title: OVERHEATS when you connect an external monitor
text:
I have had the 8-core i9 model for 2 months. Reddit it full of complaints that their macbook sounds like a jet engine and overheats if they connect to an external monitor. Apple customer support has no clue, or claims this is intended behavior. After careful search, I have observed that this is due to a series of fundamental design flaws.

1. You can only use the discrete AMD GPU when connecting an external monitor. Other laptops can use the Intel GPU. Also, you can only use the AMD GPU on Bootcamp. This makes battery life ~3 hours on Bootcamp.
2. The AMD GPU is a power hog. My laptop is pulling over 100 Watts from the wall, measured with a meter. It increases my energy bill.
3. Things are worse in Windows (Bootcamp). If I play a light video game (such as AoE2), the laptop gets so hot and draws so much power that the battery starts to empty. After 30-60' of gameplay, battery drops to 70%-50% of charge, while plugged in.
4. The heat sink of the GPU and CPU are connected. The CPU goes up to 80 Celsius at idle when connecting an external monitor, while idling.
5. The final nail in the coffin. When the CPU gets hot, macOS launches a process called kernel_task. One of the functions of the kernel task process is to help manage the temperature of your CPU. Ironically kernel_task then takes up all of my 8 cores. This shows up as 800% CPU use on the activity monitor. This unavoidably makes the CPU much hotter, and triggers a vicious circle. Then my 16" macbook becomes unusable and I have to reboot. If you think this behavior is insane, and must be a bug, guess again. Apple intends for mac OS to behave this way. Google 'apple support HT207359'.

Other issues include.
-No Nvidia/CUDA support. Even if I want to plug in an external Nvidia GPU, Apple is now blocking it.
(All my old Macs support Nvidia in High Sierra, but this one only runs Catalina.)
-No touch/stylus support. I cannot use the touchbar to draw figures when I teach/present.
-No 32-bit application support. I can no longer use my equation editors.
-Severe screen ghosting issues. Google it.
-Severe random crash/restart issues.
-Power delivery issues. It starts discharging when plugged in if I am doing computational work.
-Not sure why reviewers praise the speakers. They are bass heavy bangers. The highs are very sibilant, "S" sounds like "TH". I had to use an EQ to reduce the sibilance, but it cannot be removed completely. Also, the speakers pop when you start or stop a video. Apple claims it is a software issue, but the latest Catalina 10.15.4 has not fixed it. It only happens with low frequency sounds, which is why many users have not noticed it, but it is there.

This is just a partial list of flaws. I regret my purchase. I will sell this laptop and will buy a used 2014 Macbook with an Nvidia GPU instead.

title: Excellent Bluetooth transmitter for TV
text:
I have an LG TV (having one Optical Out) with a Yamaha Soundbar. I purchased a ZVOX AV50 set of headphones to help with my hearing of TV dialog and needed to buy a transmitter to connect my headphones to my TV. The ISelector 5.0 transmitter / receiver is a very good solution. What I like:
1) It supports the latest 5.0 Bluetooth standard and APTX latency mitigation. Ths ZVOX headphones support APX and I find the combination of ISelector and ZVOX has zero latency on dialog.
2) Pairing is easy with a simple double click of the ISelector pairing button. The ISelector has a visual cue showing a solid blue light when your headphone is paired.
3) The ISelector is much smaller than the Amazon picture indicates, which is great
4) Build quality is excellent (It is plastic)
5) It comes with all the necessary cables for attachment to your TV. Note that the Toslink cable is the thinnest cable I ever saw. It worked fine, but I replaced it with an Amazon Basic Toslink cable which has a much better build quality.
6) The range is excellent. This is installed in my basement and I could receive audio all the way to my third floor of the house. This is transmitting through multiple obstructions (walls and floors) and it still worked.
7) Installation is easy, simply plug and play. Note that the documentation is pretty basic. It also refers to the product as BTMAGIC vs. ISelector, which was a bit confusing.
8) The unit has a built-in battery. it charges via a USB Cable (Included). I plugged this into a USB port on the TV. So when I turn on the TV power the ISelector charges while I am using my headphones. There is a red light on the unit that turns on when it is charging. It does not charge when the TV is off, but this does not appear to be a problem at all. Since it has a built-in battery, I can simply unplug the unit from my basement TV and move it to my family room TV if needed and plug it into the famly room's Toslink cable and easily use the transmitter at its new location. The battery lasts for over 12 hours, so no need for a USB charging cord on my second TV.
9) It connects to two headphones at the same time.
10) Price was competitive to other products on Amazon (about $40)

I did not buy this for connections to a stereo so I did not test or need the receiver.

The two negatives that I found are:
1) it does not support Dolby Digital Audio, you need to change your TV to PCM sound output.
2) As I mentioned in my set up, I have a soundbar with one optical out from the TV. Even though the ISelector has a Bypass mode please be aware that even though you can connect your soundbar through the iSelector you CANNOT listen to your soundbar and Bluetooth headphones at the same time (you could listen via your headphones if you connected the headphones directly to the ISelector with a physical connection). Sadly It is either one or the other. This causes a problem if another person wants to watch TV with you and are not using headphones. The easy solution I found was to purchase a powered Optical "Splitter" (not a switch) that takes the input from my TV than simultaneously transmits the signal to the soundbar and the ISelector. This works great and because it is powred there is no degradation in the optical signal. For those who need a solution similar to mine, I purchase on Amazon the J-Tech 1 in x 3 out digital switch (about $20). Note that there might be Bluetooth Transmitters on Amazon that do support simultaneous BlueTooth and a Soundbar without the need of an optical splitter.

I would recommend this unit.

title: Pleasant updates to the "base" Kindle
text:
November 8, 2020 update:
I still really like this Kindle, and I stand by my review's pros and cons as I discussed below. I've read over 50 books on it since I purchased it and I'm a happy camper.

April 15, 2019 (Original review):
I had a Kindle touch years ago and had stopped using it. But I want to be able to focus on reading and not pop-ups from other apps so I bought this new Kindle to avoid the distractions of reading on my phone.

The device is smaller than both my original Kindle touch and my husband's Kindle Paperwhite. I was able to quickly get connect to the internet and begin downloading Kindle books I checked out via Overdrive. The device can be held in one hand comfortably, and it's lightweight enough to feel quite portable without appearing flimsy.

This Kindle has some buggy-feeling holdovers from previous generations: occasional leftover pixels during page/screen pages. However, I find the touch screen to be responsive without being jumpy. The bottom/power button sometimes takes an extra push to activate, or perhaps just needs me to focus a bit more. I don't mind the "special offers" and generally ignore them completely, yes, this is a generally annoying feature, but I'd rather spend that $20 on books. The backlight can be adjusted to read outdoors or in your bedroom in the dark (handy if your partner nags about keeping a booklight on).

Another reviewer commented on the PPI. Personally, as I don't use the device for pictures/illustrations/detailed charts, I frankly don't care. The images that appear in the special offers are clear enough, and the default sized print is crisp and clean and I have no issues reading without my glasses. If you frequently read books that are illustration/graphic-heavy, you may prefer a Paperwhite or other device.

I'll adjust my review if my sentiments change but for now I am very happy with my new Kindle.

title: Super fast reads, sub-par writes
text:
I recently tested a number of 16 and 32gb cards for use in a Raspberry Pi application. The tests were performed in CrystalDiskMark 7.0 using the "Real World" profile. Although this card showed a super-fast sequential read speed of 88MB/s and an acceptable 4k random read speed of 9.7MB/s, its write speed of 10.5MB/s sequential and 2.9MB/s random barely qualifies it as a Class 10, much less an A1 card.

If you're looking for a fast inexpensive Micro SD, have a look at this one: https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B0834R2C6T/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o03_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1
For about the same cost per card, you get twice the capacity and about 4 times the speed.

title: Very meh. Even for a sale price ~$15, questionable if worth it
text:
I've been using this since April. I usually use KVM switches, but my preferred brand's new Displayport 1.4 models aren't compatible with my Dell WD19TB dock, so I decided to just use my monitor's DP and HDMI ports to switch between computers and something like this plugged into a hub. I had a number of problems with it, but i worked past most of them until recently.

I plugged a USB hub into the input for this, and port A into my laptop dock and B into my desktop. My mouse, keyboard, gamepad, and one or two other things were plugged into the USB hub. Note, this is a powered hub so power draw should be a non-issue.

1. Regularly, something would just stop working until I unplugged it and plugged it back in to the hub. I tried a couple different hubs, same model different units and another from a completely different manufacturer, same problem no matter what.
2. It'll auto select kind of randomly. Not as in "it randomly decides to switch inputs," that would be much worse, but I leave my desktop off most of the time. If I do happen to shutdown/unplug this from my laptop dock, it'll sometimes default to switching to the desktop and sometimes won't. Not a big deal, just unpredictable when I'm doing some as simple as rewiring (Shelter at Home/starting to work from home has meant a lot of "what if I moved this..." situations).
3. I decided to alleviate some of these issues by getting a separate, dedicated USB hub switch for my keyboard/mouse/gamepad and plug this into my USB audio DAC. I figured it'd be nice to be able to leave the audio on my laptop dock if I need to switch over to my desktop just for a moment. I got a new Sabrent USB hub that's hire wattage, and plugged that directly into my laptop dock and plugged this USB switcher into that. USB audio would just die before a song finished playing while I was testing it. Plugged it into a USB-C adapter on my laptop dock (it has very limited USB ports), worked for a while, but after ~30-45 minutes stopped again.

Right now it's sitting unplugged. I might keep playing with it, I honestly think most of the issues is that it draws power from the host devices it's plugged into. Seems logical, but I think the way it's implemented is bad.

If you just need something simple, or you're going to use for a device you don't use frequently, it's probably fine. You may need to futz with it regularly, but it'll probably work for the most part. A few people report that it's blown up their computers... which is why I'm fairly confident it's a power draw problem.

title: Very nice device spoiled by the irritating promotional displays
text:
This is a nicely made and presented device that has an excellent screen and slightly muffled sound.

Setup is very simple (it picked up all my settings and connected itself to my network etc. without any input from me. I suspect it must be talking to the other Echo devices on my network and then gets the rest of the info from my account). Amazon have done an amazing job in getting the setup to be as simple as possible.

The screen quality is excellent and configuration was very straightforward. Sound (as has been indicated in other reviews) lacks high frequencies so sounds a little muffled (and it is not my ears, as the other Echo speakers I have do not have this issue) but sounds pleasant on music with a pleasant balance. Speech is a little more difficult to understand at times.

So what are my issues? Firstly you cannot configure a British accented voice, as you can with the other Echos. So we have the generic female American accent. I am from the UK (but lived in the US for over 30 years) and retain a strong British English accent which is why I usually switch to UK English for the language option. This gives Alexa a better chance of understanding me. I have not encountered any issue so far, since I tend to use American terms for things rather than English terms ( as I say it, I am an Englishman with an American vocabulary), however I find it odd that the Show Echo 5 does not support multiple accents.

My other issue, and this has been mentioned by other reviewers, is that the screen, which is intended to show the time and temperature, is interrupted constantly with internal promotional messages (no outright advertising). I have found it irritating that I look at it from time to time to find the current time from the across the bedroom only to find some irrelevant promotional message with the time and temperature confined to an unreadable size in the top left corner.

I am trying to use this as a combined Alexa device and clock and it is so close (I tried the Echo Spot with clock, but that plain did not work for me). Just get rid of that promotional material please Amazon.

Edit: Reduced to 2 stars We decided to return it as we could not find anyway to stop the device showing irrelevant information and making the time unreadable from a distance. On top of that if you choose photographs from your photo library the clock display is effectively useless as it is displayed in the top left corner and never displays full screen. All we need is an option to display the clock full size without the other interfering screens. The hardware is excellent, Amazon's software is the culprit and made it useless for our purpose.

title: Does NOT work with Galaxy 9 or 10
text:
I bought this drive to backup my Samsung Galaxy 9. After I received it, I found THAT IT DOES NOT WORK ON A GALAXY 9 (OR LATER). It's designed to work with phones that use a standard MICRO USB connection. The Galaxy 9 (and later) use an USB-C connection. (If you're not certain, if you can plug in your power connector either right-side up or upside down, it's an USB-C and THIS JUMP DRIVE WILL NOT WORK.

But the good news is, you really DON'T NEED IT!

Simply take your power cord, unplug the USB cord from the transformer (the part that plugs into the wall recept) and plug that end into your PC's USB jack. The USB-C end plugs into the phone as usual. (If the phone asks for access, go ahead and grant it).

The contents of your phone will appear as a new drive. (Mine showed up as Galaxy S9).

Move to the Galaxy S9> Phone> DCIM> Camera and your photos and videos will appear. Mark them (control A will select all of them) right click and select "copy" then select a folder on your PC, click on it and select "paste". Ta da!

text:
[[VIDEOID:3ef25ae1926fd96b5adf5a00c7892c2a]] This review is for the Amcrest SmartHome AI Human Detection WiFi Camera, ASH21-W.

At this price point this is a great value. The image and video resolution is clear. You have recording options of the cloud, SD card, NVR, or the phone app. A wall mount kit is included. The PTZ is a little more responsive than prior models. The night vision is better than the prior models as well.

The AI motion tracking is a bit of a hoot. It does track whatever moves so be sure you’re wanting this feature. You can setup motion detection zones if you only want to track within a viewing range although I didn’t try that. In my case, I turned motion detection off because the alerts were driving me nuts for where I have it but if I were to put it in a room where there is less motion it would be great. Also, you can setup a schedule for the motion detection. A great use would be to set it just at night when things aren’t supposed to be moving in certain places. I do notice that the motor is a little noisy on the video recordings when it’s tracking. That really doesn’t bother me much.

I had a bit of a challenge with setup because I didn’t realize this can only be setup from the Amcrest Smart Home App. Once I figured that out ( reading is important, I know) setup was a breeze. I was able to set the camera up as a P2P camera on the Amcrest View Pro app where I have my other cameras. I was also able to setup the camera on my Amcrest NVR.

I recommend this camera especially for people that want to record to and manage the camera in the cloud.

title: Read this if planning to upgrade from i3 to i7 with integrated H57 graphics
text:
I'm posting this review of my experience in the hopes it may help someone else. I was a little skeptical about purchasing a refurbished CPU. However, the part arrived well packaged in bubble wrap through the mail days earlier than was estimated. Everything looked in good shape. However, I could not make it work in my system. I just got three beeps on startup and no video. I returned the item through Amazon and the expect the refund to go through without issues. This is no fault of the seller and I would try refurbished again in the future.

After additional research today, I have learned that some motherboards with integrated H57 chip graphics will require an external graphics card for use with i7 CPUs. Apparently, the i7 CPU cannot support the integrated graphics. This was NOT CLEAR from reviewing the HP upgrade information for my PC model. It simply states that the motherboard MS-7613 (lona-GL8E) supports i7-8xx. However, when I further looked at the graphics section there is a small clue stating "Integrated graphics using Intel H57 chipset (when compatible CPU is installed)". It took me quite some time to find the root cause of my failure online, so I'm posting it here in case it can help someone else. Since I was upgrading an older PC, I didn't want to invest in another graphics card. However, I believe the system would have probably worked if I did.

title: Almost Perfect!
text:
The price is sure right. But what you get is a drive that for all intents and purposes appears to be brand-new. Even the SMART monitoring data is all reset to zero.
This makes me uncomfortable. If the drives are new, then great. But if these drives have whatever amount of time on them, I want to know it at the outset. It is like buying a car. If you buy a car, sold to you as USED, but the odometer says "0000000.0" then you get rightly worried. The only way that could happen, is if the odometer is damaged and replaced. But then there is paperwork that is provided with the car telling you of the odometer replacement. Not so with these drives; they have zero in the SMART area and that's that.
Regardless, I put the four drives through very intense testing and they are perfect.
Mechanically, they are very quiet, smooth and HOT. These are server class drives. They spin at 7200 rpm, seek rapidly, and totally capable of 100% random loading for any length of time. But, that takes electricity, and when electricity is translated to work. the outcome is heat. You need a decent case or drives carrier that has some forced air cooling. I have two of the drives in a very nice desktop enclosure that has no fans, and the drives will reach 140 degrees Fahrenheit. Almost too hot to touch. The two drives inside the gaming case have a quiet, slow fan blowing on both and they run at 110 degrees.
If you are looking for a good, high performance 4TB drives, these are an excellent bargain.

title: APC BR1350MS -received Jan 2019
text:
APC Sine Wave UPS Battery Backup & Surge Protector, 1350VA, APC Back-UPS Pro (BR1350MS)

Received with obvious warehouse damage to box BUT, due to APC's great packaging effort, there was zero damage to the product. -Note that the boxed UPS was shipped inside of a shipping box that did not have damage that would account for the product packaging to be so damaged.

The UPS came with about 90% charge and I set it up to charge fully before doing much else.
Accessing and connecting the battery was very easy. I had recently had carpal tunnel surgery and could barely use my right hand... so yeah, great job to APC since all of my other units (older APC's) were a bit of a pain with two fully usable hands.
I purchased this to replace my older APC Back-UPS Pro 700, which does not have the near natural sine wave.
I recently learned a bit more about computer hardware, PSU's in particular, and see that the 80+ with Active PFC do not play well with Stepped Sine Wave. (might explain what happened to my last MoBo).
I currently use the old 700 for everything except the computer and the USB Hub, which are plugged into this new APC. Likely move the 700 to other tasks since this one can more than handle what I am throwing at it but was taxing the 700.
This unit is longer, taller and wider than my 700 but hey, it does more and IS more in every way.

The short of it:
Came 90% charged
Easy to connect battery cable
No whine, even under heavy testing load
Set Sensitivity to highest and no annoying sounds -does click when we have brown power
I like the PowerChute option which I had never installed before. I hope I do not need to test the shutdown feature but know that it is just a matter of time where I live.

The mount is all but useless really. You can't leave anything plugged into the port when using it and it doesn't include all the hardware to mount it to anything. It assumes you already have things to mount an action camera to and if you don't you're left with not much info on what you're supposed to do with it.

The wi-fi/bluetooth adaptor is the only thing of any real value as it's the only thing that doesn't make the device actively worse at the same time. But, at least for me, it's buggy and slow. You won't want to use it when you can just plug the device into your phone. It doubles as an extra wide stand base but doesn't offer automatic uploads or a tripod mount or anything like that. It is essential when you use the scroll wheel assuming you want to though as it will now be the only way to connect to your phone.

All in all the utility here is slim at best and seems to run counter to the simplicity in design the Osmo Pocket offers. Maybe with software and firmware updates things would be better but as it stands unless you're dead serious about the wheel control and want to be able to adjust settings at the same time (over wifi/bluetooth with the phone) then just skip this.

title: Works! Very simple to setup!
text:
We switched broadband carriers recently and decided a new mesh system would fit our needs best - lots of phones, laptops, TVs, gaming PCs and tablets in our house of 6.

We now have a Gig connection so I have the gaming PCs on a gig Ethernet switch and decided 500 Mps would be more than sufficient for wireless. I pre-ordered the new Eero 6 system and it came in today. While I have over 30 years in networking I decided to just follow the directions and see how things went.

Truly simple. Install the app, turn off your broadband, connected the first Eero, turn broadband back on and let the app find your initial device. I got the three pack so I did that a couple of more times around that house and was done.

I might move one of the hot points as there is a lot of interference in the Den but the far bedroom is pulling 300 plus Mbps and it's a the farthest point possible from the initial Eero device.

The app is nice and you get a month of Amazon security, not sure what all I can do with this paired with AWS but it looks promising. I haven't played with the zigabee (sp?) network yet but it found all my Echos etc...

Very pleased. Yes it's the first day and I will update should things change but for a newly released device, I wanted to get my initial impressions noted in case someone was holding off buying one.

It works, it works well and is truly simple to setup. You don't need to be a network engineer to get this going, anyone can do it in probably 15 minutes or less!

title: Didn't work well for me ....
text:
I just upgraded our Comcast "Blast" Internet service to the Gigabit speed, and added Comcast voice service (moving over from Vonage).

Comcast provided me their XB6 "XFi" router to use, but like many people -- I didn't want to pay $13/month rental for it. My existing Motorola cable modem had worked great for the last year, but wasn't DOCSIS 3.1 compatible and didn't support enough channels to do gigabit speed. When I started researching my options, I realized there was really nothing on the market yet that does DOCSIS 3.1 and has integrated voice support except for this new Netgear CM1150v.

I bought it and tried to set it up. Unfortunately, that led to an entire weekend of frustration and sitting on hold with various folks at Comcast. The main problem is, even with a laptop plugged straight into the back of the Netgear modem, using a 1 gigabit wired Ethernet connection, I was only seeing speeds of around 450mbit/second tops, on downloads. (At first, my upload speeds were only about 11mbit/sec too, but after multiple attempts to re-provision the modem, they did get that fixed so it was doing 40mbits/sec like the gigabit tier is supposed to offer.)

Comcast had a technician scheduled to come out to the house (a required part of ordering gigabit packages from them, even though they turned the service on immediately). He verified that my signal strength was "excellent" and shouldn't have been an issue -- but agreed we couldn't achieve the speeds I was paying for.

When the XB6 modem was put back on the network instead and provisioned, though, it got a pretty consistent 940mbit/sec download speed.

(Getting the modems switched back and forth and properly activated was like pulling teeth each time, too! The automatic activation page you get when you first hook up a different modem kept telling me to call in. The process when calling in took hours because I had to have one person get the data figured out, followed by getting transferred to another department who got the phone portion working. They *still* didn't process my request to port my old number from Vonage. I have no faith they'll even get that accomplished at this point. Each time I call in - they find a problem and claim it was fixed, and the port will complete in 24 hours. Never happens.)

So .... I'm returning this Netgear CM1150v. A shame I couldn't get it working better, but I think it may be a compatibility issue with its chipset and Comcast's network in certain areas?

title: Not bad, but mine failed - not sure exactly how
text:
Bought a 50m LC terminated cable for a project at home. Everything seemed of decent quality except the “Y” crimp just before the LC connector. Tested OK, but one element must have broken before installation was complete.

I had to pull this cable (with lube) through a 3/4” pipe about 30’ long. All smooth edges and only two wide 90 degree bends. Sadly the supple rubber outer jacket of this armored cable is relatively “sticky”, so lube was required. I pulled carefully, and cable still tested good afterward. I then routed the cable around the inside perimeter of my pole building garage up out of the way so it would not get pinched by tools or other things being stored. After this simple routing, the cable would no longer pass light on one of the elements.

Since the cable is no longer good for anything (I don’t have the means to re-terminate), I cut it apart for other folks here to see what’s inside.

I decided to try again using a more typical yellow patch cable, and things worked fine. I believe this cable is probably pretty good, just maybe not up to the task of ANY pulling through conduit. I would like to try a few more for shorter runs or other jobs that don’t involve conduit to see how they hold up.

The armor is some kind of steel - almost seems like stainless. It allows for a pretty tight bend - maybe too tight, but would certainly hold up well to other abuse. Would be fun to do some torture tests.

title: Utter trash.
text:
This is the second of these boards I've tried (one from Newegg, one from Amazon (as Neweggs RMA process was glacial). Build is a 10700K, 64 GB (2x32GB) Gskill 3600 RAM, Samsung 970 EVO Plus 1TB. Both builds are unstable with the default settings on the mobo and absolutely no overclocking other than stock Turbo Boost. Testing with all the new parts ordered and with known good RAM and an HDD from an older rig, as well as with a second 10700K (as my son and I are building twin, identical gaming rigs) and with both the installed BIOS and flashed to a new version.

In both cases, in all configurations, the systems were unstable *unless* Turbo Boost was completely turned off in the BIOS. We've wasted hours of our time trying to get a stable build with no success unless Turbo Boost is turned off.

Our suspicion is bad/overly aggressive Auto power settings in the Gigabyte BIOSes though we cannot definitively confirm this. That being said, the only common denominator at this point given all of the new and old known-good parts we've swapped in and out would be the firmware, as it would seem to be a near impossibility that we've gotten two bad motherboards, two bad CPUs, or some combination of both.

Returning and going with ASUS as we should have done in the first place.

Sometimes when I logged on to the Windows, sometimes when playing around on a web browser, sometimes doing nothing, sometimes when logging off. I couldn't really find any way to consistently reproduce it.

I tried with tech support, but their only suggestion was to reinstall Windows, which I did and it didn't work. Then, I tried to only use the peripherals that came with the PC. Again, that didn't work. I tried running memory and hard drive tests, but I couldn't find any problems. So, in the end I don't really know what the issue was. I ran out of time to try to figure it out because they had to have the machine back in their hands within 30 days of ordering or else they wouldn't take it back. (It took about a week to ship from their warehouse in Canada to my house in the continental USA, so there really wasn't any time left.)

That's the bad part. The good part is that when I Was actually able to play games, they looked *amazing*. The system booted fast, and there were plenty of options to expand (extra hard drive bay, extra RAM slots, etc). In all reality, I did not want to get rid of this computer if there was any way to fix it, but it just did not work.

***I noticed that some people comment on flickering, and I am not sure how tech savvy those people are, but I had the same problem with my monitor and GPU upgrade.

I went from a 60 Hz monitor to a 144 Hz monitor and experienced major flickering. My PC did not auto-adjust for the upgraded refresh rate of the new monitor, which caused the GPU to down-clock and produce the flicker.

MY SOLUTION: I resolved this issue by going to my DISPLAY SETTINGS and adjusting both monitors (dual setup) to the max supported refresh rate, and now everything works perfectly. If you have this issue then I hope this solution works for you.
Look up "display settings refresh adjust" for more details on the fix

title: Non-tech review from somebody who loves these!
text:
I got these to upgrade my very basic Sony wireless headset (model WH-CH510) & a MAJOR upgrade they are!
(My main use is for streaming while my husband is watching something else or sleeping, so noise cancelling matters.)
The padded presentation box they come in is a clue: these are gonna be nice!
A hard case is included, as well as a charging cable, an airplane adapter, & a 3.5mm jack with microphone for hands free calling.

They’re quite substantial compared to what I’ve been using which also means they’re heavier... even so, they’re very comfortable. The ear cushions completely envelope my ears like they’re pillows. The adjustable headband is fine for this big ol’ head.
Connecting via Bluetooth is seamless & I settled in to check these babies out...

Welcome to my own audio world. Started with the opening scene of Jack Ryan & the helicopters literally circled my head, the bombs dropped behind me, & I could hear the blades of grass as the boots trampled through it. Crystal clear doesn’t even begin to describe the clarity. Moved over to Disney+ to try The Sound of Music soundtrack (don’t judge- ha!) & I heard the songs of my childhood like never before.
I am not knowledgeable in sound words besides the basic bass & treble-type stuff but I know the difference of average (the Sonys) & superb (these AKGs).
Charged as instructed for 2.5 hrs. initially & have used them for about 12 hrs so far. I will explore the hands free calling & listen to my Amazon music playlists ASAP but, for the moment, I can’t stop enjoying this new viewing/listening experience!

title: Works great for N64
text:
I compared this along with some other options for scaling my my Nintendo 64 to use on our big screen. I know that the TV itself has no display lag when using HDMI since I have connected a computer to it previously. Though it has direct RCA AV input, it introduces upscaling to convert the signal to 720p (from the N64's 240p). This adds, in my estimation, around 200 to 250ms of delay, which is very noticeable in most any game, particularly when inputs are time sensitive (such as racing or rhythm games).

I have heard mixed reviews on the MINI AV2HDMI, and was skeptical given its small stature. The switch on the side to select 720 or 1080 is also upside down? Sliding to the 1080 side, the TV reports a 720 signal, and vice versa. To its credit, thought, the unit's height allows it to be easily affixed to the rear of my wall mounted TV with double sided tape.

Initially, the converter did have a fair amount of lag, 100-150ms, so I had discounted it from my winning list. But, a second kick at the can (after rebooting the TV, changing games, and placing the converter at 720p) proved to have much less lag, into the sub-50ms range, which ended up being the best option for me besides a dedicated CRT. This amount of display lag is not generally noticeable since a frame of animation (at 30fps) is around 34ms, meaning 1-2 frames of lag for upscaling. I switched back to the first game (wave race) and did notice the delay again when changing menus, while the second game (super smash bros) on its second boot again did not have the lag, so this could be just be part of the N64 system.

Because I am only testing with an N64, I cannot comment on picture quality to any great extent, since I can count the pixels on one hand, but quality appears to be about equivalent to the internal upscaler on my TV when using AV input methods.

The unit does need external power, though i do not know if it would be able to run on the 50mA that HDMI could provide from the TV. My shipment included, however, a USB cable (which i connected directly to my TV, so that it would receive power when the TV was on.)

A complete package would have included a short (3 foot) HDMI cable as well, but one could be picked up for just a few dollars on Amazon, if a spare is not readily available.

title: Go GREEN or go home.
text:
I'd like to start off by saying I REALLY gave this card a chance. I've had around 10 different Nvidia cards since I started PC gaming, all of which have given me 0 problems at all, aside from one that was DOA, which happens. This card is amazing in a benchmarking scenario, great scores, value for money, temps are great. As soon as I play any game I get stutters, freezing and FPS drops of 40+. When people say Radeon drivers are horrible, they're downplaying it, they are a DISASTER. I need to go in and tweak EVERY setting possible in Adrenaline to get a smooth gaming experience, but why? I got this card to save some money and enjoy some great performance, which I can only achieve by spending extra time messing with things that for some reason AMD has not figured out. Another really annoying note, the memory clock runs at max if your screen is over 120hz, and is a confirmed issue from AMD, so enjoy the extra power draw from that!

I popped in a 2070 Super, which I spent a total of$70 more than this card on, and wow. Coming from a GTX 1080, the 5700XT gave me a nice boost in benchmark performance, but nothing else. Honestly, if you NEED to save the $70-$100 on your GPU and are willing to compromise, sure this card would do it for you, at the expense of even more time tweaking settings you have no business needing to change.

In short, fork over the extra cash and get a Nvidia card. Pop that thing in and watch it go, optimized drivers, great performance and no hassle.

I took my Shure SE535 to the swim (1st Right on Photo 1): it works perfect under water.

So don't wast any your money to buy those poor sound quality 'waterproof' earphone. You will be surprise many 'normal' earbud DOES work underwater and provide much better quality sound!

Update on 30th December 2019:

After so sick with those poor sound quality so call 'waterproof earphone' as above, I bough a new Shure SE215 (photo 6) as my every day swimming earphone now, which is work PERFECT with very nice sound quality.

As many people wouldn't spend that much money for a pair of earbud, so I order a pair of Creative EP-630 (Phone 4, $15.99) and Panasonic ErgoFit RP-HJE120-S (Silver, Photo 5, $7.84) from Amazon to took them for swim! As I expect they ALL work prefect with swimming!

Other than that, it's great. It's a 7" display photo frame that auto plays all the pictures you put on the stick - very vivid picture, zero complaints there. It's got a remote and controls on the back and various other options. I'm not terribly demanding, I'm just using it to throw on photos and rotate, but it sounds like there are options to program times to turn it off/on. It won't work in old-school areas on the wall (unless you work some magic for the cord to be tucked behind the drywall, which is unrealistic), so play on finding a nice table top to use near an outlet that will hide the cable sufficiently.

All in all, I'm very happy with it. Nice entry pricepoint. It was a great gift.

title: Good Sound, Nice Large Screen
text:
I love Old Time Radio, and there are many stations on the Internet to tune in, but I also like Internet radios so I can listen in different rooms, so I have several. The auna IR-160 Internet Radio is a nice unit with a screen big enough to read (crucial for my old eyes). There are many facets of the menu, and at first it's a little confusing, but easy to become familiar with, and I was able to locate and add stations to My Favorites. There are a couple stumbling blocks that made this radio a little difficult to program. It uses a dial and a right-left arrow to enter letters, numbers and symbols, but I found myself pushing the round "enter" knob at times, thus adding a misspelled or incomplete station name to a list, and for the life of me, I can't determine how to erase or edit those names. Maybe someone else knows.

I did learn (at last) how to add MediaU to the radio, a free website where I have playlists and station favorites set up. You have to ENABLE MediaU (Configuration/Manage My MediaU/Enable), go to MediaU, sign in and add the radio's MAC number, then (very important) UNPLUG the radio and wait three to five minutes. Now when you turn it on, one of the accessible categories is MediaU with all your favorite and manually added stations , and they appear like magic. As long as I was signed in at MediaU and had this radio listed, I did not have to sign in on the radio. Very nice.

For the price it's a good radio and you'll probably be satisfied.

title: It just works
text: I used this item to control three laptops running various flavors of Linux with a single Logitech "marble" mouse and a Visio illuminated keyboard.  The way it works is to plug in your output device, i.e.: mouse and/or keyboard... maybe a flash drive or camera.  This uses the standard USB cable and socket.  They get plugged in to the "output" side of the switch as expected using the standard USB cables they came with.  The computers get connected using the cables the switch came with and look like standard USB printer cables.  Use the printer port end of the cable at the switch and plug the other end of the cable(s) into the computer(s) you want to control.  The push-button switch on the device alternates between each of the control ports in an intuitive way.  The fourth port is unused at present, but I see no reason it could not be used in conjunction with the appropriate USB devices to control all three of the computers simultaneously, e.e.: for logging in simultaneously if all the machines have the same username and password, or maybe issuing the same command to use DNF to update all of the computers at the same time.... or I suppose I could hook up another computer and expand my semi-circle to four.  Switching between computers is effortless, though there may be a slight delay depending upon the processing speed of the individual machine one is accessing.  All in all, I don't see how it could be improved upon.  Nicely done, gentlemen!

Thin bezels make this machine feel very modern

Cons

Other notes
I ran into an issue which necessitated an exchange. LG support was relatively competent in determining the defect, and Amazon was great in the exchange. New one has no problems.

Ended up upgrading the SSD to a Samsung 970 EVO since the slot the original SSD is in supports 4 channel NVME. Swapped it over, reinstalled windows. Windows apparently managed to pull the digital license from the original install somehow since it already said activated when I loaded it up, so that was nice. Now it runs even faster than right out of the box :)

I am not a fan of the fingerprint reader that forces you to have your fingerprint read anytime you hit power, but the reader software can be disabled and a standard circular blackout sticker fits perfectly over top of the reader itself.

Conclusion
Would I recommend this laptop? Well it is on the expensive side, but is such a joy to actually use. The couple downsides can be worked around (upgrading SSD, bluetooth speakers), and there is nothing else like it on the market. There are other laptops a bit more powerful, but it feels very snappy and anything faster has downsides (lower battery life, louder fans). This laptop feels like it strikes a happy medium between performance and portability that is rare for something so light, and impossible to find on any other 17". If you can afford it I would absolutely recommend this machine.

title: Outstanding earbuds for the price!
text:
I bought these earbuds after reading a review on CNet.com about them, and I'm so glad I did. I was looking for a reasonably priced second pair of earbuds. I also own a pair of Jabra Elite 65t earbuds, and—at one-third the price—the EarFun earbuds are a better value.

tl;dr: definitely recommended!

The pros:
1. The EarFuns sound nearly as good as the Jabras (there's just a bit less bass with the EarFuns, but definitely not enough to justify the 3x price premium of the Jabras).
2. The EarFuns fit better in my ears than the Jabras (of course this will vary for each person). The CNet reviewer stressed getting a tight fit for good sound, but I don't have any problem with the fit. Sound isolation is just as good as the Jabras.
3. The EarFuns seem to stay connected (to the phone and to each other) better than the Jabras, and experience less interference. The Jabra's encounter static and dropoouts whenever I walk through automatic doors (say at the supermarket) and even in certain places around my house (maybe due to my wifi repeaters). This also happens at the gym if I'm in certain places. I haven't experienced this issue at all with the EarFuns—the connection to the phone and each other is rock solid, and the bluetooth range is excellent.
4. The EarFun's storage/charging case is MUCH better than the Jabra's. For one thing it's flat on the bottom (the Jabra's case is curved and cannot sit upright on a flat surface). The EarFun case also has magnets that hold the earbuds in the case while charging; the Jabra earbuds just sit loosely in their case. The EarFun case can also be charged wirelessly (as well as with the included USB-C charging cable); the Jabra case uses a micro USB charging cable. If you already have a wireless charging pad for your phone, this is a great bonus, since you don't have to worry about the charging connector wearing out over time.

Cons:
1. The EarFuns can't control the sound volume. I realize this is a premium feature, but I miss it compared to the Jabras.
2. The EarFuns don't have the auto-pause feature that the Jabras do (removing one earbud from your ear pauses the music until you put it back in your ear). Again, a premium feature, and you *can* pause the music from either EarFun earbud by tapping the button.
3. The EarFuns seemed a bit picky about pairing with multiple devices, at least initially. I had to re-pair them a couple times, and once even had to reset their connection to each other (this is covered in the instructions). But I haven't had to do either of those recently, so maybe that was just me getting used to operating them.
4. The print in the user's manual is SUPER TINY and printed in gray, not black, ink. I'm in my 50s, and even with reading glasses I couldn't make out the text and infographics. I had to use my phone's camera as a magnifying glass to read the instructions. It's possible they're available online (I didn't try to find out), but I suspect even younger folks will have trouble reading the instructions.

To be determined:
I use earbuds mostly for music listening, not making phone calls. I know the Jabras work reasonably well for that, but I haven't had the opportunity to use the EarFuns on a call, so I can't comment on how well they work for that.

Conclusion:
If I hadn't gotten a great deal on my Jabras (I paid less than half the list price due to a couple of online deals I was able to take advantage of), I would be really pissed that I'd paid so much when I could have bought the EarFuns for 1/3 the price and gotten an overall better value. The EarFuns are going to stay in my gym bag, and I'll use the Jabras around the house. I'm, even considering buying another pair of EarFuns for listening in bed.

As I write this in mid-December 2019, I've only had the EarFuns for a few days, so it's possible my rosy outlook will change if they turn out to be duds later. I will update this review in a few weeks after I've used them for a while. But as of right now, I definitely recommend them to anyone looking for a reasonably priced set of earbuds that have terrific sound. The pros definitely outweigh the cons, and for the price you can't beat them.

UPDATE October 15, 2020: still loving my Ear Fun Free earbuds! In fact, I just bought a second pair, and the new model has volume controls, which The last model didn't have, and Even other earbuds that are twice the price don't have this feature. You will not go wrong with these earbuds!

title: Great Wifi Mesh for different mix of usage with 3rd band back-haul
text:
****5/30/2020 update review: New FW added QoS on the app for easy settings for priorities. Due to shelter in place, WFH has change my ways using the network. I love the new features that I can prioritize meeting calls over network on daytime and switch back to normal use for the family at night time, given I already have fast internet but that quick QoS changes do matters. I also added more cameras as the mesh reaches more places now. Working well for me still

***Update review 3/20/20: New FW released for both GT-5300 and Zenwifi made mesh more stable on 3rd band backhaul. Connection speed is more smooth and faster on transfers.***

I had been looking and studying Mesh technology for the past 2 years as my main router cannot provide stable speed to some of my devices on certain location. Google Wifi is one of my first pick. However, Google mesh cannot manually split the bands in diff SSID which will cause incompatibility to some of my smart devices at home. Then out of no where ZenWifi got announced, which in my surprise can mesh into my GT-AC5300. This is a big plus for me as it also can take advantage of the 3rd band for dedicated back-haul.

My usage at home is consist of 2x NAS, 2x diff sets security cameras, plus more than 15 diff mixed devices. Took me a while to get the proper location set on the ZenWifi to balance coverage as my main router is positioned on end of the lower house. I also run full 7 days to test them all out.
Pros:
- Can mesh to my existing Asus GT-AC5300.
- App is a breeze to use and easy to setup (Android based user).
- Each of the ZenWifi has full function of router including LAN ports I utilized.
- FW can be updated thru app.
- PC can now transfer to NAS at 50+MB/s and up which is better than before at 15~20MB/s. Back haul plays a big role here. This is a major change for me using wireless connection to access NAS.
- Wife and Kids devices now has stable connection and can maintain network for games and TV streaming on any side of the house.
- Streaming to the NAS from any Wifi devices can now run without hiccups even from any side of the house and backyard.
- My security cameras and smart devices can now easily get wifi signal if i reboot them.

Cons:
- Power connector orientation blocks power switch. It does not affect function but just inconvenience to power-cycle the router.
- It takes a while to finish booting before you can use on each power cycle on the ZenWifi, so far it minimal impact my usage as I don't usually reboot my routers.

title: Would be worth the price if it did everything it claimed
text:
First off, the cameras themselves are very good. Great quality. Solid construction. Excellent installation instructions with careful consideration to making the install neat and secure. If you follow their instructions and paint the wire itself, it nearly disappears which is nice.

The problem is some of the more advanced features don't live up to their claims. I recently replaced seven Ring cameras (which I loved for the solar power option) with seven Nest cameras. The cameras are all outdoor including one doorbell.

I was paying $100 per year for 60 days of Ring history on seven cameras. With Nest I am paying $230 for only *five* days of history. The difference is Nest records everything and Ring only records activity. The idea is Nest has all the history but intelligently alerts you only about the important stuff.

But that's the problem. Those alerts don't work very well:

1: lots of lag

It can take 5-10 seconds before I get even a simple doorbell alert on my phone. That's a long time for someone to wait for you to answer. Same with other alerts - too long to get an alert. With Ring, it was 2-3 seconds.

2: smart alerts don't work

I was so excited to stop getting alerts every time my dogs ran past the camera or barked. But I have 100s of alerts that Nest spotted a person in my backyard only to click on the app and watch a video of my dog running by. Same for the camera detecting someone talking. Turns out to be dogs barking 99% of the time.

3: Facial recognition on the more expensive cameras just doesn't work.

I get the Nest saw someone new message over and over for the same people in my family. Light level is good, camera angle is good, it just doesn't work. Any variation in clothing, the person's position, etc. throws off the recognition.

My last two issues aren't about alerts but rather about the lack of a Ring Chime equivalent and no solar power option.

It would be nice if Nest had a small device to make a doorbell sound at the back of the house without having to install a smart speaker. Ring has a very inexpensive chime device the size of a USB charger that plugs in anywhere and uses wifi to just make the door bell sound anywhere in your house. Great, simple feature.

And having a small solar panel with a batter in the camera is a great feature on Ring that makes installations much simpler when there is no power nearby.

I'll probably stick with Nest despite paying more than double the annual cost for 1/12 the storage duration solely because of the better video quality but I'm very disappointed with their cloud based features - they just don't work.

title: USB Random / Shuffle = GARBAGE
text:
As the title says, the random/shuffle feature through USB is a terrible, steaming pile of canine fecal matter. The factory radio in a 2006-2012 Rav4 did a perfect job with that function, so it's inexcusable that a "new" radio can't perform this task. The factory radio is made by Panasonic, so perhaps their engineers 14+ years ago knew something Pioneer's engineers can't figure out. Even old Winamp's shuffle feature was better than this radio's, and anyone who used Winamp a lot knew that it sucked pretty hard in that area.

This radio will select 2 folders on startup and only play songs from those two folders. If you manually change folders, then it will start playing from that folder and another one. Most poorly programmed shuffle functions will pre-select a group of songs from all folders and repeat those. I've never encountered a device that would only pre-select folders and play songs from them.
It's unfortunate that the desired shuffle feature is 90% of how I listen to my music - the other 10% is the old school FM radio. If I didn't spend the time & money to install this radio then I would return it immediately. Either way I will never buy another Pioneer radio due to this feature (lack of).

Other than the radio not doing the one thing I really need it to - the screen is clear & responsive and sound is way better than stock (still using factory amp & speakers).

title: Sony, King of the Dumb Features
text:
First, this product worked as advertised. It plays all regions of blu-ray and DVD. What I don't like about it is everything else. It is literally the biggest POS disc player I've ever owned. It has a "feature" where it shuts itself off after about 20 minutes of inactivity. There is no way to adjust this or disable it. It is unbelievably annoying.

I like to use my Bluetooth headphones with this, and they disconnect every time it shuts itself off. So I have to re-pair the headphones, not to mention sit through all the garbage they put at the beginning of discs again.

Also, press any button on the remote and it turns the unit on. So, accidentally hit a button, and your player is on. Does Sony really think people find it that difficult to find the power button?

Worse still, it has a very difficult time recognizing a disc. This should be priority #1, like all it SHOULD do. I don't care about all the streaming crap they put on it. I can access that stuff on literally every other device I've got. My TV, dvr, Playstation, phone. Why do I need this on my Blu-ray player?

So I have to eject and reinsert the disc until it recognizes it, that is, unless the player freezes. This happens a lot. So in this case, you have to unplug it, wait, and try again.

Oh, if my disc player would only play a disc. Total garbage, and my final Sony.

Update 7/4/19: This player now has a habit of randomly disconnecting my Bluetooth headphones.

Also, yesterday it refused to pair with my headphones. I thought for certain this was a problem with the headphones, which worried me, because I actually like them (plus they were pricey). On a whim, I tried the old trick of unplugging the Sony player, waiting, and plugging it back in. Very next try, my headphones connected. Yes, it turned out the problem was, once again, with this stupid disc player.

Update 10/10/19: My remote stopped working. I thought it was dead. Batteries, not the problem. I once had another Sony remote that stopped working. I threw it in the trash. Later, I read that it needed "resetting". I didn't know remotes needed to be reset. So I tried that with this one. Three different "remedies" I found online. Nothing worked. What do you do when all else fails? Unplug the freaking thing. Guess what? My remote miraculously works again.

Why do I continue to use this doorstop? I don't have another region-free player, or another bluetooth-compatible one.

title: THIS PRODUCT IS EASY TO USE
text:
This little device actually does transfer your cassette music to iTunes with a few little clicks of your mouse. I've copies dozens of songs which were on a dozen different cassettes and it consistently works fine. Once you figure out how to use it, you just need to check a couple of software settings, start the cassette to play and click the "start button" on the screen, then click the stop button on the screen when the song is finished, save it to the desktop and then drag the saved icon into iTunes. In I-Tunes, you can then enter the usual identification information.

I didn't give it five stars because they updated their software without updating their documentation. I couldn't figure out what they were talking about when I tried to follow the few simple steps described in the little User Booklet that was included with my device. I spent hours messing with it and almost sent the device back. But after a few days of frustration in trying to understand how to use the extremely sophisticated software package Audacity, I finally figured out the few simple steps that I should follow that the documentation SHOULD have told me and was able to get the device to work.

Even though the cassette and its software is extremely simple to use to do a simple transfer of songs to I-Tunes, the software Audacity that is used in the background is an extremely sophisticated musicians' tool and with quite a bit of effort to understand, you would be capable of manipulating and improving your music in almost any way you wanted. Its capabilities are the equivalent of Garage Band's. But you don't need to understand Audacity to use this product. All you need is an ACCURATE user's booklet.

The sound quality of what goes to iTunes of course is dependent on the sound quality of the cassette. I copied every cassette with the sound volume turned as high as it goes, assuming that I can always turn down the volume if it is too loud.

So the bottom line is this would be a great product if you receive an ACCURATE User's booklet.

By the way, the Amazon technical support that is advertised with the product is worthless! The Amazon "technical person" I contacted hardly knew what I was talking about and didn't know anything about the product.

title: Nice laptops but Win 10 Home to Pro upgrade process may be more than you want to deal with
text:
I have updated this review from 1 to 3 stars. Something to be very aware of is these ship with Windows 10 Home with an upgrade key to Pro.

The short story: This is a headache you might want to avoid and just find this laptop that ships with Pro. The vendor took care of it but it took a few days of back-and-forth.

Long story: Out of five of these I ordered for a small business none of the keys that were included worked. The vendor was able to replace the keys after a few days of back-and-forth e-mails but it's a tricky situation you may need to be patient with... Apparently they buy bulk license keys purchased from a third-party (in other words these don't come with a key dedicated just to them that was shipped with it from HP), at least in my case, and apparently sometimes people take advantage of that and use the key more than once (so my assumption is by the time I got mine all uses of they key had been taken). Again the vendor after a slight delay was able to get me a new key and I eventually got all 5 laptops updated to Pro although in two occasions it has lost the key and I had to re-enter it. It wasn't just a power up the laptops and away we go situation though!

The laptops themselves are really nice and run great once you get rid of McAfee (and potentially deal with the above headache). They look really nice, I'm not sure they're the most durable (the really nice milled edges already have a minor scuff and it's mostly just sat at my desk).

title: The opposite of Klipsch speakers
text:
I have owned these for a couple years and used them for everything imaginable. If you're looking for a pair of small speakers to jam out with, they're hard to beat. You will hear surprising bass along with pleasing treble. You can push them basically as hard as you want; I feed them 100W RMS each and they laugh.

Where do they fall short? Well, there's a big canyon in the frequency response curve in the upper middle range. You can tune around it to some extent with an equalizer, but they'll never yell at you like a pair of Klipsch speakers would- and I'm mostly OK with that. It is a small liability sometimes when hooking them up to a TV.

Also, at 85db these are just about as inefficient a speaker as you're likely to run into in 2020. So you will frequently find yourself setting your volume to 40+. Hindsight being 20/20, I might buy something different, but these definitely come as advertised. If you hate your girlfriend's annoying buddy's Klipsch speakers, and you have an amplifier that is stronger than a motel hair dryer, you will like these.

title: Very good, very happy with this purchase (with pics)
text:
I bought the MagicHold 2 after looking at many other options throughout the internet. What I found is that out of the dozen or so laptop/monitor stands offered on Amazon, there's only 3-4 actual different designs. Most are the same ODM stands rebranded for different importers. This stand seems to be the exact same stand as the "Viozon Monitor and Laptop Mount" right down to having identical pictures. The instruction manual for the MagicHold 2 has "OLL-3L" on the instruction manual, while the Viozon's product number is "OL-3L". I chose the MagicHold 2 because it comes in black.

NOTE: The stand I received is different/updated from the stands in the reviewer pictures from 2015.

My Setup > Laptop: 15.6" screen Lenovo P1 > Monitor: 27"

PROS:
- nice looking (compared to most of the other cheaper ones)
- easy to install - under 5 minutes, 10 minutes with cable routing
- good quality for the price (with the exception below)
- cable hiding is pretty good, they can be routed internally, unlike most of the cheaper ones
- stability is very good, so far I haven't had any problems with drooping
- adjustability is excellent (with the exception below)

CONS:
- I immediately broke a thumbscrew (see picture) with very little force - the part is definitely defective, so I ran down to the hardware store and bought an M6 screw to fit.
- The VESA mount included was an extremely tight fit on my monitor - I don't know if the VESA mount is slightly too big or my monitor's mounting space is too small
- Unless the laptop is facing straight forward or completely flat, the laptop screen will not be vertical and parallel to the monitor - the gap between the 2 will be a very annoying "V". This is a common problem with lots of stands I looked into. There are several solutions to making the screens butt cleanly together (like in my pictures), and I chose to use a Dremel tool to modify the base of the laptop mount by removing a protrusion from the cast aluminum part (see pictures). Now the laptop rotates in the 3rd dimension, and I have full adjustability. (I scratched the base in the pic while using a hacksaw to speed up the cutting, but NBD no one's going to see it.)

Overall, I would recommend this stand to anyone trying to clean up their desktop. The arms and base are a much nicer design than most of the others.

title: Does the Job For A Steep Price
text:
I am a renter which means I cannot drill into my walls. I’ve been looking everywhere for a workaround for my home theatre and this is it! It does the job perfectly. It’s flush with the wall and fits underneath my console cabinet. I may paint the stand to blend with the wall but I don’t really mind the white either. It was easy to assemble, but lifting your tv up onto the mount is definitely a two person job. And once it’s up, it’s HEAVY and difficult to slide around so make sure you have it exactly centered before adding the tv onto the stand.

A couple things: this thing is really expensive ($300 as of this writing). Is it worth it? My answer is maybe. The materials are very sturdy - solid metal, absolutely no fear of the thing falling apart while you’re watching tv. But $300 is more than many people pay for the tv itself. For me, completing my home theatre set up was worth the cost but it was still very steep. I think $150 would be a more appropriate figure.

Secondly, on the Amazon listing they say that the StandIt 400 suits TVs up to 65”. This isn’t the case: the instructions included in the box say 55”. Now, I have an OLED 65” and I decided to hang it on this anyway since the tv is paper thin and only about 40 lb. But be advised if you have a larger set you should get the StandIt 600 (if your wallet can take it). I found hiding the wires behind the set a little difficult since my tv’s power cable doesn’t detach for easy threading but that’s more an issue with my set than the stand.

It’s worth it to get the mounted look without drilling. But just make sure you are ready to drop some cash for that look!

Cons: The auto-focus is among the worst I've experienced. Any change in the camera's PTZ and it hunts constantly for a focus, especially during a zoom. title: Buy this amplifier!
text: I installed the lava hd 8008 omni-directional antenna on my roof about 3-1/2 years ago. It made a huge difference with my reception and picked up stations with towers an hour away! Anyway, this antenna came with an inline amplifier to amplify the signal. In the last 6 months or so, i noticed local channels becoming more and more pixilated if they came in at all. This, even after regularly rescanning through the tv's tuner. I tried a number of things...unplugged the antenna, rescanned to clear the tv's cache, disconnected and checked all connections, etc. and to no avail. I figured this either had to do with the FCC changes to over the air frequencies or my antenna was just done. Well, after researching more ways to troubleshoot and exploring antenna replacement options, i decided to just try replacing the inline amplifier at the tv. This would be cheaper than replacing the antenna and had nothing to lose except a few bucks at this point. So i ordered it, got it, installed it, rescanned the channels and BAM! Got my channels back! Turns out my amplifier just stopped amplifying the signal. You'll still need to periodically rescan your channels because stations are still changing over to the new frequencies.

title: An essential tool, for beginners and professionals, for making digital art.
text:
[[VIDEOID:5607dde5b9a5577fe16ebae80446d929]] Full-Disclosure: Wacom sent me this new Cintiq 22 to review. I was not given any parameters of how to review it or persuaded in anyway to review it with a predetermined outlook. The following are my own personal views and opinions.

Background: My name is Kyle and I am the owner of Freshwater Bay Creative design studio. I have been a creative professional since 1996 doing everything from video game backgrounds, conceptual art, storyboarding, illustration, editorial graphic design, craft beer label/can design and everything in between. Over the past twenty years I’ve used several Wacom products starting with the Intuos line of tablets in the late ‘90s and even the first Cintiq 21UX back in ‘04/’05. I’ve personally owned/own the Intuos2, Cintiq 12wx, Cintiq Companion Hybrid, MobileStudio Pro 16 and now the Cintiq 22.

Review: While I may mention some specifications this is not a review about specs. If you want those they are listed in the product description. I'm far more interested in how the device works for making art.

Pros:
- Full HD 1920x1080 screen resolution.
- Large screen for big, broad pen strokes.
- Heavy weight, solid stand attached to the back is fantastic and very easy to adjust.
- Screen surface is smooth, not slick.
- Works beautifully with the supplied Pro Pen 2. Works even better with the Pro Pen Slim!
- It’s big!
- Refresh rate makes for very quick pen strokes with no noticeable lag.
- Stays cool. Does not get hot after working on it for several hours straight.

Cons:
- Full HD 1920x1080 will seem a bit soft after using a 4K screen
- Color gamut, even after calibrating the screen, seems a bit dark and lacks some saturation.
- No express keys.
- No Touch input
- It’s big! (Not really a con, just make sure you have the desk space for it.)
- Three separate cables attached instead of 3-in-1 cable.
- No USB ports on the sides for thumb drives, etc.

At the time of this writing I’ve been using the Cintiq 22 daily for about a week on a Windows 10 computer. But for the past several years I’ve been producing the majority of my work on a Companion Hybrid hooked up to my primary work station as well as a MobileStudio Pro 16. So moving from a 13” screen and 16” screen, respectively, had an immediate and positive impact on my drawing movements. Being able to draw using my entire arm because of a larger surface space along with drawing in details while having more of the image visible is incredible. One can do beautiful work on a smaller screen but if you appreciate large, sweeping arm movements to create your work then this is definitely a great size for that. There is also plenty of space for floating menus, etc.
The attached monitor stand, which comes standard with the Cintiq 22, makes for excellent ergonomics and comfort while working. It is beautifully engineered for easy adjustment, solidly built and heavy with the rubber grips (located on a solid metal bar along with rubber grips located on the bottom edge of the device itself) keep the Cintiq 22 in place. There is no wobble, sliding or give when drawing with reasonable pressure. Resolution is a bit soft when doing line work, especially having used a 4K screen, but one can still put down very smooth and quick cross hatching, feathering or paint strokes. [Note: check your App Scaling settings in Win10 and make sure it is set to 100% for best results.]

The screen surface has a non-reflective coating that gives a slight bit of tooth for drawing. Since it isn’t etched glass some may not like the slight parallax distance between the pen tip and the cursor. However, I’ve never had an issue with this after properly calibrating the pen tool.
The biggest thing missing from this tablet are programmable Express Keys. I tend to use a keyboard for many actions but on other tablets I have Express Keys programmed for multiple uses. I honestly didn’t realize how often I used them until I didn’t have them anymore. I still find myself grabbing the left edge of the Cintiq 22 expecting to press a button only to find nothing there. It’s definitely a feature I miss. (Wacom does have a programmable remote with Express Keys but it is sold separately. I might be investing in one soon.) On screen menus can still be accessed through the Pro Pen buttons though. But even then you can only interact with them through the use of the Pro Pen since there is no touch input. Forget zooming or rotating your canvas with your free hand. I personally don’t use this feature much (it’s usually turned off) so I don’t miss it. But if that is a deal breaker for you then you’ll need to look at the Cintiq Pro line instead.

This next thing isn’t a negative but just something to be aware of...The device is big and needs plenty of space both in width and depth for it to be comfortable on a desk. Especially if you like to work with a second monitor and/or keyboard set next to it. When the monitor is stood straight up the stand extends 9” behind it. When lowered it will need up to the full depth of the device including space for the connected cables. (That’s approximately 15” of open space behind the device.) There are three separate cables (HDMI, USB, Power) that protrude from the back, top left of the machine. Apparently the Cintiq 16 version of this device comes with a single 3-in-1 cable for all of this. I would have preferred that cable over the three separate cables but it is hardly an issue. If you have the space and keep them managed with your other computer cables it won’t be a problem.

Color on the device isn’t as sharp or saturated as I’d prefer. I used a ColorMunki device to calibrate both my primary monitor and the Cintiq 22. It got them matched remarkably close but some colors and values (particularly bright/saturated) come off a bit soft and lack some contrast. Also, areas of black aren’t as inky and rich. None of this is a deal killer. I’m being extremely nit-picky in my assessment. Drawing and inking line art is no problem and looks great. Painting and coloring, if calibrated properly, will give you very close color approximation. But working in tandem with a second monitor and/or double checking your work on another screen or two is always recommended.

Another thing to note that I’m extremely happy about is the lack of heat! Working other Cintiq devices they can get a little warm when going non-stop all day. Working on the 22 it never once got hot or even warm.

Set-up was also extremely easy. Make sure you have the latest Wacom driver and it will work right away. All you'll need to do to start working is calibrate your pen, monitor color and, if you want, program your onscreen menus.

Finally, the Cintiq 22 is Wacom’s answer to the “entry level” tablet market. But don’t let that fool you. The Cintiq 22 is a high-end creative tablet perfectly capable of creating your professional quality artwork on, in my opinion. Yes, the “Pro” Cintiq line sports higher resolution screens, better color gamut and more bells and whistles but if you’re an independent freelancer that doesn’t want to break the bank then this will absolutely get the job done.

I didn’t talk about the Pro Pen 2 because it’s been around and it’s fantastic. But if you haven’t tried the Pro Pen Slim yet, it’s a must have. Feels great in the hand, light weight, feels like a brush or pencil and is amazing on a large screen like the 22. Check it out.

I'm sure I missed something. So if you have any questions give me a shout.

title: Really poor solder connection results in unstable serial connection
text: The solder connection between the USB plug and the PCB is weak and easily bent.  Most PCB's like this have the ground lugs soldered down extremely well to prevent this sort of failure, but this one does not.  Also, the plastic housing falls open way too easily.  The easily bent connections has resulted in serial connection failures when the power line glitches.  Otherwise, this works great.  If you decide to purchase, I highly recommend soldering the ground lugs, touching up the 4 data/power pins, and then either gluing or taping shut the case as an extra strain relief.  I'm taking 3 stars off my review because this should have been done at the factory and was not.

text:

There are problems with design, engineering and manufacturing.

The friction-based locking mechanism has very little contact surface.
Materials used are sub-par. It is made of molded aluminum alloy, rather than CNC T6061 that we are used to for camera support, even from cheap Chinese manufacturers. There is too much play around bolts and threads. The threads on the main axis bolts looks like I don't know what, ragged and uneven. Proof is the amount of brass filings that can be found when unscrewing the lock lever - the bolt threads just eat through the brass when tightened..
The concept is interesting but this falls short for anything beyond a phone, if even that.
I'll keep it for future modding.

title: Not quite five stars
text:
I have always loved these cases and frequently test many different brands. When I purchased the iPad Pro 11" I immediately looked for the New Trent case for my new iPad. It was not yet released. I purchased a different case and patiently waited until the release. I received an email notification and purchased it immediately.

I paid full price for this iPad. This is not a sponsored review in any way.

So here is my review.

Pros:
It is designed much like previous versions.
It has a hard shell which is enveloped by a softer rubber shell.
It has a screen protector built in.
It has a leather handle that is adjustable.
It has a metal kickstand that you can rotate 360 degrees.
It supports both portrait and landscape mode.
It appears to be fairly well built.
The hard shell is thinner than previous models. This makes the case overall weigh less. It does not appear that this makes the case less protective.

Cons:
The tolerances are not as close as previous models. For example, all previous models "snap" solidly together. This one failed to snap on one side. I made sure the iPad was seated properly and the two halves were together properly. It just was not able to snap together.

There is a definite air gap between the screen protector and the iPad. This can ultimately cause problems if water or dirt gets inside the gap. Of course this can always happen with any case that has a built in screen protector but the gap makes the problem more likely. Again, the tolerance is not as close as previous models. I don't know if this is a design defect or a quality control issue.

The rubber portion that covers the USB-C port is a little flimsy. Not terribly flimsy but certainly not as strong as previous models. I am concerned that over time it will tear off. But only time will tell.

Suggestions:

I think this case might be improved in a few ways:

1) A removable screen protector would be a huge improvement. First, it would let you use the iPad without it if you don't like screen protectors. Second, if you DO like screen protectors it would provide a mechanism for replacing the screen protector without replacing the entire case.

2) Tighter tolerances would make this a five star case.

3) Although not required to improve the case, a few color choices would be nice. Black is rather boring and for my "crew" it means that we often pick up the wrong iPad because we all use the same case.

Update

Having used this case for a while now, I have found that many cables will not fit. The opening for the USB-C cable is much too narrow. I eventually decided to file the cable opening down. This permits most cables to fit.

It's unfortunate that the company hasn't addressed this. The cable opening is an essential issue.
