title: GT-AX11000 AX11000 w Stock Firmware 3.0.0.4.384_5252
text:
GT-AX11000 is an outstanding product. Please note that most of the negative reviews are a result of ID10T error in setup.
I am using stock firmware as it is stable so far. Unit is paired to 1Gig Xfinity service via DOCSIS 3.1 modem. The connection is stable, I had the unit run 18 days without a reboot. My setup includes over 35 devices, some old, some new. 2.4Gz band is locked to a channel I selected manually. 5GHz bands run on Band Steering with zero customization. The clients are utilizing either of the two 5GHz bands. iPhones, iPads, Android phone, FireTV sticks, etc. work and connect fine. I had issue connecting an iPhone once, which was resolved by rebooting the iPhone. The wired devices also work fine, I have a 10 port Gig switch hanging on one of the ports. All good. Please note that I have the QoS enabled in Media mode. VoIP has no issue. I opened the port forwarding where needed. Also, I have DYNDNS domain setup, works great. OpenVPN works great too. Custom DNS servers are selected (1.1.1.1) to bypass Xfinity. I have 0 issues streaming movies on multiple TVs at the same time all in 4k. 0 issues using facetime, 0 issues with ZOOM, WebEx, Skype, Video Calls. All works great. AiProtection works great too.
Now, I did not test it with later firmware revisions. But, the upgrades in the newer firmware(s) are small and not stable yet. Please note that I did not test AiMesh.
I upgraded from AC68U mesh system (2 units) and the coverage with a single AX11000 is better. The area I am in is heavily saturated with N/AC units (20plus SSID on 2.4Ghz and 10+ on 5GHz) which is not an issue for the AX11000. The unit currently covers area of about 2400 sq ft. I would point out that this unit can be setup via an app, but, not all of the features are available in the app. One should use a browser to complete the setup. As for the speed, I have 450 Mbps on iPhone next to the unit, 200-250 almost everywhere else.
The unit is expensive, but, it is good. I would suggest getting a cooling stand for it to keep it cool - Tree New Bee TBR-K16 works like a charm.

title: Great value for music and gaming. My thoughts comparing with Samson SR850
text:
Review Update 05-26-2019:
I need to update my review. For some reason, the Equalizer APO + Peace is creating a problem with the SHP9500 and makes it sounds really weird. I got rid of the Equalizer and installed my drivers for my motherboard which has a built in Equalizer (not so detailed but with 10 bands) and some treble, bass control (among other things) in it and playing some songs using SHP9500 this way, showed what the headphone is capable of and honestly after some more tests I can say it is superior over SR850. Equalizer APO was causing a very strange behaviour which lead me to not like it as much, I will need to investigate why. Playing Heart Afire from Defqwop in SHP9500 shows its clarity, separation and bass extension and I'd say is better than SR850. The bands I like most plays better (at least some of them JInjer, Divisions, Any Given Day) in SR850 yet, but in general I consider the Philips a step up in quality, clarity, separation and range. In SR850 some instruments of percussion for example was more faded and far away. What I noticed also was if you turn bass up it interferes much, mush less in the mids and highs (and vice-versa) than in the SR850 so you can control one of them without punishing much the other. Will keep updating my experiences.

Original post:
In short, after comparing Samson SR850 and Philips SHP9500 right out of the box, my answer is: 850 sounds better specially for music.

Now, I will try (even being kinda noob to the subject) to explain what I noticed using them both in the last days. Pluggin both into my Asus 3 celphone with no EQ and playing Spotify at max quality, 850 sounds much better in every aspect and they play louder, 9500 should be louder cause it has a higher sensibility (both has impedance of 32ohms, but 850 has a sensibility of 98db against 101db of the 9500).
If we use amplifying levels and EQ on the celphone 9500 starts to get much more nice but requires lots of adjustments to make it closer to the 850 sound.
Using my Fiio A3 amp for headphones both perform better but again, 850 sounds best. 9500 needs tweaks to become more enjoyable and has a different sound signature. If I would use them only in the celphone with no EQ, amp or anything I would not keep the 9500.
In the computer, my Asus Maximus IX Hero has power enough to push them both quite well and using the driver features I could equalize each nicely but only enjoyed he 9500 after I bumped the bass around 60hz and reducing 1 to 2db around 5khz (which is where is it a bit harsh).

Sound characteristics on each:
SR850 has a wider soundstage, smoother (more rounded?) bass, has a more harsh highs around 1 to 2khz, more blended mids (instruments blends more with vocals and all), I'd say I can hear the vocals and guitars more pronnounced, responds less to equalization but if you tune the 1 to 2k a notch down and bump just a bit the bass around 150hz it gets good, very good. A good observation, some tracks gets very disturbing with no equalization due the 1 to 2k peak but if you drop down a bit there's no problem.

SHP9500 has slightly less soundstage, more hollow but deeper bass, has it's highs peak around 5khz, better instruments separation (I could hear the drums very well), vocals are slightly more backwards than in the 850, responds very well to equalization and if you tune it the right way it becomes a brand new headphone. Bass lacks more than in the 850 but bumping up (specially around 60hz) the bass gets much more interesting and alive but I felt some rumble/ressonance in my ears bumping them so you gotta find the perfect spot. I'd say I prefer the 850 bass, more natural, more like the bass you hear from speakers. I needed to tweak down the area around 5k so the highs could be less piercing but in general 9500 mids and highs are more controlled.

Build quality/confort
SR850 uses much "cheaper feel" plastic all around but it is quite strong, don't feel like it will break at all. Has velour pads which has a nice touch but feels warm after a while and gets a bit uncorfortable. The pads touches the tips of my ear but don't disturb me. The headband has a very nice adjustment on the top of the head and don't cause any disconfort but the clamping force is felt at least in the first 30 seconds of usage but I already worn the headphone for 3 to 4 hours with no problem other than heat. Doesn't have removable cable and it entirely plastic built.

SHP9500 uses much better plastic, has metal grills, the pads rotates some degrees to adjust to the head shape, has fabric pads and fabric over the headband and feels light, absolutely light and feel like I am not wearing a headphone at all, however if I look down to get something that is fell in the floor for example, the headphone slips from my head, there's zero clamping force even if you adjust the headband correctly. I am a metalhead and can't headband at all with it, but headbanging is not a problem wearing the SR850. 9500 has detachable cable (3.5mm) and metal grills which allow you to use Vmoda boom microfone or Modmic and transform it into a headset, which is not possible with the SR850. The cable in the 9500 feels very cheap, even more cheaper than the 850 one. Forgot to mention my ears didn't touch the pads but touches slightly the fabric that covers the drivers, however don't disturb me at all.

Gaming tests:
Tried the racing game Assetto Corsa in my computer with some paid mods which has great developed sounds and I can assure that with or without EQ SHP9500 sounded better than SR850 and I think was specially due the more controlled mids and highs and due separation I mentioned earlier. With EQ it got even better because I was able to bring the bass to the right and satisfatory level. Soundstage may be a bit less nice in 9500 but is slightly and taking into consideration the extra confort and the possibility to attach a mic to it the 9500 is of great value.

All I say here could only be written because I compare them both, one right after the other. After one day away from the SR850 (which I was much used to how it sounds) and using the 9500 first with the EQ on I would be very satisfied with what it delivers. To music however, I still prefer the SR850 sound signature over the 9500 though.

What else can I say? If you intend to use it in your celphone with no amp/EQ I would not recommend the SHP9500 over the SR850, if you'll gonna listen to music and will not be gaming I would not recommend it either. If you intend to use Amp/EQ or both in the celphone, both will be enough but 9500 requires a lot of tweaking to perfomr reasonable close to the 850. If you intend to listen to music and play games I would recommend 9500 but still prefer the 850 in average (despite not have the chance to plug in a mic).
I hope it helps and if anybody has both and disagree with what I said I would be glad to hear your feedback.

title: BEST BUILD QUALITY of headphones available
text:
The star of the show about these headphones I would say is this in the following order:

1.) Longevity - These headphones have a removeable/replaceable battery AND are made of METAL and REAL LEATHER. There are a few small plastic parts but the major pieces are made solid which is very important when you start looking at reviews of Sony's, Bose's, AudioTechnica's, and JBLs reviews and see people talking about stuff falling apart after a while. I have first-hand experience with the AudioTechnica MT50's falling apart after a few years. With a replaceable battery, that means the battery life limitation essentially doesn't exist and when the battery dies, you just put a new one in.

2) Sound Quality - Do yourself a favor if you have Best Buy in your area - go in there and do a side-by-side comparison between these and the rest of the headphones... I noticed a huge, dramatic difference in sound quality between these and every single other one in there. The only other sound I liked as much as these or maybe a bit more are the Sony 950BT's Extra Bass Boosted headphones but that's just because I'm a basshead. Unfortunately, again, looking up the reviews of those shows them falling apart and a bunch of upset customers.

3) Nice features - There are 4 usability features I really like about these headphones:
a.) They turn off automatically when you take them off your head
b.) They CAN be connected to TWO bluetooth devices SIMULTANEOUSLY... I've had these connected to my iPhone and my Macbook Pro at the same time and got audio out of both without having to "switch" connections!
c.) They can be used as wired headphones and the QUALITY IMPROVES accordingly.
d.) When you use them as wireless headphones, they will simuntaneously charge your battery if you use USB-C. Bose and Sony's DO NOT do this.

As far as the app goes, I would not say the app is the best audio app by any means whatsoever, but it does allow you to adjust the EQ in a unique, visual way. It's better than nothing.

NOTE ABOUT THE AUTO-OFF FEATURE: It works great but you have to TURN THE HEADPHONES ON BEFORE YOU PUT THEM ON YOUR HEAD. This allows them to "calibrate" the sensor every time you power them on. A bunch of people don't understand this and they turn them on while on their head. This causes the sensor to randomly stop playing the music and they get frustrated and angry and think they have a defective sensor. The sensor works fine, you just need to turn them on before you put them on.

title: eGPU and a MacBook Pro 16"
text:
Pros:
Bleeding edge technology with eGPUs provides desktop class graphics performance
Nvidia 2070 Super GPU runs Half-Life Alyx perfectly through my HTC Vive

Cons:
AMD GPUs work well in Mac OS for games specifically updated to use an eGPU. Other games won't run at all or are highly unstable.

AMD GPUs are at best hit-or-miss in bootcamp. Some users report success with rigging them up to work. I was not able to get an AMD Radeon RX480 to connect successfully.

Nvidia GPUs work great in bootcamp (see pros above) but are unsupported in Mac OS and don't work at all.

Windows 10 seems to have stability issues with the eGPU connected. For instance, do NOT attempt to boot with the eGPU connected. Do not let the computer hibernate. Do not let the computer sleep. Be careful not to plug in peripherals too fast or the whole system (including built-in trackpad and keyboard) will become unresponsive.

Final Thoughts:
Even with the above cons this was still a good purchase. I look forward to future system updates bringing greater stability. Now if we could just get some Nvidia drivers for Mac OS...

title: Works very well for me; no need to spend more money
text:
This quick release adapter for my tripod works just fine for this amateur photographer. I should point out that I have it attached to my reliable old (40+ years) Velbon VGB-3C aluminum tripod, and I can't speak to how it would work on other tripods.

I looked at the wide range of adapters of this type and could see no reason to buy anything more expensive. Don't get me wrong. I'm sure there are better (and certainly more feature-rich) adapters, but this is all I need. Keep in mind that this is a simple quick release adapter, not a universal ball mount or a fancy 3-axis gimbal mount. It doesn't fold or tilt. It doesn't allow you to mount the camera off to the side of the tripod axis. It doesn't do any of those things. For the modest cost of $15.99, all it does is keep you from having to screw and unscrew the camera to the tripod. And since the Velbon tripod already allows for three axes of movement, why buy a separate attachment to do the same thing?

It comes in two parts -- one part attaches to the camera and the other attaches to the tripod. The part that attaches to the tripod has a single (bullseye) leveling bubble that's very handy, especially when taking a series of shots that will be stitched into a horizontal panorama. Yes, two arc bubble levels at 90 degrees to each other would be better, but would add to the cost and take more space. The other part (camera plate) has a slot for the bolt so that it can be attached out of the way of the battery/SD card compartment. Very important! The camera plate attaches very securely to the camera using only fingers to tighten the bolt.

The tripod part has a safety feature that keeps you from accidentally moving the release lever and thereby releasing the camera. Seems pretty fundamental to me, but not all quick release adapters all have this feature. Once the camera is snapped into place on the tripod, it seems very securely attached.

This adapter seems very sturdy and durable -- made of aluminum, not plastic. I don't expect to ever need to replace it. It's a solid 5 stars as far as I'm concerned.

title: Overall solid TV, but it has it's flaws.
text:
This TV is very solid.

OS and features.

Firstly, the operating system is not bad by any means. But as a person who has hands on with the 3 major TV operating systems I feel like WebOS by LG is king. Where Android TV is dead last out of the 3 for me.

For example, from what I've seen, you can't download a system update in the background on this Samsung. It also is a bit choppy. Especially when connected to the network. Because it tries to load everything.

This offers Alexa built into it. And similar to the echo show, it gives you a visual image of certain questions and commands. But even Alexa functionality is quite choppy.

Picture:

As a person who has an 77 Inch OLED, I feel like the Q80T can't keep up with it. But this 85 inch Q80T looks beautiful regardless. The QLED technology offers substantially higher brightness than OLED's. It really makes the colors pop out. This panel is full array local dimming which is very nice. As a person who has had edge lit, Full array is miles better.

I did take some calibration settings from online. And it made my picture look a bit better.

Inputs:

This TV has 4 HDMI inputs. It has the new Enhanced ARC standard. It also has HDMI 2.1 with a catch. Because it only offers a single 2.1 port. And that's a bit disappointing. Especially if you have multiple 2.1 devices down the road. An example would be the new generation of consoles coming out. Although there will probably be HDMI 2.1 Passthroughs/ hubs available.

Sound:

I personally use an external sound system. But the sound is what you would expect from internal TV speakers. It's not much different than most TV's.

Remote:

The footprint if the remote is pretty small. You can use voice commands. I have Verizon FIOS. And it detected my cable box. So I'm able to change channels with it.

Case in point, this TV is excellent. I wanted an 85 inch TV specifically. And it definitely doesn't let me down. There are other great options on the market for this price range. Including the LG CX 77 inch. So I would definitely suggest comparing different options.

Overall, 4 out of 5 stars for me. Operating system is decent, but not exactly great. And while the picture is excellent, it can't compare to the picture quality on OLED.

title: Works just fine in transparent extension mode until it's power cycled
text:
This thing initially comes up with its own open WiFi network. You "join" that network and set it up to connect with your router. You have a choice between a manual setup or running the Genie. I tried both methods and was successful in setting it up to extend my router's 2.4GHz and 5GHz WiFi networks using either method. In my configuration, my router uses the same SSID for both WiFi nets and the same password. I run in 802.11n-only mode on each frequency band. I set the 2.4GHz signal to Channel 6 with a single 20MHz channel (I've also tried this successfully with a 40MHz channel). On the 5GHz band, I use channel 161 and a 40MHz channel width. It's a fairly simple and normal config on the router side.

Everything worked fine after the initial extender setup. The extender connected to both router signals as expected. Running a speed test from my MacBook Pro client connected to the extender gives me 95% of the throughput that I measured when previously connected directly to my router at a close physical distance. This test was run over the 5GHz band.

You should be aware that the extender isn't a completely transparent bridge to your router's network. Unless you use a static IP on your client, when you connect to any WiFi network, your client generates a DHCP request to obtain an IP address. Most routers cache the Mac address that comes with that DHCP request so when the DHCP lease expires and the client renews the lease with another DHCP request, it will get the same IP address. The extender will replace the first 3 hexadecimal numbers (octets) in the MAC address with its own OID and then forward the request to your router. This will result in your client being assigned a different IP address when it connects through the extender than when it connects to your router. For most people, this isn't an issue but it can and will break some applications as you walk around your house and switch between the extender and the router. Remember, in transparent mode, your router and extender use the same SSID so your extender sort of acts like an access point (AP).

My issue with this extender device is that it doesn't recover from a soft or hard power cycle. A soft power cycle is performed by connecting to the extender and logging in to its management app using a special URL that the extender traps for this purpose. A hard power cycle is done by unplugging the extender and plugging it back in, thereby simulating a real power outage.

When the extender comes back up from a power cycle, it appears to reconnect with the router. However, on the client side of the extender, it often has a totally different IP network inconsistent with the router's network that it bridged and extended before. For example, my router's IP network is 10.168.123.0/24, and initially, the extender extended that network to its clients with the aforementioned DHCP request MAC address twiddling. After the power cycle, it comes back up with a 192.168.0.0/16 network that doesn't route to the router's 10.168.123.0/24 subnet. Furthermore, now the damn thing seems to be running its own DHCP server for that private network now.

My MBP client can't connect through the extender to my router so no access to my 10.168.123.0/24 LAN subnet or to the internet beyond after the power is cycled. Sometimes after a power cycle, it won't even assign its clients an IP address on its isolated 192.168/16 subnet. Yes, I'm on the latest firmware. This is totally unacceptable behavior.

title: Compact and versatile, your cell phone's music playback companion for the great outdoors
text:
You’re all set for your late-summer picnic and this time it will be perfect, right down to the musical selection. You’ve got Percy Faith’s greatest hits downloaded from Apple Music to your iPhone, and your solution for broadcasting your phone’s playback is this little speaker, the EarFun Go (Model SP100). EarFun’s portable sound source is small (7” by 2” by 2.25”) but hefty in your hand.—it weighs a pound. Four hours of charging via its micro-USB port will get you 24 hours of playback, says the manufacturer.

You would never consider bothering other picnickers with a boom box; you want only enough volume to fill your picnic table. The EarFun Go will not attract hostile stares as a boom box would.

Using a 3.5 mm stereo cable (not included), you can connect the Go directly to playback devices that still incorporate this rather archaic methodology. Most users will prefer connecting to the speaker via Bluetooth 5. This new Bluetooth standard should be a little more generous in the permitted space between playback device and speaker. But as with earlier Bluetooth standards, line-of-sight is still a good idea if you want a good signal.

The EarFun Go pairs with a cell phone effortlessly, and it remembers what it’s paired with. You can even connect two Gos wirelessly to a single cell phone and get stereo playback! Another example of its versatility: the Go can double as a speakerphone should a cellular call come in.

In case your picnic gets rained on, your Go should weather the storm–its manufacturer claims it’s waterproof.

Using Bluetooth to connect the Go to my iPhone XR resulted in clear playback from its twin 40 mm transducers, each powered by a 6 watt amplifier. For such a small form factor, bass is surprisingly good. In fact, the full spectrum of the recording is reproduced faithfully. The string section in Percy’s rendering of “A Summer Place” comes through nicely, as do the grace notes from the French horn. The double-bass player plucks away, and the flutes waft above the entire airy performance. Your picnic is complete.

The portability, sound quality, battery life, compact size, wireless connection, and ease of use enable me to recommend with confidence the EarFun Go to set the musical mood for your next outdoor get-together.

title: LG 38WK95C-W vs Dell U3818DW for MacBook Pro 2019
text:
I was on the market for a 38" monitor to be used with my MacBook Pro 2019. Looking at internet reviews, Dell U3818DW was receiving a lot of praise. I decided to buy it, and quickly realized that it really is not working well with Mac. It was not recognized immediately by Mac, but after some finagling and reading on-line advice I was able to connect it. I also found out that Dell only produces its display manager app for the windows, but not for MacOS, same is true for the app to update monitor firmware. 

Reading Dell customer support forum made me even more upset, as someone named Chris M suggested to every Apple user question that Dell does not test any of its monitors with Macs, and for any questions users should go to Apple forums. It reminded me of Michael Dell's infamous quote that Apple as a company should be sold out so as to not embarrass its customers. Soon thereafter, Apple became one of the most valuable companies, while Dell struggled from one bankruptcy to another, and even a recent infusion of 2 billion dollars from Microsoft and becoming a private company did not seem to help. But I digress...

After trying my best to adapt this monitor to my needs, my frustration grew and I started to look at alternatives. I quickly realized that Dell does not manufacture the display panel (they have not really ever manufactured anything - just re-selling at profit). The display panel for this model of Dell monitor is made by LG - it is LM375QW1-SSA1. It goes for $400 for a consumer on-line. I looked at which other monitor uses the same display panel and it did not take long to find the original LG monitor LG 38WK95C-W. The best thing is - this LG monitor actually sells for $100-150 less than Dell!

I purchased this LG monitor and could not be happier. Dell has been returned. 

Since the display panel is identical, many aspects are similar, however there are few nuances that you may want to know:

1. LG monitor works very nicely with Macbook Pro 2019. It has a Mac OS app, was immediately recognized with the correct resolution and set up basically took connecting my USB-C between the Mac and the monitor. Dell as mentioned previously does not have a Mac OS app, you would not be able to upgrade the monitor firmware from Mac and most importantly it does not play well with Mac OS.

2. I prefer LG stand to the bulky Dell stand. While LG stand does not allow to rotate the monitor right and left (unlike Dell), it has not been an issue in my set-up. Also LG uses a satisfying pneumatic mechanism that allows to move the monitor up and down on the stand, while Dell stand uses metal rails. More importantly I can move the LG monitor above my Macbook when it is open (this is the setup I prefer), while Dell's stand does not allow to move the monitor that high (see pics at the max height).

3. Since the Dell monitor packs the power source inside the monitor, the monitor is much thicker, mostly in the
middle and has a ventilation screen that will collect dust overtime, while LG's power "brick" is separate from the monitor, and thus the monitor maintains a slick and thin appearance which I prefer. The downside is that LG's power source is only rated for 60W, while Dell's - 100W. Macbook Pro 2019 comes with a 95W adapter, so if you are working on video editing or other tasks that require significant power, Dell power source would be a more adequate one. However since I don't run high power apps all the time, I had no issues charging my Macbook from the monitor's USB-C connection without any issues. During this week I used an LG monitor, I worked and had to convert a video file. In the process, Mac's battery dropped to 85% over 4 hrs, but then quickly charged back to 100% without use of Mac's own power supply adapter. This is only important if you are planning to connect Mac to monitor via USB-C and can be fixed by still connecting it via its own power adapter, which is also the case if you connect to the monitor via DisplayPort or HDMI port. 

4. Both monitors come with speakers. However LG monitor speakers are 10W and Dell's 9W. More importantly, LG allows you to connect to it's speakers not only via a cord, but also via a bluetooth. Both speakers are OK, and not spectacular, but I find them pretty useful. 

5. Overall LG monitor has many more setups and more fine picture tune setups, including (pseudo)HDR when compared to Dell monitor.

title: SMR drive not fit for purpose as a NAS drive

DO NOT BUY THIS DRIVE unless you have a very specific use case: either as a single drive/mirror, or mostly read only system.

These, and other SMR drives, are NOT suitable for very busy or even moderately busy writing use cases.

title: Inexpensive, easy to use, decent quality for its price range
text:
I started with packaging photos, then product photos, then the last three pictures were taken with the camera itself.
The box is smaller than I expected, but sufficient. I suppose that is typical for items that are intended to be shipped rather than sold at retail.
It came in a padded envelope, but it's light enough that it was not damaged in shipping.
The privacy shutter came separately - it has a pre-applied self-adhesive pad. (Application directions are on the Amazon product page.) I am not using it.
The USB cable is nice quality - the stiffness may bother some, and it may impact positioning the camera, but it will be less likely to wear out or get damaged.
The base has a threaded receiver for a tripod, which is nice.
The base is not spring-loaded - it relies on being manually closed, not spring tension.
Both surfaces inside the base are rubber-coated, so it will tend to grip.
The camera has a hinge, so you can aim it up and down and not just where the base leaves it pointed, but it does not have a swivel from side to side.
The unit was automatically detected by my Windows 10 computer, and Teams picked it up and used it as the default camera.
A set of white lights come on when the camera is active. They are noticeable, but not distracting.
The resolution (as expected) is 1920x1080 for a full-HD 16x9 image. The Windows Camera app says it will do 30fps at full HD.
The color is decent for the main subject in a photo. The image has significant fisheye to get its wide-angle view, which is normal. Brightness drops off at the edges, and it's clearly fixed-focus, intending for a person at a normal working distance away, and not close-up images - the quality close-up is lousy. Which is to say this is a webcam for conferencing, not for photos. You won't want to use it for your eBay pictures. But that's not what it was intended for.
The sound is not so good, but it will work. I compared with my Logitech USB headset, and the headset had better sound when it was behind my head than the camera had when positioned properly about two feet ahead.

Summary: It will do its intended job decently, but the video will be better than the audio. If you don't have $100 to spend, it's a decent option. If you do webconferencing regularly for business, and if you can afford a Logitech camera for $100, I'd suggest going that route. If you use it for family and friends, this will work. As I write this, Logitech webcams are hard to find without scalper markups.

If the company reads this, look into a better image sensor and microphone. The microphone might be improved by different installation - it may seem worse because of the small hole, but others with small holes have better sound. I didn't take it apart to see how it's mounted inside.

Update: I used Teams with a coworker, and he said that the image quality is likely better than others in its price range. He said that in this range, a bright background (a window) usually washes everything else out, and this one doesn't. And he said he thought it sounded fine. I'll upgrade it a star.

title: Solid Performer
text:
Battery leakage destroyed the old Radio Shack AM/FM/SW radio that I'd have for more than twenty five years. I researched these radios for several weeks before deciding on this little Tecsun DR-920C. When I say little I mean its LITTLE! But even though it's small its big on performance. I mainly listen to AM radio programs and this thing performs really well on AM. The internal antenna is adequate for an station with a reasonable signal. The FM is fine for local stations. What surprised me was the performance on SW. I didn't expect much at all, especially with just the telescopic whip antenna, but it actually worked pretty well. I am adding the roll up wire antenna for good measure and can't wait to see how it performs with that.

For an emergency radio this thing is awesome. It's tiny enough to fit into a backpack or go bag type thing. It runs on only two AA batteries so keeping it powered is easy. The radio is super easy to operate. No need to learn a bunch of menus. I like that there are actual switches for functions rather than menus. Menus give me a headache, especially when you don't use the radio often. The plastic body of the radio is as rugged as my old one, although it wouldn't hurt my feelings if someone would make a radio like this but in a tougher body designed for a little rough handling.

Over all, if you need a small and very functional radio for emergency use, or even casual listening then this is a great choice.

title: BOSS my A**
text:
This is simply a lie with the output power. I feel stupid for not checking what I was buying more in depth, but here is my feeling with this Amp.

The large downfall is they advertise 1800 watts RMS into 1 ohm. I have 2 DDX-10s that take 2000 RMS. When I took the amp out of the box I noticed the fuses. 2, 35 amp fuses. DIdn't feel right to me. Little math later and I found it would only put out roughly 1000 watts (Voltage X Amp (fuses) = Watts). So I'm returning this thing for the Skar RP-2000.1D for real power. Look it up on youtube, a guy does a dyno on this amp.

Anyway the thing I do like about the amp besides the lack of power. The controls are easy to get to since they stick out. The logo lights up, which is kinda neat but where I use it not necessary. Not much else to say here...

So for me I wanted true advertised power, which I don't think this will provide because the fuses are too small. They should blow during music play. But for a person who has a budget this will do just fine.

title: too bad the zero-rated battery kills this otherwise sweet little flip top
text:
Oh well I guess my concerns were valid - the battery is even worse than I had thought. The battery began swelling portending failure), causing the bottom to "belly" out, so that all 4 feet didn't touch anymore, which made it very hard to use. Then, fully charged, it died 50 minutes into a 90-minute zoom call. OK, I should have been plugged in but that was the last straw. Returned. BTW I was unable to reset windows 10 to properly wipe data so I had to spend a lot of time cleaning it out and disguising user info. Windows is a pain in the butt, I'm switching to a chromebook!

Other problems: this may be universal in flip-tops but it was difficult to manage in tablet or tent mode, always unintentionally closing or switching the app - this is due to the narrow bezel which I liked at first. Also it would tend to show the screen upside-down on video calls, apparently thinking it was in tent mode.

Here's my original review:
Solid: pretty, sturdy, low price. Weak battery, a bit slow. I liked it enough to get 2.
I'm not a power user, do mostly web browsing, stream video, word processing, spreadsheets, powerpoints, reading books. I wanted a nice light, fairly versatile computer. I considered a tablet but need a keyboard - so the fliptop (why is that not a real name for this format?) works for me. But windows is a kind of a PITA, maybe I should try chromebook.

The good: The build quality of this little flipper is quite impressive, nice keyboard, great screen, light weight - I find nothing to complain about on appearance and feel. This looks and feels as good as an Apple IMO (but lighter). I also like the small, USB-C charger (however see battery comments below). I haven't tried casting video yet but other reviews say it works fine. I like that the solid state drive is easily upgradable.

The not so good: Of course it's not the fastest PC, takes longer to boot than my (fairly old) i5 - powered laptop, and downloads aren't super quick. It isn't slow enough to really bother me though.

The bad: battery life is pretty bad. I'm OK with it, I'm almost always near a plug and the charger is really small and light. Batteries are heavy and expensive - which explains how this little gem can be so light and cheap!

title: Total joke - impractical and barely useable
text: I have purchased over 200 FSP brand computer PSUs. They have proved to be extremely high quality and very reliable, however whoever designed these and wrote the description must have been smoking dope. On the positive side they are high quality and they run very cool so I suspect if you can get them into the case they might be reliable which is why I gave them 3 stars, however they are a total joke as regards suitability for ITX cases and to state they are modular is beyond a total a joke. EVERY PC needs to have a Motherboard and unless it has an M.2 SSD it needs one SATA power connector. Any good modular PSU comes with multiple plug in leads. If you don't need the old style LP4 connectors then you don't plug that lead in, same for the Motherboard CPU power header or the video card power connector. However this PSU has one gigantic power connector just for the 24 way Motherboard connector that doesn't even have the CPU header on it. There is only one other modular plug in so unless you have an extremely weird setup you need both plug ins (there are only 2) and all the leads just like any normal non-modular design. Worse still these are not lovely flat and all in one flat cables, the motherboard connector is connected with around 5 different flat cables twisted around like birds nest soup at the end so the correct terminals connect into the connector. Since I only needed the 1 SATA power connector then trying to get rid of around 5 other multi-connector leads neatly in an ITX case was nothing short of a nightmare. The flat cables take up more than twice the room of the equivalent FSP250-60FAG non modular normal wired PSU and why any sane person would have a Floppy Connector on a modern PC PSU when I haven't used one in 20 years beggars belief. See my photos for 2 attempts of trying to neatly install this nightmare. I bought 4 of these, I certainly would not recommend them for ITX cases and will not be buying any more.

title: Better than a standard keyboard in a dirty environment, but not the best money can buy
text:
I bought about 35 of these for use in a metal shop. They work... OK. A few of them have been a bit troublesome, with the most common annoyance being extraneous key presses being registered. For example, some of them seem to think the space bar is being pressed with almost every other key, so you have to be very ginger with it to avoid typing something like "M ED I OCR E" rather than "MEDIOCRE" - and that's what these are. Although they are flexible enough that you can *almost* type normally with them, nobody in the shop likes the "spongy" feel of them. They will certainly stand up to dirt and water far better than any standard keyboard, and for the occasional typing that our shop folks do, these are passable. But, if you need to do a lot of typing, you will probably be frustrated with these.

I won't be buying any more of these. Instead, I will get the Grandtec "virtually indestructible" keyboards. I have a handful of these in the same shop. They are considerably more expensive than the Rocksoul units, and on the GrandTecs you have to hit the rubber button keys with similar force to an old fashioned mechanical typewriter - so they are also not made for someone who needs to do a lot of typing, but they work much better than the Rocksouls and provide what ought to be an equal amount of resilience to dirt and moisture.

text:
The camera can't update the picture most of the time.

On the other-hand it works most of the time if the system hasn't prompted me of motion or if I review "motion captured" footage after it's been recorded.

The picture quality is so-so. You'd be lucky to get a plate number or positive ID for anything further than 10 or 15+ feet.

Motion sensor is hit or miss too.

Also, you're likely going to be replacing batteries faster than they claim. I've replaced my busiest camera once already since my purchase a couple of months ago. I figured this would be the case before I made the purchased but thought I'd give feedback.

Depending on your setup, this seems like the type of system that people get for their own peace of mind but ultimately will likely fall short when required to deliver real world results (my opinion based on 8 years of policing).

Overall I'm dissatisfied with this product and if I could do it again I'd spend a few more dollars on a better system.

title: Works great
text:
I found an old camcorder VHS thing in my parents attic there were a couple of VHS tapes collecting dust up there too. I asked them about it and they said they had no clue. So I set out on a journey to find an old VHS player and ALAS! I had found one in burried under a dusty box of old dog toys and leashes. Time to solve this mystery! But sadly, we had upgraded all of our TVs and had nothing that ran analog anymore. I was about to give in and accept defeat, but NO! I set out on Amazon, I bought this little adapter thing, I waited at the door for a full 2 days for it to arrive, AND THEN IT DID! It was like slow motion, I gathered everything, the tapes, the player, and the adapter. I ran into the living room and used my grubby little hands to slap all the wires together. It was set. Everything plugged in, I chose a tape at random, the only thing labeled on it was a date and a heart. My curiosity had my mind running at lightspeed. My parents walk in, they ask what I'm doing. I tell them I'm solving the worlds greatest mystery, they buy into my little act and sit down on the sofa. I double check everything. It's time. My sweaty left pointer finger hits the TV remote, it blinks on, and my right greasy pointer finger gently strokes the play button on the VHS player... and I looked up...

Yea and that's when I realized that the dog toys in the attic weren't dog toys. Dad was just into some kinky stuff. The adapter works great tho 10/10

title: A Few Things to Remember...
text:
1. The pieces of the case fit together QUITE WELL!! Since it COMPLETELY covers the SD Card slot, make sure you do everything necessary [pertaining to the Card] BEFORE assembling the case for the first time [or putting it back together again]!

2. The case has removable covers that protect the S Pen storage slot, headphone jack, and the power jack. Make sure they are securely in place [when those items are not in use] to prevent dust and debris from getting lodged within them.

3. The case insulates the device QUITE WELL!! So, when your device is in the case, try to avoid laying it down flat on 'soft, non-rigid' surfaces (beds, pillows, etc)...especially if you are doing things that are 'resource-intensive' (primarily gaming)!! Doing so will cause your tablet to warm up!! So, either use the Velcro hand strap, or the kick stand to support the device instead.

4. The carrying strap is connected to the corner straps through PLASTIC clips. Although they're rigid, it doesn't take much force to disconnect them [from the carrying strap]. Think of the clips that were used on fanny packs (Google 'fanny packs', if necessary). Therefore, avoid doing anything that would cause your device to swing excessively while it's hanging [from your neck, shoulder, etc]...and NO SUDDEN, JERKING MOVEMENTS, either!! Again, the connectors are PLASTIC CLIPS (not metal hoops)!!

title: New TN technology  is interesting.
text:
I stopped using TN panels 2 years ago after experiencing VA and IPS and personally really didn't like any of the 240hz options, tried them all. The thing I find interesting about this monitor is you can use "scenery" and tweak it to be pretty close to my VG279Q IPS panel in coloration. Then switch it to FPS, RACING, RPG or w/e for gaming.

Upon turning the monitor on for the first time it will not look great without you adjusting the settings. So I'll list mine.
Brightness: 60
Contrast: 80
Color Temp > User Mode > R-92 G-94 B-100
Vivid Pixel: 0
Adaptive Sync: On
Shadow Boost: Personal Preference I use 1 or 2 for gaming
Trace Free:(Asus's name for Overdrive) This is the important one for Asus panels as it alters the monitor speed. So please read the explanation.
I have a 2080ti and have no issue hitting 144hz or 165hz with OC in competitive games with competitive settings so I use 80 ... If your PC struggles to max fps use 40 or 60... unfortunately 100 or Max Overdrive will cause Overshoot which is inverted ghosting. So test your system using 40,60,80 and if you notice inverted ghosting adjust accordingly.

All in all I'm really impressed with this technology and love that for work related activities I can set this monitor to a preset that doesn't necessarily make it seem out of place next to IPS panels. Colors still fall off at angles but it's more extreme at vertical angles and not as bad at horizontal as past panels I've used.

text: We have thee kids in our family and it's always a concern that we might lose track of them when we go on a family trip. We I tried to turn on Yepzon to use it, it's completely dead.  I did some research and decided to purchase a Track! device. We paid for a monthly global plan ($19), and it worked exactly as described.  In Beijing and several other cities in China, we are able to track our 5 year old son's location, even in remote Jinshanling Great Wall area.  The signal is constant and I got email alerts as I set it up (speed alert, zone alert etc).  The battery life is great (no charge needed for days), and the device is small, lightweight (my son wore it as a necklace) and secure. title: Best AM FM Pocket Radio on the Market
text: This is the best pocket radio on the market. Excellent control and ergonomics, very visible  LCD readout, will tune for EUR or USA (9 or 10 KHz increments), auto timer for shutoff if using to fall asleep, works great with rechargable AA batteries, great sensitivity and selectivity on both bands, this is the one to get! Not sure why the poor reviews, but I have tried many popular pocket radios and this has the best performance, feature set and value. One small hack I have done is to put a wide rubber band around the width of the unit to keep it from sliding around on tables or if I am in bed. This is a great radio for listening to long distance (DX) stations and from my location in Chicago can reliably receive on AM stations in Nashville, NYC, Boston, Iowa, Minneapolis, Dallas and Montreal at night on AM. I have been a licensed Amateur Radio operator for over 25 years and can highly recommend this unit as one of, if not the best pocket AM, FM pocket radios on the market. Stereo on FM is great with earbuds ( I like the Panasonic earbuds). Love the locking function so that frequency dosen’t accidentally get shifted if tuning buttons are pressed if radio is in your pocket or bed. Just a great radio and I can recommend this one without any hesitation.

text:
I purchased this camera to use as a baby monitor both at home and when we travel. As soon I unpacked the camera I knew that it was a good purchase. Setup was a breeze and I was up and running very quickly by simply downloading the smart home app and scanning the QR code. The quality of the video from this camera is fantastic both during the day and at night. I am blown away by the night vision quality and can't believe how crisp and clear the video is. I designed and 3D printed a custom mount for the camera to put it on a stand that we have for our other baby camera for traveling. This makes it easy to set the camera in any room and also to travel with. The only negative I have found is that the app must be open to keep the audio feed streaming on my iPhone. It would be nice if the app would be enabled to allow background audio so that you could use it as a baby monitor for audio all the time and video when you need to see what is going on.

Overall, this is a great camera and I would recommend it as a baby cam for use at home and when traveling. If you are traveling you will need a travel router so that you can be on your own secure network. I would highly recommend this camera if you need a low cost way to monitor your baby with a camera or monitor a room in your house

2. Needs to fit my Cannon 70d with 24-105 and 70-200.
3. Needs space for my polarizing and variable ND filters.
4. Need to hold my tripod
5. Needs space for extra batteries and cleaning stuff.
6. Needs to be absolute smallest bag able to do the above while protecting the gear.

This bag does it. Love it. Full disclosure, I use both the camera section and the top for cameras, and because the top is not padded I bought a removal padded insert which took the pack from great to perfect. title: Superb mobile DAC with MQA support
text:
Wonderful sound, great design, superb technology. At the price, this is an amazing value. Best of all is the MQA support, which provides the best reproduced sound I’ve ever heard. My main system DAC is a PS Audio DirectStream, which I chose partly because of its available MQA support. I willingly paid $6000 for the PS Audio. It’s unreal that I got something that sounds and works like its little cousin for only a few hundred.

I use my xDSD attached to my iPhone via Apple’s camera connection kit, which is a simple short cable, and using the iFi-provided Velcro pads. I don’t bother with the Bluetooth capability, although I imagine others will find it convenient.

Some people complain about the shiny finish collecting fingerprints. I haven’t had that issue. Maybe I’m less finicky than others about such things. Maybe I don’t leave fingerprints, and I should consider a life of crime.... 😊

BTW, I recommend you try MQA (via Tidal and Roon, for example) in conjunction with this baby. You will be amazed. There’s some controversy in the audiophile community about MQA. I think this is mostly because people don’t understand it. Simply, it addresses the fact that humans evolved to be really good at hearing separate sounds that are very close in time to each other, closer than the time intervals in CD-level or even hi-res music. Regular digital music “blurs” these tiny time differences. MQA is a brilliant mathematical approach that recovers those timing details in the original recording master, and gets them delivered faithfully to your system so that properly-equipped devices like the xDSD can send them to your ears. I’m an MIT graduate. I’ve read the technical papers describing the technology. It’s genius stuff. It works. You will hear the difference.

Anyway, I really recommend this little giant. Get it!

title: The best hub for my MBP
text:
I have about 4 of these types of hubs that will add extra ports to a MBP and this is my favorite by far. The others use one cable and unless I am at a desk, it is dangling off of my MBP. This is not ideal for using my laptop on the couch, for example.

The Hyperdrive does use both ports on the side of my laptop, but I can give up those ports because you get both of them back in the Hyperdrive. My only small complaint is that it is hard to tell when my SD card is actually in the port properly. I have to see if it shows up in my computer folder and then mess around with it until it shows up. This is not uncommon for these type of devices. I only have one device out of the several I own that you can actual tell with the card snaps in place. All the rest of them have this same issue. I also had that issue with my older 2011 MBP, so I only knocked one star off my review for the problem (would have just been a half star if it was possible).

This also feels very sturdy in build quality. I typically just toss it into my bag with a bunch of other stuff and I haven't had any issues. The ports that are added are HDMI, 40Gb/s USB-C, 5Gb/s USB-C, SD, microSD, 2 x USB 3.1. The HDMI can handle 5k or two 4k monitors.

Outside of the one issue of seating the SD card, I am a huge fan of this for when I am on the go. Once it is attached, it feels like part of the computer. The fact that it is so capable (one of the USB-C ports is Thunderbolt 3) is a huge bonus. I recommend it over similar devices that connect with a cable unless you know you will be sitting at a table.

title: 5⭐, don't let bad reviews dissuade you.
text:
First and foremost, 16+ year Telecommunications professional. Home Automation, Fire & Sec, AV, the works. Let me say you cannot beat this projector for $200. Most within this price range only output video at 720p or 480p.

Many of the complaints I read where invalid because you can't expect a projector to do everything at this price point. If you're going to put a one-star review because it doesn't have smartcast/wi-fi built in as part of it maybe you should have read the description first. Yes it's not the best for gaming, works great with my 360, works good with my Xbox one, there is some motion blur on each but not enough to take away from your experience, but just for gaming, movies look fine.

This is a 1080p projector, nothing more, no smart features, no built-in Wi-Fi, none of the bells and whistles that most people expect BUT rarely if ever use. All that being said, $200 for an HD projector that you can pretty much run at 40-120" in is a steal any day of the week. You couldn't find a TV to match this size even as cheap as they are now.

Now if you're just wanting to have a quick projector to set up for backyard movie watching, movies on the ceiling for the kiddos sleepover, or maybe broadcasting the fight or game onto your garage wall then this is perfect for you, add a lil soundbar and you have yourself a portable, or stationary theater for less than $300 It can even run as an actual theater projector but you can't expect it to run 4K movies because it's not a 4K projector, and you can't expect it to have the refresh rate of higher-end projectors.

I'm going to use this one 4 garage and outdoor movie viewing, but I'm actually planning on buying a second one to mount above my bed to broadcast the picture to my ceiling so I can watch TV in bed because why not???

FYI, this is better than my old Optoma HD20 that was $1000 when I first got it

title: Accurate, but a really annoying company.
text:
TL;DR:
Effective basic recognition with stupid disabling of key features, making it useful but perpetually annoying. Decent product, bad company.

I am writing this review using Dragon, so you can see that it basically works. However, it still the same nuisance company, and they keep disabling key features, that would make it far more useful, and moreover comfortable, to use. I've never had to use tech support, so I'm not giving them a rating for that.

However, they do not give you access to Vocabulary Editor, so you have to do new words one at a time. It is tedious adding things one at a time and tedious deleting them one at a time, but that is what you are forced to do. Worse, perhaps (or at least more obviously stupid and obstructive) is that you can't delete most of the words, especially the very useless proper nouns that pop up. For example, it gave me "Karch" for "couch", an unbelievable mistake, but you can't force it to not recognise "Karch", however useless that word may be to you. Another downer is the options it gives you when you say "Correct that". It almost never has any alternatives. Further, when it makes a mistake, it makes it over and over, without offering to bump your word up in the priority. For example, if you want it to say "couch" and you correct it several times, it will not prioritise that word for several turns. Overall, very limited configurability, and the sales of this product are only aided by the total lack of intelligent competition.

In summary: very effective basic recognition, but the home edition used to give you access to the Vocabulary Editor, and they have now disabled it, which means that every time you buy this product, you have to check carefully for every little feature, in case they have removed something crucial. So it's a good product, with an extremely annoying company behind it.

title: Good cable, not very flexible
text:
I bought this cable as an increasing number of my devices are using USB type C connectors. This does not mean they support 3.1, 3.1 Gen2, etc but rather that manufacturers are standardizing on a new connector to replace the microUSB connector. The issue is that the included cables have a range of capabilities. For example, a pair of headphones of mine has a USB type C connector for a USB 2.0 connection. The bundled cable is a USB 2.0 A-C cable. This started to get out of hand and rather than labeling each cable with the capabilities, or lack their of... I decided to just replace all my cables with USB type C connectors with the latest 3.1 Gen2 cables. As the USB spec is generally backwards-compatible, this both future-proofs and simplifies.

I've tried Amazon Basics cables in the past, with generally positive results and the price was significantly better than competitor 3.1 Gen2 cables... so I bought one to test. This cable is exactly as it claims... a USB 3.1 Gen2 A to C cable. As 3.1 Gen2 is relatively new, I can't fully test it... but every test I've been able to administer, the cable has performed as expected. The one thing I was not expecting was how thick/stiff the cable is. I'm sure this is just a early adopter problem and later cables will be more flexible, but for now... the cable is stiff enough that it is difficult to coil/travel with. Be aware if you are looking to store it in a small space.

Over all, I'm satisfied as the stiffness was not an issue for me.

Update (10 APR 20220: I've checked a few other brands of 3.1 Gen2 A to C cables and they are all pretty inflexible. This is likely due to thicker shielding needed to support a full 10Gbps. Since this seems to be common among all 3.1 Gen2 cables, I'm bumping this from 4 to 5 stars. ALSO, I have now had a chance to test this on a setup where both devices supported Gen2. I'm pleased to verify connectivity of nearly 10Gpbs and have since bought a few more of these.

text: I purchased this backpack in October 2019. It is now August 2020. Within the time period since my purchase, they decided to make their customers pay for warranty shipments both to and from their facility. Shipping the item to them costs roughly $20. The manufacture charges $9.99 if they proceed with replacing your product under warranty. That’s roughly 50% of the cost of the backpack! My backpack lasted less than a year and I’m expected to pay 50% of the cost of the backpack in order to receive warranty service. To me, this is an example of a manufacture not backing their product. They expect it to fail, so they’ve put a system in place to re-write their warranty terms at any time and pass replacement costs onto their customers. Rather than pay the 50% to receive an inferior product and then chance dealing with this again in less than a year, I will be looking for a different backpack from a different manufacture. title: Touchscreen doesn't work; Timex app is clumsy; data is encrypted to only the Timex app
text:
29 May 2020
Highs: heartrate accuracy, stepcount accuracy
Neutral: an adequate selection of watch faces, but few include heartbeat info, which is what I bought it for
Lows:
- screen is difficult to read even when the light is on;
- the amount of time the light stays on is way too short and not customizable-not enough time to read the data displayed;
- the watch data is encrypted, so it won't work with the workout software I like and use--the software provided is on the low side of mediocre (it's supposed to connect to Google Fit, which is a little better, but I can't see where the GPS data is pushed in real time.)
- last and worst, the touch screen doesn't work--it won't swipe to other screens or let you select from options displayed; this last point is what reduced it from a three to a two

I had used the Timex Ironman with the chest strap for years. When exercising over 55, monitoring and controlling heart rate during exercise is important. The watch gave me direct feedback on when my heartrate was under or over my goal, and I loved it. When I saw this new watch with the HRM built in, I was looking forward to using a familiar tool. Unfortunately, it hasn't worked out as planned.

First, it requires the Timex app to even configure the watch for use. If you have any problems with the app or connecting the watch, you're done. I didn't have a lot of problems, although I had to fumble around a bit because the instructions are not crystal clear. But I managed to get it up and working okay. I received it in time to get it set up before my afternoon workout. To my surprise, when I tried to connect my fitness app to the HRM, it didn't show up. It doesn't show up for Google fit, either. It seems that the watch connection is encrypted so that ONLY the Timex app can read the data. And getting their app to interface and pass data to any other software is impossible. You're stuck with Timex. And if you don't like their fitness app--which I don't--you're good and stuck.

Second: workouts and goals are highly personal and come in a wide variety; no matter which feature you look at, the watch and app are limited and uncustomizable, short of complaining to Timex and then hoping that they'll fix your problem in the next software release.

Third: all of the features really depend on the watch face touch screen. This is a critical feature and should be stringently quality controlled. With the touch screen dead, it has little to offer in the way of utility.

The thing that has worked well--and the only thing that prompted a two star vice a one star rating--is the built in heart rate monitor. It's very accurate. And the watch is comfortable to wear. I can at least keep track of my rate, even if it doesn't help keep me in my exercise range like I wanted. I like the different watch faces offered, I just wish they all offered heart rate as one of the options for display.

I'll update this once I find out if Timex will fix the watch touchscreen.

title: My greatest buy this year
text:
I am a professional photographer and although I have not many years of experience, I can say that I have worked with some brands of lights. This flash has been so great and I am so happy to have it. It does have some problems, but lets start with the good things:

1. The portability is so good, its not so heavy (even with the battery) and it has a beautiful case
2. It has two flash heads that can easily give you different light
3. The battery is so good, it last forever (have not been able to tell you how many shots at full power though)
4. Great modifiers that are sold separately
5. If you have other Godox products with wifi capabilities, you have a beautiful ecosystem
6. Great price for the product that it is
7. Digital display is easy to read and it has a back light that can be turn on or off

This product does have its problems, and I will try to put some of them here:

1. The Godox support and troubleshooting is not good, even the user manual is incomplete. I had a problem where I bought a X1C-T Wireless Remote Flash Transmitter (same brand) and the flash didn't sync with the transmitter. The problem was a configuration (very hidden) that it was not specified in the manual. Before I could make it work, I sent them an email asking what could be the problem and it has not been answered. Also, even though I tried to find out about my problem in the internet (youtube, google, etc), I could not find anything about it. I was lucky to fix it.

2. It does not work with Youngnuo RF-603 triggers. I assumed that it was usable with any trigger because it does have a miniplug slave connector, but I was wrong. At the moment I connected the plug to the flash, the triggers stopped working. You do need to have a Godox trigger (or at least, it seems that way, I have not tried other brands)

3. Even though I really don't mind, the product is plastic and it does seem a little fragile, if that is a problem for you (specially the included bracket), then maybe consider other brands, but it will be expensive.

4. Additional configuration is a little hidden, and like I said in the first point, the manual is not complete, so you will not find all the options that the flash has.

5. Although this problem is easily fixable, the flash has a turn off timer, and if the flash shuts down, it won't start with the trigger, you will have to turn off and on the flash switch.

So, it's a functional web-cam that works, I guess, but not a 5-star in my book unless you're focused only on price. I kind of wonder if reviews are even useful anymore since all of these products are just flooded with 5-stars.

title: Worked far better than expected
text: First of all, I have owned and operated a computer business for over 20 years, so I have seen the good and the bad, and, probably just like the rest of you, I read the reviews of items before I buy them. For me as a business owner, I have to be careful what we buy for and sell to our customers, and this drive was just such item we ordered for a customer that needed a new hard drive as theirs had crashed. I ordered it one day and it arrived the following day. Packaging was nothing special and was what was to be expected. Going from a traditional, mechanical drive to an SSD was already a given that it was going to be an improvement, but what we did not expect was just how much of an improvement it would have been for this system. Keep in mind, the system itself was nothing special, decent processor and 8GB of memory. We installed this drive fairly quickly, used a flash drive to install Windows 10 on the system and the installation was rather quick, which caused us a little hesitation at first thinking that something went wrong since most times installation takes considerably longer, but this was done in roughly 10 minutes, if not less? We let things run as they should and the installation was perfect, however, what truly impressed us was the boot time of the system from cold start to full on Windows ready, which was roughly 10 seconds! We thought that might be a fluke, so we shut it down and restarted it from cold start, and the results were the same. Now, as a comparison, we used a similar sized traditional hard drive and performed the same installation on the same computer so that there was no room for error or saying that system A has this processor and system B had this much more memory. Installation took roughly 24 minutes on the traditional drive and boot time was about a minute and a half before you could do anything without the little circle basically telling you to wait. Let me say this, I could care less what the reviews others may provide here are, perhaps they got a bad drive, which happens, or something else happened, I do not know, but, when we see install times cut down to less than half the time and a 10 second boot time, that is impressive, period. Will this drive be perfect for EVERY installation and provide the same results EVERY time? Of course not, conditions vary, experience and skill level of the installer will vary from person to person, and if there is one thing that we have come to realize over the years in this business is that people are far more willing to blame a device than their own user error because that is far easier to explain. If we are at fault and did something that would cause an issue, we own up to it, and yes, we know that devices can fail during installation or you get a bad batch or device, it happens. But, for some people, before blaming the device for a failure, consider looking at the conditions before blaming the device, as there might be a good chance that the failure was due to user error before device error. Would we recommend this drive to others? Absolutely. Will we continue to use and install these drives in other systems? Absolutely. Are these the "magic sauce" that is going to put your system over the top and make everything perfect? No, but these drives will do the job and make you happy you bought them!

Original review:
My feeling on this speaker is....eh.
It’s small and the sound is great. Those are the good things.
The not-so-good things:
1. You can only control the volume by walking over to the speaker & pressing the up or down buttons. You can not buy a remote for it; I tried. You can not control volume through the Bose app. You literally have to press the buttons. And they’re squishy buttons that aren’t very sensitive. So, when you tell Alexa to play some Amos Lee early in the morning while you get ready for work & it comes blaring out because your husband was listening to something the day before at top volume, and you can’t get the squishy volume down button to respond quickly, it’s not pleasant.
2. The battery dies quickly when not in use even when the power is off. I’m considering leaving it on the charger all the time but that’s disappointing to have to do.
3. There’s no way to know the volume setting without playing a song. There’s no range of 0 to 10 on a readout. So if you were blasting it yesterday, it’s going to come blasting out today. But you won’t know to expect it because there’s no readout.

There’s probably no better sounding portable/rechargeable speaker, but it has its drawbacks.

title: DON'T BUY! Doesn't work. Product was changed. Extremely low microphone volume.
text:
I recently bought a Sennheiser Game One gaming headset (https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B00KK8ZLEC/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o01_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) and bought the Sabrent USB Adaptor since it was a suggested buy with the headset. It had many great reviews. It didn't work right. I have a Mac, and also have Windows 10 on Bootcamp where I play some Windows only games such as Overwatch and Destiny 2. Using the Sabrent USB device with the headset, there was decent sound, but mic input was extremely low on both macOS and Windows 10. I googled all kinds of fixes and even downloaded a volume booster that just made my voice sound like crap. I reread the reviews more carefully and found one critical review, that had an explanation of why these USB adaptors don't work anymore. He explained that Sabrent lowered the voltage on their product and obviously didn't tell anyone, or offer the difference in the description. Now if you had a dynamic mic headset it might work since it needs no power.

Anyway, I bought the Sennheiser PCV 05 Combo Audio Adapter from Amazon (https://smile.amazon.com/gp/product/B00IM36VU0/ref=ppx_yo_dt_b_asin_title_o00_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1) and when plugged in on macOS there was a HUGE world of difference and sounded fantastic. Everything worked including the microphone. When I rebooted into Windows 10, headset sounded awesome, but Windows 10 would not recognize the microphone and had generic recognition of the headset altogether. I had to use Mac computer built-in mic to talk to people. I called up Sennheiser directly. They explained that the wiring on Mac and PC's are different, and even though the Windows 10 is on a Mac, it still sees devices differently than Mac. They sent me out their brand USB adaptor for free since I already bought their headset and another adaptor of their brand.

title: You might not need this, but it is cool
text:
If you have a LAN server that's not quite busy enough (Windows or Linux), then you can download and install Omada's free Cloud Controller software and you won't need this device. Or if you have hardly any Omada access points and you don't mind manually configuring each one, then you won't need this device. I'm in the second camp (only 2 Omada AC1350 APs), but I decided to go ahead and spend the $$ on this anyway. This summer I may get an AC1200 access point for the backyard and it will fit right into my network and be controlled by this device. This hardware Cloud Controller can handle up to 50 devices.

This device is cool and I like it. You connect to it with a web browser and can check status any time or reconfigure your APs. Collectively all APs act as a single unit. And Omada APs don't contain a router, so that's 1 less function to pay for and then turn off. I have plenty of routers and firewalls now. All my Omada gear is hardwired through gigabit Ethernet to my LAN.

During setup I turned on each device and watched status on my DHCP server (I'm using pfSense on a dedicated box). My DHCP software allows me to select a device and configure it with a static IP address tied to the device's MAC address. Thus my access points and Cloud Controller all have static addresses and it was easy to do. This Cloud Controller does everything else and makes it easy. I like easy.

The photo is looking up at my basement ceiling. The joists are 2x8s on 12-inch centers (10.5 inches free space between). The biggish blue box is a POE switch (the only thing plugged into AC power). The little black box on the end of the yellow Ethernet cable is the Omada Cloud Controller (POE powered). It's only 100Mbps, but it doesn't pass any LAN traffic, so slow is okay. The two white cables go to the Omada AC1350 APs (POE powered). The gray cable goes to a patch panel that goes back to my LAN switch.

title: Killer stereo mode, surprising bass approximation, excellent party speaker
text: I'm usually not a fan of Bose's EQ strategies to make their products sound good, but for what this tiny speaker sets out to accomplish, it's hit the sweet spot for exactly what I want. Two things, stereo and small size, are particular fetishes of mine, both of which have been frustratingly difficult to satisfy on my search for decent portable bluetooth speakers. I've tried several that have relatively satisfying bass, including those by B&O and JBL. But I was recently at a birthday party barbeque, and when someone commented on the music, I was surprised when I located one of these as the sound source. There were 40-50 people attending the party, making a lot of noise, and this one tiny thing was not only cutting through, but providing a pleasant approximation of a full range of frequencies. I was blown away, and it stuck in my brain. A few weeks later, I read that this model also featured a well-implemented stereo mode, and I was sold. I bought one to test, and after a week, I bought another. Stereo has been severely overlooked in Bluetooth speakers. Many brands offer it, but in practice, it's cumbersome to activate. Not only does this model have a easy way to turn on the stereo mode without using the app, but it works well, which is more than I can say for the feature on other speakers I've tried. Adding to that, 2 of these take up as much or less space in my bag than one of those other speakers. Don't get me wrong- the sound isn't as full as larger speakers, but the balance of frequencies (it's high mid heavy balance, with a freaky approximation of frequencies in the 70-100hz range) is quite satisfying- dare I say 'musical'- and the additional stereo option provides a engulfing space that is just not available from other speakers, and adds to the illusion of size. Distortion is kept in check at just below top top volume, and battery life is great: I get 3+ hours at that sweet spot of 2 notches below loudest setting. In my opinion these are the best speakers for listening in remote places or for an effective and enjoyable portable party.

title: A Pretty Good Budget Laptop
text:
I ordered this laptop to replace an eight year old HP Pavilion laptop running Windows 7. My old laptop had a broken hinge which would be such a hassle to replace right now that I decided to just get a new budget laptop that I could use right away. My price range was $500 or under; and I wanted something light, with decent processing power. This laptop fits the bill as far as size (14 inch screen, thin form factor), weight (about 3 pounds), and value for price (about $460.00 including tax and shipping). I chose to upgrade the standard configuration by doubling the SSD size and doubling the RAM.

The seller shipped the laptop fairly quickly; it was delivered in less than two weeks (custom builds like this take longer than standard, ready-to-ship configurations). The laptop arrived in perfect condition; very well packed in the original HP box, with the original plastic wrap and removable screen shield. The power cord was also in the original packaging. Over all it looked brand new, despite the seller breaking the seal for the upgrade. (They are very upfront about this.) It was easy to set up, and I was up and running fairly quickly.

I removed on star because I dislike the Windows 10 Operating System, so this is not a reflection on the seller in any way. They were great, and responded to a question I had after purchase within 24 hours. Ultimately, this is a pretty good budget laptop for someone looking at Windows 10 machines in this category. It runs fine, looks great (silver case with HP logo), is light enough to be highly portable, and fills the basic needs of web surfing word processing, and storage.

title: DO YOUR UPDATE!
text:
I always read reviews before buying electronics, so after reading reviews on this headset I was fairly confident that I was either going to love this headset or hate it. Reviews said the mic monitoring was way too sensitive and that it made the item unusable.

The good: Sound is clear, adjustable, and surround, and the headset is comfortable. You adjust it in your Xbox settings and tell it you have surround sound on and everything changes. It's amazing. The sound is so clear and the volume is great! One problem I had with other sets is that the sound was too low. This one hasn't got that problem at all. It has volume adjustments for both game and party chat right on the side of the headset. Excellent because honestly, I don't like having to go into the xbox sound settings to adjust that. The ear pieces are very comfortable and lightweight. I wear glasses and most headsets push my glasses in on my head and it's kinda uncomfortable. This headset doesn't push on my glasses at all and is super comfortable.

The bad: The only thing bad I can think of to say about this headset is that the pad on the top of the headband is an odd kinda foam feeling pad. I think after a while it'll wear down. I like the cloth strap better on the Arctis, but hey, can we really have everything?

The important: When you get your headset, before you even sync it, plug it into a computer. Download the update program from Turtle Beach, and do your firmware update! If you do this, you won't have any problems with the mic monitoring that everybody is complaining about. DO YOUR UPDATE! It even comes with a paper inside telling you to update your firmware! If you fail to do so, your issues are not a problem with the headset...they're with your head.
