title: Tough to beat for the money!
text:
I have a Yamaha 3000W generator...that is worth EVERY PENNY I paid for it....(and there were a lot of pennies involved in buying one of them.....) But this little Wen is AMAZING!!! I bought it as the generator on my boat was acting up, and for the portability and the price, I thought I would give it a try! And OH BOY was I impressed!
I do think this is a "knock off" (I say that 1/2 joking as in MANY situations, the plans/molds for these generators are TRADED from the top level makers to a "budget" makers for parts for their "brand name" units...) of the Yamaha 2000W generator! They look very similar, and I can promise you the internals of the Yamaha (and similar Honda) are BETTER quality....but for 2000W....I am not going to be running too much heavy duty items off of it....so I won't be taxing the components as much....
I have had this thing for four years....I have brought it on MANY a boat trips and it sits on my swim platform whirring away....producing enough power to run whatever I need on the boat....MUCH quieter than the onboard unit I have, at a fraction of the fuel used! I even run it in the spring when I am working on buffing the hull of the boat as it even works well with my "yellow branded" buffer and lower RMP's, WHILE running the battery charger for the boats batteries!
The ONLY time it let me down....was when we had -25 below weather here in MN....and it would not start....but that could be because I run 15W-40 synthetic in it and I think it was just too darn cold!! (FYI.....my Yamaha STARTED in this weather!!!! ) I have not tested the sine waves to see how "accurate" and "clean" the power is....so I not sure there....but I can tell you I have run nice quality 200W Powered speakers off of it....TV's...and it seems to be FINE!!!
I have heard a saying..."you know why they named it 'Wen'? You will need to throw it away WEN it breaks...." But mine has been going strong for 4+ years with NO issues.....And at this point....I expect another 4 years out of it!!!! (Or more!!!)

I bought this mainly to use as a clock radio to wake me up in the morning. The sound is great, as is the radio reception. However, there are a couple of serious flaws that keep me from giving it a higher rating.

title: Fire Hazard
text:
I waited to write this review, to do some testing as to if this would last. The preface, we don't use our Wii a ton. Once a week for an hour is about the most this gets used: I am by no means a power user.

THIS UNIT FAILED after light use. I expect all units sold from this vendor to have the same failure mode at some point in their lifetime, as the design of the power supply is flawed and lacks important safety features.

I'm an electrical engineer by trade, and so naturally when this unit failed, I opened it up to look. What I saw was that the manufacturer cut corners to deliver a product that could start a fire. It packed proper fuses, and components are undersized for their tasks. For instance, instead of using one properly size power resistor, the designer used three smaller and cheaper resistors. In my case, the slight imbalance inherent in all components caused one unit to fail. This failure pushed too much power through the other two components, and caused a cascade failure.

Pictures attached show not only the poorly designed power supply, but the poor quality workmanship that went into assembly of this device.

If you want to risk starting a fire, then this product is a good choice. Otherwise spend the extra dollar and buy a real Nintendo power supply. If the supply your recieve feels light, or rattles, you should return it. A properly designed power supply will be heavy, like the OEM one was or like a laptop power supply.

Don't buy this.

title: does not work as balancer
text:
Received the board rather quickly. Have not used it yet, decided to look on the balancing electrical circuit. It is very "on the budget" design. Precision reference chip (TL431) is used in place of a zener diode. If you put the values of resistors (R1 = 68k; R2 = 101k (two resistors in series, 100k and 1k)) into the formula (see the screen shot from TL431 datasheet), you will get Vka = 4.31V (keep in mind, Iref for TL431 is in the range of 2uA). It means that THIS balancer starts to by-pass the charging current (through ballast resister R3) when voltage on the battery reaches 4.31V. Before that, all the current goes through the battery (no balancing).
OK, lets calculate the balancing current (via R3, which is 51 Ohm). Let's say, we overcharged the battery by 100mV (in this case, 4.41V), balancing current in this schematic will be 100mV / 51ohm = 2mA. Wow! Whooping 2mA ! And this is for the BMS which has rating for 20A. It will take days (or probably weeks) before batteries will be balanced.
That is, this board will probably work as a battery protector, but as a balancer it will certainly fail.
Look elsewhere if you need a working balancer.

title: Great!
text:
I did a lot of research before I bought this. (I was kind of obsessed about it actually.) The Node2i gets great reviews in all of the on-line audio magazines that I read. I was hesitant to buy it though because some Amazon reviews indicate problems with frequent wi-fi drop-outs and buggy software.

I finally made the puchase 3 weeks ago, and I’m very happy. I have the Node2i connected by wi-fi to my router about 25 feet away. Luckily, no problems with drop-outs, even with hi res streaming!

Setting up the Node2i with the BluOS app took all of 10 minutes. I use an iPad with the BluOS app to control the Node2i, and it works well, although there is a bit of a learning curve. The integration with Tidal is good enough. You can navigate through your playlists, albums and artists. Editing your Tidal playlists in BluOS isn’t really possible though – you can create Tidal playlists, but you have to use the Tidal app to delete a track. Integration with Amazon Music HD is disappointing - you can’t navigate from from playlists to albums to artists or manage playlists. The ability to play internet radio via TuneIn is great.

Streaming via Apple Airplay from a Macbook, iPad or iPhone works well, but I don’t use it much. (Airplay supports CD-quality streams, but not high res streams such as Tidal's MQA or Amazon’s Ultra-HD, although in truth I’m not sure I can tell the difference.)

The Node2i handles simple Alexa commands well – eg. turn it up, turn it down, skip this song. I also often use Alexa to switch between TuneIn internet radio streams that I have as pre-sets in BluOS. I haven’t tried to get Alexa to play specific artists, playlists or tracks. (I’m not sure it would work.)

The best thing about the Node2i is that the sound lives up to the glowing reviews: it’s detailed and warm. Tidal and Amazon Music HD sound fantastic. I’m also impressed by how good some of the better internet radio streams sound.

If I have trouble with the Node2i, I’ll update this review, but for now it’s 5 stars.

title: Works fine on Windows/RPi, doesn't support simultaneous Glonass and GPS
text:
Summary: it works on Windows 10 and raspberry Pi, and is reasonably sensitive. It will take some time and technical ability to get it going as there is no included documentation. Glosnass can not be used simultaneously with GPS/WAAS so it's of limited use for most. Build quality is okay, don’t abuse it and you will be fine.
-----------
This review is long and aimed at technical users. The VK172 does not include any instructions, software, drivers, etc. It utilizes the u-blox 7020 chip and outputs a stream of standard NMEA-0183 messages readable by most GPS software. When utilizing u-blox u-center software, special configuration messages (ubx) can be sent/received (also possible without the software, just not as easy).

For initial testing I used Windows 10. After plugging it in, it was assigned a serial comm port without needing to install any drivers. Others have reported needing to install Windows drivers so it depends on what drivers you already have installed.

I used device manager to find the correct comm port number, then used PuTTY terminal software to connect to it. It immediately showed the NMEA sentences streaming by, it didn't matter what the baud rate was set to, although 4800 is the NMEA standard. I next downloaded the UBLOX "u-center for windows" software to verify functionality. Once connected, I saw satellites start to appear and within a couple of minutes I had a position lock and the blue led started to regularly flash. This was indoors away from windows. After a while it picked up a WAAS signal and was receiving 8 to 12 GPS satellites.

After 20 minutes or so I felt the device, it was barely warm, a good sign. I then tested with Google Earth in realtime GPS mode and it worked just fine.

The following morning I tried it again at the same location, it took nearly 5 minutes to get a 3D fix. Part of this may be day vs night, as night time RF signals get less interference or perhaps it didn’t retain the ephemeris data. The PDOP at night was around 2, during the day it was over 3-4 at the same location. When moving the receiver close to a window, eventually two WAAS satellites were picked up and several more satellites. The daytime PDOP near the window eventually improved to 1.3-1.8. A full cold start (initiated through u-center) in this location took 5 minutes and 20 seconds to get an initial fix. A hot start took less than 3 seconds. A warm start took 31 seconds.

Although it’s advertised as working with Glonass satellites, it’s not too useful in reality. When looking at the configuration through the u-center software, it appears Glonass isn’t enabled. The u-blox 7 documentation states that either GPS/SBAS/QZSS or Glosnass can be enabled, but not both. After unchecking “enable” for all other systems, I could enable Glonass and it did work. GPS is generally better than Glosnass, so the only advantage would be if it receives both simultaneously. Since it doesn’t, there is little point in bothering with Glosnass.

After playing with Windows, I did a quick test on a raspberry Pi 3. No driver was needed and a serial port was created as /dev/ttyACM0 which I connected to using putty and I saw the expected NMEA strings streaming by. Gpsd also seemed to work after a bit of effort.

I next took a look inside. The notable components are the ublox G7020-KT GPS chip, a ft25h04s 4Mbit serial flash, a small battery like component, and the patch antenna (note- the antenna is on the side with the LED so best reception occurs with that side up). The battery (or supercapacitor) is approximately 4.8mm x 1.5 mm, and measured just over 1 volt. The markings are obscured, but I think it's an XH414 which is rechargeable and it's likely only used to retain the ephemeris data for a hot/warm start. The soldering was good, except for the USB connector’s mechanical contact points which had not flowed properly (often an issue due to the connector acting as a heat sink), the signal pins were fine. I touched up the weak solder joints, but not really necessary.

Overall a decent unit as long you don’t need Glonass and GPS simultaneously.

title: After months of use, I regret this purchase.
text:
We’ve been using Ring for a few months now and quite honestly, it doesn’t live up to the hype. Setup was ok (except issues with no guide for stucco installation) but customer service reached out when I posted issues at first and was great at getting back to me with troubleshooting.

Problem is primarily with the App and the ongoing “cloud subscription”.

The App:

1. Notification spam/click bait is constant for “crime report”, “your...report!” Basically any urgent tagline to try and get you to open the App. There’s NO WAY to turn these spam notifications’ off unless you don’t want any notifications at all for anybody actually at your door. title: Stellar audio but extremely bad microphone
text:
I’ll be upfront and honest, I’m a huge fan of RHA. Whenever a friend, family, or coworker asks for earbud recommendations you best believe RHA is at the top of the list. I’ve been using the RHA T10 for the past 5 years and the right side has finally decided to go out. This is in no part RHA’s fault as I was very rough with them, tangling and folding wires to stay them in my backpack, accidentally getting the cable caught in my longboard as I skated to work and school yet they still kept chugging along. Now that they’re broke I was set on replacing them and the T20 wireless was the obvious choice. Wired and wireless options? Meaning I can retire my T10 and my broken Beats X? This is too good to be true! Well it was and it wasn’t. In terms of audio quality it was great, exactly what I loved about my T10, I recommend checking out the T10/T20 wired reviews and you’ll get an idea of what I’m talking about if you’re unfamiliar. Battery life via Bluetooth was truly amazing ~11 hours and I never felt the need to crank the volume because the seal was so great in my ear canal that not much noise leaked in or out. Build quality was great as well, the cable isn’t as thick as the t10 and the metal connectors felt lighter but it’s of higher quality compared to the 95% of the remaining market. Now why did I give it three stars then? The microphone on the Bluetooth cord (because the standard 3.5mm cable doesn’t have a mic in line) was absolute garbage. It would pick up so much ambient noise, cable noise was a serious problem as well. It made receiving calls a nightmare and earsplitting for the person on the end of the line. If you even think of moving it will pick up some noise and relay it. Maybe I received a defective device? I hope so because I really want to recommend this device. I’ve used the Apple AirPod, AirPod Pro, Jaybirds, and Beats X for use daily as I listen to music on my motorcycle and I receive countless calls throughout the day at work. The AirPods/Pro never sit in my ears properly and fell out along with lower audio quality. The Jaybirds could barely fit as well, the beats x were surprisingly good but their battery life wasn’t as good. The RHA was king in terms of audio, battery, fitment (their included ear tips are the stuff of legend), looks (in my opinion they’re pretty sleek, charging (type-c tyvm RHA for killing the aging micro usb connectors I loathe to see). However the mic is abysmal and the wired option doesn’t have a mic, and in my case I required a mic to daily use. Disappointed that this product didn’t work, or may have been defective, but I still love you RHA and will recommend some other products you offer.

I’ll update this as necessary if any changes occur if I ever procure another pair

title: A good quality laptop with some in consistent QC issues.
text:
Bottom line up front: It is a well made and practical update to the previous generation XPS. I found the display in mine to perform well (I've read about QC issues with the OLED though and it is something to look into before buying). The keyboard is crisp. The battery life is average (5-8 hours for me) and the touch pad is annoyance when doing lots of typing.

It is fairly light and thin. The keypad hasn't changed much from the previous version. It is firm, but shallow. Using a mechanical keyboard most of the time means I need to consciously adjust my typing when I switch to my laptop.

The NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 and 16 gigs of onboard memory mean pretty good performance. Where my HP Elitebook struggles running VM Player if I am going anything else, the Dell has no issue.

The Samsung OLED display is very nice. The lighting is even and the colors crisp. The blacks are very dark, though there seems to be some grainess on certain colors such as grays and lighter blacks. The whites can be painful to look at though and I needed to use Night Light to make it bearable over long sessions.

Despite not being 'a gaming laptop' there is no reason that you shouldn't be able to play games on it. The high end CPU and 16 gigs of memory should give a respectable performance. The biggest issue seemed to be the CPU throttling that Dell shipped it with. This has been rectified to a good degree with their release of the 1.2.3 BIOS update. While not a purpose built gaming machine there is no reason you shouldn't be able to enjoy some gaming on your new XPS.

You can't disable palm check on the touch pad, which can make typing a challenge at times. The only work around is to play with the sensitivity settings which is less than ideal. The black interior of the case means it shows every smudge and mark.

The power button on mine tends to stick, so I have to be gentle when I wake it up from sleep or I will end up powering down my system.

The speakers are downward facing and very underpowered. You will definitely want to use headphones.

All in all I am happy with this laptop, it performs well for me the tasks I use it for. It is a fast, thin and light laptop with good performance and high quality components. That said reading about others issues with it as a results of hit or miss QC is concerning for a laptop in this price range. I think it is worth the risk, but the issues are something to be aware of.

title: Challenging, Fun, Great Sound
text:
Is the kit perfect. No. It's 100% challenging 100% fun. For less than $20 great sound, really, really good. A circuit schematic is included which has at least one mistake, C2 1uF cap should be 10uF. The component installation diagram is perfect tho and well marked. Some of the components are less quality than you might hope for, but nothing terrible. The speakers seem very high quality. The plastic where the screws hold the case will not take a lot of torque. The 1/8” connector is flimsy but easy to overcome by careful attention to wire position and a bit of electrical tape.

Construction starts right off requiring the mount of a tiny surface mount IC. I used Scotch Magic tape to hold the chip in place. On the left speaker circuit board the yellow wire hole was too small for the wire pair - fixed with a 3/64” drill bit. The advice of a couple of other reviewers was helpful. Using some longer standoffs the circuit board was mounted backwards exposing the pots to the rear. 1/8” holes were drilled in the plastic so adjustments to the pots could be made. This really helps when you need to balance the speakers volume. 8 #4-40 x 1/2” machine screws and nuts were used to mount the speakers – the furnished screws were a stretch. For mounting plastic panels a bit of tape was folded over so it could be easily removed, then the nut placed on the tape on the tabletop. Placed the panel over the nut then threaded the screws. Sound really is amazing.

title: Great Budge Monitor....
text:
[[VIDEOID:bcbc9b47285721879956d1b52767095d]] Construction
So starting with the physical description of the product it is huge even for 7 inch monitor ,t’s not something that you want to use on top of your camera especially with the small mirrorless cameras but I would rather consider as a monitor that you can use it in a studio or maybe on just the light stand and then you can monitor your display easily while keeping the camera small. As far as the construction it is made out of plastic except the mounting points around and it is not at all heavy in the weight as well, The only weight that you will be caring will be just your couple of batteries on the back but it does get heavy once you put large Sony NPF 970 style of batteries. On the right as well as the left side we have a couple of quarter inch mount and in the middle we have rosette mount with a M6 of screw. On the bottom of again we have a couple of quarrel each mount and in the middle we have one Rosette mount with M6 in of screw. on the top we have a different system then the other monitors so we have four different function buttons first and then we also have two more buttons that is F5 and f6 to control the brightness of the monitor self and on the right side again we have one more function button f7 and then the last one is on and off button. On left side we have one scroll button to go to the menu and then it also has a click so you can select particular function. Buttons are little bit mushy, there is really not a click to it but all the keys and the scroll button makes a really easy to navigate menu system even without using a touch screen.

Looking on the back side of the monitor, on the left side we have DC in as well as DC out port, and it does come with the DC cable as well so you can power this monitor and also use this DC output to power your camera at the same time in the center we have a headphone jack to monitor the audio. On the right side we have HDMI in and HDMI out one USB male port for the firmware updates and to install LUTS in the monitor. And finally on the right bottom, there is a place to connect your j^ key remote.

Batteries are hot swappable.

SCREEN QUALITY
So, before we dive into the technical stuff, let’s first talk about the screen quality in my opinion. The screen is 1920 x 1080 that means HD but it does accept 4k signal and also can output 4k signal if you use HDMI out. By the way if you happen to buy SDI version, there is not cross conversion in between HDMI & SDI so that is something to keep in mind.

Brightness is 450 nits, which is probably half of all today’s top tier smartphones, so you can use this with hood outdoors and it’s definately better than your camera screen but if you have to pull focus then it can still less brighter. Hood is also of a really good quality, its easy to put it on but it does take fair amount of time to take it of, so something to keep in mind. Viewing angles are also really good, colors are almost accurate but I’ll talk about that in just a bit a second. Contrast and black are also deep, it also gives you very nice saturated image if you are susing a proper LUT on top of your footage. As far as sharpness, I did bump a little bit otherwise it does look little bit soft if you were comparing it to 4k but since it's a 7” screen, it’s totally fine with 1080p pixels. Yes, about the colors, so when I received it, if you go under the basic temp under the colortemp, I received it at 6500K which was very off but when I switch it to 9300K it’s accurate, so that’s that.

EXPOSURE FUNCTIONS
Let’s talk about the exposure tools because that is probably one of the biggest reason you want to add monitor on top of your camera. So, this monitor does have a decent amount of exposure tool but it does miss out quite a few. So, it has false color, in fact two different type of falso color scale and the good thing is, it also shows scale on the side,. It also has a zebra and then you can also select your zebra value. And I think, that’s preytty much it as far as the exposure tools, there is histogram but personally I think histogram is really inaccurate representaion of exposure especially if you are going for the contrasty scenes.

What is missing, number one is of cource, Waveform, very important exposure tool, I don’t know if it can be implemented by software update or not but I really wish they would in future. There is also no RGB Parade and the last important tool to check correct hue and that is vecteroscope. Vecteroscope is also one of the tool that I use every signle time to check whether I am getting a correct skin tone or not but it is missing in this monitor.

FOCUS CONTROLS
Focusing is also one of the other feature and reason to use an external monitor and we do have focus peaking on this monitor as well. You can assign a separate function button to it and then you can also set two levels of peakig you want with it. I really wish though it has a focus assist feature that increases contrast to make everything look sharper on the focus point. It really really helpful and much better than focus peaking, you can increase sharpness of the screen but then it applies to the whole screen instead of focused area so that is also one of the feature that I miss.

By the way, the touchscreen is really good, you can always drag your finger and zoom in to check your focus on the screen.

Other then that, the rest of the menu is also really intuitive and with the presence of 7 different function keys, you really don’t have to go inside it and honestly I have kept my touchscreen off most of the times.

Besides all of that, what else I can think of, there are 3 different anamorphic modes, you can also monitor your audio using the audio bars, you can place different and custom aspects of safety markers, unfortunately and I hope I am wrong but there is also no way show gridlines on the screen, which is I think really important for framing your scene, I hope they bring that in the future update.

Lastly the LUT support, so there are some in built luts inside the monitor itself which are helpful, there is an slog2, slog3, vlog and hlg and fotga lut, fotga lut which is kind of faded and log like look itselft but I couldn’t install any LUT by connecting it to the computer, so I will update this as soon as I am able to do install my own LUT in the monitor.

You can also bring the quick menu by swiping it from the side so now you can see all your function button and even change function of each button and you can use this slider to change the brightness of the monitor, and there is battery bar on the side.

And that’s pretty much, hope I didn’t bore you on that one but I did wanted to cover everything before wrapping up. If I missed anything or if you have any question, let me know in the comment section below, link to the product is in the description below as well and if you have made it this far subscribe to see more videos like this and as always thanks for watching.

title: Simply the Best! Punches Above the Weight!
text:
I had a summer code, so I got this directly from manufacturer. I conducted a living room mini shoot out between a bunch of digital coax cables, and DH Labs was clearly the winner both in price and quality punching above its weight. Now before you say digital is digital hence cable would not matter, I would point out that SPDIF protocol was designed in the 80s with limited error reporting and error recovery. It’s a unidirectional one-way transfer protocol working at ultra high speeds prone to timing-errors, reflection jitters, impedance mismatch, and so forth. It neither has packet resend/recovery nor does have HDMI powerful error corrections. To those who claim if the digital cable is bad, there should be either no sound or audible clicks in the sound: true if you lose significant number of bits/packets, but what if you only lose a few here and there? How do you know how your receiving device is programmed to handle lost data? Does it just ignore the bad apples, or it tries to average out and interpolate to recreate or compensate the missing values based on nearby neighbors? We all know how interpolation turned out for OLED TVs and fast motion! I still sigh in despair on a daily basis after having OLED for more than a year. Anyways, there are a lot of factors involved, and SPDIF protocol, unlike TCP/IP, does not have a guaranteed delivery on packets and data integrity. I am a CSci major by the way, so if you like to talk RFCs and design schemes all day, we can!

Back to cables comparison, I tried WireWorld UltraViolet, Audio Quest Cinnamon, Audio Quest Carbon, and DH Labs D-750 all in the same system and listened to same tracks over and over again. It wasn’t even a reference system, just my Apple TV 4K connected via HDMI to Sony OLED, which outputted PCM over HDMI ARC port to a digital coax converter connected to Hegel H190 coax port. My speakers are Focal Electra 1008BE2 with beryllium tweeters. In theory, this normal setup should not have any sonic difference based on different coax cable, but it does! I could clearly hear differences between all of the cables. In a blind test, I probably will be having a hard time picking WW and Cinnamon apart, but Carbon has a distinctive sound that you can pick immediately. So here are my personal observations regarding each cable:

4- WireWord Ultraviolet: very good sounding cable for the price, but once you try better cables, you realize the upper frequencies are a little muffled and the dynamic range is a bit compressed.

3- Audio Quest Cinnamon: best cable for the money, period. Sounds very natural and pleasing, but again, lacks a bit of detail of the higher end cousins. The low end frequencies are very nice and blended too.

2- Audio Quest Carbon: it was very bright and brittle at first, but got significantly better after 15 hours. The RCA connector is pure silver directly hanging over copper wire, so it should eliminitate the impedance mismatch that is common in RCA connectors. The cable is also well made with very nice jacket and finish. Sound quality is very revealing and analytical. It’s the only cable that has that 3D sound effect. High frequencies have a spike, and it goes lower than other cables. However, I feel the sub frequencies more with my body than hearing them. It’s either that the middle sub frequencies are subdued or they’re masked, but whatever the reason, this cable has the most character of them all. I still have mixed feelings whether I like it or not, but it sure is different. I think it’s worth the money if you like the sound, but it’s hard to beat the value of Cinnamon. If you can afford Carbon, go for it.

1- DH Labs D-750 is the only cable that claims it has true 75ohm RCA plugs. In other cables, even if the cable is 75ohm, the RCA plugs and soldering will change their impedance. I really like this cable. It’s the most balanced cable in this group, and neither a single frequency stands out nor do I hear any spikes. The bass is full and high frequencies are all there. It has the fullest sound of all these cables. It doesn’t have that 3D sound effect that Audio Quest Carbon produces, but I’m not convinced if that 3D effect is because you hear the right things or it’s a byproduct of some missing or subdued parts. Carbon is a little harder to listen to than the D-750 because sometimes the 3D effects get too distracting. Retail on DH Labs is about 30% less than the Carbon, and with the frequent direct sales from the manufacturer, you can find D-750 for about 40% to 50% less than AQ Carbon. It’s a steal at these sale prices for what you get sonically and also in physical built. My only complain is that D-750 outer jacket is thick and not as flexible as AQ, so I had to be careful with it on the back of my equipment cabinet. Best sound quality in this range and the winner for me. Just remember that manufacturer suggested break-in time is 60 hours, and Empirical Audio article suggests that 1.5m is the sweet spot to avoid reflection jitters in digital coax.

Final thoughts, it’s weird that digital cables introduce coloration to music. I’m still baffled myself, but it’s there. I listened to many pieces of music and watched a couple of movies, but for a reference, try this song on Apple Music: Serpiente by Fernando Milagros. At about 56 seconds in, there’s a high frequency instrument in the background that comes in at about half a second intervals and sounds like “ding... ding... ding... ding...”. WireWorld masked that effect almost completely. AQ Cinnamon rendered a less detailed version of them, and D750 had all the details but did not project them high and up in the room. AQ Carbon throw those ding sounds so strongly that they almost sounded like a spike or burst. If you’ve a bunch of cables around, you can easily conduct your own tests. As for me and my budget, I’ll keep the D-750. Thanks for reading and YMMV.

*** Possible Future Upgrade:
VH Labs has a solid core pure silver 75ohm coaxial cable with silver RCA plugs that they say has the most accurate impedance of all cables. They claim that they even go through the trouble of throwing a lot of the cable away as a waste to make it a true 75ohm at finished lengths. Depend on RCA plugs you choose, they range from 340-410, and they claim it will compete favorably against reference cables in 2K to 3K price range. I don’t know about reference cables, but it should be interesting to compare VH Labs pure silver cable directly with the cables listed above and also the Audio Quest Coffee to see how accurate they are with their claims.

title: Great laptop, bit heavy
text:
Overall this is a great laptop, though I have only been using it for a couple days. The bezels are a bit large on the top and bottom compared to many others these days, but I cared more about having the number pad, which say the Dell XPS 15 I was also looking at did not offer.

Speakers are good, though a bit hairy. My 6 yr old Acer Aspire ($700 when I bought it) has pretty considerably better speakers (Dolby Digital Home Theater), though they have been the best I have heard on any laptop by a country mile. The speakers on this HP I would consider well above average, but the clipping I hear on anything above 40 or so is annoying to me since I'm used to the Acer's.

The build quality is excellent. The screen is maybe a bit wobbly compared to my old Acer's but I didn't notice it until I pushed it (and I use my laptop on my lap generally) so I can't imagine that would be an issue for anybody unless they are fishing for things to be annoyed about.

It is surprisingly heavy and thinker than I imagined, both more so than my Acer's, but I much prefer a metal body construction (this one is aluminum) for heat dissipation so that will naturally come with the territory. It is not uncomfortably heavy, however, just a this thing feels expensive kind of heavy.

The power block gets I would say ~30 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than my Acer's and bigger (though still a standard size, about 6'' x 3'' x 3/4'' eye balling it}), but the Acer is an ultrabook and is much less powerful, so that isn't very surprising.

The screen is 4k so enough said there.

Keyboard feels great and is backlight, offering 2 brightness settings which is nice.

I must mention that the graphics chips are an intel UHD 630 default (for efficiency) and a GTX 1650 [Max-Q], not a 1650 Mobile which is ~20% more powerful.

Also, this laptop does NOT come with a 64 GB flashdrive as advertised. It does have a nice faux leather carrying sleeve though, which is not shown. It also does come with the pen (battery included). It comes with Windows 10 Home preinstalled and a 10 Pro key on the box which I used to upgrade, but honestly there is not point unless this is going to be a work computer. There is probably a small performance degrade with Pro so I should have just left it with Home instead.

The body is a matte finish and feels comfortable and robust.

Had a question for the seller and the responded very promptly and courteously so no problems there.

Overall, pretty great, don't regret the purchase.

title: Perfect for spring cleaning your Macbook to make it run cool
text:
My Macbook Pro (2012), still running perfectly well, would heat up with fans blaring just a few minutes after I would connect it to a monitor or if a website had videos or animations. Web searches led me to believe that this was because the Nvidia GPU would kick in, heating the laptop and the heat was not dissipating because of dust trapped in the fan and vents.

I ordered this toolset from Amazon. The tools seem to be of good quality and the screwdrivers are magnetic making it easy to work with the tiny screws without losing them. I opened the back of my laptop to find that indeed there was a lot of dust trapped on the fans and the vents were practically clogged. Another web search showed a video on how to clean it using compressed air. Luckily I had a can of compressed air available. A few minutes later all the dust was gone. I have seen an incredible difference in the heat and fan levels since the cleanup.

I would highly recommend spring cleaning your Macbook every few years. All I needed was one screwdriver in this toolset but well worth the investment. If you do decide to clean, then remember this important note. Not all screws on the bottom of the Macbook are the exact same length. In my case 2 of the 10 screws were about half a mm shorter than the others. This is not easily discernible unless you put them side by side and look closely. I assumed all were the same length until I put them back. I then had to trial and error my way into finding the right ones.

title: Amazing Consumer/Enthusiast Camera - Not so much for pros
text:
I purchased this camera mainly to use with Matterport for real estate 3D scanning. For that, it works amazingly well. I also love the cool features such as hyperlapse and bullet time, as I'm a junky for time and space bending tricks. I'm a filmmaking pro and was curious how well it can be used with a film production and brought it on a b-roll shoot.

Unfortunately, from a pro perspective, the image quality is lacking - especially with hyperlapse. This could be a byproduct from the only way to process the images being on the phone app. At the same time, the images straight out of the camera show a bit of aliasing and blurriness. Unfortunately the processed footage just didn't cut well with the rest of my edit so I decided not to use it.

BUT, this thing is amazing for social media and and personal use. I posted some really fun stuff on instagram and facebook. It's a great alternative to using a gopro due to stabilization and more time bendy tricks to play with. When it comes to non-360 output image quality, however, the gopro wins since the sensor pixels aren't spread out to the 360 capture.

title: Didn’t know the quality was going to be THIS BAD...
text: Long time photographer, and I have transitioned from film to digital in 1998. I have used dozens of pro camera bodies from the original 5D, to the 5DSR, to medium format digitals such as the FUJI GFX50/100 these days. I am an outdoors guy, and have owned roughly 10 sets of tripods (mostly by Gitzo / RRS) so I think I got a good frame of reference here. I have used PD straps (good) and bags (good), but lately I bought into their hype of this “steady, light weight, compact” tripod hype piece, so I ordered one a few days ago. Long story short: EXTREMELY disappointed. I have never seen a tripod this flimsy in my life. Even a sub $100 tripod can beat the stability and quality of this $600+ Peak Design tripod. The neck of the PD tripod head is pencil-thin, and the legs are just as thin too!! You can bend the legs with your pinky!! You can literally cause vibration by BLOWING air from your mouth on the thinnest segments of the legs. It is that bad. I requested a return within 24 hours after receiving it. The tripod is not much lighter than the Gitzo traveler series, or many other cheaper brands. The only thing Peak Design did better is the packaging, but we all know packaging is not what takes good photos. Conclusion: this is not a tripod for serious photographers.

title: Sound Quality
text: For most of us, we buy the sound bar because the speakers on the televisions these days are very inferior and or point in a direction that is not optimal for listening pleasure. In my case, I paid $500 for a 32 inch Samsung tv with absolutely wonderful picture quality and I received terrible sound quality for my money. I was forced to purchase a sound bar to make the tv sound at least tolerable. I had a very limited space for the sound bar and need one less than 28 inches for the tv stand. This size requirement limited my choices dramatically. After much research I stumbled on the Bestisan sound bar ( made and/or sold by Megacra ). For $76 I got a 20 inch sound bar. This sound bar far exceeded my sound quality expectations, especially for the size. I feared I might should have purchased one with a sub-woofer , but fear not, this little dynamo has wonderful base and treble adjustments, and with a single little bass bump, it has all the Bass I need. I don't think tv's should be sold with inferior sound, as a tv is a viewing and listening experience , not just a visual experience.....but for now , it is the world we live in. So with that in mind I don't think you should have to pay an arm and a leg for a speaker system to enjoy your television. This sound bar more than meets the needs of most people , unless you have an enormous room you are trying to fill, and honestly, I'm not sure this still wouldn't get the job done. Watched a war movie recently and this sound bar had me ducking for cover. If you have a limited budget or need the sound bar to fit in a tight area, you will be very happy with this item. The only downside..... the remote from the tv does not recognize the sound bar , so you have to use 2 remotes.

title: Extremely portable and comfortable buds with great sound for music and phone calls.
text:
I really love these Soundpeats TrueAir2 earbuds. The sound quality is excellent and has a good bass, something that is missing in most other earbuds I have tried. Phone calls are clear on both ends of the conversation due to the dual mics active noise canceling system and because the shape has the microphones angled pointing toward your mouth. This is also great for Zoom meetings and other online uses.
The case is so small and thin (see attached photo) that you will take them everywhere without an annoying bulge in your pocket. It hold 25 hours of charge, enough to recharge your buds 5 times.
Most other buds have a rubber like disc that fits into the ear canal snugly and can be uncomfortable. These buds are all hard material and they fit into the notch on the bottom of your earlobe and are so comfortable you'll forget they are there. The touch pad controls are very responsive and control volume, next and previous song and pause, answer phone and connect to Google or Alexa for needed info. These buds are so easy to pair with your device. Just take them out of the case and they connect automatically.
I highly recommend the TrueAir2 and know you will get much enjoyment from your music and phone calls.

The leg extensions on the back on are only held on by two tiny rubbery/plastic parts (like a small mushroom that is cut in half) and one of those failed the moment I used it (see photo). No way it can be fixed with glue or any other DYI method. Going to have to send them back and maybe try another set but at this point... I'm really not sure if I can trust it long term. title: It’s great for the price, but keep away from phones
text:
Overall, this preamp sounds great for its price. This is also a DAC and it sounds great when plugged into By USB. You would hear a the difference in quality when plug into the jack of the preamp, computer, vs iPhone XR (Lightning to 3.5 mm jack adapter). Every device has a DAC (digital to analog converter), such as phones, computers, music players, etc. Better DACs, better quality. Change my tube to JAN 5654W by Riverstone to get better quality (comparing both tubes, JAN 5654W gives a more warmer sound signature when compared to stock (still usable in my opinion). Volume nob has a good click.

Pros-
Warm sound

Cons-
Bluetooth (quality drops, it’s still usable If you like slight muddy or muffled bass and treble. Analog still works)

Isolation (I don’t know if all amps are like this but keep it away from phones. It makes a slight static when listening on a headphone, not noticeable when it’s on speaker. Static becomes more audible when on call. Don’t know about other frequencies, but phones has a frequency of 800/1900 MHz)

Would be a 5/5 but the Bluetooth was off compared USB or RCA(if you other DAC) but still usable. Isolation to keep from interference mention above.

text:
[[VIDEOID:5bda5a0fa9338cc95f7e530072a56724]] For those who complained they can't get the thing to go higher than 4x didn't bother raising or lowering the scope against the specimen to increase the magnification optically vs the digital 1-4x zoom. Watch the attached video as I prove them wrong and zoom into the individual scales of a butterfly wing (which I found outside -- no butterflies were harmed for this video). This little thing is awesome! I can see those who work with micro soldering and board repair or zooming into small components would find this extremely handy! I bought it for the son for purely for purposes of exploration and education.

The ability to capture snapshots and video directly onto the included memory card is a huge bonus.

While the instructions are a little lacking and don't clearly lay out the zoom issue folks didn't understand, it only takes a few seconds of playing with it to figure out how it works. Watch the video and see what I'm talking about by raising/lowering the scope (optical zoom) vs the buttons changing 1-4x of digital zoom. The wing wasn't exactly flat on the platform, so you have to raise/lower and focus just like you'd do with a traditional microscope.

title: Check your old C drive FIRST, if you're cloning it and moving your OS to the SSD
text:
After many, many frustrating hours of freezes at 99% with Samsung's migration software, running CHKDSK C: /r in CMD mode from Windows search ,as well as trying Macrium's, and EaseUS's cloning and backup software [including several hours with the latter's helpful tech support ], HDTune Pro identified bad physical sectors on my old C: drive. CHKDSK and other disk repair apps can fix damaged soft sectors, but not hard ones.
SO, I created a bootable USB drive using Microsoft's Media Creation Tool. [takes a long time]
Then, I powered down, and unplugged the SATA cable to my old C drive.
I mounted and plugged in the new SSD drive, and booted via the USB [also takes much longer than normal after the BIOS beep]
The installation software then takes over. I did have my product key. Unfortunately, despite the supposed option of moving all my apps to the new drive, the installation software would do only a clean install.
The SSD is fine, and fast. It also runs cool, which surprised me somewhat.
Bottom line: You cannot clone drives with [hard] damaged sectors.

title: Super Rapid Setup in 30 Seconds!! You won't be disappointed!!
text:
This is a SUPER solid softbox!! I bought this softbox for both my vlogging studio as well as for a convenient softbox to use on my many photography sessions. The bowens mount on this softbox is made of solid metal and is extremely solid.
One of the things I love about this softbox is how fast I can pull this out of the bag and set this up for a shoot. If you ever used a softbox where it comes with the soft exterior, the central ring, and a bunch of loose rods then you know what an exercise in frustration is. With those cheap softboxes it takes forever to set up and after a short period of time the little pockets in the soft exterior that the rods sit in rip and then the softbox is useless and you are throwing it away. Trust me when I say, do NOT ever get one of those. This softbox has all of the rods built into the central ring on a solid locking hinge. You simply pull up on one of the rods until it clicks and rinse and repeat for the rest of the rods and you are ready to start shooting. It takes me about 30 seconds to set up this softbox which is insanely fast!! Collapsing the softbox is just as fast. You just pull up a tiny bit on the rod while pushing the locking button and the rod is released.
The next thing that is awesome about this softbox is what comes with it. The carrying case for this softbox is really nice. It has a solid zipper and can hold the softbox along with all of the accessories with room to spare for additional umbrellas you want to bring along on your shoot. The accessories that come with this softbox are an inner diffuser, an outer diffuser, AND a grid. The fact that it comes with the grid is terrific. I have a Westcott Rapid Box XL and it didn’t come with a grid. The Westcott grid comes separately at a whopping $229!! Needless to say I never dropped the cash on the Westcott grid but the Mivitar softbox comes with it right in the bag and it is a nice sturdy grid as well.
I really struggle to find anything wrong with this softbox. It is sturdy, super convenient to set up, comes with everything you could ever want with a softbox, and it is only $120. The Westcott equivalent is $298 plus another $229 for the grid which combined is a total of $527!! If this was available 3 years ago when I bought my Westcott softbox I would have definitely gotten the Mivitar one instead.

title: One nut wonder
text:
-------------------- TL/DR: --------------------------
20+C drop in CPU temps during gaming! Mid teens drop at idle. Exceptional performance with almost inaudible fans at 100% speed (case on floor 3ft away). at 100%, if any other sound were going on in the room, at any reasonable level, the fans would not be audible. It's a soft rushing air sound (i'm using 3 filtered intake, 1 exhaust in my case btw). it would be a pleasing, though low, white noise to sleep to btw. My MS Surface laptop fan just kicked on and is louder at arms length from me than these fans at 100% 3ft away. I'd say that's impressive. My impressions of Arctic: they are a smaller manufacturer who decided to spend some R&D to build and sell some superior products without the marketing overhead of others. Arctic has 120/240/360 & 280 models, buy one if it fits your needs, you are likely to be impressed. (And yes, there is a plug under the cpu pump housing if you must unplug the VRM fan)

------------------------- full review + 2 updates -------------------------------------------------
Why one nut wonder? The CPU pump housing only has one nut!! Like a healthy man, it's supposed to have two, and really needs two.

Suffice it to say, it looks big and gorgeous. And by big, I do mean big. A youtube review called it "Optimus Prime's cod piece", and yeah, that's pretty accurate! :D I probably should have gotten the 240. I have a moveable HD mount thankfully which I had to move rearward to it's last mount to make installation possible. It's going to be impressive once I get the replacement.

As for what I can speak on, it looks very solid and we'll made. The hoses have serious gerth, the braiding looks great, and the pump housing definitely looks like Optimus Prime's cod piece as one YouTube reviewer joked.

Packaging is very good, even if the box looks a tad generic. But let's be honest, save $20 on designing/printing a prettier box and charge me $20 less, yeah me!!

If sent artic an email so I'll come back later with an update as to how quickly they respond and how well they take care of me. I'm really not wanting to have to return then reorder as I don't have the additional room on my account atm. Step up Artic, please 🥰

UPDATE#1
Support responded to my late Thurs night email early Fri, and an hour later had approval to ship me a new unit along with a shipping label to send the 1st unit back. So Mon or Tues I hope to receive the new unit. more to follow...

UPDATE#2
Received replacement Tuesday, date I guessed it would arrive based on quickness of shipping of original item. thankfully, this unit is a two nut wonder, and i was able to successful mount it. So, now that I have it working, on with some real comments.

Installation: Unit is very large, and a bit cumbersome, yet, that is exactly what one would expect from a AIO CLC cooler of this size. Thankfully, due to the failed first install, I had already reorganized my case, and only needed to remove 2 front fans and the AMD cooler. The Fans do need to be reversed as I need to use the unit in pull mode, and it comes from the factory in Push mode (manual shows an expectation of top mount vs front. Only question mark, it felt like the pump head was connected to the hoses upside down, as the natural ark of the hoses seemed to want the VRM fan pointed at the GPU (in hind sight, i should have mounted it that way, to blow air on the back of the GPU since my board has properly sinked VRMs (AC Carbon Pro). Alas, i did mount it with the fan facing the VRM's, and it was a little tough as the backplate wouldn't stay in place and I had to put the box the pump was shipped in under the case to hold the plate so I could get the screws in.

Performance: this is the all important part for most. As it good? does it work? the short answer, Hell Yeah!.
Prior to installation, i ran a couple benchmarks, plus I'd watched the CPU temps while gaming. Generally the CPU would be 70-80C while gaming at 4150 MHz (R5 3600, using standard AMD overclock). I also ran in "silent" mode, with the CPU under-clocked to 2800. CPU would get to about 50 in gaming with minimal loss of FPS. In both bench tests, impact of about 2 - 5 FPS. Heaven benchmark saw less than a 2 FPS change between this speed and max of 4150. also benched with AC Odyssey's built in benchmark. Here, there was a 5 FPS difference.

Temps: idle - while typing, I'm in silent, temp is 36C, fan 20%/365 rpm. During Heaven, with the AMD cooler, 45C base, 57C during benchmark. With the AC280, it was idling at 34C and peaked at 42.3C. So under load, didn't reach temp the AMD cooler was at idle. At MAX CPU speed (note the test program, Heaven or AC Odyssey, is still running when I change the CPU setting), Heaven on the AMD cooler was idling 52C, during bench saw 74 max with an avg in the mid 60's. on the AC280, idle ~39, max was 60.1, yet avg is 50 or less.

AC Odyssey, AMD cooler on silent has an idle ~50, max of 63, and avg between 60-62C. With Max CPU speed, idle ~52, max of 85.9, avg in the mid 70s with lots of spikes to over 80. On the AC 280, CPU silent mode idle ~37, max of 48, avg of 41-43 (so 20C less than stock!). at Max CPU, idle is ~40-42 (noticed, the cpu fan indicates 1500 rpm and 100%, which doesn't match my fan curves, so not sure. I can sort of hear the fans, though they aren't even as loud as the white noise I play when sleeping). Max temp was 60.9, avg in the low 50's, ~53. So more than 20C cooler than stock!

Conclusions: Clearly, this thing performs. if you can get a 280 to fit, I'd recommend it for the extra $10 just because. Otherwise, if you can only fit the 240, I'd expect the same awesome performance. DO NOTE, the Arctic radiator is about 50% thicker than most other brands. This unit requires room. Quality of the build is surprising, considering the packaging looks like a standard low cost OEM manufacturer. I love they are spending money on R&D more than marketing. Let word of mouth do your marketing. Bravo.

I'd like to give some other temp results as well. Setting my CPU to Balanced (stock 3600MHz mode), temp is 32C fans 35% (front cover removed). Temp increased 1C when I put the cover back on. Setting to Silent (2800MHz), the fans drop to 20%, temp hovers between 32/33. Setting to Extreme/Max (4151MHz) temp jumps to 38C with fans at 100%. Using a custom fan curve, CPU still at 4151, temp gets to 38, then jumps to 48 then drops to 38 then pops back up. Perhaps my curve needs some tweaking now. At 38 the fans are at 37%, at 48 they are running 50%. Can't hear them at all. My work Surface 2 Laptop fans are louder (it kicked in while I had these fans running 100% to observe the noise level).

So, should you consider this over all the other CLC AIO units on the market? if you couldn't care less about RGB, yes. If you want RGB, buy the others unless you just want a rad this large. Clearly Arctic is following in the Hyundai/Kia mold of producing a good product with a better than standard warranty, yet spending minimal on marketing to keep costs below anyone else in the market and letting word of mouth do their marketing. Arctic is putting a 10yr warranty on their fans now, and while this only get 2, it's still 2 years on something this complex with their own internal pump design, not the same ole rehashed pump everyone else uses from a 3rd party. You could be forgiven for thinking Arctic is the Microcenter house brand for fans, their boxes are 2 color, blue/while, with little marketing gimmicks. I applaud that approach. So combining that approach with exceptional pricing, I had to give this a try. I do not think I'll be disappointed long term. I hope not at least.

text:
I am 64 years old back in the day high quality sound required big speakers with high power amplifiers, I guess things have changed. I have never cared for any kind of ear bud thingies because back in the day they all sounded like poo, why bother.
My pride and joy was a mid 85's top shelf Yamaha amp with a pair of klipsh towers. High quality stereo sound for sure. That was a bad ass set up. Wife hated it. Burglars re leaved me of that rig so I bought a klipsh surround sound set up to pacify my wife. (But honey they sound so good) The surround sound system is fine but not quite the quality of those towers, just saying.
I currently have audio-technica ATH-M50 headphones for discrete listening, they sound very good but not perfect and a little slack (a lot actually) on the base. But I think for the $150 price I paid I got what I paid for I like the headphones, a good value I'd say.
I see the youngsters with their ear buds and think how convenient but there is no way there is any kind of quality sound coming out of something that small, but what if I'm wrong.
I don't want to spent $200 on Bluetooth earbuds unless they are really good.
I find these klipsh wired T5M wired buds and find that they use the same technology for the Bluetooth so same sound more money less wire. OK lets give them a try, if I like them Bluetooth buds may be in my future.
I am amazed, these things have big sound the mid and high range is excellent. When I first started listening to them they seemed a bit bright with very anemic bass however after burning in the drivers the sound has improved noticeably, mid and hi range no longer sounds bright but very accurate, and the bass is much better.
A good fit in the ear definitely improves bass and I found the large covers to work better for me the medium ones which were a bit fussy but the large ones pop right in nice and tight. The burn in was also important overall the buds sound better after burn in.
There is big sound here for $45 bucks no joke, you will not get sub woofer thumping bass but the bass is good. For $45 dollars I did not expect teeth rattling bass but it is good.
Just so you will know I have ordered some 1More Quad buds for more than twice the money just so see if big bass can really be reproduced in a freaking earbud. Once I have them I will add to this post. Honestly I will be amazed if the 1More Quad buds can justify the extra $125, these T5M buds are seriously good.
They definitely sound better than the audio-technica headphones, noticeably better in the low med and high ranges.
This old dog just learned a new trick.

title: Lights stay on all the time when powered by your header unit
text:
[UPDATED REVIEW 3/23/2020] I am changing my rating for this camera to 5 stars because it clearly does need the lights that I said I drilled out in my earlier review. I don't know how they've done it, but this camera does an excellent job gathering ambient light to show your surroundings while backing up. It is far superior to the 8 year old camera that I had to replace. Furthermore, the vendor "cold" contacted me to let me know that they have seen the reviews from those of us who are disappointed over the inability to turn the lights off. And they stated that a new version of the camera will be coming out soon with a brown wire that can be cut to disable the lights. I am leaving my original review below just so folks who are interested can read how disable the lights with a drill. Again though, I now believe this to be a superior camera, and I am looking forward to seeing the new one with brown wire for disabling the lights. Excellent customer service as well!

[Original review]
As several others have noted, when you power this camera by wiring it directly to your header unit, the LED lights will turn on (and stay on) when the car is running. Apparently, it is an all or nothing deal. When the camera has power, the lights also have power. This is less then ideal for those of us who want to access the camera while driving. For example, I like to turn on the camera when I am towing my trailer to make sure everything is okay and nothing is flapping around or loose. The only way to not have the lights on all the time seems to be by "piggy-backing" the power from the back up lights. But then this would mean that I would also not be able to view the camera except for when I am backing the car up.

I'm guessing what I really need is a product that uses separate power sources for both the LED lights and the camera. Maybe the LED lights could separately be wired to the backup lights while the camera gets its power from the header unit? I'm not sure if anyone actually makes a camera with lights that are powered by a separate source, but it seems there might be a market for that based on some of the other reviews I have read here.

Anyway, I just followed the advice of another reviewer and I drilled out the 4 corner LEDs and sealed them shut with water proof Gorilla glue. Other then that, the picture from this camera is pretty good. I just wish I could have had the backup lights while only backing up.

title: Best M43 Panasonic you can buy at the moment.
text:
If you are a Panasonic user with some great quality glass you've accumulated over the last few years (Leica 15mm, Leica 25mm, Leica 12-60, etc) this is the finest I have ever had. I have been superbly happy with the GX8 and probably that is a better used alternative at a cheaper price (Maybe $500) but if you want the better one get the G9 for around $900.

It's heavier but it has two card slots, and more useful features, and frankly the removal of an anti-aliasing filter does allow the Premium 12-60 lens to pop more with your landscapes.

I planned to sell the GX8 but I still love it as well. It's probably dumb to have both but call me dumb.

in some ways the G9 defeats the purpose of the smaller, lighter formula I love with the M43 format, but what a sweet camera in your hands. The top lighted panel like on fancy DSLRs is highly usable as well. The dials are highly useful and the 6k is a super cool feature.

I am very satisfied with the photo quality both Jpg and Raw. I am a Panasonic fan of how they color render and have been since I purchased a GM1 a long time ago. (Still have that one mated to a 20mm for travel and inside stuff)

I think anyone who has been putting together a collection of Panny lens over the years deserves to own the currently best M43 they make. Get the G9. It's an awesome piece of camera equipment. I got mine hardly used for $800!

Go for it.

title: Great product
text:
I purchased the Ring peephole to replace my old optical peephole and to add a bit of security. The hole from the optical peephole was a bit big but the Ring was easy to install and the 2 pieces (3 counting the back cover) fit easily and covered the door hole on both sides of the door completely.
The battery that came with the Ring needed to be charged which took a few hours but it came with a usb cable so it did not need a proprietary exotic charger, any usb wall charger will do.
The removal of the original peephole was easy, just a pair of channel locks did the trick. The Ring came with a small simple tool to help with removing/install, but since my original peephole did not have "notches" on the eyepiece where the Ring tool would fit, channel locks were needed and worked great.
Mounting the Ring was easy but be aware you will need both hands to hold the camera on the outside of the door and the mounting plate on the inside of the door and to screw on the mounting nut, this too was easy and the Ring tool worked great to tighten the mounting nut.
Ensure your camera cable is pulled fully through the Ring peephole support tube (which also acts as a optical peephole) and is not twisted or kinked. Once the camera and back plate are orientated how you want them, fully tighten down the mounting nut and insert the fully charged battery.
Setup is also fairly easy, and typical for new device setups. The Ring peephole connects via wifi and only takes a few minutes, if it appears to take a delayed period of time to connect to your wifi, there's a small orange reset button on the left side of the back mounting plate (I had to use the reset button myself) which restarts the wifi connect process and should connect just fine as mine did.
You will have to log the Ring to your wifi account complete with your password and create a Ring account, once this is done you are ready to set your Ring options. Overall, it took me only around 20 minutes from removal of old peephole to having a fully functioning Ring. The options you will have to experiment with to achieve your desired settings.
Linking my Android phone, my wife's iphone and both of our ipads to the Ring was also easy, just needed to download the Ring app to all the devices, log on to my newly created Ring account...done
The camera quality is very good, especially for daytime, a nice clear picture with a fisheye view. The Ring peephole comes equipped with a door bell and speaker/microphone for communication with out opening the door. The door bell feature is great and sends alerts to your device when pushed, again you will need to adjust your Ring settings for each device for what alerts/notifications you want for them.
Night view is also good though my porch light is directly above my Ring so there is a small bit of washing however, the Ring does a pretty good job of adjusting itself to give me a better than average viewing, with my porch light off, my viewing quality increases. If your porch light is placed to the side of the front door, your results may be better than mine but I am pleased with the quality I receive.
I do suggest purchasing an extra battery (I did) and keep it charged to prevent any downtime when replacement is needed.
NOTE: There is NO continuous live viewing!! Live view will timeout after about 3 to 5 minutes, then will ask you to reconnect for live viewing. This is something that Ring is aware of and future software updates may be in the works but for now no. Just don't buy this if you think you can use as an overnight video monitoring device for baby's room or property security..it can and does (depending on your settings) activate with movement/activity but not full on video monitoring. You have live viewing at will, just not for long durations.
The "non continuous" viewing is the ONLY reason I didn't give this product a 5 star rating..it was easy to install, easy to setup, very good camera quality especially during the day (good night time) and lots of settings to adjust for your needs.
I do highly recommend this product and will buy again

title: Excellent keychain flash drive
text: I keep this on my keychain.  Often I need to get audio files from the church or bring power point for songs.  Great to always have it with me.  I use a Mac and the church has all Windows, so I formatted it for FAT32 on my Mac.  Windows will want to only format it as 32GB when using FAT32 because Microsoft wanted people to be switching to their proprietary NTFS which does not work well for removable drives that need to be shared across different platforms. Even though it's formatted for 64GB, the Windows XP and 10 systems will still write and read--it's just when you try and format it on Windows it may be a problem.  It does get a bit warm when plugged into USB 3 (more speed = more heat on any USB drive) but not hot enough that I would be concerned.  Any USB of equivalent speed feeling cooler on the outside, I would be concerned that the heat is not being dissipated properly and reducing life of the drive.

title: Old OP SYS for a new 2020 model
text:
After reading the manual that was not well done I reviewed the reviews and that was very telling. While doing so I came upon a string of 5 star entries, back-to-back, with one word reviews and generic and email addresses it explains my concerns that the software and remote viewing would be a problem. So check out the reviews and here is mine.

The DVR is very simple, very light and there are oddities that make a hardwired system overly complicated and based on the re-labeling, a rebranding deal. We will see how the cameras handle the weather. They are not built to handle the exposure, and generally a low quality product. I expect to replace it in 3-5 years as first the IR lights fail then the motion sensing and HDD because an SSDD cannot or should not be used, in an unvented housing without a fan cooling or heat sink config. To be smart I had to make a number of significant modifications to basically use and old system sold in a modern wrapper. Why keep it, because it is cheap, and my alterations were easily done and I already had the tools and parts to do so. I replaced the HDD with a quality 2TB 3.5" laptop unit, drilled vents through the case and installed a cpu cooling fan where the PSU is located. Also used heat shrink tube over the camera end connections, I find those to be a weak point in all short pigtails, especially when running the cables through an attic and the camera under an eave or soffit. Using a high quality lube to protect and waterproof the articulating camera mount also will slow its corrosion, as the metals appear to be an aluminum alloy, or there may be dissimilar metals situation.

Plus, the system sat in a box beyond the return date and that is that, I am stuck with it.

title: Nice little screens
text:
[[VIDEOID:692d8799f8d1ae5e61e4d3937f9bd03f]] I got 3 screens as advertised, each in a tiny protective case. The screens are nice and bright, with very saturated colors. The video I uploaded makes the colors look dull, but they're pretty vibrant when seen with your own eyes. I ordered the yellow/blue screen, and one thing to note about this screen is that you get a full 128x64 pixels, but there's a gap separating the yellow section and the blue section. So you get 128x16 yellow pixels at the top, and 128x48 pixels below it, all usable, with both parts separated by a gap approximately equivalent to the width of 2 pixels. As others have stated, address 0x78 is silkscreened on the back of the device. The actual I2C address is 0x3C. 0x78 is 0x3C left-shifted by 1 bit, which is how i2c addresses are sent on the bus. I don't know why they decided to print the left-shifted address instead of the actual address, as it just leads to confusion as shown in these reviews.

There was some white crud all along where the ribbon cable is soldered, and where the header pins are. This appears to be a byproduct of the soldering flux used. I was able to remove it by using a little bit of isopropyl alcohol along with an old toothbrush and gently brushing away the leftover flux. All of the solder joints appeared to be fine.

One of the 3 screens I received was defective, displaying glitchy artifacts and with every other row of pixels unusable. I initiated a return and replacement request as soon as I realized this, and 2 days later got the replacement screens (all 3 of the replacements I received worked perfectly, for the record). Now I just have to ship back three of the screens before the deadline. Minor inconvenience, especially since I was able to at least work with the other two working screens in the meantime.

text:

The picture quality is good even from quite close, the small size makes it nice to store, and the Bluetooth is a nice feature for connecting with my home speakers. It also autocorrected for the keystone effect, which is nice. It also has a lot of connectivity options, which was one of the features I was looking for. Overall I'm very happy with this projector.

My only complaints are that it's not very bright when projected to the full 100", but it looks fine in a dark room. The battery feature is nice but it auto-dims the output, which is a built-in setting you can't disable. It's also a little annoying that it doesn't auto-focus.

I specifically bought this projector for the wifi and Bluetooth options - not many projectors offer both. I've been unable to get it to connect to my Windows 10 PC (sees on the network but won't connect) or my Moto G7 phone. After doing some research it seems the wifi option is only compatible with older versions of Windows and Android. I ended up buying a Roku Stick which works fine, but does add to the clutter/footprint.

Overall I'm mostly happy but disappointed that I can't use it as I had intended.

My final note is that you can get it for much cheaper, NEW, on a certain online EGG-themed tech supplier.

title: The Adapter works as advertised
text:
I tried using this adapter in a variety of configurations:

Scenario #1 – Connected the Galaxy 8 smartphone using the GAOJAY adapter directly to a regular HDMI input on the Sony 4k TV. Attempted to play a video from the smartphone that was resident on the phone – so no Internet connectivity was being used. Result: perfect screen resolution, and sound came through the sound bar, as the ARC connections between the TV and the soundbar remained connected.

Scenario #2 – Connected a Lenovo ThinkPad using the C power port to the TV’s regular HDMI input, playing the same video that was resident on the smartphone. Result: same as the smartphone – all excellent.

Scenario #3 - Connected a Lenovo ThinkPad using the C power port to the TV’s regular HDMI input, playing a video from YouTube. Also played a PowerPoint from the laptop. Result: same as the smartphone – all excellent.
I repeated Scenarios 2 and 3 using the thunderbolt port on the laptop; results were the same.
In fact, all the videos displayed on the TV from the laptop showed more realistic color than the laptop’s screen.

Scenario #4 – Replaced the cable TV HDMI input on the Sony soundbar with the Galaxy 8 smartphone using the GAOJAY adapter. The ARC out on the soundbar remained connected to the Sony 4K TV’s ARC HDMI port. Attempted to play the same video from the smartphone that was resident on the phone in Scenario #1. No Internet connectivity was being used. This configuration did not work. It appears that the adapter is not compatible with the ARC port on the Sony soundbar in this configuration. Note that sound did play correctly through the soundbar when the adapter was plugged directly to a regular HDMI input port on the TV, as described on Scenarios 1 through 3, above.

Conclusion: This cable provides an excellent connection to a 4K TV’s HDMI ports from a C port for both display and sound from a smartphone and from a laptop.
