title: The best mid-range tablet around, Samsung nailed it with this one.
text:
First impressions of this device are solid, the screen is bright, the battery life is impressive, the speakers sound awesome, and the software is feature-rich and well-thought-out. TLDR, a very fairly priced high quality mid-range tablet with great performance, respectable battery life, and a great display.

Design
This tablet is designed very similarly to the nearly double priced Galaxy Tab S6, with the only removal being the pins for the first party keyboard. It does however, gain a 3.5 mm headphone jack, which is a must-have for any high quality headphone user. It is made of aluminum and glass, with the only plastic being for the Wi-Fi / LTE antenna bands. Very modern and sleek with minimal bezels that aren't too small, nor too large making the tablet look dated. However, I wanted to protect this tablet for years to come so I won't be looking at the bare metal chassis too much, as I purchased a case for it. I recommend doing that, since it will keep the resale value of the device high, and prevent it from being damaged as easily. That and a screen protector are a must-have for this tablet. I recommend the Poetic Revolution case.

Features
This tablet features, two speakers tuned by AKG certified for Dolby Atmos, facial and pattern unlock, the latest Bluetooth and Wi-Fi standards, a 3.5 mm headphone jack, an 8 megapixel rear camera, and a 5-megapixel front-facing camera. No fingerprint reader unfortunately, that is something in the higher-priced regular S6. 64 or 128gb of storage. This tablet also includes a passive S-Pen that does not require charging and can magnetically stick to multiple places on the tablet.

Software
As of 2021, this tablet is running Android 10, with Samsung One UI 2.5. Android 10 is a great operating system, but is even better when paired with One UI 2.5. Samsung really knows how to make a good tablet OS, but considering they're pretty much the only company who's making decent Android tablets, there's not much to compare it with. I would be here all day talking about every little detail, and I don't think I found everything yet. But here's some of the highlights. Dark mode, smart select which allows you to take screenshots of a custom size using the S-Pen, Samsung Notes which allow you to take notes with the S Pen, allowing apps one time or partial location only when in use, better battery management, better notification handling, and many other things that I haven't discovered or noticed yet. What you should take away from this, is the operating system is very well-balanced and has very few bugs that I have discovered, Samsung knows what they're doing.

Hardware
The Samsung Galaxy Tab S6 Lite is running an Exynos 9611 Octa Core processor (4x2.3GHz + 4x1.7GHz) with 4GB of ram. While the processor is a bit weak, it is acceptable for multitasking and moderate gaming. This tablet runs Minecraft, Terraria, Call of Duty mobile, and Asphalt 9 with decent frame rates. Note it does not run fortnite officially, and unofficially very poorly. Some of that is due to poor optimization, but if you want to game at high settings buy a tab S6 or S7. It is perfectly acceptable for watching videos or TV, and the 4GB of ram makes multitasking very effective. It's much more powerful than a Fire tab or something cheaper, so it's certainly very usable.

Storage
By default this tablet comes with 64 or 128 GB of storage, with around 20 GB of it being reserved for the system. It has plenty of space for all your apps, and a decent amount of downloaded content. Not to mention it also has MicroSD expansion, which allows you to expand the storage up to 2TB, not that you could actually find 2TB micro SD cards for a decent price, or at all. To save some money, I would recommend buying the 64GB model, and buying an SD card later.

Screen
This tablet is using a 2000 x 1200 resolution LCD display. While it is certainly not an AMOLED display, it is bright, vibrant, and certainly high resolution enough for mostly anybody. It's actually visibly brighter and sharper than my old Galaxy S6 Edge screen, but that's a first or second gen OLED. If you want a high-quality OLED screen, buy a tab S5E or S6. It certainly perfect for watching movies or TV, and unless you are directly comparing it with an OLED you won't notice much difference. There is some slight backlight bleed but it is not noticeable in my unit.

Battery
This tablet is using a 7040mAh lithium ion battery, which is unchanged from the tab S6. So naturally since this tablet has a lower power consumption it's battery life is slightly better, I went through almost an entire day and still had 35% battery left. As for the battery health, it's still perfectly fine now, but this tablet is less than a month old, so have yet to see how much it will degrade over time. Charging this tablet has been somewhat interesting. On my original Samsung Galaxy S6 Edge wall adapter it actually fast charges over the spec of the wall adapter. Measured on the app Ampere, the charger is rated for 2.1 amps but the tablet charges at up to 2.6. This shouldn't be an issue, as the charger has in-built safety features that will shut it off if it gets too hot or if something draws too much current. I've also tested it on an Anker Powercore 26800 power bank, and an Anker Powerport Speed 5 USB charger. Interestingly, it does fast charge using the blue ports on my USB charger, it does not fast charge using the black ports nor any of the ports on my power bank. It's not totally an issue, because it's only about a 30-minute decrease in time for the fast charging ports, just somewhat annoying. Keeping in mind all of these ports can deliver the current and voltage required to fast charge.

Camera
The camera on this tablet is perfectly fine. While it's no Flagship smartphone camera, it's certainly good enough for scanning documents or video calling, since I doubt you're going to be hauling your tablet around taking pictures with it. The rear camera is 8 megapixels, and front facing camera is 5 megapixels. Both 1080P, and the rear shooter can shoot video in 1080P 30fps.

S Pen
Ah yes, the S Pen. The S Pen is Samsung's claim to fame with this tablet, this S Pen is different from the one on the regular S6, as the one on the S6 is active and needs charging for the fancy Bluetooth features. This S Pen however is a passive stylus, made internally by Wacom and licensed to Samsung. Samsung made the right call in this decision, as the S Pen feels great, is well-balanced and not too heavy, and has minimal latency when drawing fast. Even though the S pen is made of plastic, It Is by no means cheap plastic and feels very quality in the hand. It does have replaceable nibs, as it rubs off a little bit on the screen protector I have. If you lose or break your S Pen, since it's a passive stylus it's only $60 for a new one. Still expensive, but not too bad. The S-Pen stows away on the side of the tablet with the point facing up, using magnets it is quite a strong hold and the pen is unlikely to fall off unless you bump it. With the case I chose, the pen is still in that location, just with a bit of plastic in the way of the tablet. This is not really affect the magnets, and the pen stays where it's put. Certain apps don't support the S Pen, but most of the first party Google ones and Samsung ones do, and Samsung has built in some extra features like screen write, that takes a screenshot and that allows you to write on it immediately, smart select which allows you to capture a custom size screenshots of most content except most streaming services, and some added functionality with Google Translate. I actually found myself using the S-Pen to navigate the tablet, rather than just writing. It's very precise and easy to use, and easy to put away when you're done.

Conclusion
Overall this is an outstanding tablet, a very major upgrade from A Fire tab, or a cheap Chinese one. With it's relatively low-cost especially if you can get it on sale, decent performance, well thought-out software, large storage with expansion, great LCD display, and free S Pen, this tablet should be a major consideration in anybody's tablet buying process. 5/5 Stars.

title: The worst of 2 worlds
text:
To start off with, I did NOT receive a damaged or older device as some others have. I received exactly what I paid for. As such, my complaints are with the actual device design and performance.

This is supposed to be a 2 in 1, right? Magazine and internet articles keep talking this thing up with ridiculous statements eluding to Microsoft having perfected the design. The "Best of both worlds!" they proclaim. No way. It's not going to be a good device, to begin with since it runs Windows 10, which is horrible. It's basically an inferior version of Win7 with an Xbox-like interface. Underneath, it's still an M$ mess. There's really no reason for it other than to run newer games, which I wouldn't recommend this thing. It's too slow and cumbersome. But I didn't buy it for gaming. I have a hot-rod custom rig for that. I bought for both basic and professional visual design work. For the basics, my smartphone does a better job. For the visual work, I have a large collection of software I bought and paid for. I've given up trying. This thing is slow, the screen (even with a decent ppi) has low brightness, terrible contrast, and a limited color gamut. The touchscreen has a poor response to both finger and pen. The i7 doesn't perform well, heats up, and has an annoying fan. The digital storage, tiny capacity, and all, doesn't feel much quicker than an old mechanical drive. The battery life is pathetic, even with all the settings turned down to a crawl; when it's slow on maximum. So, as a laptop replacement, I cannot take it seriously.

As a tablet, it's probably the worst in history. I already mentioned how terrible the screen response is, but if Win10 desktop is bad, the tablet version is downright horrible. I'd rather use a regular pencil and paper. Comparing to an iPad, in both device and software, wouldn't even be funny. But, a first-generation Android-powered tablet runs circles around it too.

Alas, no one made me buy it. My decision, my wasted money, my fault.

title: Wifi does not work, flimsy tablet
text:
I was hoping to replace my old Wacom Intuos (medium) tablet that I've had for several years with something newer, lighter, and most importantly, with a built-in wireless option (the old Wacom can be made into a wireless one but the optional Wifi combo costs as much as some tablets).
Not wanting to spend hundreds of dollars again on another Wacom I looked into XP Pen and Huion offerings. Reviews looked good for both companies. I didn't expect the same level of quality as the Wacom stuff but I did expect that the one feature I needed most - wireless capabilities - to work.
It didn't.
I'm on Windows 10, updated and patched. Only essential programs installed, no bloat. Main programs I use tablets with are Photoshop and Lightroom.

When connected via the included cable, the tablet actually works fine. In fact, one doesn't necessarily need the software/driver, and you don't have to turn on the tablet on the back either. Again, that's if you only use this tablet while tethered with the cable, only need the writing/drawing feature to work, and you don't need shortcut keys or anything else.
Otherwise, you will need the driver. There are 2 to choose from on their web site. The newer one is in beta but has a much better UI. I tried them both. Neither got the wireless feature to work.

I followed every instruction for installing and connecting the tablet (from their Amazon page here as well as from their own support site). Uninstalled all Wacom drivers, did a fresh install, did the button/Off-switch dance over and over, re-installed the drivers, restarted when needed, etc etc. I'm sitting 2 feet away from the receiver and the tablet just does not work wirelessly.

Besides wireless not working at all for me, I find the overall feel to be a bit flimsy and ....just odd, in particular the feel of the pen on the surface. Cheap feeling, like the surface just doesn't glide as well. And yes, I did peel off that protective film cover they put on. This is a fairly minor complaint though. One could probably get used to it, and I think for most folks this is something that might be worth the cost savings compared to a Wacom.

Overall, I think for the price this would be a very good option for those who only need drawing tablet occasionally, and need it to be lightweight, cheap, and are OK with being tethered.

Since what I needed most is wireless to work, this item goes back to Amazon. I'll check out the competition or go back to Wacom.

title: Review from a handbag & luggage designer. Poorly designed. Fails to protect computers.
text:
Honest review from a travel goods designer:

Pros: It's a nice looking tote and the photo accurately represents colors in the real product. The floral graphics are a refreshing offering compared to so many bland computer totes.

Cons: The reason people buy computer totes is because they want to protect their computers. Unfortunately the 'laptop compartment' is very poorly designed and entirely fails to offer adequate protection for a laptop.

There is only foam padding on 2 sides of the compartment so a laptop CAN & WILL slide to the unpadded edge of the bottom and hit the ground with no protection when the bag set down.

Bottom line: If you are considering buying this tote primarily to protect your laptop, do not buy this unless you are willing to place a hand towel or other padding in the bottom to protect your computer.

Suggestions to the manufacturer:
Regarding the pass through charging port: It really doesn't add any value at all. The plastic USB connector on the outside of the bag is unsightly and awkward and it would be much easier for a user to just have the cord coming up through the top of the bag while it's fully zipped. When the bag is fully zipped there is still plenty of room on one end of the zipper for a charging cable to fit through.

If you decide to design a next generation version of this bag, you should improve the padding the storage storage compartment to offer padding on all three sides. I would also consider designing the interior of the laptop compartment as a 'sling compartment' so it is impossible for the computer to hit the ground.

I am giving it a one star review because this fails to protect computers as it is.

Additionally one of the faux leather straps has a dent in it.

title: Clarity is over 9000
text:
I've listened to these on my Samsung note 9, on my PC with onboard crystal sound 2 audio, on a sound blasterx g6 dac/amp, and plugged into my topping d50 dac + topping a30 amp. In all instances these headphones sound great (assuming you give it enought volume) but you will see a big boost in fidelity when using a dedicated dac/amp. When comparing my audio-technica adg1 vs the Sennheiser 598 SE, I noticed the 598s were muddy in the mid range and lacked detail, and overall soundstage in comparison. Comparing the 660s vs the audio-technicas I noticed 660s had even more detail and clarity, which I wasn't expecting to be so noticeable. Furthermore that muddiness in the 598 SE were nowhere to be found here. These headphones reveal details in my music collection that I never heard before--this is true for lossless music files and low quality mp3s alike. Vocals are crystal clear, instrument separation is phenomenal, and the bass is tight (something the adg1 was lacking). And while the soundstage isn't as wide as my audio-technica ath-adg1 (ath-ad700x) it is a very natural soundstage with very, very accurate imaging. If you close your eyes and place yourself in the room you'll be able to point out where each instrument was placed.

The only drawback is the initial tight clamp force which has been alleviated after a few weeks of use. Now I can easily listen to music, watch movies, and play PC games with these for hours on end.

title: Works well to clean up VGA and S-Video signals
text:
I purchased this to use with a Nintendo 64 game console S-Video output connection. In comparison to the HDMI to N64 cable sold by Hyperkin, this combinations of products for the N64 works just as well or better in my opinion to obtain an HDMI display signal for modern displays from the N64. This just outputs the S-Video or VGA connection to an HDMI connection so you cannot expect a truly digital signal, but it does work very well to clean up the signal.

The box overall is smaller than you would expect, has the connections conveniently located, includes a power adapter and does not get hot.

I have also tried this device with a Playstation and Playstation 2 using VGA cables and it does well to clean up the signals. I would recommend a component solution for the Playstation 2 however as it can output a digital signal.

If you are using this in conjunction with an S-Video enabled device such as an N64, VHS, LaserDisc, or PC circa Windows 98SE/ME/2000, it will work well for your needs to connect these devices to a modern display using an HDMI cable.

title: Great camera for the price
text:
This is a great little camera. There are still things I am figuring out but after running it for a full 24 hours I like it. I originally bought it to keep a watchful eye over my mailbox after someone knocked it off it's stand but I have come to learn the limitations of a 55$ camera. My mailbox is simply to far away, during the day at highest motion sensitivity the camera will detect people walking in the street. But at night time even at highest motion sensitivity walking in the street does not set off the MD, however all the bugs coming up to check out the infrared lights do. I mounted it on the soffit and I had some problems with the install as a 3/4 inch hole saw as recommended in the install guide did not make a big enough hole. You can get the top part of the water proofing cap through the hole but it then gets stuck on the part that holds the ethernet cord. I took a stanley knife to the plug and cut off enough of the plastic for the plug to fit. I would recommend going up one size and using a 7/8 inch hole saw, which is what I will do if I install another one of these. I've changed the recording now to do motion sensor during the day and normal recording at night time. I'm still not sure I'll catch anyone knocking off my mailbox, I think I'll actually need to upgrade to a model with zoom for that, but I can't fault the camera for that.
I think the windows client app works well once you get the hang of it, it can be a little confusing that there are settings directly for the camera, in the case of an SD card being inserted, and then settings for the windows client app. I have not done any recording onto an SD card so I can't speak to that. The iPhone app works great, simple setup, and when I initially plugged the camera into my POE switch the app detected it right away.

All in all a great camera for what it is.

I really wanted the Note for the S-Pen, that was the only feature my Galaxy S9+ did not have. The release of the Note 10 was a major disappointment for me which was one of the main reasons I looked at the year-old flagship Note 9. Unlike the Note 10 which took several steps back, the Note 9 has the headphone jack, dedicated Bixby button (Extremely useful for remapping for various functions), MicroSD card support, and a fingerprint sensor on the back. All features I need as a power user.

I was pleasantly surprised when I received the product and found it to be in near flawless condition with only minor scratches that aren't noticeable unless you explain the phone closely. The stylus was there and works well. The battery was in good condition and like-new. When I turned on the phone I knew it was running the unlocked firmware since I am also running the unlocked firmware for my Galaxy S9+ and it has no carrier bloatware. When I put my T-mobile SIM card it worked nearly instantly. After using it for two weeks there has been no problems with it so far, all features seem to be working as intended.

I can safely say this is the best phone I have ever used and may be the best Note Samsung may ever produce.

title: Intermittent disconnects after 2 months of ownership
text: This router started to have multiple (>5-10) several second long disconnects after 2 months of ownership. It happens intermittently, and causes me to lose connectivity with my remote desktop and internet outage with my laptop and other devices. In the 2 months, I had not scheduled regular restarts. My base stations are connected via an ethernet backhaul. I'm not able to isolate which base station (or both) is experiencing the issue. I restarted the router and since the past day after doing that, it has not been having the problem. In my opinion, it is unacceptable that a router should need a regular restart to prevent this problem. I have seen other reviewers state the need for regular restarts to quell any random problems they are having. In fact, the system settings includes a "schedule restarts" function, which in my opinion is the poorest duct tape solution to software bugs that they can't iron out, and it's inclusion is basically an admission that they have low quality software development and can't/won't do anything about it. Another minor gripe is the weird fixation on dedicating the 5Ghz-2 (160MHz) channels to backhaul only, even when you have a wired backhaul. You can use the 160Mhz channels for data, but it requires finagling with the settings which shouldn't have to be this hard. I have seen other reviewers mention this and knew this going in, and with the wifi congestion around my neighborhood the 5GHz-1 channels work better for me anyway, so I can't complain. Aside from this, the router does have excellent range, excellent connectivity speeds as advertised, and relatively easy setup for my uses.

title: HONEST Review of HPUSN Softbox
text:
My review is 3 parts, for the most common steps:

1. Setup - No instructions. You have to watch 3rd party videos to figure out how to install the bulb and to mount the softbox onto the tripod. However, once you figure it out the first time, THEN it's easy.

2. Usage - This is where the product shines (pun intended). The lights are bright and are properly diffused for the best lighting on the subject.

title: Worst Technical Support Ever
text:
Not more than a week after buying this the DVR would no longer output video to the monitor. I was able to connect via network and the Swann HomeSafe View software and the first thing I noticed was the 1 Tb hard drive this came packaged with wasn't being read by the DVR. Naturally, you would think 'Oh. The hard drive is messed up.' and you would be right.

Considering how new the item was I attempted to contact Swann via amazon to which i was directed to their support website. Returning this wasn't really an option considering the number of wired camera's I had already installed and I figured it would just be either a DVR replacement or hard drive replacement.

The FIRST support tech I chatted with took me through his script which basically revolved around the power supply and without much ado I was dismissed to a technical support article about 'making sure you are using the right power supply.' Well I knew it wasn't the power supply for a number of reasons. I have a number of the same power supplies PLUS I am an electronic's technician and hobbyist. I know how to test a supply.

So I went to amazon and to be honest I am a little disappointed in their response. They insisted I touch base with Swann again which I did. The SECOND support technician, I kid you not, asked me about 15 troubleshooting questions all about the power supply -- was it working, did I try a different one, was there power to the DVR, did I try a different outlet, did I recently suffer a power outage, was it plugged in, did I try turning it off and on again, try turning it off and on one more time, was there a HD indicator light on the front.

Let me point out that I gave them a very thorough report of what the problem actually was - which was the hard drive. But no matter how much I explained how I knew this guy kept coming back around to electricity-related questions from their script. Eventually he told me that this required further troubleshooting and that I should call their number or submit a ticket.

Seriously.

I submitted a ticket to Swann - that I never got a response to. I went back to Amazon and they offered me a $53 refund - that I never received. "Our records show a refund was submitted." Chatted with them twice about this mythical refund. This was about three weeks ago - and even if it was going to come in late - my credit card got stolen last week so that will never happen.

In the end I opened up the DVR and took out the hard drive and attached it to my computer and tested it. Quite a few sectors on the disk were scrambled and opening it up in Disk Management allowed me to re-volume the drive and put it back in.

But still....WORST TECHNICAL SUPPORT EVER!

title: Best headphones I've ever owned but -1 star for several minor usability issues
text:
As of about three years ago, I was an earbuds guy. The wireless over-hear headphones I had tried previously never could approximate the kind of audio immersion you get when you wedge little speakers directly into your ear canals. I never found over-hear headphone noise cancellation to work that well - often, turning it on would create more noise than it cancelled, compromising audio quality and, well, just sucking generally. Not to mention the inconsistent and typically non-intuitive affordances for powering on/off, pairing, and controlling playback on these things.

But then I picked up a pair of Sony's WH-H900N noise cancelling wireless headphones. I basically fell in love with them on day one and used the heck out of them over the past 3 years. So, now I'm an over-ear headphones guy. Specifically, THIS line of over-ear headphones that Sony is putting out.

I still love my H900Ns. But we all know that in tech a lot can change in 3 years time. In fact, I was about to upgrade to the WH-1000XM3s a few months ago but held off after learning about the imminent release of the M4s. So I waited. Then I pre-ordered. Yesterday, I received them.

I've now had about 24 hours to toy around with them and I'm already prepared to say that these are clearly the best headphones I've ever owned. Which is to say: They're everything I love about my WH-900Ns, but better:

- They're noticeably lighter, and based on about 5 hours of use I'm convinced they're more comfortable to wear
- Sound quality is significantly better. I didn't actually expect this amount of improvement, but it's definitely noticeable at both low and high end. Separation of layers is particularly amazing: vocals shine with total clarity, heavy bass tracks shake and vibrate my skull without any noticeable distortion; high-hats and snares are crisp and clear. Very happy with this so far, which i should mention is just using the default settings with songs downloaded from Spotify. I'm looking forward to optimizing further with custom equalizer settings in the sound connect app.
- Small thing but the semi-hardshell case with dedicated accessory storage (pictured) is really nice to have (900Ns just came with a bag...)
- Clarity of phone calls - both input and output (i.e., the mic works well) - is excellent. This is key as I plan to use these to listen to music and take meetings while WFH for the foreseeable future. The 900Ns were also very good in this regard, but the ability to connect to both my work computer and my mobile device simultaneously will really help me out during the work week.

CONNECTING TO TWO DEVICES SIMULTANEOUSLY

One of the issues is figuring out how to connect to these things to two devices at the same time. Given that this is a new and much-anticipated feature, I would have thought Sony would have thought to make it crystal clear to new users how to actually do this. Maybe I missed it, but I couldn't find instructions for how to do this. Here are the steps I discovered through trial and error that allowed me to simultaneously connect to both my iPhone and Mac Mini:

1. You may have to enable the feature from within the Headphones mobile app. For me, it was disabled. See photo I uploaded showing the relevant part of the application.
2. You need to first pair the headphones to each device separately before it is possible to connect to them simultaneously. As far as I can tell, there is no way to put the headphones in pairing mode when they're connected to a device.
3. Then, when the headphones are connected to one of the devices, you should be able to connect your second device to the headphones using the second device's bluetooth preferences.
4. If the second device successfully connects, you'll hear a voice notification through the headphones: "Bluetooth device 2 connected". You'll also see two devices listed under the "Status" tab of the Headphones Connect application.

Not a big deal, but seems silly that something like the above wasn't just in Sony's own documentation.

OTHER MINOR GRIEVANCES AND NITPICKS

It seems that the only way to get the most out of these is to use them with your Android or iOS device. This is because a lot of functionality - such as the ability to customize sound - is only available on iOS/Android devices with the Sony Headphones Connect application. The iOS app is decidedly intended for use on iPhones - it only runs in portrait orientation, making it a pain to use on my iPad (which I almost always use in landscape orientation). But the worst thing about this is that I can't customize anything when listening on a MacOS device, which these days is a lot of the time. Fortunately, these sound excellent even with the default settings - just wish the capabilities of these headphones wasn't dependent on which device I was using them with.

Final minor grievance (for now) is this adaptive sound control feature that Sony got me to try out. It requires location sharing and by default fires annoying and surprisingly frequent notifications on my iPhone about how it's apparently adapting to my ambient environment. I figured out how to mute the notifications but still need to figure out how to shut the feature off entirely, which I frankly have had enough of. My advice is to opt out of this feature when you first set your headphones up. Very disruptive with totally unclear benefits.

FINAL WORD (FOR NOW)

Again, best headphones I've ever owned, and I'm very happy with my purchase. But the minor issues I describe above, combined with the high cost of these things, were enough to knock a star off my rating. Buyer beware :)

title: Meets most Cat7 standards, reduced CRC errors
text:
There are many cables on Amazon that claim to be Cat7, Cat 7 cables require individually shielded wires then the entire bundle also needs to be shielded, of the many cables available these Amazon Basics cables seem to meet the "basic" requirements to be classified as Cat7. I would prefer if they were 22AWG instead of 24 but much better than the "flat" Cat7 cables by others with 32 AWG wires that aren't even shielded around the wire bundle, basically Cat6a running at a higher frequency. These cables are stiffer compared to CAt6a or Cat5e, but that means that they are properly shielded unlike the highly flexible Cat7 flat variants.
I was running Cat5e cables on my network and recieving a large number of CRC errors to the point whereas my router would restart periodically, I figured layer 1 problem and started with the basics, new switch & new cables. I replaced those tired outdated cables with these properly shielded Cat7 cables and reduced my CRC errors drastically, I know it's difficult to get nearly zero CRC errors from a DSL connection as the quality/ condition of the Cat3 (my house is almost 50 years old) wiring coming into my home can make a difference (I'm also running ethernet over powerline) and an ISPs overall connection quality varies, especially Century Link's quality, but so far I am pleased.

title: Firmware defect
text:
I got these headphones less than a month ago and once the battery charge dropped to 80% the headphones keep repeating on a loop "more than 12 hours playtime." It won't stop, even with resetting the headphones, turning them on/off. When it happened the first time I just recharged them but then it happened again, and it's always when the battery is only at 80%. I looked this up and apparently a lot of other customers have experienced this issue. When I gave technical support a call, they seemed to have no idea this issue existed, even though I've seen multiple other customers complain of the same issue and mention they talked to customer support and ended up returning the product.

If it weren't for this strange issue, these would be great headphones especially with the battery life. But the website and my experience with three customer support agents makes me feel like there's something shady with this company. I'd recommend looking elsewhere for your wireless headphone needs.

title: Needs non-corrosive contacts
text: I have had this for about 9 mos, connected to a Ring spotlight cam, and it worked great initially.  The cam battery would last a bit less than a month (lots of raccoons and critters setting it off as they roam near the fence the cam is mounted on, draining the battery), and made the battery lifetime "infinite".  However, in the depths of winter, it stopped charging the battery -- and yes, I did brush the snow off of it.  But, it started working as the temps warmed up.  Now, it has stopped working again, and I discovered that both the cam and solar panel sides of the connectors (male/female) have significant corrosion, even though the connector was seated very firmly with the two screws.  I haven't checked the output of the panel yet, but I fear it may be moot, as the connector may no longer work.  There were obviously precautions taken to prevent water ingress, but water always finds a way, and in this case, probably trashed the electrical connection between the two.  I have tried to clean off both sides, but it doesn't seem to be sufficient.  A note of advice to you all: look for a hood or cover that extends over the connector or put some sort of box on that part of it.

title: A disappointment in several ways.
text:
I own three Garmin devices: this watch, an Edge 520 Plus for bicycling, and an In-Reach Explorer for use in the wilderness backcountry. I'm not a serious runner, so the various features for workouts, split-times, challenges, etc., are not really important to me. However, I've never owned a watch like this and wanted to give it a try, particularly because it stores music.

Pros: Great battery life, customizable, transfer of music from I-tunes is easy. Setup with Garmin Connect is straightforward. Email notifications work well.

Cons: I use the Bose Sound Sport ear buds, which is a brand on Garmin's suggested list of bluetooth devices. However, when I run, the connection is not consistent and music cuts in and out. To get a clear connection I can't cover the watch with long sleeves, and I frequently have to keep my wrist a bit higher than I normally would. Also the watch doesn't connect to the headphone is quickly as it should.

The biggest disappointment has to do with the GPS accuracy. When hiking, it grossly overestimates the distance travelled. For example, on a New Hampshire section of the AT, where distance signposts are typically quite accurate, the watch gave a distance that was .4 miles different than the true 3.2. On a bicycle ride of only 20 miles, it gave an ascent that differed by 150 feet from what my Edge 520 simultaneously recorded.

As for the Garmin Pay, this is a feature I haven't been able to utilize. My two banks, which cover a large section of the Midwest, aren't on the available list, a fact I feel is due to the banks' policies. However, the list of banks is quite long and if you do business with the First Ukranian National Bank, you're all set!

In summary, I'm somewhat disappointed, particularly for the price, and wouldn't purchase this device if I had the decision to do so again.

title: Great adapter - performance might be limited on older computers
text:
The compact size is a great feature. It links at 5.0 Gbps in Linux (fedora).
iperf3 throughput though, due to limitations of the 2013 computer its plugged into, is about 2.8 Gbps.
This is still 2.8x faster than the native 1 GbE so there are no complaints there.

The only weakness I have found is in the Linux driver itself. It needs time to mature. It's slow to initialize and, as such, doesn't come ready quickly enough at system boot. Network mounted shares sometimes need to be mounted manually from the power-off state.

At this price point, it's worth the money and breathes new life into a machine with limited options in the same manner as a SATA-3 SSD in a traditional HDD machine does.

title: Sound quality is NOT up to par.
text:
Pros:
- Multiple audio sources (Bluetooth, USB, CD, MP3 CD, FM Radio, line-in)
- Portable (uses 4 C batteries)
- Looks nice
- Price

Cons:
- Poor sound quality (deal breaker)
- FM radio reception not very good (and there is no AM radio)
- Volume knob can be finicky (not a huge deal, but gets a little annoying at times)

The functions all work, input, output, bluetooth, radio, etc. Having USB and bluetooth is especially welcome.
There's even a primitive equalizer that helps a little. Also, it's a nice looking little radio. But the features and style are not the problem. Since the primary function of this thing no matter what the input (CD, radio, bluetooth, USB, etc.) is to play audio... shouldn't sound quality be first on the list? Who wants a device that gives them 6 different high-tec options to produce crappy sound? Not me. I'll be returning it and looking for something probably twice the price that (hopefully) sounds decent.

With the prevalence of high quality bluetooth speakers these days, the poor sound quality of this device is not acceptable. Raise the price $5 or $10 and put some decent speaker inside and it would be well worth it.

I should also note that the radio antenna does not pick up local stations very well, and the volume knob skips volume levels sometimes. Also, there is no AM radio, which I would probably never use, but would like to have anyway.

title: An Excellent Solution to a common modern problem
text:
(Disclaimer: I'd ordered a Prosumer 3-Port HDMI switch previously, so I was identified to try out this unit.)

This unit helped me create an ideal media setup and solve a problem I didn't even know I had.

I work from home and use my TV as a monitor, and I have for years. I'm also an avid gamer. I like to listen to media (regardless of source) through my surround sound system, or through high quality headphones when I feel like it. I'd been using my speaker system as a receiver, switching inputs from Xbox, to PC, etc.

Here's my setup:

TV
Satellite Receiver
Surround system
PC - Windows
PC - Ubuntu
Xbox
Turtle Beach wireless headset (runs off optical, mic is connected to Xbox at all times)

My ideal setup means that all my devices can be run through my Xbox, primarily so I can get great wireless sound through my headphones.

Since the Xbox only has one HDMI in (whatever is being sent there is shown in the OneGuide app) and a single HDMI out, I was able to run all my other HDMI devices into the HDMI switch, and then run one HDMI cable from the switch to my Xbox. The Xbox then feeds into my surround system and outputs optical audio to my headphones. My surround system then outputs to TV.

I know that's a lot, and I literally had to draw a little flowchart to work out how I wanted everything connected, but the result is I am typing this on a PC that is running through the OneGuide app on my Xbox (so if I get Xbox notifications, they overlay on my screen), and at any point I can mute my surround system and get PC audio through my headphones. I can do all that with single, small HDMI switch added to my setup.

TL;DR - If you have multiple HDMI sources and want them all to run through your Xbox, this unit makes it easy.

Then I checked Device Manager and, although it showed the soundbar right there on the screen, the properties stated: "This device cannot start. (Code 10) The object was not found."
Did a lot of troubleshooting online and everything I tried (drivers, reinstall, different USB ports, etc.) failed. So, I figured it must just be a bad soundbar. So, I ordered another ($23 isn't too bad), and when it arrived I plugged it in and, voila! Sound!... until I rebooted and... no sound.
If you order this I suggest you keep the box and test it thoroughly (including reboots). If any issues come up, just box it up and send it back. Apparently, if this device decides it doesn't want to work on your particular system, there's nothing you can do to get it to work.

title: Good Overall Device. Would Buy Again.
text:
To begin with, I didn't purchase this device on Amazon (Ebay one this time), but figured this was a good place to share my thoughts about this device since it is generally my first stop when shopping.

Let’s start with aesthetics. This laptop is beautiful. By far the nicest looking laptop I’ve ever owned. It doesn't look like a gaming laptop. The bezels are thin, it’s low profile, and the fan vents aren’t exaggerated like some other gaming type laptops.

With regards to weight, it's a bit heavy, but not too bad. I’d say it feels like a quality sturdy product rather than a heavy one. The power brick is quite large in area, but pretty slim. It is a bit heavy, but not too bad.

Panel

The screen is amazing. The colors are vibrant, and the blacks are deep, as you would expect with an OLED panel. I had a hard time deciding between this panel and the 1080P high refresh rate panel. I figured that I would use this more for editing video / photos and also watching videos.

One issue you should be aware of is the color calibration. Basically, if apps aren’t able to use your color space or a wide gamut, the content will appear over saturated. This is actually a major issue. Apps that are over saturated, to name a few, are DaVinci Resolve (couldn’t find setting in app), Windows Photos, Steam (in game settings may offer wide gamut), etc. Luckily Capture One seems to work fine. I don’t use Adobe products, so I can’t comment on those.

If this panel is going to be your primary or only panel for color related work, make sure you know how to get accurate colors in your application of choice. This has been a bit of an issue for me. Luckily I have another monitor where I can see an estimate of what a final export will look like.

Keyboard

The keyboard does take some getting used to (and is a bit of a fingerprint magnet), but I can type pretty quickly on it. I’ve heard some complaints about the QWERTY portion being off center, but that has not bother me. That’s how my desktop keyboard seems to be as well, so not a big deal in my book.

The keys are tactile and feel good when you’re typing. The RGB back lighting is nice, particularly at night. I’ve turned it off for now, which can be done using the FN key and the space bar. The main issue I’ve had is hitting the numlock button when trying to backspace. I am getting used to this though.

The arrow keys don’t feel natural to reach for. They seem a touch too far to the left. I have to look at them to use them.

10 Key Number Pad

Having a number pad is nice as well. The only issue I have with this is the placement of the 0 key. I seem to hit the right arrow every time I try to enter 0. I’d also say, don’t expect to be as fast with this 10 key as you would be on a regular keyboard. I can’t pinpoint why, but I seem to have to look at it when entering data. Still, I’d rather have it than not have it.

Touch Pad

The touchpad isn’t great, and I’d suggest sticking with a mouse. For me, this is true for most laptops. I’ve had a two major issues with this touchpad.

First, when I’m typing, my left palm slightly touches the touchpad and often moves my cursor while I’m typing. since I’m using an external mouse, I set the touchpad to turn off when a mouse is plugged in.

Second, when clicking on the pad, it is very common to get a right click instead of a left click. This mostly happens when trying to hold left click to select text.

On the side of the touchpad is a fingerprint scanner, which works amazingly well. Seems faster than the one on my Pixel 2.

Speakers

There’s nothing to write home about regarding these speakers. They are on the top of the keyboard (as shown above) and sound okay. Serious users will prefer a headset or external speakers. However, for casual media consumption, they are fine.

Webcam

The webcam here is fine. It’s nice because there is a cover you can slide closed (good for those paranoid types such as myself). It’s positioned at the top of the keyboard and does point up at you, so you will have that awkward view. Since I don’t use this much, I prefer it here as opposed to the top of the display.

Killer Wi-Fi

I’ve had some issues with the Killer Wi-Fi, which for the most part, I was able to troubleshoot with some extensive web searching and trial and error. One issue was that the Gigabyte laptop would disconnect from the internet about every 2 minutes. It also caused all my devices to disconnect including a laptop, desktop, and two android devices. Turns out that my Wi-Fi router has a single channel of 2.4 GHZ. I hooked up another router that was dual band 2.4 GHZ and 5 GHZ and this fixed the main issue.

Prior to this, I did uninstall all Killer applications and installed the drivers only, which you can find on the Killer site. This didn’t help, but one less piece of poor software is good. I still get some random disconnects where the troubleshooter mentions a bad gateway. I think I’ll replace this card with an Intel one at some point.

Manufactures, please read all the complaints online about the Killer Wi-Fi cards and stop using them. These things are awful!

Ports

To sum up the ports, simply amazing. In my opinion, you have all that you’ll ever need.

USB 3.1 Gen 1: #3
Display Port 1.4 / USB 3.1 (Type C): #1
Thunderbolt 3 / Type C: #1
HDMI 2.0: #1
SD Card Reader: #1
Ethernet (RJ 45): #1
Combo Audio Jack: #1

Bloatware

Bloatware hasn’t been intrusive, and I didn’t find much of it. There are some Gigabyte applications, but they haven’t caused any problems. It wasn’t enough to do a clean Windows install which some people using previous generations have suggested to do. The only items I uninstalled were Spotify and some Candy Crush games (gross).

Performance

I’ve done quite a bit of work and testing using this laptop with my findings listed below. Hopefully the sectioning of the content helps you locate performance characteristics for your use case. Keep in mind, I am not a professional, just an Average Joe fiddling around with cool free applications!

Power

With regular use such as word processing, spreadsheet work, YouTube and web browsing I got about 5 hours at the default unplugged brightness setting of 29, which is pretty low. Given the quality of the panel, I didn’t feel like I needed full brightness for the activities I was conducting.

While gaming at full brightness, you will be lucky to get one hour from a charge. I played Sunset Overdrive at 4K and hit 10% battery power after an hour. It wasn’t too bad, but not great.

One other issue is that the laptop seems to be throttled when not plugged in. It seems this occurs at about 20% power. You could hardly hear the fans running and performance took a big hit, with frame drops and eventual full on stuttering after about 50 minutes of play. Still not bad.

Gaming

I was only able to test a couple of games, and they may not bet the typical games that are tested for performance. Nevertheless, the following gives an overview of gaming performance under limited tests.

I began with Sunset Overdrive, which looked great at 4K, 1440P, and 1080P. It struggled to maintain 30 frames per second (FPS) at 4k but performed pretty well at 1440P and 1080P. It felt like a pretty solid 60 FPS at 1080P, but there were some stutters and dropped frames. This game doesn’t have many graphical options.

I also tested some Player Unknowns Battlegrounds at 4K and it seemed fine running at 60FPS with graphics on the highest settings. I was surprised here.

Overall, I’d say the laptop is okay for gaming, but you’re probably best running it at 1080P or setting graphics options to low at 4K. Either way you play, the panel looks great, but is over saturated due to the panel / application issue I noted above.

Photo Editing

With regards to photo editing, I did not encounter any issues using Darktable or Capture One. Adding many modules and edits did not slow the device down and edited photos exported quickly.

Video Encoding

One of the primary reasons for purchasing this laptop was to do video editing in any location. I created some videos with a GoPro Hero 7 and a Fujifilm X-T30, edited them in DaVinci Resolve (color grading, sharpening, LUT), and exported them in 4k MP4. 5 min of 60P footage took about 25 min to export. 5 min of 30P footage took about 15 min to export.

One issue to note is that as you add fusion items and color grading, the playback within DaVinci Resolve can run slowly and scrubbing is choppy. You can solve those issues by changing a few settings within Resolve.

Graphic Design

I created some graphics in Inkscape and GIMP and did not have any issues whatsoever. This laptop works very well with these applications. To be honest, I haven’t thrown anything too difficult at these applications, but for what I’ve used it for (basic graphics, YouTube cover art, featured blog images, bitmap tracing, etc.) there have not been any issues.

Summary

Overall, I am mostly satisfied with the Gigabyte Aero 15. It is a very capable device, with plenty of port options, a beautiful crisp display, and a great form factor. Aside from the Killer Wi-Fi card, the trackpad, and applications not accepting the wide gamut, this device is perfect for my use case.

title: Amazing, flat, would be good for producing/monitors!
text:
I REALLY love these headphones, out of all the headphones I've bought on Amazon (and most were at LEAST twice as expensive) they sound the best and most accurate! I'm not a professional sound engineer, but I do produce and and DJ and definitely know accurate headphones when I heard them! I will say the fit is slightly weird, but they do come with multiple sizes for the silicone ear tips. I haven't tested the microphone, but again I can't find a complaint about the sound quality, other than you may get a crisper high-end on headphones that cost $200+ (like Seinnheiser).

One final note, these headphones produce a good amount of bass, but not too much, they don't boost/extend the bass at all, but they also don't "not produce enough". Generally speaking, I find headphones with "extra bass" to be lower quality.

Comparison to other brands:

Products like Bose and Beats tend to "cut" the sound, and while they may make certain songs sound "smoother" and even "better" in some ways, they'll also make other songs sound significantly worse, as they cannot create accurate renditions of songs. Also, as far as headphones with this enhanced smoothing quality these two brands are EXTREMELY overpriced, you can find similar sounding (smoothing) products for much much cheaper. Headphones at that price range should be aimed at extreme accuracy for production/studio monitors. Weirdly enough the mid-cut sound quality is much cheaper to produce than flat/accurate sound.

Speakers like KRKs will sound highly accurate and clean/almost "precise" in the high-end, but again, they DO enhance/colorize the sound slightly – that said, they'll make almost every song sound better.

Apple headphones provide a small boost in the way lower-mids that make songs sound deeper, but overall they're pretty good headphones _for the price_ (you can get them very cheap on eBay), however these headphones, IMO, sound better.

Skullcandy/Sony headphones sound pretty decent too, but they sound a little (only SLIGHTLY!) crunchy/digital in the very high-end (listen to the high-hats, it's sorta in the "ssssss" sounds).

Seinnheiser is a great brand for higher-end studio monitors, and I'd say they're the closest to these headphones, they sound slightly better in the high-end, and many models won't produce as much bass/sub-bass as most headphones, honestly to the point of lacking accuracy at times.

The pcb trace widths are about 5mm for 3.3v and 12v, and 5mm+3mm for 5v, so it should handle a reasonable amount of current. Mine came with four 25A250V fuses, so you'll probably want to replace those with something appropriate for your application.

It's cheaper than the 24pin ATX power cable extender that I would cannibalize in order to make something similar, so I would get this again.

title: +: threads are accurate;  - :  too much relief on 1/4" threads
text:
I suppose others will want to use this adapter, as I do, to mount a mic on what is normally a camera tripod. But...
The adapter has about 0.10" at each end where there is no 5/8"-27 thread, and on the end with the slot, the 1/4"-20 thread doesn't start for about 0.15" into the adapter. Presumably, you'd put the adapter into the mic holder with the slotted end out, so you can tighten with a coin or similar. The mic holder I have in my hand has only 0.203" thread depth (for the 5/8"-27 thread); I suppose it's typical. That means I only get a little less than 3 turns of thread engagement when I put in the adapter. But even worse, the 1/4"-20 threads on my tripods and other camera adapters are all short, so short in fact that they don't engage with the adapter at all! So, for now, I have to turn the adapter around with the slotted end fit into the mic holder, so I can use the 1/4"-20 threads that go all the way to the end that's sticking out of the mic holder. -- I'm thinking that eventually I'll put the adapters on my metal lathe and remove some material from both ends, so that the 5/8"-27 threads have more engagement, and so a (re-slotted) slotted end will have 1/4"-20 threads to the end. Also, as delivered, the length is quite a bit more than I need, so it'll be nice to not have so much gold color sticking out of my black mic setup. Net, I haven't saved much effort over having just turned an adapter "from scratch" on my lathe!
Update: I did remove material from the slotted end of the adapter with a lathe, and slotted the other end (the end that the 1/4-20 threads go all the way to the end) so I can still tighten the adapter with a coin, and it works well on my tripods and in my mic adapter now.

title: Good quality, great deal
text:
I bought my laptop (ENVY 17-u275cl) at Costco, and it was still within the free extended warranty period (2 years) when the battery got so bad the laptop put up a warning every time it powered up (it's usually on the charger). When I called to make a claim, they said I'd have to ship it for service, and it would take around 2 weeks. Oh, and by the way, their standard procedure is to wipe the hard disk to the original factory image! I have backups, but the time and inconvenience would have been huge. (They said I could request that they not wipe it, but I didn't feel very secure about that.) So, I decided to replace the battery myself. HP said that the correct part number is 849315-856, and the only place I could find one (from the list of authorized distributors they gave me) was at ITPAS, for $125. This unit seemed like a better deal, and I figured I'd take a chance on it. Glad I did!

Swapping out the old battery was not particularly hard. I found some helpful instructional videos on the HP Support Video Gallery website (search for "ENVY m7" once you're there there). Amazon won't let me post the direct URLs, but one is titled, "Removing and Replacing the Base Enclosure on the HP ENVY m7 Notebooks", and the other, "Removing and Replacing the Battery on the HP ENVY m7 Notebook". However, note that the first video was incorrect about the 3 screws under the rear rubber "foot" -- on my machine they are P1 Philips-head screws (NOT T6 Torx-head). Also, be careful to gently lift the double-sided adhesive strip together with the foot.

I folded over the wire harness underneath the new battery, to match the original battery, and didn't feel like it created stress on the wires. The screw holes on the new battery lined up perfectly with the old one. I like that the screwdrivers provided with the battery are magnetic! Helps avoid dropping the tiny screws.

The old battery was bulging pretty badly. Please recycle your battery properly! Check the Call2Recycle locator for a dropoff location in your area. A lot of Home Depot, Lowe's, and Staples stores take them.

After I closed everything up, I attached the charger and turned on power. The screen showed a message that the CMOS memory had been cleared -- I guess there's no other backup battery for it. I entered the BIOS settings screen to set the date and time, as well as a couple of other preferences that had been lost. Then I saved changes and exited to start Windows. It felt like it took longer than usual to boot up.

Everything seemed fine, and by this time the battery showed a charge of almost 70%. I disconnected the charger to let it drain to 3%, as suggested in the pamphlet. It seemed to be working well, taking a while to get down to 45%. I stepped away and let my son use the laptop for a bit. He also stepped away, but not very long after he told me the computer had powered itself down, much sooner than I'd anticipated. (This laptop has never been good at warning that the battery is getting low.) I attached the charger and turned on power, and it came out of hibernation with a 3% charge, so at least it didn't get all the way to 0%. My guess is that it started draining quicker once it got to the lower range, though it's possible that my son's usage was heavier than I thought. In any case, I charged it all the way to 100%. Since then (just a couple of weeks so far) it seems to be working fine, though I haven't let the charge get below 50%. The last time we were using it on the battery, just watching web video (brightness set to 75%), it seemed to be on track for 4 hours of life.

I used HP's Battery Check, and, as others reported, it has a little less design capacity than the original ("before and after" screenshots attached). It appears to have been almost 8 months old on the day of delivery (11/7), which is a little more than I expected (when I first bought the laptop, the original battery was just over 3 months old). Finally, I'm still a bit perturbed by the non-linear discharge that first time. (The pamphlet suggests draining to 3% every several months, but based on what I've read about Li-Ion batteries, I'll try to avoid going below 15%.) So, I'd initially rate battery life at 4 stars, pending more experience. However, given the value, it gets 5 stars overall.

On the first Sunday, we put the unit outside, and transmitted to it from about 100' feet. During the service, the livestream was repeatedly interrupted. After the service, the unit was hot. It was in the upper 80s, so definitely a warm/hot day.

On the second Sunday, we kept the unit inside, near a window. It was another day in the upper 80s, but the sun wasn't hitting the unit. Again, the livestream was repeatedly interrupted.

title: GREAT Cameras if you understand their limitations
text: First of all I have had Blink cameras in various models, indoor models , outdoor capable XT  (as soon as they came out ) and now the XT2. I have them for YEARS now. I now only buy the XT models as I found the indoor models OK but too limiting to me. You have limited record capability (30 sec clips max) and you will burn through batteries with numerous motions events if enabled. it pays to heed suggestions for placement if you plan to record certain events. Yes there is a slight lag but it is minimal when it records a clip. Considering they are wireless video its acceptable performance to me. I love the ability to mount these anywhere due to the battery option. If you plan to use these as more of a true security camera I recommend plugging it in for power. Battery power become backup to line power loss. It will not charge rechargeable batteries (not recommended anyway). Plug it in if you find you burn through batteries. There are many outdoor case options that support very long power cords if necessary. My primary use is as a general surveillance camera with motion only on certain cameras and only scheduled (yes you can do that). Those motion cameras will burn through batteries faster but I do have one at the end of my driveway pointing toward the house to catch pull-ins in my driveway (basically a video equipped driveway sensor) It lasts at least year for me. Generally I recommend a defense in depth with Blink cameras as only PART of your video security. I personally also have a Ring Doorbell pro and an ADT pulse system with cameras as well.  I also pay for a residential security patrol. If you think that is overkill, that is my choice. Also great to check on your pets when they are left at home. Be aware EVERY camera out there has limitations either relatively high storage fees and initial cost or more limited free storage like Blink with less expensive initial cost. Camera vary in quality and price but Blinks are relatively cheap and easy to set up. For those of you who may have issues setting one up when using battery power I suggest plugging it in to power when setting it up. That usually works for me. I have not had one camera failure in the years I have been buying these. I gave these to my sons as Christmas presents and they use the in their apartments and rental houses. Great but with known limitations. If cost is you primary concern, they are by far the overall least expensive option. Blink cameras are prefect for me but as only part of an overall security strategy. Please understand battery camera limitations and advantages and make determination yourself if they will work for you.

title: CEC works great. HDMI signal does not.
text:
For CEC this works great no issues. There is an open source library that you can use to created your own CEC control apps. There are also 3rd party apps that allow you sleep and wake your TV like a monitor or switch off your AV receiver; which is probably why you’re looking for this product anyway. If you have problems sleeping your PC its probably a software issue. Look for another 3rd party app or change your USB sleep settings.

As noted by the manufacturer this product will not work at 18Gbps. This means high bandwidth modes such as 4K 4:4:4 @ 60Hz does not work. Since it is a passive coupler it will pass the signal but it degrades the signal too much to work reliably. It really should be updated to work with current HDMI standards since $5 couplers work without issue.

If you need full HDMI 2.0b functionality you’ll need to buy a splitter to split your video card output between the TV or other AV equipment and this adapter. Make sure the TV side of this adapter is plugged into the one of the splitter outputs. Some splitters will not split the signal if it does not detect a valid HDMI device. In that case you’ll need an additional cable to run to your TV or better yet use a HDMI dummy plug to spoof EDID. If you want the technical details: CEC works over a shared 1-wire bus. That means as long as your splitter supports CEC passthrough it will work. The same signal travels bidrectionally between all connected devices; when you issue a command every device receives it and then determines if it was intended to it.

You can also use a custom cable with the CEC pins (13 & 17) split out but this is a far less practical solution for most people since an improperly shielded cable will likely degrade the signal anyway.

title: Beware: Product Quality is highly unreliable.
text:
I rarely write reviews. In fact, it takes either a great experience or an absolutely terrible one for me to make a comment about a business. I own a business and mediocre reviews are useless. Of course you should satisfy your customers--that's why you're in business.

This product, out of the box, was actually pretty decent. Simple (not easy) to setup, and depending on what you're looking for, is a decent enough product. It was a little slow, a little buggy, but the picture was very clear and the recording worked. So, you know, a 3.5-4 star review. Never would've heard from me.

Then, about a month in, one camera stopped working. Didn't think anything of it, except maybe a faulty camera. I went home, went to sleep, and when I went back to the business, all four cameras stopped working. I immediately reached out to customer support, and they had me go through several juvenile attempts to fix the problem before sending me a new drive. The reason we landing on it being a new drive is because, well, why else would 4 cameras and 4 wires stop working?

Except that didn't resolve the problem. Not at all. I let them know that, and I haven't heard back. Nothing. I gave up for a while and now it's too late.

This means that the problem to getting these working is one of two things:

1) somehow either all 4 cameras or all 4 wires went bad. I don't know how this would be possible, but if it is, it's not a company I can quietly let others donate their money to. The other thing is that it took me nearly 6 hours to setup the wires so they are completely hidden. To undo and redo them for that to maybe fix the problem is absolutely cray.

2) They sent me two bad drives. I believe this is far less likely, but either way support was useless. I would be willing to give the company one more try, but I wouldn't buy this specific product. Hopefully their wireless is better and their customer service steps up, because as of right now i'm just out my money with absolutely nothing to show for it.

title: Quick Pairing with BT 5.0 devices, excellent sound quality
text:
Here is what I found after one afternoon of paring and range testing followed by nearly two months of use:

(1) Range - I am extremely impressed with the range of the transmitter, beats other 5.0 long range transmitter (https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07GZLSFGP) I have - 5 stars
(2) Pairing - Very quick to pair with some of my receivers, difficult to pair with others - so, I would give 4 star
(3) Sound Quality - excellent, I am using LL and HD - 5 stars

Another observation is that even though the manual says volume + - does not work in transmit mode, it seems to.

Now for some of the challenges I had::
(1) Cannot pair a second bluetooth receiver to the transmitter - https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07CJJ9V1F - I have five of these, this is my staple receiver that I use for listening while watching TV - after a two months, this does not bother me that much
(2) Using https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B075WSFS7M or https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07DZPDWQ8, I can connect two devices - but sound is distorted, which does NOT happen when I use them with https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07GZLSFGP - this I am told has been fixed in the latest firmware
(3) I use the headphone jack input on the device to connect my TV. For some reason, L and R channels are in reverse. i.e, Left speaker sound comes out the right headset. I have plugged in four other transmitters to the same cable, they all produce the sound right - I am told that this has been fixed in the latest firmware

After two months of continuous use for several hours a day, I am quite happy with the overall performance of the product. So, I am giving it a five star.

[I asked for and was provide two identical devices so that I could test TX/RX combination - this pair produced the longest range, and best sound quality that I have heard to date ]

title: Absolute beast!
text:
I was in the process of updating my PC SSD, so I needed an external enclosure, this Asus ROG Strix Arion enclosure therefore served me two purposes; to hold my new SSD to be cloned and then to house my old SSD afterwards.

For anyone not in the know, ROG stands for Republic of Gamers, and represents the gaming division of Asus so this SSD enclosure is oriented towards gamers but can be used by anyone looking for a high quality SSD enclosure.

Off the bat the presentation is top notch, high profile, glossy, full colored box that contains the ROG Strix Arion SSD enclosure nestled within a dense foam container. No cheap plastic product containers here and of course it is a little bit of overkill, but the presentation cannot be denied.

Inside the box is the ROG Strix Arion SSD enclosure, a short USB-C to USB-C cable, another short USB-C to USB-A cable, a rubberized protective covering for the unit that has a built in handle for the included strap and very plastic carabiner clip shaped into a "R" to represent ROG. The only shortcoming that I have with this is how extremely cheap the carabiner clip is, needless to say I will not be using it at all.

Holding the ROG Strix Arion SSD for the first time, wow! This aluminum enclosure is one very solidly built device! It has some heft to it without being heavy and the fit and finish is top notch all around including the super awesome RGB LED lights.

SSD installing is a breeze as this SSD enclosure opens up with just a pin eject tool, the same kind that opens up the SIM/SD card slot on cell phones. Inside there is a thumbscrew that is easily turned by hand, and if need be the pin eject tool can be used as a quick screwdriver. Place the NVME SSD inside the slot, reattach the thumbscrew, close the unit and you are ready to go.

Connected to a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port on my desktop PC, I was getting 941 MB/s read and 882 MB/s write, good results if just a tad slow but very much in line with most other USB 3.2 Gen 2 external NVME drives, I also tested this on my laptop with Thunderbolt 3 and I was getting 1,050 MB/s read and write, much better and closer to the threshold for USB 3.2 Gen 2 which is approximately 1,250 MB/s. The drive inside is a 250 Gb Samsung 981a which is capable of 3,000 MB/s read and 2,200 MB/s write.

I didn’t test the RGB software because I most likely won’t be using this drive for my PC, more than likely as a miscellaneous drive for maybe Xbox or music or something else so I’m not really concerned with whatever color it is but I do like the RGBs on this device, one of the reasons I chose it. Excellent enclosure and what I think is a respectable price for a quality product of this caliber. Highly recommended.

title: Canakit provides a good deal; the RPi4 8Gb is an impressive SBC
text:
I've noticed a lot of people upset after purchasing this CanaKit...& It seems to be from many newcomers making their leap into the Raspberry Pi Single Board Computer (SBC) experience. For those unfamiliar with SBCs, this might not be the ideal CanaKit to go with...BUT! Generally speaking, CanaKit offers several different Raspberry Pi kits that are fairly well priced.

This Kit—Take care to note, this CanaKit does not include everything required to operate the RPi4—you are getting a Power Supply, the RPi4 board itself, some basic heat sinks, & some instructional literature to help get setup. You will still need to purchase:
– A Micro HDMI to HDMI cable (the RPi4 supports dual displays, so your normal HDMI cable won't work with the RPi4).
— A Micro SD Card–look for one that is UHS–I, UHS Type 1 or 3 (designated by a "U" with a number inside it), & Class 10. 16GB would be sufficient, but you can certainly go up from there! The 32Gb mSD Card & below will be referenced as an "SDHC" & 64Gb & up will be referenced as an "SDXC" – these are just mSD Card Capacity Standardized Designations. Also, one with an adapter card would be ideal
—A Case or even 2.5mm stand-offs to keep it contained or elevated ~1" or so
—A Mouse & Keyboard
—A Monitor or Television with an HDMI port

That is the sufficient list of items to set up the RPi4 (in addition to what's included in this Kit; CanaKit offers kits with all of these items in one otherwise). Those would probably be ideal for anyone just breaking into SBCs for the 1st time. Nonetheless, items can be ordered piecemeal on Amazon with this CanaKit.

Since I already had everything except for the RPi4, a Power Supply, & a micro HDMI adapter, this CanaKit worked out quite nicely. I had been looking for just the board, but the 8Gb model was selling out so fast; CanaKit had some in stock, seeing this Kit and pricing out a power supply (with a switch!), this Kit actually saved me money.

Now, as far as the board is concerned, the 8Gb model is the Raspberry Pi Foundation really trying to broaden appeal for their SBC lineup; and since they are the oft copied "Credit Card Sized Computer," the Foundation really asserted a new standard...and continues still—the board will increase in functionality in the near future.

The ARM chip is a Quad A72-Core, clocked to 1.5GHz & proprietary GPU, clocked to 600MHz (The RPi4 is simple to overclock & I've already done so...those clock speeds are off the top of my head, or, ~approx.). The board will have a Standard Release of the Raspberry Pi Operating System, which is 64-bit native for the RPi4; &! Recently announced, Vulkan 3D drivers will soon be made available for the SBC. The current release is a 32-bit Raspberry Pi OS, but plenty of Linux distributions are available; Windows 10 can be installed on the board.

Also, Android 10 has been compiled as well. That was particularly the selling point for me as it would then be capable of Project xCloud Game Pass Streaming from Microsoft (Xbox Controller Required). And sure enough, it was rather simple to get up and running. That's a major value for the RPi4 – even the 4 Gb model would be more than capable too.

The only complaints I have with the RPi4 is the change to micro HDMI, but it makes sense with two displays (which I probably won't use?). And an SSD or mmc module would have been nice to have a slot on the board.... BUT! That is just nitpicking though. I am really quite amazed by the Rapsberry Pi 4B... (an SSD will work via USB3 adapter).

The RPi4 is a standalone computer if you want it to be. It will run Zoom, Skype, etc... YouTube performance is getting better. Game Emulation is already very good, but will soon be even better. The board is a learning platform at its core, but the dedicated Community is just getting warmed up and in short order, its scope will rapidly expand.

If you're considering getting a Raspberry Pi 4B 8Gb, then I am certainly willing to recommend the board and from CanaKit too.

text:
I saw a lot of reviews that claimed this is the one Thunderbolt 3 dock that actually works. Sadly there seems to be a lot of cases in which it doesn't. One of those cases is the situation I wanted to use it in the most - to hook a laptop up to a keyboard, mouse, monitor, ethernet connection, etc. at home.

For handling most of those somewhat well, this dock gets a couple stars. That's all it gets, though, because of a couple flaws. First and somewhat minor, the devices connected through the dock will not be able to wake the laptop. I worked around this by plugging my mouse's receiver directly into the laptop instead. Second - and this is a big inconvenience for laptop users - the DisplayPort simply stops working after resuming from sleep mode. To fix this, you need to unplug the dock from the laptop and then plug it back in.

I'll be switching back to my non-TB3 USB-C travel dock that costs 1/10th the price and simply works better albeit with fewer ports.

title: Bought for the AKG K240 Studio
text:
UPDATE - 7/25/2020

The one complaint I have about these is I don't like the seams inside the earcups. It's a bad place for a seam both in terms of durability and comfort. I can feel the seam on my ears and it's a bit itchy or something.

Also, I noticed that one of the seams has a very small gap in it that seems like it might get bigger eventually. I may be able to repair this with some thread. I'm not sure.

Anyway, I wish there was a way for these pads to be exactly what they are but just for them to have slightly bigger holes for my ears. One thing I always hated about the stock K240 Studio pads was that they squished the tops of my ears. These are the same size on the inner hole so obviously, they also squish my ears. It doesn't exactly hurt like it did with the hard fake leather of the stock pads but it kinda becomes unpleasant after wearing them for a couple of hours.

I don't know. Maybe there's a pad that I can make fit that has a larger opening. I will have to look into it.

END UPDATE
-----------

ORIGINAL REVIEW
After at least 5 years of daily use, the stock earpads on my AKG K240 Studio headphones had had it. They were never very comfortable to start with (as you may know if you own these) and over the years had gotten increasingly uncomfortable as the "leather" hardened and flattened and tortured my ears. I literally had painful red marks on the tips of my ears that never went away from where they squished them constantly.

Finally, unable to take any more, I bought these. They were easier to install than I expected and compared to the stock ones (even when new) there just is no comparison on the comfort. Huge improvement! The material actually probably makes the biggest difference, since it is super soft by it's very nature.

If you're still suffering with the stock pads on these headphones, do not think twice! It's worth buying these even if they don't last too long (obviously it's hard to tell how long they will last when they're new). No real huge difference in sound quality. Well, on my headphones the sound with these pads is clearer than it was because I had to cut out the stock foam on my original pads years ago and replace it with some kind of fabric, which actually made the sound a bit muffled and I just lived with it.

If you own these headphones and you're reading this review, you probably need these pads. Unless you hate the material they're made of, you can't go wrong.
