My reason for buying this was for EDC purpose, to hold a variety of every day use items, except for a laptop (I’m more of a desktop kind of guy). My brother has a similar bag and says it holds his laptop and other items very well by the way.

Anyways, I got this bag to replace my decade old Jansport bag. Instead of wearing that bag down to the point of breaking, I decided I should get a more stylish yet rugged and useful carry bag that would look decent in any scenario really.

On with the review...
On the first day of receiving this pack, I will admit I was not completely sold. It didn‘t look very good to me, I think this was just caused by my own lack of vision and style. But after filling my bag with my items, this bag definitely grew on me, both figuratively and literally. I definitely believe I could carry up to three times what I have in my bag currently, thanks to the top flap and folding rim of the bag, you can really carry a lot!

The stitching on the bag is very solid, and the interior padding makes this bag very sturdy and comfortable. I have read that this bag is not waterproof, but thats ok. It is comfortable to carry once you have it fitted to you. The buttons and straps are also very sturdy and should hold up for a long while. The magnetic buttons were a bit tedious for me to align without actually looking at what I was doing, but this was solved easily by adjusting the buckle to the correct size depending on how filled the bag actually is. I have received many compliments on this bag, and I feel like my money really went a long way when buying this bag. I am also glad I got the large size bag and in OD green. I kept reading reviews that the bag is smaller than expected, so for me this was exactly what I was looking for: a bag that can carry a lot and not look excessively large. My only complaint is that the bag could use some more pockets in the inside, but with some creativity, you can fit this bag to suit your needs.

title: Had issues but ring support was great!
text:
[[VIDEOID:f25f74b2417b533e466b096ce60624b3]] I love Ring and their products! so why the bad review? Glad you asked. Let me explain. I am literally a walking poster boy for Ring, since the Doorbot and before Shark tank I was All in. I own every single Ring product, I’m not kidding. The Ring indoor camera, while at a Great Price point and small form factor to compete with up and comers Wyze cam, this model is Flawed! You can read it in the reviews I have video proof! I currently have many security cams protecting my home 10 of which are Ring and the New indoor cam is only one giving me issues! It constantly disconnects from my EERO WI-FI network and is the ONLY cam to do so. All other ring cams and cams from other MFR have ZERO disconnects! This Ring indoor cam is about 6ft from my router Shows an EXCELLENT RSSI of -29 and yet it will disconnect at least 5 times a day, or more! What will happen is the cam will detect motion then crash and emit audio static via speaker and in app show Wi-Fi connection Is lost. This crash lasts about 30 seconds before it reboots automatically. Or I can manually reboot by unplugging and replug in the camera if I am in area during the crash. This makes the camera unreliable for home security! During the day the picture quality is excellent, the audio quality is good, night vision is really clear as well. I do have a complaint if you use the color night vision option in settings it adds a purplish hue to video color at night. Before you say “it’s a problem with camera placement such as Wi-Fi dead zone”...I would like to add that where I currently have the new ring indoor camera I had a wired ring stick up cam 2nd GEN in the exact same spot It NEVER had this issue. I moved the ring stick up cam 2nd GEN to my garage and while further away from my router with an RSSI of -41 the stick up cam now in my garage never drops. So as for new Ring indoor cam If not for the constant disconnects this would be a very nice camera to add to the Ring portfolio but in its current state I would say stay away. ***UPDATE 11/20/19*** the Ring indoor cam FINALLY DIED! It’s still had the same Wi-Fi disconnect issues, and the same static issues but late last night it started to show a black screen only would not show any video. attempts to unplug and replug did not help. so I tried to remove from the Ring app reset the device and set it up again. it was stuck on a permanent red LED and was nonresponsive the good news is ring is taking care of me in the sending me a new replacement.
***Update 12/4/19***
Well my ring camera did have some pretty serious issues I will say that after ring got in touch with me they were quick to resolve the issue my replacement was brand new and has zero flaws in it whatsoever so it seems I just got a bad camera as the new replacement seems to be working great no disconnect whatsoever!

title: Excellent Portable USB-C hub
text:
Ever since Apple switched to USB-C ports for the MacBook Pro, I have been looking for a great portable hub that would allow me to connect multiple USB devices and a 4k TV or monitor via HDMI. I have been through quite a few in my hunt for one that works as promised, is portable enough not to take any room in my bag and gives me the connectivity flexibility I need.

I recently purchased a Koopman Premium USB Type-C Hub and it works perfectly for me. With one USB-C connection, I now have 3 USB 3.0 ports, a 4k HDMI port and an additional USB-C port. While the additional USB-C is not a big deal on the 15" MacBook Pro, which has three others, it would be incredibly helpful on the one USB-C port 12" MacBook or the two USB-C non Touch Bar 13".

As importantly as anything, it works flawlessly. I plugged my 4k Sony TV into the HDMI on the hub and got an instant perfect 4k signal.

What I also really like is that a couple of the other hubs I have tried are hard connected to a cable. The Koopman comes with a USB-C to USB-C cable but can easy be swapped for a USB cable or a USB-C to USB cable - providing extra flexibility.

One nice additional advantage of this hub is it works great with my Nintendo Switch, which, along with the MacBook Pro, is typically in my bag. I can easily connect a 4k TV or Monitor to the Switch.

Hopefully, one day, as Apple seemingly envisions, the world will be all USB-C. Until that time, this nice hub avoids the needs for most of my other dongles.

title: AUDIO IS JUNK! Going back to the 65t
text:
Wow wow wow! These are Trash compared to the 65ts. Before buying the 75ts I tried my dad's 65ts. I was afraid that they wouldnt sound as good as my wired headphones when listeng to music. But I was very impressed and decided to try out the new 75ts. Unfortunately once I got them I was extremely disappointed.

First the positives:
I love the small case with the magnetic snaps, I love the USB-C, I love the smaller size and the longer battery life. And the pass-through sounds MUCH clearer than the 65ts.
(side note, Jabra please double the available gain on the pass-through, it really needs a boost)

The bad:
I don't like the way the 75ts fit in my ears. The 65ts twist in and lock into the shape of my ears. They fit perfect! When I try to put in the 75ts I have a difficult time deciding if they are properly in place. They shake out a little easier too.
The Big bad... I am an audiophile and believe I have fairly good hearing across all frequencies. It seems someone let a bass head with no top end hearing design these new buds. The bass is completely over driven and makes the entire low end sound like mud. If I turn down the bass in the equalizer all I get is quieter mud. The highs are also pushed too high and loose all their clarity. I couldn't believe it. All these great new features but junk audio! All the features in the world can't sell me on a pair of headphones that sound bad. Man did they screw these things up! Maybe if you never use them for music you won't be bothered.

I tried my dad's 65ts again and man do they sound amazing! I could do with a tad more bass, I do love bass so long as it's clean, but the 65ts have enough to satisfy. I'll be returning the 75ts and buying the older 65ts instead.

title: Good looking case with bad quality
text:

1. You need to install 2 additional copper columns before you put in your mobo, but they cannot be fully inserted to the pre-drilled holes. Therefore, the 2 copper columns you installed will always be higher than the others, making it impossible to have your mobo sit 100% vertical. (i.e. the right hand side of mobo will be 1-3mm higher than the left hand side - this is bad for PCB)

title: Super comfortable replacement for M40x headphones
text:
I've only had these two days, but I absolutely love the difference they make. I've had my M40x headphones for probably 5 years, with nearly daily wear, and the headphone pads were starting to flake off. Now, I have a small head, and the stock pads were perfectly fine for me; they didn't really wear down that much in squishiness over time. However, when looking for new ones, I saw these, and thought they might be better. Indeed they are!

I have a small head, and I wear glasses. The M40x have a pretty good clamp around the head, so after a day of wear, the pressure on the glasses on the sides of my head got uncomfortable. I have not had this problem with the memory foam of these pads; they form around the glasses stems instead. I was a little worried about the large size of these, and with my small head, they do come all the way down past my jaw a bit, but it's not uncomfortable. They cup all the way around my ears very nicely.

I took the advice of the "most recommended" post and put them with the wider part forward, which is definitely the right way for the M40x. With the narrow part forward, they would have slid off backwards. I also followed the recommendation from the install of new stock M40x pads, and removed the little foam insert from my previous pads and put it in these before putting them on the headphones. Having done so, the sound of the headphones changed very little. I use these for transcription, and even with the pads moved over, the treble and mid are a little more present in speaking voices, but I think that clears up the sound a little. I didn't want to change the sound of the headphones the way the person in the "most recommended" post was looking for, but by keeping the old foam pads, I think I've got the best of both worlds. They are also a little more noise cancelling this way; still not designed for noise cancellation, but I use a mechanical keyboard and it intrudes on the audio less than I am used to.

TL;DR -- My M40x headphones are more comfortable and sound better with these pads. I can't say how they affect any other headphones, but for M40x, totally get these!

title: Nostalgic look keyboard brings back nice memories
text:
Before I start my review, if you are figuring out how to put this keyboard in pairing mode, press FN + C (see my screenshot).

I was looking for a tenkeyless bluetooth keyboard when I stumbled on this keyboard. The round key caps reminds me of my fun high school years when everybody were still using typewriters. The nostalgia is what urged me to buy this keyboard. I'm glad I did. I am currently using this keyboard as I type this review.

The packaging is plain and simple. Inside the box was just the keyboard and a quick start guide (written in Chinese). Immediately upon touching the keyboard, I fell in love. The key caps looks and feels very premium just like my $150 gaming keyboard. Unlike gaming keyboards, the base of this keyboard is made of hard plastic instead of aluminum, which is fine because it makes it lighter and portable. The tactile feedback is very satisfying that I could type on this keyboard the whole day. If you are wondering about the tactile feedback, it feels like Cherry MX Red switches. It has a soft and silent key press that has slight resistance before the actuation of the keys. Although this keyboard can connect to multiple devices, there is no shortcut key to switch between devices. Since I am only going to use this on a single device, I don't mind about fast switching. My only gripe on this keyboard is the user manual, it is written in Chinese. Good thing I have an older bluetooth keyboard that connects the same way (FN + C), and when I tried it, it works. For battery life, this keyboard automatically sleeps and wakes up when you press the keys, so at 2 hours per day actual usage, the battery can last more than a month.

Overall, I love using this keyboard, it feels great. The nostalgic design is very nice to show off. If you are looking for a high quality keyboard with a vintage look, this keyboard is highly recommended.

title: So many problems! I cannot recommend this board because of poor QA and support by ASUS
text:
PROS:
Nice budget board. It has LEDs that light up on boot to tell you how each component is doing in post. It has a sexy look with a decorative LED display that you'll enjoy if you have a transparent case side. The I/O back plate is sturdier than usual, and has a nice branded paint job. The boot up screen shows the TUF logo, which I think looks awesome. You can turn it off if you don't like it.

CONS (and there are many):
Unfortunately, and technical support has confirms this, you are not going to get x16 PCI-E for your video card if you mount an M.2 NVMe SSD card. The SSD card causes the video to run at x8. I don't understand why it happens when there is another NVMe slot and two more PCI-E video slots, though. There have to be enough lanes available. Z390 chipset quirk? ASUS quirk? What?

This glitch is *not* in the documentation. I initially thought I had a support issue. I asked them to please put this fact into the manual. I was getting ready to return the board.

Eventually, I did have to return the board.

Quality has been sketchy. I had the (first) board installed for only half a year before the video started to get unstable, and then began to run at x4 and crash the machine regularly. It also wouldn't boot with the video card in the second PCI-E x16 slot, so it was easy to diagnose as a mainboard problem and I replaced it with a new purchase, because the computer had been in service for months, I needed it to stay up, and ASUS won't cross-ship.

The replacement was DOA. That's right. Two bad boards in a row.

Finally -- third time is the charm? -- apparently not. Though I have a stable board that will boot video off of all PCI-E slots, now the front USB 3.0 header only gives me one fully functional front USB port to run as 3.0. The other port will work as USB 2.0, but as soon as you try to do anything with 3.0, like transfer a file to a v3.0 flash drive, it crashes out and causes Windows to tell you something went wrong with the device. It is definitely another mainboard bug, because I plugged the case's front USB cable into the other USB outlet on the bottom of the board and now I have two working USB 3.0 ports on the front of my case.

So, to recap, board 1) PCI-E lane failure after six months, followed by 2) a DOA replacement. Then 3) everything else works but now the front USB port is messed up?

It's disappointing. ASUS is clearly having quality-control problems, and their support is lousy when you have a problem with their broken hardware. They don't want to cross ship a new part and will insist upon a repair, which effectively means if anything goes wrong you basically have yourself a full-price refurb.

If I pay full price, I want a new part as a replacement that works. They should ship me new product until one of them works. If they don't like this, they should do what they can to ship working product, not hassle me with a mail-in refurbishment. In this case, I bought a second board because I didn't want to deal with their lousy support thinking that it couldn't just keep going wrong. That was DOA, and Amazon allowed me to return it to them and replace it with a new part that also doesn't completely work right. Three strikes. No more ASUS.

I'm exhausted. I've mounted the heat sink like five times now rebuilding this thing with ASUS parts that are in varying states of disrepair. I give up. You win ASUS. I'll keep the broken product and hope it doesn't deteriorate like the first one.

So a two star rating: Great product if it works, but I was either very unlucky or there is chronic bad build quality, especially considering the selling point of the TUF series is durability.

I am unlikely to ever buy one of ASUS' products again, and would warn everyone off the TUF Z390-Pro. Three bad boards in a row is unlikely to be bad luck. It's just a bad product.

text: We use these for watching TV. At first I bought 2 sets to use withe the Oasis Plus transciever for watching TV. A few weeks later (about 9 months after the original purchase), and in spite of the extra care while pluggin in, the second set went bad, exactly the same as the first - power pin disintegrated. This was, after all, one of the original two I had bought, so again, benefit of the doubt, maybe I had not been careful enough connecting to the charging cable in the months before the first one broke... but not enough benefit of the doubt to buy another replacement set. Well, now the third set - i.e. the one we have been babying since the day it arrived - has broken in EXACTLY the same way - power pin has disentegrated just like the one shown in the pic, just like the first one, just like the second one. Three out of three, junk. And not to mention, the transceiver is now junk as well because obviously three times a fool is enough for me. We have at least a dozen other micro USB devices that we use regularly, some of them over 5 years old - and have never had any issues with the charging ports. Given that it was the power pin the disintegraded every time, I would suspect these units are allowing too much current causing the power pin to run hot and degrade over time.

As for the lights themselves, the adjustable brightness is great. It doesn’t always remember the previous setting, but the switch is easy to use and the blue LED to help find the switch when the lights are off is a great touch.

The color covers work, but none of them seem to play well with my green screen. That means I use only the plain white light, which can very easily make me look washed out on camera.

To fix this, I suggest pointing the lights off-center, to the outside by about 45 degrees, as though you’re trying to light something behind and beside you rather than your own face. That reduces glare, makes it easier for me to see, doesn’t wash out my skin tone, and still lights me way better than no light at all.

The above recommendation works ESPECIALLY wel with a green screen, as it makes my background really stand out. It’s much easier for the camera to get a super-sharp boundary between me and the virtual background image. More than one colleague has commented on it!

All told, for the price these lights can’t be beat, but you should experiment with them to determine your own best results.

Rather than go over another typical laptop review I mean there is really nothing I can add except tell you why I choose it over the competition.

What I want in a laptop: looks, good battery life, good keyboard, nice display, thin/light, reliable, good price and decent performance.

The go versus:

Asus 425/433/434: these are probably the biggest competition in price, looks and performance, The issue with the 434 is the lack of reliability with numerous reports for users. At 3.2 lbs it is kinda heavy, and the 433 has a cheap keyboard deck

Hp/Dell 14 inch: I put these both together because they are similar and they both are very heavy approaching closer to 4 lbs. To give you an idea my 15.6 gaming laptop weighs 4.8 lbs. The dell is not very attractive to me and more bland. The HP is attractive but still heavy, not a bad choice, but not the best option IMO.

Acer Spin 13: very premium, but more of an industrial design, also heavy, great performance though. UHD display.

Pixelbook: probably the best alternative, and checks a lot of boxes but I find the large bezels very dated. Still expensive if you want to buy it new.

Samsung plus V2: another good alternative with a metal lid. Under 3 lbs and not bad looking. The bottom portion is plastic and it does feel like it. Plain 1080p panel.

The pixelbook go has a good 1080p panel which you don’t find often in chromebooks unfortunately. Outside of the pixelbook the go is the only other one under 2.5 lbs. It is also thin. Slim side bezels. Great speakers and keyboard. The go checks all my boxes for a laptop perfect for this my masters program.

When I first heard the go announced I was upset in the pricing, but then I compared it to the competition. At regular price almost all the competition sells at $599. The base pixelbook go that I bought is $649. The go is $50 dollars more but compared to the rivals it has a leg up on build quality and looks with many of them. Now most of the other laptops I mention they have been on sale for significantly lower than msrp so you might want to consider that. There also is no fold-able display like many of the others, which for me has less meaning for the way I use the device.

What google did was refine the basic laptop and wrapped it in a pretty bow, which is the same thing that surface laptop, macbook air have done.

title: Even more versatile than they advertise !!
text:
I am a retired Electrical Engineer who has been in the computing industry for over 50 years. I actually purchased this unit to use a travel and backup device. Since I only use an iPad Pro when I travel the intent was to augment the storage capability with an external device so that I could have all of my important and working files with me as well as have a place to offload the thousands of photos I take on every trip abroad.

This SSK device with its high capacity HDD meets and in most cases exceeds my expectations and needs. It not only works as advertised but I have found that with a little knowledge you can connect it in other ways for even more flexibility. Here are a few of these:
- when in Wireless Bridge Mode you can map the drive to a Windows or Mac File Manager System. In Win 10 File Explorer you just need to MAP the device as follows: \\(local ip address)\Share_sda1 for the HDD and you can also map the external drive as follows: \\(local ip address)\Share_sdb1 (remove the parenthesis when you set this up). The local ip address can be found in your router or in the SSK App Remote Management section. Once mapped you can read / write as if the SSK unit was inside your pc !! To use the following be sure to turn on Samba in the SSK App first.
- you can also map the SSK unit to your pc when connected to your network in Wired AP (access point) Mode. To do this you need to first set your router to port forward the local ip address (see above) to port 445. You will also need to know your WAN IP address provided by your ISP (Internet Service Provider) that can be found in your router settings or by aiming a browser on your network to https://whatismyipaddress.com/ You then MAP Win 10 or Mac File Manager to \\(my WAN ip):445\Share_sda1 for the internal HDD or to \\(my WAN ip):445\Share_sdb1 for the external drive connected to the Host port.
- A extra nice feature is to be abnle to actually use the iOS iPhone / iPad File Manager to access files on the SKK Drive. To do this when connected in Wired AP Mode you simply open the iOS File Manager; touch the 3 dots in the upper right hand corner; select Connect to Server; the type in the smb://(local IP address) -then touch Connect and in the following window type in the user ID and Password. The device will then pop up under Shared in the Browse Window of the App. You can then read and write as you would to any connected drive.

To access your SSK unit when it is connected to your network at home via the internet do the same as above but in this case type in the following: smb://(WAN IP address):445 - as the remote connection above the local ip address of the device has to be pre setup to forward port 445 to your LAN ip address.
- Access via a File Manager App such as FB Pro will give you significantly more options for sorting and accessing files. To use these apps you will need to use their setup instructions and use the following options:
- use address \\(local ip address) to connect to the SSK locally and \\(WAN IP Address):445 to be able to connect remotely. In either approach make sure that Samba 2 if shown is selected and port 445 is selected

The only issues I have with the device are ass follows:
- user manual was awful, however a revised one is available on the support@ssk.cn web site;
- it would be nice if they could speed up the wi-fi connectivity. This is especially true if you are using the SSK unit in Wireless Bridge Mode where it requires 2 different wi-fi connections to work. When in Wired AP Mode the unit is faster but could still use improvement. It would also be nice if they could 5Ghz support
- when connecting external devices to the Host port if you use other than a usb Thumbdrive you will likely need to connect a powered device or USB HUB. This is especially true if you connect a HDD or a USB type C device. A recommended change to the SSk unit would be to change the design to accommodate USB C type connector so that external devices can be powered without a HUB or power supply.
- one other thing to note is that once you start using the SSK unit you will find that there are pre configured folders already setup on the HDD you MUST LEAVE THESE as they are for the device to work correctly. You can add additional folders here in the root area or you can add additional folders to the already existing folders but you MUST leave these folders named as they are.
- the SSK unit will operate with 2 different local ip addresses. It will use one when connected in Wireless Bridge Mode and a different one when connected in Wired AP Mode. Because of this, if you want to use any of the connection methods identified above you may need to set each up 2 ways. If using ONLY the SSK App for access to the internal or external drives then the App will automatically resolve this ip address issue as it will try to connect both ways when started. Myself, I like the options provided above as I can freely move files and folders anywhere and display folder contents in different ways. The good thing is you only need to set these up once and then you will be good to go for as long as you use the SSK device.

All in all I found this to be and excellent device. It works well, is quite easy to configure and use; has excellent compatibility for nearly any way someone might like to use and is manufactured very well. The price is also excellent !!!

Stay tuned. Although I know that it will void the warranty I will be attempting to install a 2TB SSD in place of the HDD in the near future. I will add additional comments here when I do.

I hope that this review has helped you.

Well done SSK !!

title: Great kit
text:
This is a great kit overall for anyone looking to get into electronics with a raspberry pi. Someone completely new to electronics and programming will probably struggle a bit, so you'd have to be motivated to do some googling if you get confused/struck. For perspective, this review is coming from someone somewhat experienced with electronics and programming but has never used a raspberry pi before.

First off, note that while this kit comes with almost everything you'd need to get going, you will also need the raspberry pi itself, a usb power cable for it (micro or usb-c depending on your model), a micro sd card for the pi, and a micro hdmi cable (unless you plan to only remote desktop into the pi, which works pretty well).

Several items in the kit are essential to do any sort of interfacing with electronic components from the pi, most notably the breadboard, GPIO breakout board, and GPIO ribbon cable. These will let you have all the input/output pins from the pi securely connected to the breadboard and clearly labeled, so that you'll be able to send and receive signals too all the various components that are included.

The good:

All the included components seem pretty thoughtfully chosen, these are not just random electronics thrown in a box. You'll have enough wires for about anything you'd do with a pi, and many of the components are not standard things a hobbyist would have lying around, like the LCD module, raindrop module, and ultrasonic sensor.

The included manuals and code are actually pretty good. There are tons of tutorials for almost anything you'd want to do with a raspberry pi online, but it's very nice to have them written for the exact parts and setup that you have. There's about 30 or so tutorial pdfs for each of the major components that are included, beginning with just turning on and off an LED up through the more complicated parts like controlling motors. Each of these walk you through setting up a circuit for the component and gives an overview of the basic operating principals. Each tutorial includes code in both C and Python too that will run a simple demonstration once you have the circuit hooked up. This was very nice for me to have this code as starting point, since I could then quickly adapt it make something I was interested in, without having to lookup what modules I needed to import or how that specific component interfaced with the GPIO.

The bad:

The storage box is a little flimsy and a little small. Everything is packed in pretty tightly, and you'll probably have a hard time getting it all back in. Some of the larger components though, like the broad board and ribbon cable, you'll probably have out indefinitely, in which case space is less of an issue. There are a good amount of compartments and dividers in it, I just think it'll probably crack when I invariably leave in on the floor and step on it.

The tutorials really are better than I expected. There are occasional typos in them though and in the code (all the code runs correctly, mostly just a few mis-labeling of variables), that might briefly confuse someone new to this sort of thing. I wish that the the tutorials gave a few ideas or what else to do with a component. They walk you through the initial setup, but that's basically it. I also think the code could be slightly better suited to experimenting/adapting for new users--even simple things like having more variable set as parameters for a function rather than embedded within the code. Not at all an issue for anyone who has their own ideas for projects and is a little experienced, but other people might be a bit disappointed.

Conclusion:

Overall, this kit is a lot of fun and a pretty good value. You could probably assemble all the components yourself for a little less, but really not by that much. Many of these parts cost a few dollars at least if you're not buying in bulk. There's enough included to do all kinds of simple projects, and to get you started for something more advanced. I've gone through most of the tutorials and had a lot of fun. I'll probably get a few extra motors soon and make a brachiograph and a plant moister meter/waterer before retiring the raspberry pi to a quiet life as a home media server. If I miss tinkering with it, I'll probably get a second, cheaper pi model to use with it permanently.

text:
USAGE REPORT
After one year usage, I usually review electronics and here's this one. The main use I give this keyboard is for gaming [hardcore gaming]. I don't have a loud mechanical aberration. Instead, I use this fancy, quiet, inexpensive little comfort keyboard. I stress out the word comfort because the pad, after a year of use, has been standing out strong. I play about 5 hours each day, more on the weekends and this is THE keyboard to have. Other than gaming, whenever I need to type, the keyboard keys feel strong and have a nice "clicking" sound but not abnormal as a mechanical keyboard because this is NOT a mechanical keyboard, which is the reason I bought it.

CARE/MAINTENANCE
As every gamer will know, there's an inevitable habit of eating at your PC and I am not the exception. Sometimes I eat chips or other mildly-greasing foods while playing or otherwise using my computer. Besides me being squeamish about having oily fingertips, I really do take care of the keyboard and clean it at least once a week during my "battlestation" weekly maintenance care routine.

SUMMARY
So there you have it, a heavily-used keyboard that has been beat and abused many times and still holds well. A well-built product for everyday computing and even gaming. I recommend it.

title: Excellent Desktop Replacement
text:
I've been using it for about a month, and I have only good things to say about it. Note that my typical usage is as a desktop replacement / mobile desktop. Overall it feels like a quality build with premium features.

Performance:
It's incredibly fast. You can find benchmarks around, but encoding videos is fast. If you stream or record gaming sessions, this machine can handle it no problem.
The screen was surprising as I haven't kept up with the tech. The colors are fantastic. Blacks are deep. And the smoothness of the 240 Hz display is palpable. Granted, in Apex Legends I ONLY get 120 Hz (slight sarcasm. That's an excellent framerate and looks fantastic).
I am able to play Half-Life Alyx (VR) using Oculus Link feature of the Oculus Quest with an Anker USB 3 cable, and it plays great on highest settings.
The fans can get loud under heavy load which may be an issue depending on your usage. I have no problems with it when wearing headphones.
The USB ports are ALL USB 3 which allows for a lot of flexibility and future proofing. Most of the ports are on the left side which better suited to right handed folks, though the power plug is on the right along with a two of the USB inputs.

Keyboard:
I just like that it's lit, but I admit that playing with the per-key colors can be fun. The space between keys are better suited for gaming than typing. Any other gripes about key placement (e.g. Windows and Fn keys swapped) were resolved by remapping the keys through MSI center or SteelSeries software.
Trackpad is good. I like that it uses physical buttons.

Battery:
I keep it plugged in most of the time, so battery life doesn't affect me much. Battery performance is not that great, but I honestly haven't tested much past seeing it drain quickly when unplugged. I've read that disabling MSI center helps with that, but I use MSI center for its battery saver feature and to enable/disable high performance mode when needed.

Software:
It came with some bloat, but uninstalling most things was easy. I kept a few things around like the Nahimic software which has some good audio options for surround sound and static and noise cancellation for microphones. The only issue I had was that the MSI dragon center kept pinning itself to the task bar, but I eventually found some hidden XML file from windows to get it to stop (LayoutModification.xml).

Upgradeable
It came with a SATA adapter in the box to add a SATA 2.5" drive. I can't review this part, though. I intend to eventually upgrade the disk storage and maybe RAM. Supposedly it's easy to do.

Overall, I enjoy it. It's nice having a premium computer for a change. If I run into any issues within the year, I'll update the review.

title: Amazon Warehouse hit or miss as always
text:
I ordered this from Amazon Warehouse where it indicated the item was used and bonus material was missing.

What I received was a brand new motherboard with all bonus material included in a distressed box.

So consider this an Amazon Warehouse hit.

These ship with BIOS 4.40 (newest is 4.5 as of this review), but the BIOS is new enough to support all 8th and 9th gen CPUs up to the 9900ks and 9100F.

This is a basic board with slightly below average VRMs. I tried a 9900k in it that is known to hold 5.2 no problem in another board, but this board stalled at 4.9 before the VRMs overheated at 1.3v. But that wasn't why I bought it. It is a lower tier board really not meant for major overclocking and higher voltages. I tested a 9900ks I have which runs at 5ghz @ ~1.2v no problem and it handled it just fine.

My build was with a 9100f which this board could handle very easy.

Installation was straight forward. I paired it with a set of Corsair Vengeance LPX 3200 XMP memory (2x8GB), and it worked instantly and flawlessly and passed an overnight memtest run no problem.

A few cons:

No RGB header
Only one mid and top fan aux connector
No cooling on the VRMs
chipset heatsink runs right up against the M.2 devices installed in the lower part of the board

Overall, for the price, (~79USD), it does what I need and built out just fine and passed all stress tests (Memtest, CB15, CB20, TimeSpy)

5/5

title: No Power, No Joy
text:
I was so excited to score this innovative TV! My intent was to put it up on my wall and use it as a computer monitor in my office, watch some Netflix programming and have some cool wall art when I'm away.

The box arrived and my excitement was furthered. It was a slim box and everything packed nice and neat! As I unboxed it my confusion grew a little bit. Instead of a standard power cable with various video ports in the TV itself, this thing is complicated with a control box. I suppose it could be to simplify the wall art idea (i.e. 1 fewer cable coming out of it maybe?)

But in pursuit of this engineering miracle, the brilliance of Samsung introduced unnecessary complexity - there's a giant cable that must be connected from the TV into the control box. Your power and HDMI, etc. then plug into it thus adding an additional connection point that could fail.

Anyways my somewhat complicated setup was complete! I installed the batteries into the oddly shaped remote control Then, with my excitement reaching a crescendo that could only culminate in the beautiful "SAMSUNG" blue and white image splashed on the screen that I so eagerly anticipated, all that remained was the simple, final push of the power button. With a measured flick of my right thumb, this newfound pleasure would be mine! AND.....

Nothing.

A little red light flashed on the remote. "Hmm" I thought. I flicked again. Nothing.

After a third flick brought no change I checked all the connections, un-doing and re-doing in the overly specific and risky order that apparently is required of such an amazing engineering marvel. I plugged and unplugged the power.

Flick. Nothing.

Being a veteran of years of PC support, I seemlessly and ever so carefully moved the unit to another power outlet. Triple checked the connections.

Flick. Nothing. DOA.

Patience worn thin, frothy anticipation turned completely flat like a 3-day old beer, I packed up the unit and sent it back never to buy one of these again. Turns out my experience was like that of the 1995 film "Waterworld". Couldn't wait to see it, couldn't have been more disappointed once I did (in fairness the movie projector actually worked at the theater and at least I did see Waterworld, but still...).

Sometimes even Samsung, the Kevin Costner of electronics can't thrill you. Save your money. This thing is probably cool when it works. That is, if you can ever power it on.

title: Defective -  Buyer Beware!!!  $3,000+
text:
I just wanted what I paid for. I needed this for intense college programs and the computer came defective with screen clouding, a dead pixel, and a defective trackpad. This computer took hours of my time trying to fix this with support.

How does this defective product get fixed? Well... it doesn’t. It can’t be fixed by the company. Either return it and pay for another one (a total of $3,000+ on your credit) or send it back and be without a computer for an extended period of time. Neither of these were reasonable options being a college student.

The Bad:
———————
-The quality of this screen is unacceptable for its “brand new” gaming laptop price and for its refresh rate. (Dead Pixel and Screen Clouding)

-The trackpad does not work correctly. Don’t use it as a mouse. It doesn’t register half the time and stops working in the middle of it.

-The battery pack is heavier and larger than most. Not the best, but not the worst, battery life. (About 3-5 hours of casual non-gaming default lighting use on a full charge.)

-Lack of paper manual. There was limited paper documentation other than an obvious “how to power on” getting started guide.

-Separate Mic and Headphone Jack.

-Does not come with a webcam cover.

-That red on the trackpad doesn’t actually light up.

The Good:
———————
-Cool, bright, dimmable individual RGB keys and comfy keyboard
-Doesn’t get too hot/noisey
-Has k-slot
-Screen has little to no glare.
-Packed securely
-Slim design
-Right side number pad
-The seller’s had quick and english support
-Built in webcam
-In theory its internal specs are good for casual gaming

Update:
Two years later the keyboard LEDs started burning out. (They never worked right anyways, sometimes they wouldn’t change when pressing the button and sometimes they’d bug out and the only fix was restarting.)

The dead pixel either healed itself or I just don’t play it in the dark to notice it.

The trackpad still never works right and bugs out. I use a usb mouse because of that.

The powerbrick is annoyingly big and heavy for casual travel and the battery life seems to only be 1-2 hours now.

The company was no help. Highly suggest staying away from computer king.

You can’t put a webcam cover on because it closes flat there.

The computer screen goes black all the time when idling and you can only turn it on with the power button, trying to add a screensaver won’t work. Changing settings has not been able to fix this.

The fans bug out sometimes. They either wont turn off or wont turn on with its respective button. Sometimes only one goes on. Maybe they’re broken? The plastic casing broke while in my protective bag. Its a poor design. The plastic flares out making it susceptible to damage in upright-side carrying bags. I’m more careful than most people with my laptop. The design should not be able to be cracked when setting a bag down with gentle force.

I still regret this purchase and feel a grudge against the company for selling a product with so many defects.

title: General Use WiFi
text:
I really like these units. They are easy to configure, are rich in features, can be used and configured for any level of IT capability including security features against WiFi hacking and are reasonable in price. Because of the nature of my house construction (brick, rebar, and concrete) together with the internet service (high data rate fiber-optic) I configure these as routers when connected to the service. I enjoy connecting them to the internet service provider's box then connecting a laptop or desktop to one (1) of the five (5) available service ports. This is the programming configuration to be used. Going to the TP-Link support site is easy and the box is readily and easily detected and configurable at any of three (3) skill levels depending on your ability and understanding of WiFi terms and requirements. Level One is finished in three (3) steps and you are in business. Level Two (called "Basic" by RP-Link) has a number of other settings should you wish to undertake that level of configuration. Level Three (3) is Advanced and allows for a higher IT WiFi skill level to undertake configuring the box under a "drop down" selection and configuration menu. In under ten (10) or less minutes you can go from nothing to full 2.4 and/or 5.0 GHz high security WiFi operation. I have used and worked with another vendor's hardware for over ten (10) years as well as many other vendors' hardware. I found that many were extremely frustrating, required frequent "hand-holding" returns due to both the difficulty in configuring and the frequent lack of results over a days long process. Frequent returns to that process were involved particularly when any updates occurred. Compared to that and some other systems this device is a complete "walk-in-the-park" satisfying and intuitive process. I do not make this statement lightly.
This unit is very user friendly at any skill level. Support is available from the vendor though I have not, as yet, required it.

title: Works but the app has frustrating bugs
text:
[updates]
So I didn't return it and I did get it to work after I stopped swearing out loud at the app. I found that some of the bugs in the app have to do with the camera not synching with changes unless it's restarted. For example, if you turn off the IR illumination in the app it will say it is off but it isn't. If you restart the camera it will turn off. I've found similar bugs with "modes" and motion notifications.

In all this is a decent bit of hardware and the Ring eco-system is becoming more and more compelling but the fit-and-finish of their app leaves a lot of room for improvement. After looking at the competition, however, only Wyze is better and most, even Google, have much deeper problems with their products. If you just want indoor cameras I'd still say get Wyze but if you want the full Ring setup including doorbell cameras, outdoor cameras, security systems, etc. this is the right indoor camera for you.

[updates]
After being contacted by Ring support I tried again and found yet more keyboard integration bugs with the app. Here's the first one I ran into:

1. open app and click on login
2. get notification that a code was sent to my inbox.
3. switch to the gmail app and see the code.
4. switch back to the ring app.

EXPECTED:

The same code input prompt should be still showing with the keyboard on the screen.

ACTUAL:

The keyboard is missing and will no longer appear in the app. You have to force-quit the app to get the keyboard to return and cannot switch to your email app to complete the login. The only way to login to the app is using a different computer to get the code from your email.

CONCLUSION:

Please provide a *native* ios application or do not advertise support for ios.

Please, please, please please please, stop. writing. non-native. ios. apps!

<nerd-rant>If you can't afford to hire an IOS developer then don't advertise support for it and don't write a crappy Cordova (or whatever) app and put the pain off on us customers. If you need to share code write it in C which is perfectly portable across Android and iOS.</nerd-rant>

Specifically, your non-native app doesn't tie in with password manager integration through the ios keyboard. I have EXTREMELY long WPA passwords that I really can't remember. I rely on Lastpass to autofill forms but this does not work with the Ring app.

Additionally, the setup workflow is dumb. Each time it failed to connect to wifi the workflow stared over from the start instead of simply repeating from the last failed step. title: PERFECTION
text:
Replaced similar dock that was eSATA. USB C was just as fast as native eSATA but with better ability to disconnect and reconnect. After reading reviews, I decided on the OWC because one of my backup drives is a 10TB. It was immediately recognized. My eSATA dock would only recognize one drive at a time. This OWC recognizes both, even though it connects through just one USB C cable. I recommend Tripp Lite cables. This unit came with a cable but I used a 3'3" Tripp Lite.
I am using two SATA HDDs for backup of internal NVME SSDs. I did a file copy from one HDD in the dock to the other HDD in the dock, and even though the unit connects to my 4 port card with only one USB C cable, I get FULL SPEED transfer between the two drives!
I have not tested the clone function but I could not be happier. I upgraded from an older USB 3.0 dock and 3.1 has no speed limits for your HDDs.
WORTH the extra $ over the cheaper units on Amazon.
ALSO: I saw a review that the power buttons on top had a cheap feel. I disagree. I think they are fine. Out of all the docks I have owned, THIS one has the power and data ports on the SIDE, NOT the back, so the orientation of the "DRIVE 1" AND "DRIVE 2" indicators is sideways. title: Buyer beware!
text:
When Apple stopped producing the iPod Shuffle, I didn’t think finding a sweat-proof, clip style DAP would be so daunting but it is. This one was number four on my list and I thought/hoped this was going to be the one. It’s not.

It feels heftier than a Shuffle, so I thought it might be more durable, but it stopped working after almost 6 weeks of use. I used it solely for workouts, which I do for about an hour 5-6 times/week. I clipped it to the front of my shirt and went. The player has visible seams which could theoretically have allowed sweat to seep in - and I sweat a lot - so there were potential for water damage. Also, the player had been exposed to the up/down impact of aerobic activity. During the rest of my week when it was not in use (96% of the time) it sat on my desk.

I reached out to the company last week and I haven’t received a reply. I tried to leave a (poor) review on their website but conveniently it wouldn’t upload.

The company clearly put thought into the player’s concept: the sound is phenomenal; it supports a variety of files, it supports Bluetooth technology, and it’s easy to upload content (just drag and drop). They just need to work on durability. And customer care.

Update: I was able to return the faulty player through Amazon, and they replaced it. Player number two lasted 22 days which Amazon understandably did not replace. When that happened - sometime at the end of February- I once again emailed the company. As of April, I still haven’t heard back from them.

title: High build quality.
text:
Just got this a few days ago. So far, I like it.

History: I am coming from another fitness tracker probably the most popular in the business, but I have worn out two of them just by wearing them and I will not buy another.

This product so far:

1. Superior build quality. Solid. Feels good on my wrist. Looks good.
2. Band is flexible and comfortable. Does not fall off (so far).
3. Two year warranty. Better than many others. I am expecting more than two years out of this, so my questions include: what will be the costs to replace the battery or get the band replaced? Unknown at this point.

The following denotes my experience, what I found. I am not sure if this information is "officially correct" or not, so Suunto, feel free to comment:

1. Initial watch setup is fairly easy.
2. To pair it using Bluetooth to connect to your phone, the watch must be in "non power saving mode"
Settings->General->Power Saving (Off - toggle to the left). My watch came with this setting Off.
3. Download the Suunto app from the Play Store (if on Android, as I am) to your phone.
4. Download and install the SuuntoLink app from the Suunto website to your computer (Mac or Win10). In my case, Win10.
5. Connect the charging cable to your watch, and to the usb on the computer. Your watch will begin to charge, and Windows will recognize a new device.
6. Open the SuuntoLink app on your computer. It will show the watch, the charge level, and the version of the watch software. If your watch needs an update, it will offer to update your watch.
7. The current version of the watch software as of this writing is v 2.13.18, and it had to be updated upon receiving the watch to be current.
8. Create an account in the Suunto App on your phone. Under Partner Settings, choose Strava. You may have to create an account on the Strava website first (free).
9. Choose your watch face.
Settings->Watch Face.
There are several to choose from. The best for me is digital showing the date, time, and steps. Toggling the upper left button alternates steps with battery percentage remaining.
10.)When the watch is charged, choose an exercise
Exercise->Walking (this was my choice for today).
Wait for the watch to catch a GPS fix and your heart rate, (the watch will pause while it does this), then tell the watch to start the exercise. The watch will track your stats, including distance, minutes per mile, elevation, and route.
11. End your exercise (tell the watch) and sync with your phone. Your route data and stats will be transferred to the Suunto app on your phone, and Strava on the web for your viewing. The map of your route will be visible in both the Suunto app and the Strava web site.
12. It is not necessary to bring your phone or have Bluetooth on your phone on during your exercise. The data is transferred upon completion of the exercise, after the Bluetooth connection is re established.

This should get you started.

Some quirkiness with the watch:

I bought this watch with the intent that it gets me out a bit more and exercising, and so far, that has worked (yay!).

On the watch face I have chosen I can see steps. When I chose Walking, the miles traveled, exercise duration time, and some other data are displayed on the watch face, but not the steps! I would like to see a field added for steps also. The watch is tracking your steps, just not displaying them in walking mode. When you end your exercise, and return to the watch face I have chosen, the cumulative daily steps have been tracked and updated, so the data is there during the walk, just not displayed.

I will continue this review as I find out more about this product.

I started out with a full charge, and went for a 3 hr walk, and still had above 90% when I returned with power saving off (GPS tracking on).

A note about the display:

There are many reviews complaining about the display. My experience has been different.
In bright sunlight, outdoors, the display is quite readable.

Indoors, the backlight is necessary, which requires the press of a button.

Essentially, what you are purchasing seems to be a high end fitness tracker, with high build quality, that links to an app on your phone for data transfer, and that app can link to Strava for data and route archiving and review.

If you are buying it to glance at the time, indoors, without pressing the button, it will be too dark for you, and a waste of money.

So far, I like this product, and have given it five stars, and so far, I am happy with the purchase.

Update 12/30/20:

The heart rate monitor on the watch is moving around quite a bit, even though it appears snug on the wrist. The watch gave an error message about the heart rate.

So I purchased the Suunto chest monitor which arrived today for around $80. It came, and I am not too pleased as:
1. It is made in China, seems light and cheap. No on/off switch, so constantly on.
2. It would not pair with my watch or my phone.
3. Suunto support was courteous and helpful, and suggested I return it., which I did today.
4. Amazon will replace it with another.
5. At this point I am not getting accurate, consistent heart rate from the watch, or the chest monitor, and if the
replacement monitor is also bad, probably both will be returned for a refund, and I will consider other vendor.

Reduced by 1 star for above.

I intend to update this review when the replacement sensor arrives.

Update 1/3/21:

I have received a replacement chest band and successfully paired it with the Suunto 5. Increased * to 5.

Watch quality and chest band quality seems to be good.

However, Suunto is short on instructions, and like many electronics manufactures today, may expect you to learn about their product by playing with it. I however, am old school, and I like clear and complete documentation.

So, here is some "extra" information, that may help you with both the Suunto 5 and the chest strap:

1. The chest strap has no "on/off" switch. It appears to turn on when the chest contacts are moistened and strapped to your chest.
2. The chest strap has two components, the strap, and the sensor. The sensor clips into two fasteners built into the strap. It is designed to ride on the center of your chest. Clip the sensor to the strap.
3. Adjust the strap to fit, so the sensor is snug, but not too tight.
4. Moisten the contacts on the back of the chest strap. These are not metallic, but are black rubberized plastic spaced approx 2" on either side of the sensor on the back of the chest strap. They are 2"-3" long and shinier than the elastic part of the strap.
5. Turn power saving OFF on the watch. Settings/General/Power Saving
6. Pair your watch to the chest band. Settings/General/Connectivity/Pair sensor.
Note: the chest band seems to pair to the watch, not to your phone.
The watch will tell you if pairing has been successful.

Notes recording an exercise:
The watch will display steps, time, remaining battery and heart rate, depending on the watch face you choose.
To store this data and transfer it to the Suunto app and later to Strava (if you have a Strava account), you need to sync the watch with your Suunto app on your phone.
Suunto support tells me that the watch will sync automatically with your phone overnight if the watch is in NON Power Saving Mode, and is paired with your phone with Bluetooth.
My experience is a little different. I prefer to sync immediately after an exercise, manually.
Here is the procedure to do that. It assumes you have already paired your phone via Bluetooth with the watch, and you have a Strava account, and it is setup to talk with the Suunto app.

1. Bluetooth should be ON on your phone.
2. Consider rebooting the watch (left and right buttons top pressed and held simultaneously for 15 sec, then released). Consider also rebooting your phone. This may not be necessary, but can solve problems with syncing.
3. Open the Suunto app on your phone. Go to the Home page. In the upper right corner you will see a small watch icon. Press it. The app will take you to a page showing the watch and saying "Connecting".
4. The App will then say "Connected" and "Syncing." When complete it will say "Last synced: Just Now"
5. At this point, the Suunto app has your data, and Strava may have your data, Strava may instantly get your data or it may take longer, I have experienced both.

Update 1/4/21:

Suunto support says they will replace the watch band should it be damaged out of warranty for approximately USD$60. They could not give me a price on watch battery replacement as the watch is new, and they have not had to replace any batteries. They indicated that the battery is covered under the two year warranty for the watch.

1/8/21:

The watch only seems to require being OFF Power Saving Mode when it is syncing with the Suunto App on your phone. Otherwise, even with Power Saving Mode ON, the GPS will still track you. You can turn OFF Power Saving mode after the end of your exercise before syncing with your phone. Once sync is complete, you can turn ON Power Saving Mode again.

Update 1/11/21:

My preferred way of charging this watch is to attach it to a Win 10 computer with the Suunto app installed on it.
My process:
Boot the computer
Start the Suunto App
Connect the watch via USB
The Suunto App reflects that the watch is charging, the charge level, and that the watch is up to date.
When the watch reaches 99 or 100%, I disconnect it, and close the Suunto App.

I hope this is a useful review.

Update 7/26/2021: I have used this watch for some time now, and continue to like it. It is solid, and has gotten me to do a bit more walking, which is good. I no longer user Stravia, as I find everything I need is in the Suunto app. I update after my walk turning on Bluetooth and syncing with the Suunto app on my phone... this usually takes approx. a minute. Then I turn Bluetooth off. I share my walk, stats and map track with friends using email on my phone. I usually charge the watch a few minutes before each walk to 99 or 100%. I have never run out of battery during a walk, and I am always using power saving except when syncing.

So far, so good.

title: Primitive and unreliable
text: DVR's have been around for well over 10 years and you would expect that companies entering the market for the first time would not be starting behind where the pioneers started way back when. I had a Tivo back when they first came out and the cool thing was that I could pause live TV. The AirTV can't do that.  You can only pause programming that's been recorded and I find that incredible. The AirTV doesn't let you start a recording earlier than scheduled so many of the recordings are missing the first 30 seconds or so. It also won't let you stop recording later than scheduled. It occasionally stalls while watching live or recorded OTA programming for a second or two. The kicker is that if you're watching a show on a channel that has a scheduled recording coming up, you'll get a warning that the tuner is being taken away for that recording. And as soon as the recording starts, you'll lose the signal. You can start watching the in progress recording but this design is a joke. It does integrate the OTA channels into the Sling TV guide very well. But that's all it does well. Unless you really need that Sling TV integration, you should stay away from this thing. They have a lot of work to do before the AirTV is ready to compete against other DVRs.

title: Not worth the effort
text: Having lived with it now for the better part of a year I feel qualified and comfortable drafting a review/recommendation, which is, that I cannot in good conscience recommend that anyone buy it.  In the first instance, despite plenty of time for the manufacturer to fix very well-known issues with the BlueOS app, that app's integration with the unit remains so quirky as to render both device and app unusable.  I'm taking about dropped Bluetooth connections, intermittent pops/drops during music playback, handshake issues with both WiFi and wired Ethernet connections, complete failure of the app to recognize music players (e.g. Tidal, Amazon, et al).  I tried everything -- using Andriod and iPhones and iPads, nothing works as its supposed to (as Bluesound claims it does) and yet I can get the app to load on my desktop (which defeats the purpose of buying a wireless unit).  I need the Node to function as advertised. I ended up spending  countless hours troubleshooting, which by the way, in connection with troubleshooting, on Blue's website is an unhelpful waste of time.  Just visit Bluesound's Support Page and you'll see what I am referring to.  In the second instance, when I use the device outside of the Blue OS app, I still have to deal with all of the intermittent drops, etc. but I found that it doesn't offer any sonic difference/benefit that a Cambridge or Yamaha or Schitt or Marantz device offers.  Needing to convince myself of that, I brought all of those devices in to A/B test.  It turns out that they all do the same thing in terms of delivering a pleasant sonic reproduction.  I have a very revealing 2-channel playback system and while I might have been able to pick out minuscule, discrete differences in playback sonics, I found that I really had to concentrate hard to identify what those were -- if any -- there was nothing that I or anyone else could point to and remark, "Oh yeah, that's SO obviously noticeable/preferable, etc."  I bought the Bluesound because I wanted an MQA-compatible device for Tidal-MQA tracks.  I thought it was going to be a seamless user experience.  After a while it felt as though I invested in a Kickstarter-funded device/OS managed by a group of high-schoolers who leveraged their daddy's connections to slap together and sell a "cool idea" with the attitude of "we'll fix any issues customers report to us post-sale" and "use those customers as our R&D".  I ended up with a Marantz and haven't look back but I could have just as easily gone with any of the other devices I tested.  I'm one of those audiophiles who simply wants to go down to my listening room, turn on the devices, and hit play and enjoy.
