title: Warm sound, Comfy fit & Detachable Cables?  Yes, please!
text:
My sincere thanks to BQEYZ for reaching out to get my feedback on the BQEYZ product line.

Full disclosure:
I've no affiliation with BQEYZ and receive no remuneration for the review other than retaining the review sample.

The BQEYZ K2 and KC2 arrived on my doorstep in one package, side by side. Before receiving them I had determined that I would make a concerted effort to put my own particular preferences and biases aside in order to give each model its due attention and fair assessment. I reassured myself that I would approach the task objectively; I would check my ego and habitual preferences at the door. At least, these were my intentions before hearing either the K2 or KC2.

About me:

I tend to prefer a relatively neutral sound signature with a slight emphasis in both bass and lower treble, which is basically a mild "U" shaped sound signature where midrange frequencies are left intact and unaffected. I find that an absolute neutral sound signature usually lacks enough energy for the genres I enjoy most, which are Classic Trance and Progressive (early Tiesto, Markus Schulz, Otello, DT8 Project), Chill Out, Breakbeat (Hybrid & Burufunk Remixes) and 80's & 90's (New Order, Secession, The Cure, Siouxie & The Banshees, Depeche Mode). Sure I listen to Verve Remixed, Sade, Bach, Ella Fitzgerald and everything in between, but as of late the bulk of my listening pleasure is focused on the aforementioned genres.

About IEMs:

Take note when you read IEM reviews that when the reviewer gives his/her opinion regarding the sound that there are many factors that shape the final sound an IEM delivers to one's ear.

Those factors include:
1 - Shape & size of reviewer's ear canals. (shallow/deep, wide/narrow)
2 - Shape & size of eartips (round/cone, single, double or triple flange)
3 - Materials of eartips (silicone/foam)
4 - Shape of IEM (and/or angle of nozzle) can cause fitment issues for some.
5 - Source (quality of DAC in smartphone, laptop, digital audio player)
6 - Source (power rating) is it amplified/unamplified.
7 - The IEM itself (driver flex/trapping air in canal causing muffled sound.
8 - The Reviewers ability to hear all frequency ranges (age plays a factor).

Most consumers are unaware of how much weight each of these factors hold in rendering a final verdict. This is why there is such a wide variance in not only ratings, but the description of an IEMs sound. An unaware consumer purchases a perfectly fine IEM but has difficulty keeping the IEM in the ear or he/she does not satisfactorily seal the ear canal with the included silicone eartips (this is a common occurrence) and the consumer summarily dismisses the IEM as sub par. Another consumer purchases the same IEM but experiences a perfect fit and seal and has nothing but praise for the same IEM. Sealing the ear canals AND HAVING THE EARTIP FIRMLY AFFIXED to the IEM nozzle is the only proper way to use in-ear monitors. I can think of no audio equipment that is subjected to such praise or ridicule as the in-ear monitor. As if that's not enough, there is no "one-size-fits-all" when it comes to IEM eartips.

Materials (silicone/foam) have different dampening effects on final sound.
Shape of the eartips (olive-shaped, cone-shaped or other-shaped) can have different dampening effects on final sound based on how much space is between the IEM nozzle and your eardrum and how well the eartip has sealed the ear canal.
The aperture of the eartip's opening (wide-bore/narrow-bore) will have dampening effects on the final sound.

The easiest way for you to experience the different effects I am discussing is to take your current on-ear headphones or over-ear headphones, pick a song full of energy, put the earphones on and let them sit naturally over or on your ears. Listen to the music for two minutes. After two minutes, using your hands, slightly press the headphones closer to your eardrums. Notice the change in the sound. Is there more/less bass? Is there more/less treble? Did the vocals slightly slip forward/back?

Consider that on-ear and over-ear headphones have a driver that sits approximately 1 1/2 inches to 2 inches from your eardrums and by pressing the headphones 1/4" closer to your eardrums the sound changed. Now consider that an IEM driver sits anywhere from 3/4" to 1/4" from your eardrums and the slightest changes (angle, depth, shape, material) can have up to three times more of an effect due to the proximity of the IEM to the eardrum.

For this reason, I think it is wise to invest a nominal dollar amount on different eartips to find an eartip that works well for your particular ear's anatomy. This way you experience everything the earphone tuner intended for you to experience. Some IEM manufacturers supply multiple sizes (S/M/L) and/or materials (silicone/foam) of eartips to increase the odds that the consumer achieves a satisfactory seal, but even this is not foolproof. If this information holds any interest for you, there are a plethora of aftermarket eartip brands to look into, such as "JVC Spiral Dots", "Spinfits", "Comply Foam Eartips" or "Znari Foam Eartips", "Creative Aurvana" and others. If you really want to fine tune things, then you might find yourself doing what I do, which is scouring Amazon for inexpensive earphones that appear to have silicone eartips that have a shape that typically work well with my ear's anatomy.

The BQEYZ K2:

My BQEYZ journey began with two very similar sounding models, the KC2 and K2. I was determined to document all minor or major differences I could hear when comparing them. This BQEYZ K2, like the KC2, is a 2 balanced armature plus 2 dynamic driver configuration enclosed in sturdy but comfortable metal housings.

My initial impression of the BQEYZ lineup was that most of the models looked a bit bulky and uncomfortable. Rest assured that I was mistaken. The K2 sits very comfortably in my outer ear. The K2's rounded corners place no pressure up, down, inside or out of my ears once I insert them. Yes, they do look as though they were chiseled from an aluminum billet but don't let the photo images scare you off; these are very comfortable in-ears.

I Iike the high-end metal finish of the IEM but I'm not crazy about the somewhat pedestrian look of the 2-pin plastic connector. A more rectangular or square METAL housing for their connectors would compliment some of BQEYZ designs (K2 KC2, BQ3). There is NO ONE making square METAL housing for 2-pin connectors but there are IEMs that would benefit from such a design. In addition to BQEYZ's K2, KC2 and BQ3; the KZ BA10 and ZSA come to mind. Just a thought.

The cable itself is fine; it's supple enough when you compare it to what is typically packaged with most $50+/- in-ears but the eartips leave a little something to be desired....for me, anyway.

The 90° 3.5mm jack and "y-split" strain relief seem sturdy enough to sustain long-term abuse and BQEYZ was thoughtful enough to include a cable cinch.

There was minimal effort employed with the packaging but really....who cares? You get basic eartips (S, M & L), a decent cable and great earphones....for $50+/-! A more premium cable and more eartips would be great but I think BQEYZ has no illusions about who their initial customers will be (the hobbyist). Many of us customize our IEMs with aftermarket cables and/or eartips. The hobbyist looks for an IEM that is well built and sounds great. Once we find said IEM at an acceptable price point we then upgrade the accessories at a nominal cost (starting with $1 eartips and/or $7 cables). For $75+/- one can obtain a great sounding yet personalized IEM. No, I won't be complaining about sparse packaging.

Sound:

The eartips used for all IEMs mentioned are Tennmak "Whirlwinds" which are wide-bore eartips that keep the presentation as diffuse and open as possible.

While reviewing the KC2 I routinely sampled the K2 for comparison purposes and, as stated in my KC2 review, I found that the K2 is essentially the same sound signature with a slight lift in the mid-bass region.

The phrase "essentially the same sound signature" is easy to proclaim but the key word in the phrase to focus on is "essentially". I suppose the material point is how the "slight lift in the mid-bass" effects the overall presentation. Make no mistake, the presentation does differ.

In essence, the K2 presentation is a slightly warmer and smoother KC2. The KC2 has a more neutral lower frequency presence which allows the midrange and treble to come forward and breathe a tad more. Midrange and treble are more vivid on the KC2.

The two areas that I am most critical of with in-ear monitors are the mid-bass region and the upper midrange region. I dislike mid-bass that oversteps reasonable boundaries. I suppose the "boundary" is in my head and is therefore subjective but, to my ears, too much mid-bass tends to reduce clarity and pilfer some of the "air" and "presence" in the higher frequencies. Too little mid-bass tends to let the upper midrange come forward a bit. On poorly tuned earphones the upper midrange can then exhibit strident behavior which is simply too uncomfortable for long listening sessions and you'll likely have to keep the volume very low just to avoid any offensive behaviour.

Fortunately, the K2 has been tuned properly, avoiding any aforementioned "pitfalls".

As stated in my KC2 review, my favorite Budget-Fi IEM for the last 18 months has been the KZ ZS6. I love it's airy and energetic nature. The ZS6's treble extension (10khz) is problematic for some folks, though I don't have an issue with it. Just be aware that my shallow ear canals may have something to do with my ability to tolerate the ZS6's treble extension. Your ears are likely completely different so insertion depth and resonance areas will differ as well.

The K2 and ZS6 both sport a 2+2 configuration at the $50+/- price point and come with well-designed metal housings.

The three main areas that the K2 sound signature differs from the ZS6's sound signature are as follows:

1) Soundstage depth
ZS6 soundstage depth is deeper allowing more space between instruments.
K2 soundstage depth is decent but of average depth.

2) Bass texture and impact
ZS6 bass texture has more body with slower decay which facilitates impact.
K2 bass texture is more dry and clean with quicker attack and decay.

3) Treble response
ZS6 treble is extended to a fault and a "no-go" if you are treble-sensitive.
K2 treble is well extended but slightly rolled off at the extremes for comfort.

One could say that both IEMs take an "almost" analytical approach in their delivery but that would depend entirely on which other in-ear monitors you'd be comparing these two with. Both IEMs offer a great sense of detail but you'd find that the ZS6 and the K2 offer a more "entertaining" presentation if you compare either of them to some of the more neutral or even "balanced" in-ears at this particular price point.

Let's move on.

Bass:

Despite the K2's slight lift in the mid-bass, the bass is clean and quick leaning more toward a dry presentation. The dry...ish mid-bass avoids bleeding into the midrange which means the midrange avoids sounding congested. Vocals do have more presence on the KC2 but this K2 had more "toe-tapping" verve and punch when listening to The Police's "Roxanne".

Similar to the KC2, the K2's sub-bass does roll off. A dry mid-bass lift with sub-bass roll off means the bass is well controlled. The trade-off, of course, is that the low frequency impact isn't as visceral as I prefer. Sarah McLachlan's "Ice (Dusted Mix) was more pleasing on the K2 (as opposed to the KC2) due to the additional mid-bass presence but what I appreciated even more was the K2's ability to lift mid-bass presence without smearing the transition into the midrange. That (mid-bass enhancement WITHOUT cluttering the lower midrange presentation) is a rarity at the $50+/- price point.

Again, the main difference between the K2 and ZS6 lower frequency presentation comes down to bass impact. The ZS6 has a more wet and visceral god-smack type of impact whereas the K2 is determined to deliver a dryer/cleaner presentation. Both are sufficient but the deliveries are quite different.

Midrange:

Midrange timbre remains intact with good weight and density for both male and female vocals. Transparency and clarity remain mostly intact on recordings like Tracy Chapman's "Fast Car". The KC2 had a more forward midrange whereas this K2's vocals are a bit warmer, smoother and centered (neither forward nor recessed).

The K2 exhibits zero strident behavior. The only caveat being the quality of the mastering of the recording. Some of the remastered ("digitized") tracks I listened to sound awful on a transparent sounding IEM like the K2. I typically prefer to pull tracks from older Compact Discs as opposed to "remastered" releases. Most of the time the older CD's sound less "digitized" to my ears.

Treble:

The K2 treble is very button-down reserved despite it's decent extension. This is ideal for avoiding fatigue and enjoying extended listening sessions. Like the KC2, the K2 effectively eliminates upper midrange stridency and lower treble pierce by scooping the troublesome area between 4500hz and approximately 11000hz. To my ears, drawing down this region too severely tends to temper the dynamics a bit giving the upper midrange a veil-like or dulling effect on vocals and higher-pitched stringed instruments. The K2 seems to deftly walk the tightrope in balancing timbre and presence with a smooth delivery. Given the choice I'll always vote for increased dynamics (for EDM) but this type of delivery is right up my alley for Bach, Vivaldi and other baroque masters. Violins, oboes and trumpets all sound alive and well-rendered with rich timbre and good presence.

That said, the sparkle I find present in the ZS6 is not present in the K2. That's good news for the treble-sensitive I suppose but I maintain my position that well-tamed upper frequencies could lend more realism to the overall sound signature. As with the KC2, the "sparkle" of the bells/triangles in Toni Braxton's "He Wasn't Man Enough" were definitely missing. The percussion up top on Basement Jaxx's "Stay Close" did not have the sense of air I am used to. This is clearly due to the K2's treble roll off. A micro-detail junkie (me) will miss the sparkle and shimmer but the treble-sensitive listener (and most listeners) will be very happy with the K2's treble presentation.

Soundstage:

Like the KC2, this K2 has a good sense of air along with its ability to layer. Layering is good but it's mostly hindered by the KC2's average soundstage depth. More soundstage depth would give the KC2 a more dynamic presentation.

Bottom line: decent width with average depth.

Perhaps the BQEYZ BQ3 will improve on "soundstage depth" and dynamics with its reported "W" shaped sound signature. I'll be reviewing the BQ3 next so stay tuned.

What about response to EQ?

If your DAP has a very good EQ then you will find out just how well the K2 responds to it.

When I plugged the K2 in to my Cowon Plenue and hit "BBE" the K2 shifts into high gear. More toe tapping. More head bopping. Just more fun! In fact, just as much fun as my ZS6. The Cowon's "BBE" just unleashes the K2's real potential with more visceral bass impact and better texture, slightly wider soundstage and even a slight improvement in depth; again, not ZS6 depth but the sound signature remains clean while delivering more depth. It's sufficient to get your blood pumping. Be aware though that not all DAPs are created equal; Cowon DSP is, in my humble opinion, class-leading and quite extensive. You can tweak your music with an almost infinite number of setups.

Summary:

Everything is carefully measured to deliver a smooth and detailed presentation that never oversteps. The bass has added punch but avoids boom. The midrange avoids the uncomfortable strident behavior that other $50+/- hybrids models display (BGVP DM5) and the K2 treble avoids pierce. In short, the K2 emphasizes things just beyond the boundaries of having a balanced presentation but if "balanced" is your goal you should be looking at the KC2.

It is clear to me that BQEYZ focused their attention on tuning their product line and the K2 was tuned with a sense of smoothness and kick in mind. It's a little bit warmer and a tad smoother than the KC2. You'll enjoy these more if you listen to pop or more modern genres. The KC2 is slightly more vivid and transparent for vocal-oriented genres (folk, country, bluegrass, etc.). Both models are great for Jazz so it's a toss up.

Do you prefer smooth or do you prefer vivid?

Pick your poison.

The KC2 for a balanced presentation or this K2 for a smoother presentation with a little more kick.

An upgraded cable isn't necessary but you can personalize your IEM by finding eartips that work best for your ears. My favorite eartips are wide-bore Tennmak "Whirlwind" eartips but eartips with a more narrow bore may increase bass response and/or increase the midrange focus.

These really respond well to EQ but I just press the "BBE" button (Cowon Plenue) and it's on!

....all for $50, mind you!

They're quite good at a competitive price point.

Hope this was helpful.

Doc

title: Great product, but has some issues
text:
*** 1 Year Review Update ***

I decided to keep the system. After a few firmware updates and once TP-Link fixed the AP only mode such that the main and guest networks are truly separated I switched over from using it as a router to an AP solution. It has worked flawlessly since and without any performance degradation's.

I still do not like the app-centric approach for "management" (cannot call it that honestly); insight would probably be more appropriate. But, I will be moving in the future to an enterprise grade solution (this solution purchase has just been a stop-gap until that time and I finalize my network architecture). For the average home consumer that is not very tech-savvy (which is the audience this product really targets) it is overall very simple to get up and running with very few issues, especially at this price point.

I have submitted over a dozen feature requests to TP-Link and almost all of them have been discarded by the manufacturer (but at least acknowledged); of the ones that were "accepted" they were very trivial.

As of today, Sep 21 20201, the system via the app is no longer able to check for updates (it receives an error). I believe this is not due to the units themselves but instead TP-Link's update portal that the units use to check for updates. Checking on the main site reveals an update published on July 15 2021 (S4 2.0_en_1.5.0 Build 20210607 Rel. 56436_US_EU_AU_JP_up.bin) that is available which is one update newer than my currently applied firmware published on September 30 2020 (S4 2.0_en_1.4.3 Build 20200918 Rel. 77820_US_EU_AU_JP_up.bin). Looks like I will have to update the units manually using the download links provided by TP-Link and by logging into the web UI (note: each unit will have its own web UI but one - the master - will show a different one by showing you the topology of the mesh; a manual firmward update can be applied using that unit).

= Summary

Overall this is a great product. It definitely addresses the WiFi coverage in our new home. It has only been a few days since I set them up. However, a star in my rating had to be knocked off which will become evident shortly. I may update this review after some more time has passed. But it is currently appearing I might be returning this.

I operate these in access point mode and not router mode. I have a better router than what these units provide and do not need double NAT'ing on my house wide network. That, and, I will be replacing the house wide router with a substantially better one anyway in the coming months.

This review, however, covers my utilization and experience in both modes. Also note that I am an IT professional and deal with network infrastructure (along with many other things) day to day for over 20 years.

In this review the term “satellite” is used to denote a Deco unit that is not the main Deco unit.

I have intentionally saved the worst points of my review as the last section.

= Topology Setup

I have fiber to the premise gateway, still with the gateways’ Wi-Fi fully enabled on both 2.4Ghz and 5Ghz bands. My home is over 2,650 sqft, single story, built this year, with gigabit Cat5e cables to each room the Deco S4 units are situated. All Deco units use the Ethernet backhaul. All Cat5e runs and cables have been tested to support gigabit speeds point-to-point (with of course the obligatory TCP/IP overhead). Placement wise each of the Deco units are almost in a straight line, a function of my floor plan and where I need Wi-Fi coverage the most. Relative distances between Deco units:

- 25 linear feet between first satellite and second, main Deco unit with one interior door between. This I refer to as satellite 1.
- 45 linear feet between second satellite and main Deco unit with 3 interior only walls between. This I refer to as satellite 2.

= Performance

The throughput performance on these is fantastic, especially at the price point. I have fiber gigabit Internet service. I use speedtest.net for all bench marks. I get the following throughput on a Samsung Galaxy Note 8 (US), stock firmware, latest software and security patches. Distance is always the distance between my test device and a specific Deco unit and with line of sight between the test device and the target Deco unit.

| Deco | Distance | Downstream | Upstream |
Satellite 1 | 1 ft | 344 | 392 |
Main | 1 ft | 446 | 389 |
Satellite 2 | 1 ft | 460 | 392 |
Satellite 1 | 3 ft | 279 | 422 |
Main | 3 ft | 485 | 409 |
Satellite 2 | 3 ft | 392 | 383 |
Satellite 1 | 6 ft | 355 | 350 |
Main | 6 ft | 477 | 390 |
Satellite 2 | 6 ft | 483 | 461 |
Satellite 1 | 9 ft | 361 | 475 |
Main | 9 ft | 482 | 374 |
Satellite 2 | 9 ft | 477 | 466 |
Satellite 1 | 12 ft | 385 | 460 |
Main | 12 ft | 451 | 458 |
Satellite 2 | 12 ft | 501 | 528 |
Satellite 1 | 15 ft | 445 | 389 |
Main | 15 ft | 461 | 453 |
Satellite 2 | 15 ft | 500 | 432 |

A 15 foot distance between a Deco unit and a connected device is most likely acceptable considering average housing room sizes. However, in my house floor plan, I have an easy 25 foot line of sight from the main Deco unit to where I did a test. Results came in as 251 Mbps downstream and 117 Mbps upstream. Still, highly acceptable. At my maximum floor plan range to that same Deco unit and still maintaining line of sight of 33 feet I wind up getting an unexpectedly impressive 493 Mbps downstream and 388 Mbps upstream. While I cannot check in the app to see specifically which Deco unit my test device was connected to due to either app or overall product system issues, I am left with only one avenue of explanation: the Deco system has successfully performed link aggregation for my test device. If, in the first place, I am correct in this very poor conclusion due to the lack of data, then, this is indeed impressive and can very well be THE single most discriminator in overall product performance vs issues vs cost.

I realize these performance tests are not representative of real world scenarios. Fact is, most people do not go to such lengths to test their products and relevant environments, much less describe their environments.
When a little more time goes by I will update this review with more realistic real world performance tests in terms of longer distances and obstructions.

= The Good

I do not need parental controls, so, access point mode removes that for me, thankfully. Because I operate this in access point mode not having quality of service on the Deco's is just fine as is not having DHCP handled by the Deco's. Again, my current infrastructure handles all of these elegantly and more than sufficiently.

In order to get a proper pass off while going from one end of the house to the other I had to enable fast roaming. Without enabling this resulting in unbearably long hand offs from one unit to the other based on proximity to units. The net result of this was severe performance degradation. This seems to work without issue and solved the hand off issue.

The app is straightforward to use and easy to understand, ranging from initial installation to adding additional Deco's to day to day activities. The app also provides notifications of new devices when they are added to / detected on the network (both in router and access point modes).

As expected you can define a main Wi-Fi network and a guest network. This is standard fare. You can select if you want both 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands active or be more selective. Again, this is standard fare.

You can rename connected devices in the app. Useful especially when connected devices do not allow you to set their DHCP host name. The units try to profile a connected device type (e.g., Phone, PC, etc) in which the result of this is also easily accessible via the app. But, when it cannot or gets it wrong you can override this in the app, very useful feature indeed. The app will also show you basic information such as allocated IP address, MAC address (wish it was in colon delimited notation and not hypen as the former is the standard representation for MAC addresses), connection type (main or guest network and frequency band) and which Deco unit the device is currently linked to.

Unfortunately you cannot get the same level of information regarding devices connected to the guest network. Having visibility into this is just as important to give you another data point in your connected IoT devices. Oh, yeah, I suppose that people visiting your home is good too. Regardless, it is utterly unclear whether or not connected devices on the guest network have visibility to one another (e.g., can see each other), and much less have any reach into the main Wi-Fi or rest of your network. At a minimum, the default of any guest Wi-Fi network should be nothing can see anything else on the guest Wi-Fi , cannot see the main Wi-Fi, cannot see the rest of your network and can only see the Internet.

Any Deco unit can serve as the main. In router mode, this means that the main unit has routing capabilities. Likewise, a different unit can be specified as the main via the app.

= The Bad

There is no white listing of devices, only a black list. Security best practice is white listing devices that are authorized for access. Having only a black list is unacceptable. It is on this ground alone these units may very well be returned. It escapes me why TP-Link would fail to include the ability to white list. Since this product seems to be targeted to the less network technologically bound than myself I can understand why only a black list is available (to prevent the less technologically adept folks from effectively locking themselves out). However, not including a white list capability does an injustice to everyone and is, security wise, shameful and puts consumers’ home networks at additional unnecessary risk of exploitation. Yes, using a white list to winds up meaning having to go through a little more trouble to allow a new device onto the network. For me, and every other IT security professional out there, white listing is an essential tool in the security posture arsenal and is one that should never be omitted.

The only firmware release is the initial firmware release: Deco S4(US)_V2_191023 from December 25, 2019 (TP-Link support site). In the Deco app it reports no new updates for the firmware with a current version of 1.1.5 Build 20191023 Rel. 67285. Unzipping the firmware release on the support site shows the same firmware version as the app shows (specifically: S4 2.0_en_1.1.5 Build 20191023 Rel. 67285_US_EU_AU_JP_up.bin). Half a year later I would expect at least an additional firmware release. While not having any could be a good thing, generally, this is never the case. There are always bugs and vulnerabilities in every piece of software, and, firmware is no exception. Clearly a firmware update is needed at least to add a white list feature.

There is a barely usable web UI for the Deco's beyond that of just using the Deco app. I have found a landing page for each Deco connected to my router via the IP assigned to each. All UI's require authentication. The UI is different depending on which Deco you connect to. The Deco's that are not the main Deco provide the following features: update the firmware, pull the system log or reboot. Accessing the system log allows you to save it, email it or clear it. In contrast, connecting to the UI for the main Deco yields a subset of the features compared to the app but adds visibility into the units' CPU and memory usage. Said subset of features are mainly read only via the interface, again, not very useful. Thus there is no real point in using anything but the app if one is looking for access to more robust features.

Connected device presence status (online / offline) is wholly inaccurate as reported by the app. The only connected devices that are accurately reported for presence are those that have not left the Wi-Fi range and not power cycled. For example, all of my Fire TV sticks show as being online but all mobile devices that left the Wi-Fi range now show as offline despite being back within Wi-Fi range of the units for several hours. Even manually refreshing the view still yields in the app reporting these same mobile devices as being offline. More testing still needs to be performed, but, there is no reason why the device list status page in the app is this inaccurate.

Bandwidth utilization by connected device in the device list is great to have. The only problem is that it too is completely inaccurate to the same degree as mentioned previously regarding connected device presence status. For those devices that actually show as being online the bandwidth utilization shown in this same view is always 0Kbps up and downstream. Since installation of the units I have yet to see this populated and have seen, once, and only once, a single connected device bandwidth utilization being reported if I select the said device in the list.

There is no ability to perform a wireless site survey.

There is no ability to use 802.11x.

From a network management perspective there is no way to rename a specific Deco in terms of the host name that it will present to the rest of your network. All units show up simply as "deco-S4" from DHCP. Not useful.
There is no way to designate the guest network LAN IP address range.

= The Ugly

Initial set up was in router mode, the default. Setup of main and satellite 1 Deco’s went flawlessly and took but a few minutes per. Meanwhile, satellite 2 refuses to join the mesh in router mode and always leaves me staring at a red blinking light. The app reports “Unable to add these Decos” and “Move these Decos closer to a Deco that you’ve already set up, then tap TRY AGAIN.” Why would anyone have to move a Deco unit closer to another? They have an Ethernet backhaul, and by definition, can communicate with each other!

Meanwhile, the engineer within me takes a different stance: while all Deco units indeed have a gigabit Ethernet backhaul each unit must be able to verify a minimal Wi-Fi signal level from its closest neighbor. And, since I am a customer facing type of person that voice inside of me would scream: in order to assure the best possible experience please ensure all Deco units have no physical obstructions between them and that none are surrounded by things that can block radio frequencies such as metal and concrete.

Point is, I have yet to get all three Deco units online in router mode at all. It is NOT an option to bring any units closer together. Satellite 2 Deco has been power cycled and reset (via the reset button on the bottom of the unit) half a dozen times per with precisely the same results.

Now, putting the system into access point mode results in a perfectly usable system without any of these problems. Wish I knew why. Regardless, this is a telltale sign to me of poor engineering. Of course, switching system modes from router to access point (or vice versa) results in the system rebooting all Deco’s. The majority of most modern residential Wi-Fi capable routers do not require a reboot when making this change.

This is so problematic that it is cause, alone, for me to return the product.

title: Mediocre feaures in a supermodel skin.
text:
I am extremely technologically inclined, i understood before purchasing this product its limitations and purchased it anyway for its looks and build quality.

Suunto is an excellent manufacturer, there dive computers are the ultimate in the field.
Positives:
The watch is absolutely beautiful, large (reason i bought it) and exceedingly well built/ high quality. The watch is water resistent rated so a quick dip/shower/rain should be no trouble. The wear OS system has many usefull apps available, the suunto fitness framework is excellent with many different fitness modes, offline map functionality, gps tracking, heart rate monitor works very well, it is accurate and quick. The heat maps are interesting if not extremely useful. Suunto fitness app is full of features and its very accurate and useful in many ways. The watch has NFC for google pay which works on most POS card readers/ all card readers with touchless functionality. (this is my first smart watch and i really wanted the Samsung gear s3 for its MST technology where you can pay with your watch on any terminal NFC compatible or not ! just like samsung phones, but the watch is years old, discontinued and still high priced / hard to find brand new). The google pay works perfectly, the watch faces have 3 customizable buttons, i keep weather, google pay, and batter info on mine and its perfect throughout the day for functionality. The watch can act as a google translator which its built in mic, you can have a conversation with a speaker of another language right on your wrist, and it works great. The watch will display every notification from your phone, you can reply to text message and start new text messages, you can make calls that pickup on your phone, you are alerted of incoming calls even though you cannot take them. you can reply and write new emails outlook app is available as well as gmail i believe. the gps works great and google maps is available so you can get directions right from your wrist as you walk or drive. it has a timer, stopwatch , compass app is available it has weather app contacts and messages the play store and google assistant which can search the web for you. battery saver feature is available as well as ring my phone to find it. The watch connects to the phone via bluetooth but also has built in wifi and can have full functionality without blutooth if the watch is on wifi and the phone has data service of any kind, i like that feature. the screen lock options are good and secure the speech to text works smooth and accurately and the on screen keyboard is tiny but surprisingly easy to use and accurate/functional despite its small size and my fat fingers. you can customize two of the 4 buttons to open any app you want,, and more watch faces are availabe through the play store from 3rd party sources. its very comfortable to wear all day, its extremely solid, i love it despite the few negatives i outline below.

Negatives:
The Suunto 7 falls short in a few categories. As a smart watch it lacks some basic features, you cannot make phone calls directly through the watch is has no speaker, it can control media playback on the phone but cannot play music it has no speaker. It has no camera, the watch has its own built in GPS module but GPS must be turned on in the phone as well for it to connect, that bothers me. The 7 has no sim card slot and is not a standalone phone so the phone must always be in bluetooth range for functionality. The battery will last two days but no more, no matter what the use case it lasts two days. when the watch is on continuous display it will last about a day. with the watch on raise arm to display mode the watch face does not appear long enough for me and that cannot be changed. I had an issue uninstalling an app that turned out to be useless and the watch didnt seem to complete the uninstall of the app, i reset the watch and started over which is a fairly lengthy process. Sometimes the wear os connectivity with the phone fails for no reason and the phone cannot be reached message comes up while every other connectivity with the phone is fine. the built in watch faces are very limited. Wear OS is a google product and if you are not a fan of google like me you are pretty much stuck with relying on google for the watches operation however this is common among some smart watches. web browser options are very limited on this watch. there is no youtube, it has okay google listening functionality but it has stopped working for me and i find that rather annoying because i actually use OKay google quite often on my phone tablets etc.

title: Great device, one lesson learned for new buyers...
text:
All in all this tuner is terrific and works as advertised. I set it up alongside Plex and it works great.

One lesson learned however: When I initially was setting the HDHomeRun up, I connected it to an indoor OTA antenna that had one of the little usb-powered signal amplifiers. (alot of the indoor antennas seem to come with these now). I found that when scanning for channels I was only getting roughly 6 channels when I expected to be getting alot more. After alot of fiddling and trial and error, I connected the antenna directly to the HDHomeRun without the little usb-powered amplifier, and this completely solved my issue. Scanning picked up 35 channels and their signal quality is great. I'm guessing that there may be a signal amplifier built into the HDHomeRun and that having the little usb-powered one amplifying the signal as well was somehow interfering with that.

title: Music, in your ear, without wires? Holy Future Batman
text:
So I've owned these bad boys for a little bit over a week. I've made some phone call, listened to some music, miraculously haven't lost them (knowing myself that's a huge feat) So you may ask, what can I tell you about them ... Here we go...

Sound Quality: you know when you but a budget pair of headphones that exceed all expectations and you feel like a MENSA genius for getting such a great deal? Now multiply that by at least 7. These earbuds sound pretty damn awesome regardless of genre, like not $40/$50 awesome, legitimately awesome. Not true wireless earbuds awesome, but any earbud wired awesome. These things will sound great with your high fidelity ripped straight from vinyl recordings, you don't need a DAC and Preamp you snob, just enjoy the ultimate convenience and portability. Also, super sound isolating with many fitment options.

Durability: well so far they've held up, and have been put through the ringer. Only complaint would be the hinge for the lid of the charging case, I would like that to feel a little more overbuilt but that may be more of a personal issue. Otherwise, hell yeah for now.

Wirelessness: they don't have them.

Call quality: dual microphones seem to work very very well, no noticable dropoff in quality during phone calls, so that's cool

Misc Complaints/Thoughts:. It would be cool to have a "find my earbuds" feature in the future with some app support, also app support to change sound profiles like other Back Bay devices are able to do. Would love to see a more durable case, perhaps some earbud tips that aren't so spectacularly noise cancelling, letting some ambient noise in would be great especially when earbuds are used primarily in a workplace setting or for phone calls

Battery life: so far so good, seems to last as long as stated, which is incredible considering poor battery performance on other wireless options.

All in all, these things are most definitely worth the cost, they punch 2-3x above their weight class. I couldn't be happier with my purchase, but would be just as happy if I had paid twice the price.

Glad to finally be on trend for something.
Another spectacular product by Back Bay Audio

text:
Okay, I will first say that I am no "Pro" or "reputable" source but I do love photography. Since going over to Fujifilm, I've been in the market for a 23mm lens but the only choices I had were the Fujifilm made ones. I like the portability of the f/2 but I always liked the rendering of the f/1.4. When I heard that Viltrox was offering their 23, 33, and 56 at these prices, I figured I had to have them all. I use the 23mm Fujifilm X-T3 and X-H1. The auto-focus has been very fast, comparable to the Fujinon 35mm and way faster than the 18-55 kit. Low light shooting has been good as well. The only thing I wish I could have would be weather sealing but I have to remember this lens is only $330. For me, this lens punches above it's price. The only issues are the chromatic aberrations (which can be fixed in post) but it's not that significant. Also this lens renders like an old film lens. You'll get some elements of "character" that'll feel very welcomed if you're in to that.

If you're looking for a 23mm for the Fujifilm X-system and on the fence, just buy this. It's cheaper than the OEMs and performs just as well.

This product is a true pioneer on the market for 4K UHD dash camera. I can tell that the customer service team has been trying to collect feedback and take the feedback very seriously. Supporting team continues to improve the product and upgrade their software very frequently with new improvements. I have been communicating with Helen from customer service team since I bought the camera. She is very patient and responsive. And for the super great customer service -- always reachable and stand behind their product, which really gave me a peace of mind and built up my confidence of using this camera.

Update (05/24/2021): today my dashcame went dead. It first kept on and off by itself. The it went black completely. title: Great monitor but false advertisement
text:
I gave everything 5 starts but the overall 2 stars. Here are why -
It is a great monitor after I set it up, no dead pixel for me, back-light issue is minimum to me, but just compare to the front page images or video provided along with this selling item, they are photoshopped.

The display does not go all the way to the frame edge, there is an almost 3/8 inch (1cm) gap between the frame and to the display area/margin. When you have two monitors side by side, the gap is more than the plastic frames. To me - If you showed people the full-screen display (regardless the outer frame) in your ads, you should sell the same product. I agree with other reviewers for this false advertisement this really misleads people to buy it because of that fake images. I do see they used "Edgeless" in the product descriptions, so this is very much a false advertisement.

Other than that, VERY noticeable glare (see pictures) even in the gap/black areas (inside the plastic frame to the real display areas). Solution is to use a dark background. For backlight issue - adjust the "backlight" (in OSD / Picture) to about 25. (Default is 80), this may help.

Monitor does 75 Hz. For people who claimed not be able to get the 75Hz it seems a human error.

The last thing - the VESA mount is at its BOTTOM part at the back of the monitor. If you have a two monitors mounting arm, then you can't balance the height if you have any older monitor.

title: This is real BT 5!
text:
So I bought several usb bluetooth adaptors from ebay mainly to use to connect to my headphone to listen to music on my headphone (Bose NC700). I am often more then 20 to 30 feet away from the computer or in the next room over or down in the basement or upstair. The main reason for getting BT 5 is because the range was better and I don't get sound drop or crackling. No surprise, the ones from ebay were BT4 with the with the old name erased and a "v5.0" printed on. It didn't let me step more than a few feet away before dropping or not connecting at all.
On this last attempt, I thought I would give this a try. Reading the spec, I thought it was only BT4. At first when you plug it into your PC, it doesn't detect it as BT 5 device, you have to upgrade the driver using the CD they included. After software install and a restart. I came up as "Realtek Bluetooth 5.0 Adaptor" I didn't believe it, so I tested it using Bluetooth Version Finder and it shows as 5.1!
I've been using this for a couple of weeks now with my headphone. Overall the sound quality is great and I can be 20 to 30 feet away without crackling or drop. I went to the next room, basement (right below), and upstairs; there were a few crackling once in a while when I'm on the move, but once steady it went through the walls just fine.
I have not tested this with other devices such as Bluetooth keyboard or mouse, but headphone works great.
I would definitely recommend this to anyone looking for cheap BT5 adaptor to work with your headphone.

title: It works fine
text:
This was the least expensive of such available devices, and it does work. And they supply enough screws and mounting hardware that even if you lose a piece, you can still make things work. The case is small and sleek and feels right. It gets warm when the drive is running.

I did not install the "thermal conduction pad" because it would then cover the label on the drive and make things like serial numbers inaccessible, and also because I occasionally swap drives, so what's the point? But the WD Black drive I'm currently using doesn't run too hot (under 40 degrees C).

My one issue with the device is that the USB-C female connector on it is not sufficiently deep so that cables sit flush with the case using any of my many USB-C cables. This makes the connection feel slightly insecure, and in fact at one point the access speeds dropped to half from their normal speed, and reseating the supplied cable at the drive end brought performance back to normal. One star off for that.

Be aware that they are very clear that this supports 10Gbps speeds while USB-C supports higher speeds than that, and so your very, very fast Nvme drive will likely perform at roughly half the speed of which it is capable. That was OK for me, as I mostly use this for data storage and backup applications, but I wanted to note it if your use was more dependent on speed. Frankly, the perceived difference between 1500 Mb/s and 3000 Mb/s read speeds in real life is a rounding error.

If you're looking for something like this, I would recommend this one.

title: ALMOST the perfect budget earphones for most people.
text:
Pros
+Decent sound for the price ($20)
+Extremely comfortable. The foam tips create a secure fit without the rest of the earphones touching my ears at all.
+Seemingly high build quality. I doubt these will break over time.

Cons:
-Cable is noisy when shaken around. This wouldn't be an issue if we could use the "loop over the ears" method, which completely removes this issue, however the volume control module is way, way too high up the cable, so you end up looking like you're wearing a volume control earring when you loop them over your ears.
-There ARE better sounding earphones around this price range, although they come with their own list of cons (namely quality control).
-Only one set of foam tips; the spares are silicone. Considering that the foam tips are a selling point of the product, there should probably be more included.

Overall, if these stay in working condition and don't exhibit any hidden comfort issues, they are a fine set of earphones for use while standing or sitting. If the volume module is moved lower down the cable, allow these earphones to be looped over the ears, use while running or exercising would be easier to recommend. At that point, they would be the perfect general use earphones, and excellent backups for audiophiles to carry around.

This review will be updated if anything unusual comes up.

title: Excellent noise figure; high Gain amplifier for observing the Milky Way.
text:
A group of high school teachers is working with West Virginia University and the National Science Foundation to build and test student build radio telescopes for observing the Milky Way Galaxy. These will teach the students about electronics and astronomy.

A critical part of the radio telescope is the first, low noise amplifier. The NooElec Amplifier is custom designed for radio astronomy observations. It has high gain and a good RF filter for reducing interference. The 1st figure (with Red ruler) shows the amplifier attached to the feed horn. The second figure shows the NooElec Amplifier in a test horn pointing at the ground. In the background is the larger horn we use for the Milky Way Observations.

The three plots show the observations with the test horn. The figure with two separate graphs shows the "HOT" load, looking at the ground (Red upper line) and "COLD" load (lower, looking at the sky). The x axis is frequency in MHz, and y axis intensity in raw counts.

To make astronomical measurements requires calibration. Computing the ratio of HOT and COLD gives the temperature plot, with an excellent receiver temperature of between 90-110 Kelvin. This is very good performance. The Milky Way Spiral Arms are seen in the broad feature in the middle of the plot. The narrower lines are interference.

The 3rd plot shows the Milky Way galaxy with a baseline subtracted. The data were taken only with the all aluminum test horn (14 inches in diameter). The x axis is velocity of the hydrogen relative to the Earth and the y axis is intensity of the hydrogen at that velocity.

title: Most things are good (even Very Good), 2 Complaints (1 BIG Complaint)
text:
TCL overlooks a VERY IMPORTANT element of TV viewing: Over the Air ("OTA") Programming (which actually provides higher quality video than most streaming sources). Previously, TCL didn't even include a TV Tuner--it erroneously assumed nobody uses OTA (antenna) reception anymore. Fortunately they have corrected this oversight by including an adequate TV Tuner, yet they still make OTA programming extremely difficult to watch, by providing a totally inadequate Remote Control that doesn't have a number keypad to select the Channel that you want to watch (instead of switching through all of them, one at a time). I like my local Channel 4.1 "NBC," my local Channel 50.2 "PBS" and several others. Switching between them with the Pathetic Remote that is included is Extremely Time Consuming AND Frustrating. Surely Roku doesn't require them to include such an Inadequate Remote!!! I have searched, and so far I am not able to find a third party Remote that is stated to provide this function---and I'm not particularly interested in buying third party Remotes just to see if they might in fact provide this function on the 65R617. (Seems like an adequate Remote would be a small investment for TCL to make a Good TV, GREAT.)

My second complaint is the fact that with todays cornucopia of entertainment sources, 3 HDMI ports is simply inadequate---it can't be that difficult or expensive to include more HDMI ports. (AGAIN, a small investment for TCL to make a Good TV, GREAT.)

title: Great little headphones for lifting or running
text:
I was initially blown away by the ease of use of this product. You only have to pair the headset once and you're set forever.

Now, I will give my ONLY complaint up front. It has no power button. You'd think it would be a huge issue but the device powers off when it is placed back in the case and turns on when removed. Just be aware of this if you suddenly need to take a call or turn them off. Additionally, the case recharges the earbuds and the battery life has been impressive.

The headsets have a great pairing distance and do not suffer from constant disconnects like you see in many wireless earbuds in this style. The ear buds can also be used single or both at any time. The controls on the side of the headset are not a button but are simple touch.

Touch once, the music pauses. Touch again, resume. Double tap the right ear to skip songs or double tap left ear to go back. The instructions are ....not the best but once you grasp what they're trying to tell you it clicks quickly.

I've been very impressed with the sound quality at this price point. Is this the best sound you'll ever hear? No. Is it better than almost all other 20 dollar wireless earbud? Yes.

I've also already logged about 10 miles jogging in these and have had no issues with them falling out or the need for constant adjustment. They come with 3 different ear sizes and its important you set that correctly before going on a run.

Overall I'm impressed that you get so much at this price point. I would definitely recommend these for sports and outdoors. If you accidentally lose them, you're not out 200 dollars and you don't look like a DJ trying to lift in the gym.

title: Update: Fragile? Great for travel. Included cord isnt great.
text:
Update: Product just stopped working after brief use over these three months.

Overall, this miniature dock is a fantastic accesory to travel with. The tilting feature, all be it a bit finicky to snap it in place, is useful for certain seating arrangements. I only used the HDMI feature once, but in that one time there was no issue with it.

I originally bought this so that I can play Super Smash Brother Ultimate with my gamecube controllers, and for that it is really solid. I don't use the included charging cord because it does seem a bit cheap, but that isn't an issue since my Anker battery came with one when I used the portable battery to power the dock to play with my wired controllers. I usually hook the dock up with the Switch power brick if I want to charge the Switch while in use. I find myself using it for more games than just Smash while I'm at my desk, though. Another point of concern is the docking itself, it does wiggle a bit if keep trying to adjust the position or if the surface it's on is unstable. However, this is to be expected when you rest a large switch onto a small dock with a usb-c port and a roughly 1.5 cm notch. There is also no feedback when you initially dock it like with the first party dock. Which goes without saying, but don't keep pushing down on the dock expecting a click or a noise like the original dock. Power is no issue so far to the battery of the Switch, especially compared to some other third party docks.

So all things considered. Some pros are that this product is great for tavelling, great if you prefer to play with a stand that isn't the Switch kick stand, convenient and sleek. Some cons are that the included cord isn't the best quality and for some who are clumsy may break the port if they misuse the product or are rough with both the console and product (i.e. children).

title: Prints Anything and Everything From Galaxy Phone; Easy to Set Up
text:
I really like this HP ENVY 6055 WIRELESS ALL-IN-ONE PRINTER (5SE16A). Finally I’m able to print anything and everything from my Samsung Galaxy S10 cell phone! To set it up with an Android phone, you need two apps from Google Play: HPSmart, and HP Print Service Plugin.

SETUP. Once you have HPSmart, you turn on the printer, open the app, and follow the prompts. The app finds the printer, helps you connect it to your home network, and takes you through the process of loading paper, installing two ink cartridges, and aligning the copier. From time to time, a prompt will tell you to press a lighted or flashing button on the printer in order to proceed.

The setup process isn’t difficult, but you should start it when you have maybe 20-30 minutes to devote to it. There are enough steps that you don’t want to get interrupted in the middle.

HPSMART APP. Something that I really love about the printer, is that I can use my phone to make it scan a document and send the document to an email address. The phone can control all of the printer functions through the HPSmart display--it just takes a tap on a virtual button. I asked the printer to print a photo from my phone’s Gallery, and it came out beautifully. The photo that I took outside my home with the phone’s camera and immediately sent to the printer also came out beautifully.

MANUAL CONTROLS. You can also control the printer manually, at least for copying. When you open the printer cover, the buttons for the number of copies and copying light up. However, this printer is easiest to control with the HPSmart app. (I need to visit the HP web site and download the full manual--the closest now is the Envy 6400 all-in-one printer manual--because the lighted buttons aren’t quite intuitive.) Other mobile devices on my home network (e.g., my iPad Air) are able to find the printer and use it like any other printer on my network.

SPEED; COPY QUALITY; INK The printer is quite fast, and the quality of the printing is excellent. The ink colors are bright and the printing is extremely crisp and clear (even with fine print). The printer uses HP 67 ink cartridges--which are definitely NOT discontinued (as another reviewer reported). My local Staples store has the ink in stock right now (July 2020).

INSTANT INK PROGRAM. If you like, you can sign up for the optional HP Instant Ink program, and the printer will automatically order ink for you. I chose the “Moderate” program, which assumes printing about 100 pages per month, for $4.99 a month (after the first 2 months’ free trial). If you don’t print that many pages, you can carry over the unused pages to a later month (up to a set number of pages). You can cancel the Instant Ink program at any time.

APPEARANCE. The printer has a sleek, low profile. It’s white, which means it will blend in with the decor of any room.

title: Dummy battery makes bad contact with Fuji XT3
text:
The dummy battery (the "battery" portion of this item) is slightly smaller than the battery for the Fuji XT3. It's shorter by less than a milimeter, but that's enough for the metal strips on the dummy battery to sometimes fail to make contact with the camera. For example, when using the camera as a webcam for zoom, even bumping the tripod a bit will often cause the dummy battery to lose contact and hence for the camera to turn off. I can tell it's a problem with contact because if I push the dummy battery further into the battery compartment, the camera will turn back on. Sometimes it takes many minutes of adjusting to make it regain contact and hence to make the camera stay on. I've since fixed it by adding a few strips of scotch tape to pad out the bottom of the battery, which makes it artificially longer, but this was a christmas gift to my mom and if I weren't around there's no way she would have been able to fix it, which would have made it effectively worthless.

I know this item does not advertise compatibility with the XT3, but it does advertise compatibility with the XT2, which uses the same battery as the XT3, so I can only assume the same problem would occur on the XT2.

title: Excellent way to upgrade from mp3s.
text:
I was content with playing mp3s through my phone until I got a set of studio monitor speakers for home recording on my Mac. Then I realized: there IS a difference. Even as a 55 year old with mild tinnitus I could hear the difference, I could hear things I'd never heard before on recordings I'd listened to for years. So flac is good, there IS something to be gained by upgrading.

I shopped around and compared with my dearth of knowledge. My logical point was that Plenue makes high end players that I could never rationalize buying, but that means they must know their stuff. So I bought the far more affordable Plenue J, knowing I'd be sacrificing screen size and graphics glitz for sound quality.

I haven't had the opportunity to compare this to other brands on a level playing field, but I am very happy with what I got. It is true that the graphics interface is not fantastic, but this thing is small, battery life is excellent, and the sound is what I was hoping for. Now I'm picking apart the production of the music, rather than the limitations of my player. You expect jazz and classical to sound good, but Judas Priest - Defenders of the Faith was a revelation. I will be checking producer credits on albums from now on.

So yes, I got what I wanted, and I recommend it. There are better and more expensive players out there, but the price/quality ratio likely doesn't get much better than this.

title: Comfortable earbuds with good dynamic range
text:
I like the MORPHEUS PULSE 360 for the comfort and dynamic range.

If booming Bass is a criteria then these are not the earbuds to get. But for a good crisp sound across the audio range with distinct instrument performance these are the earbuds that fit. The Bass does pop with drums. Listening to a drum solo the drum sound was responsive and not flat but reverberated. String Bass had good bounce. In the mid range these ear buds really shine. Orchestra, Big Band, Classical Music, Rock Groups and individual instruments all sound clear, good tonality, vibrant and dynamic sound. Instruments like the Banjo and Mandolin could be heard with the very distinct sound each produce. The Banjo with the twange and a little reverb.

Separation and reverb are excellent. Playing electronic music with the funky sound switching from one side to the other back and forth quickly and then voice in the center these earbuds gave a superb performance. In the classical and opera pieces the quiet passages were .....quiet!

The earbuds arrived partially charged. I placed a full charge on them prior to Review Test. The two charge lights are a red/blue color indicating charge required. When charge is complete the lights turn solid blue then turn off. To PAIR, the Device is placed into Bluetooth mode. The LEFT Earbud (only) is removed from the case and it’s name appeared on the device. Then the Right Earbud is removed from the case and it will pair with the left. It required two times for the earbuds to pair with one another. But then no issues. There is a USB Charge Cable and two extra sets of Silicone ear tips. I found the ones already fitted from the factory very comfortable for me.

Recommended - Four 😃😃😃😃 Star

I've tried a couple of other loupes from different manufacturers in an attempt to save money, but they did not work as well as this original Hoodman loupe. Perfect fit for my Nikon D810. Does a great job with blocking out light in the environment, but I don't want to have to hold it in place. Those elastic bands from Hoodman are too expensive and really don't work very well, according to several reviewers. I want to use adhesive to attach this loupe to my D810's snap-on screen protector which is made of plastic, but I'm unsure which adhesive would be best for this task. I will do some more research on this and may post an updated review. The advantage would be my Hoodman loupe being more securely attached to my D810, held in place by the snap-on points of the Nikon BM-12 screen protector, which also makes it removable when I want to use just the screen without a loupe...or I could just unclip and remove the eyepiece portion of my Hoodman H32MB loupe, leaving just the base still attached.

title: several problems with this thing
text:
First, the unit is so light that the cables decide where it will reside. The solution is to glue it down with double-sided that, but that presents another problem.

The indicator lights DON'T. They don't light up at all or too tiny to be seen unless, maybe, you are sitting 3 inches away from them,. Right now I have this thing hooked up feeding a 34" LG monitor from (a) a W10 box w/i7-2600K and (b) a Cheese Grater Mac Pro 4.1/5.1, both of this are 9-10 years old. And I'm viewing the Mojave OS screen on the LG and writing this.

To get to the W10 screen all I can do is push the button until it pops up. And there is a noticeable lag. NO INDICATOR LIGHTS come on. I had to push the button 4-5 times and wait 3-6 seconds for each potential screen to come up. And when it does, the screens are scrambled.

I suspect some of this is due to lack of a device power supply but I don't know.

I would recommend looking for one of these with a real power supply. And maybe a remote control.

This is a sorry piece of work.

title: Its a zippy machine. The windows experience rivals my 3900x Desktop.
text:
Was kinda blown away with how fast this CPU is on a laptop. Laptop looks nice, its a nice weight, nice keyboard, display has nice vibrance and clarity. 144hz is great for a laptop. Only issue I have with it is it gets too hot, but I got a cooling pad which helps it stay cooler. Intensive games will get it up to 80s Celcius even with the pad though. This is acceptable for my usage of the laptop which will be intermittent, but I do not recommend this machine if you are planning on using it every day or for several hours a day, as the heat will undoubtedly cause longevity issues with constant use. Obviously if you get a lower tier GPU it wont get as hot. I read around online that I can do some undervolting as well to cool it down, will fiddle with that eventually, but supposedly the temps are 'fine for a laptop'. *shrug*.

Still happy with it

title: Hardware and DVR Client Fail To Deliver
text:
I purchased this DVR to pair with my HD Home Run Connect Quattro and my clear QAM cable TV. I read reviews that talked about how it interfaced simply with other Silicon Dust products. Before I purchased I searched the support forums and read of issues with the client including audio not being in sync with the video, the lack of a grid-style guide and the glitches in the client after the June upgrade but I decided to give it a try regardless.

After a couple of weeks I have reverted back to my old DVR solution. The DVR setup with other Silicon Dust products was seamless. Just as expected, I plugged it into the same switch as my Quattro tuner and ran through the setup. Within minutes it was configured.

The deal breaker for me is the DVR client. It is nowhere near as refined as it should be. In the support forums the Silicon Dust support staff recommend using other hardware and clients (NVidia Shield seems to be the preferred option) to get around the inadequacies of their DVR client. This would be an option for some but not for me as I am already an Amazon Fire TV, Windows PC, Samsung Galaxy and Xbox user. It all seemed great for a few days as I learned the ins and outs of the DVR app. I ran into a few things that I thought were user error but they were repeatable and I soon realized that the client was not going to live up to my expectations.

Perhaps after a major DVR client upgrade I will give it another try but for now my family and I have too many complaints about this product and its' related software.

title: Great customer service, still to be determined on the product
text:
I am probably going to edit this review as time goes on. I gave 4 stars for sound quality, material quality, and battery life but I gave 5 stars overall? The reason is because of quality customer service. I’m not an audiophile so I’ll never rate something better than 4 stars when it comes to sound. But, in my ‘non-audiophile’ opinion, these sound pretty good. My purpose for getting them though was not to listen to music, but to listen to my television while I ran/jogged on a treadmill. With the aptX-LL, it was perfect for me. There was absolutely no lag between video and audio, I’m very happy with regard to that. Unfortunately, after one use, one of the earbuds separated. I’m sure it was an anomaly and I contacted the company and they sent a replacement to me right away. I received that one and used it just fine, once. Unfortunately, this one ‘disconnected’ gave me a ‘low battery’ and never worked again. Hopefully this is another anomaly. Again, I contacted the company, and they sent me another one that same day. This 3rd one is going to be the one that tells the tale for me. If all goes well, this stays a well rated product. Another problem and I’ll adjust my review to reflect, ask for a refund, and cut my losses. I don’t think I can give an unbiased review on the battery life as I will never get to the point where I don’t have battery life left before I plug in to recharge. Overall, when I have used these, I’ve really loved them, I’m just hoping that the pairs that I received were just hiccups.
EDIT #1: I have downgraded the rating from a 5 to a 2. You guessed it, the THIRD pair that the company sent me, only lasted me 3 uses. At the second use, I noticed a 'crackling' coming from the left earbud. Kind of sound you'd expect from a broken wire that was connecting and disconnecting. I'd adjust the wire to it and it'd go away for awhile. By the third use, the crackling was permanent and painful to listen to. Another thing was it gave me the "low battery" warning. Didn't last as long as I'd like, but 3 uses I can live with before I recharge. I plugged it in, and let it charge over night, came back to it and it didn't charge at all. The little red light was still on. I put it back in, and between all the crackling, it said it had a "low battery". Plugged it back in, went to work, came home (many hours later) and little red light is still on. As I said, when I contacted the company, they were very responsive and apologetic for the product. But this is strike 3 and I think it's time to cut my losses. I used when I would jog/run on my treadmill. I break a pretty good sweat when I run. Maybe the issue is that they aren't really sweat resistant? Maybe if I used these to sit on a couch and watch tv or sit in a cubicle and watch videos or listen to music, they would work fine. I used them to run with, to sweat on and to pretty much have a constant jostle as I ran, they didn't work for me.

title: Versatile battery tester. Clumsy to use. Cheapish construction.
text:
I had a similar unit from Radio Shack that served me well for more than twenty years until I misplaced it.

Several similar, if not identical, units are offered on Amazon. I’d suggest going with the lowest priced one.

Construction feels a bit on the cheapish side, but with careful handling, I suspect it will last a long time.

There’s a platform that is used to check voltage on AAA, AA, C, D ad some button at batteries.. Battery handling is a bit clumsy. The platform is flat and there are no guides for holding the batteries and I found it a bit tricky to properly position and hold batteries on the platform. You slide a piece along the platform to make contact and get your readout on the color coded meter.

On one end of the unit, there are contacts for measuring 9V batteries.

Overall, I’m reasonably pleased with this purchase.

Jerry

title: Fits Alienware m15 -- five sleeves reviewed!
text:
TL;DR
Winner = Tomantek is my choice https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B073QFMPK1/

Full story:
I recently bought an m15 and spent WAY too much time searching for a case/sleeve for it. Hoping to save other m15 owners some time.

I was having trouble finding one that was large enough to accommodate the unusual dimensions of the m15 AND yet also be small enough to fit in my Wenger Synergy backpack's designated laptop pouch.

Wenger Synergy Backpack, Gray (GA-7305-14F00)
https://www.amazon.com/Wenger-Synergy-Backpack-Gray-GA-7305-14F00/

I eventually found 5 cases/sleeves that the m15 would fit in, but some were just too wide for the backpack. And by “wide” I mean, when stored rotated 90-degrees, it would stick out and I could not zip closed my backpack. Either way, I'm going to share my results for other m15 owners...

These are the 5 sleeves I bought for testing:

1. ZinMark Laptop Case Sleeve 15.6-Inch, Spill-Resistant Protective Case for 15.4-Inch MacBook Pro A1286 / Retina A1398 and Most 15.6-Inch Laptop Ultrabook Netbook, (15.67 x 11.02 in) Dark Gray
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B0733B1FF5/

2. Lacdo 15.6 Inch Laptop Sleeve Bag Compatible Acer Aspire/Predator, Toshiba, Dell Inspiron, ASUS P-Series, HP Pavilion, Lenovo, MSI GL62M, Chromebook Notebook Carrying Case, Water Resistant, Gray
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B01MRYRI9N/

3. Evecase Laptop Sleeve, 15~15.6 inch Diamond Foam Splash & Shock Resistant Neoprene Universal Sleeve Zipper Case Bag for Dell HP Gaming Chromebook Ultrabook Notebook - Black
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00LFJ88SQ/

4. MOSISO Laptop Sleeve Bag Compatible 15-15.6 Inch MacBook Pro, Ultrabook Netbook Tablet with Small Case, Shock Resistant Diamond Foam Water Repellent Neoprene Protective Carrying Cover, Black
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B071VX1YZM/

5. TOMANTEK [Best Comfortable Laptop Sleeve Ever] TOMANTEK 15-15.6 Inch PU Polyester Slow-recovery Sponge Shockproof & Water-resistant Laptop Sleeve Case Bag/Ultrabook Laptop Tablet Bag Case/Skin Cover, Black
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B073QFMPK1/

Note: For comparison purposes, my particular m15 laptop weighs exactly 5lbs, 1.0oz (2.3kg).

The Zinmark is a nice dark gray with two metal zipper pulls. The opening extends on the long edge. It has a nice furry interior and an extra zipper pocket running the full height of the sleeve. I like two zippers over one because it allows me to zip it closed with an AC adapter still connected. Plus, if one zipper breaks, you're not screwed. Unfortunately, there is some resistance to zip it closed due to the depth of the m15 (measuring from the front to back of the laptop), so it’s a bit tight there, and at 16" wide, it doesn't fit in my backpack.
Weight = 8.7oz (246g)
Total weight with m15 laptop = 5lbs, 9.7 oz. (2.54kg).

I like the Lacdo a lot with its extra pockets (two zippered pockets on front + one pouch on the back. It’s great if you just carry your laptop around or have enough room in your backpack/briefcase for it. But at 16.5” wide, it wouldn’t fit in mine. Plus, you really are limited to slim items in the zippered pockets (pens, notebooks, USB drives, etc.). A travel mouse would add a lot of bulk (unless you have the one from Microsoft that folds flat – that’s what I use). Two metal zipper pulls plus a soft felt lining with no tags inside make this an ideal case for an m15 owner that wants the ability to store and carry other items including files folders and documents. Those extra pockets do add significant weight, though. It’s the heaviest of the bunch.
Weight = 11.4 oz (324g)
Total weight with m15 laptop = 5lbs, 12.6oz (2.63kg)

The Evecase is great, if you don’t mind neoprene. The thick pyramid-shaped exterior pattern offers good crush protection, but since it’s only the points of each pyramid are what come in contact with whatever surface it’s on, it slides around easy, such as on a car seat. Being pointy neoprene, it’s quite flimsy when empty and, quite thick when a laptop is stored inside. Also, an “Evecase” logo is stitched on one side of the soft felt liner. That could possibly cause scratches or wear marks on your laptop over time. While I do like the think rubber zipper pull, there is only one pull, and I prefer two.
Weight = 7.8 oz (220g).
Total weight with m15 laptop = 5lbs, 8.9oz (2.52kg).

The MOSISO is identical to the Evecase above, except it has two metal zipper pulls instead of one rubber pull. It also comes with a smaller version good for a travel mouse, portable hard drive, or cables, etc. It’s much to small to fit in an AC adapter.
Weight (excluding bonus carry pouch) = 7.8 oz (220g).
Total weight with m15 laptop = 5lbs, 8.9oz (2.52kg).

Last, but not least, is my personal favorite/winner. The TOMANTEK sleeve has everything I wanted: light weight (it’s the lightest of the group), two zippers, nicely padded, not flimsy, and fits in my backpack – just barely. It has the most interesting outer texture and feel. It’s grippy, so it wouldn’t slide around on car seats as easily as the others and has this sort of firm/spongy feel to it. While it does lack any extra pockets or pouches, that’s fine with me since that’s what the rest of my backpack is for. The height of the case is perfect for the m15 and with the laptop inside, there is roughly 2cm (one finger width) worth of wiggle room width-wide. While the case COULD be ½ smaller in the width for a snug fit (and a better fit in my backpack), inserting and removing the laptop from such a snug-fitting case could be a bit cumbersome. So, I like the fact that there is some wiggle room width-wise. I also love the fact that zipper teeth are not exposed at all when it’s zipped closed. That could quite possibly help keep out any moisture or splashes. This one’s a keeper for me.
Weight = 7.7oz (218g).
Total weight with m15 laptop = 5lbs, 8.8oz (2.52kg)
