title: Best 3.1 DOCSIS Modem for XFinity
text:
I was weary of some negative reviews at first, but after reading online reviews from reputable sources, and trying it for myself, this modem is simply amazing!

First off, setup was super easy. In a nutshell:

1.) Power it up.
2.) Connect Ethernet cable from modem to laptop and go to xfinity.com/activate
3.) All you need to do is login like you're about to pay a bill and that's it - no account numbers or anything!
4.) CALL XFINITY TO ACTIVATE YOUR EQUIPMENT!!! Do not skip this step!
5.) Tell them the Serial Number and MAC Address (DOCSIS 3.1, not the DOCSIS 3.0 - look closely on the unit, not on the box, there are (2) MAC addresses, provide the 3.1 number).
6.) Connect modem to router via Ethernet (Cat 6 minimum), connect phone line, and you're gucci.

Literally all those steps took me less than 15 minutes, including the call to XFinity.

I had been wanting to switch to my own modem and start saving $11 per month (plus taxes) for a while, and finally decided to go for it. I hated paying the rental and then I also found out another little detail, you know that free XFinity hotspot thing they keep talking about, ever wonder where that comes from, that's right, your rental modem/router. That sucker is turned on by default and XFinity is using your electricity to power up a public XFinity hotspot. Totally lame, I killed it ASAP in the XFinity My Account application as soon as I realized that. Next thing I did with the rental was turn off the WiFi by switching the unit into Bridge mode. Just some advice for people still renting. I highly recommend switching to bridge and using your own router, it's way better than theirs. Better yet, buy your own modem and route. Ok, rant over, back to review.

It is easily two times, if not three times smaller than the rental modem/router unit. Kinda goes as a given since it's one device replacing two. And to that point, it is better to have two discrete devices than two devices in one package for reliability and ease of diagnosis. The device is also very discrete looking and sufficiently aesthetic, at least to me, to be in plain sight. Overall, the build quality, construction, and overall perception does seem to line up with the price tag. I feel like I'm getting my money's worth for the time being. Reliability will ultimately solidify or uproot that.

It boots up way quicker than the rental (~1-2 min) and performs better. The latency on my speed tests went down from 12-15 to about 7-9ms aand I'm getting just slightly better downloads but not by much. However, this is one of two of the only XFinity approved DOCSIS 3.1 modems - think up to 10Gbps connection. Now I'm on blast - 250mbps (getting all 250 and then some) but am thinking of going to 1Gbps. And while we're dreaming, this modem will do 2Gbps with link aggregation, but the software update is still in the works. Basically two Ethernet cables from your modem going to your router, each 1Gbps but acting like a "single" cable to provide 2Gbps of total throughput. Way out of the league of most people, but XFinity does have a 2Gbps option over coax so I figured I'd throw it out there.

I have only had it for a few days, but was so thrilled with the easy set-up and exceptional performance, I decided to leave a review. I will update ofcourse over the years with reliability and how it holds up, but so far, very promising.

title: The smartest upgrade I have done on my home network.
text:
Worth every penny and then some. I was able to separate my two networks of traffic to improve latency, download time, etc. If you experience issues while working from home (video drop, lagging, etc), this is must. I had no idea the significant difference hardware can actually make.

Background: My network is primarily Synology with RT2600AC router. I implemented the Ubiquiti
EdgeRouter ER-4 with immediate and undeniable results.

March 17 2020 I began to work from home due to COVID-19. My family of four were all competing for not only bandwidth, but QoS and port needs. My daily use of Microsoft Teams video and WebEx were dropping. Probably the worse crisis of all is my son could not game and chat via headsets with his friends and my daughter was complaining of Netflix not being fast enough! Oh my!

I have an IT background and have a solid setup with my own routers, mesh-wifi, etc. I have approximately 56 devices connected to my network with most being wired (new home build). Everything had been working great until now with latency in the 29ms range. I had opened support tickets with my current router technology company and signed-up for Site24x7.com monitoring of packet drops and connectivity loss from outside the network (to the edge fo the router).

PLEASE SEE ATTACHED IMAGE. This is the proof from switch from Synology RT2600 to Ubiquiti EdgeRouter 4. (drop the mic)

My Setup:
- Port 1 - My son's PS4 network. No restrictions. His own DHCP with one IP connected.
- Port 2 - My entire house network with WiFi, TVs, 26Tb NAS, SmartHome, etc, etc.

All traffic flows to OPENDNS (free acct) to protect against malicious threats, etc.

title: Quality Sound
text:
Pro bundle with Sub Overview

Pro: Quality Built, Quality Sound, Functionality, Small form factor, Volume (low and high), Perfect amount of Base

Cons: Connecting all three to act like a system is finicky and dosen't work when you set it as an alarm. Only will play off one so you miss out on some of the rich sound when waking up. But a plus since it isn't as loud.

Long Review:
I have to say these are amazing. I have had a lot of amazon products and these surprised me the moment I started them up. First off these get loud for their size and the audio clarity is amazing. They are crisp, clear and sound amazing. Now if you like heavy heavy base then these aren't the speakers for you. I bought the package with 2 speakers and the sub and they are perfect for me. The base is well controlled and gives the sound that is lacking in many speakers but if you want the base to shake the walls and make it sound like a floor speaker with a 12 inch amplified drum then don't try. But if you are looking for a clean, rich, bold and sophisticated listening experience then these are amazing. Much better than anything I have tried in the $350 price point.

If you want something that is loud, base heavy with good high and mid tones better than this then look at spending 700 or more. I listen to everything from classical music to EDM, Rock, rap, pop, country, jazz and folk and these just keep impressing me. The vocals aren't drowned out and you can hear all the instruments and the base fills in the lows at the perfect listening experience.

Summary: If you are looking for rich, deep, bold music this is the set for you. Better than anything in the 350 to 450 market. (I have tried 20 in this market) If you are looking for wall pounding, rave quality base then you better live on your own or in a frat house cause more than this you will need a floor speaker with amplifier and thick walls. PS I own a full amplified speaker set housed in my living room for when I was in college and a fraternity. Nothing against them but horrible for all day listening and having friends over to talk and not drink all day haha

Note: I have both echos and the sub in my bedroom and the room is too small for all 3. I barley raise the volume past level 3, maybe 4 if I am listening to them in the shower. I moved them to my living room for the pre and post Superbowl party and they filled a medium 4 bedroom 3 bath house with crystal clear music.

title: Amazing screen, Harmony Remote capable, bad remote, too short of power cable
text:
If you can get beyond the cheap remote, short power cable, and requirement that this be delivered via a crappy shipper (was like $70 shipping that is charged after purchase regardless of Prime), this is an amazing screen!

First the bad: The remote sucks. It is cheaply made and has buttons on it that aren't even hooked up to anything (it is a third party generic remote). Only the Up/DOWN/STOP do anything (which is fine as that's all you need to do) You have to point it directly -and I mean DIRECTLY - at the under side left on the screen (the little IR window). The power cord is hard wired to the unit which sucks because you can't add another longer cable and have to use an extension cord to power it (which makes it look like crap if you need to run it down a wall like we do).

The not so good: as with any projector set up, unless you have a super bright projector, it is very hard to watch in the day time even with blinds closed. Because of the tiny holes in the screen for the acoustic transparency some light comes through the back (even when we close the blind on the windows behind the screen).

Now the good: This screen has great picture quality (we do 1080p) and the acoustically transparent feature works flawlessly. We have had this screen for 9 months and never once has the motor jammed. Their tech support is great and prompt (had a few issues with how to use the remote)

...and now the truly amazing: you CAN connect this to Alex using a Harmony Remote, app and hub (further referred to as Harmony). YOU DO NOT NEED TO BUY THEIR EXTRA REMOTE! (although you do need to buy the Harmony Remote with hub). The Harmony comes with an IR emitter that is on a long cable. If you position this under and a bit forward of the screen , the Harmony will control it when you add the Elite Screen IR into the app (scroll through the device options and Elite Screens will be a choice). After adding all of my other home theater devices to the Harmony app and setting up a "scene" (called it 'TV'), I can, with a single press of a button, make the screen come down, turn my projector on and turn my receiver on to the correct input. Then, with the Harmony Alexa skill, you can control it all with Alexa. We just say "Echo, turn on TV" and it sends the code to the Harmony and activates the TV scene. Then, we programmed an 'OFF' sequence in the scene so when we say "Echo, turn off TV" it turns everything off!

Oh, and absolutely let this screen hang open for a couple days. Any wrinkles in the screen (yes, they all have them) will work themselves out. At least they did on mine...

title: Awesome camera at a great price!
text:
The first thing I noticed when opening my package from Amazon was how economically packaged the camera was. Amcrest doesn't pass the cost of fancy packaging onto its customers. With that said, the packaging was more than sufficient to protect the camera and the other contents for shipping.

The camera itself appears to be contained in an aluminum or some other lightweight metal. The base itself (the part with the Amcrest logo) itself is a hardy plastic. All mounting hardware you need is included.

Only the Quick Start guide is included in the box, but the actual manual details all of the UI settings. I wish tooltips or a digital manual were included in the UI as opposed to having to look up the information in a PDF.

I initially ran my setup via IP on the web browser but found that remote performance with the Amcrest View Pro app was troublesome. I didn't want to go through the trouble of manual port forwarding in my router just to get remote viewing on the app, so I reran the setup in the app using the P2P mode. This made the camera available from both home and remote with ease. If you already have access to the web interface, you can access the QR code from the browser to set up your app.

I mounted mine up high (10 feet maybe) on one side of the garage door. The video quality is fantastic as is the large viewing angle. There is a slight fisheye effect which is to be expected with wide-angle lenses, but it is not so extreme as to be distracting. Low light performance is amazing, especially in BLC mode. I found that this mode provided the best low light results of all the options.

I have basic motion detection set up in the app to send push notifications for motion. You can specify motion zones so that passing cars or blowing flags don't trigger notifications.

The only problem I have with this camera is that System -> Upgrade -> Check Version doesn't appear to function. I have not investigated this much, but it has been this way since installation. I checked Amcrest's website for firmware, but this model wasn't listed at the time of this review.

I can't speak to recording or playback just yet as I have not NVR or SD card for this camera but will be investigating one or both in the future.

In conclusion, a great camera. I will most definitely be looking into some additional cameras as well as a PoE switch to supply them.

title: Best Value for 1440p and 144Hz with Ray Tracing and HDR. It even handles 4k and 144Hz.
text:
This card has been performing extremely well in games with Ray Tracing and HDR enabled. I have a 1440p, 144 Hz monitor that really shines with the 2080 Super. In Shadow of the Tomb Raider, I have the image settings at Ultra, Ray Tracing Shadows at High, and HDR enabled. It benchmarked at 100 fps max, 55 fps avg, and 37 fps min. I have also played Metro Exodus with similar settings, as well as DLSS enabled, and had similar or better benchmark scores. Call of Duty Modern Warfare 2019 performs even better. I was able to play the same games on a 4k, 144Hz monitor with lower FPS, but smooth game play that never dipped below 30 FPS. There was no stuttering or artifacting. The card with it's triple fan cooler never went above 68 Centigrade and the fans never ran more than 1200 rpm. The card remained silent throughout the games and testing. I haven't overclocked it yet because there really has been no need to. I will probably give the beta MSI After Burner program for RTX card overclocking a try. It seems very simple because it will do all the overclocking automatically, except for the memory. The card is visually pleasant to look at with its RGB rainbow scheme. Aside from price this card is a real winner. It definitely makes more sense than the RTX 2080 Ti, since there are rumors of a Ti Super coming in early 2020, as well as the AMD "nvidia killer" coming by summer next year. Save the $500 difference and wait to see what comes. If you own a 1080 Ti you might want to wait till next year when the new cards come out, unless you really want RTX now. I hope this has been helpful.
Edit: I finally did overclock the card with MSI AfterBurner which gave me a modest boost that resulted in about 10% performance boost without any overheating, throttling or other problems. This is an excellent card.

title: Makes loading and using apps a cinch!
text:
I wanted a tablet for two reasons. One, I was completely out of room on my phone and wanted to test how easy it was to use apps with the Android platform on the Tango tablet. Second, I was looking for something that was lighter weight but seemed to be easier to read. This tablet satisfied all my requirements. I turned it on and had it up and running within minutes. Using my wireless network, I was able to grab all my Android apps from my phone and copy/move them onto the tablet. There was a built in feature on the tablet that did this for me. I have arthritic, shaky hands but took a high-quality clear picture within seconds with the built in camera. The quality of the screen display was clear and beautiful. I was able to attach the keyboard to the tablet very easily. I found I personally liked using the touchscreen more than the keyboard. The touchscreen was much more responsive but I used both. I tested the sound quality and the ability to play a heavier video games. The game (Runescape) played the same on this tablet as on a phone or computer. We listened to YouTube music videos which sounded great. There seems to be plenty of space and ram for my purposes. When I need more, it appears I can easily do so with an SD drive.
The only downsides I found were that the battery took longer to charge than my phone so I wish that was faster. Also, when I was using my Chrome browser, I would accidentally pull down the menu (at the top) displaying charge left, etc. I wasn’t sure how to move this to a different side of the screen.
Overall, I would highly recommend this tablet for work, school or pleasure purposes.

title: An Improvement To My System
text:
I have a late 70’s McIntosh System. The phono pre-amp on my 40 year old C28 Pre-amp started failing. A friend of mine brought over his Pro-Ject Tube Box S2 to try on my system. I really liked the way the tubes took the edge off the output on my solid state system. I decided to buy a S2 instead of spending that money trying to troubleshoot and fix my C28 phono out.
The S2 was easy to set up. However, one of the tubes quit working within a few weeks of purchase. My friend had updated his stock Pro-Ject tubes to Tung-sol brand tubes. I ordered a matched pair of Tung-Sol 12AX7 Tubes and replaced the Pro-Ject tubes. I haven’t had any problems with the unit since replacing the burnt out tube. So hopefully it was just a bad tube.
Now I’m sitting in the sweet spot. I have a Pro-Ject DC Turntable with an Ortofon 2M Bronze MM Phono Cartridge. Playing records through the S2 sounds better than it ever did through my old McIntosh phono pre-amp. And, changing to the Tung-sol brand tubes made a noticeable difference in sound quality as well. With the signal passing through the S2 my vinyl records just sound better. With the tubes, I feel the output has more clarity, tone, and richness, especially in the mid to upper ranges.
At this price point, I am really pleased with the sound quality of this little S2. But I would recommend upgrading the stock Pro-Ject brand tubes. You will get more out of your S2. You will also need to find the specifications of your current cartridge so you can properly set the S2 to your cartridge’s output. You can usually find cartridge info pretty easy through an online search. The included instructions with the S2 will help explain how to dial your S2 into your cartridge’s output.

title: Don't have to worry about storage any time soon!
text:
With the size of today's video games, storage is getting harder and harder to manage. Personally I like to have all my games in one location along with their launchers, to reduce any issues that can arise from having games and launchers on different drives.

With 8TB of storage, I have enough room to keep all the games that I enjoy playing installed. Even with all my favorite games, I still have plenty of room for new titles to come out and install.

I was hesitant on buying this, because I was worried about the noise level. While you can hear it while playing games that are installed on it, or if you're updating/ installing new games on it, while it's not being accessed it is silent. Also when I am playing games I have headphones and don't notice it, and it is not loud enough to be picked up by my microphone.

Comparing this drive to my last internal drive I used for my games, the only thing I have noticed is a slow down on allocating disk space when installing and updating games.

I am slightly disappointed in the connection WD used on the Drive. It connects via USB 3.2 Gen 1 (or the original usb 3.0) which is limited to a transfer speed of 5Gbp/s. While there might not be any problem there, I feel like could have used at least USB 3.2 Gen 2 (typically most usb c cables) with transfer speeds up to 10Gbp/s to eliminate any potential for a bottle neck.

Overall I am very pleased with the drive, and have recommended it to all of my friends that worry about storage because of large games.

title: Buggy, insecure software, but great hardware. IT professionals only, others should steer clear!
text:
Overall, a cheap IP camera that can be networked with other cameras to create your own security system, or in my case, act as a good baby monitor for the baby room. The infrared (night) vision is spectacular, but offset that with the horrible experience setting it up and the even worse security vulnerabilities that I don't trust have been patched... Still... >_>

Here's what's good:

- Night vision
- supports RTSP (no need for the Foscam official app to view video stream)
- no cloud subscription necessary for main functionality

Here's what's bad:

- Requires downloading and installing a dubious program to figure out what port the HTTP server is running on to configure it (or just use nmap if you're techy)
- Requires downloading and installing a program that runs a local HTTP service to do things any web browser released in the last 5 years (mobile or desktop) could handle. Seriously, it sends cmands to it and gets back instructions on how to render the page. It's stupid.
- Security vulnerability was exposed for all Foscam cameras and it's unclear whether it was patched. Like, making the feed available for viewing with hardcoded, unchangeable credentials. I'd rather my camera feed of the baby room not show up to pervs on the internet...
- Only easy way to view the camera stream is from desktop or the official Foscam mobile app, which requires an account

Here's what I did to fix the things I didn't like:

- Used nmap to map all the open ports on the device and tried until I found the right port for the http server
- Used pyfoscam python library (available via pip install) to configure it and allow controlling it without the questionable program always running in the background
- Added a no-internet-access subnet and only allowed the camera to join wifi on that subnet
- Used VLC media player (for desktop, iOS, and Android) to view the RTSP stream from anywhere so long as it's on the same wifi network

For the price, the bones of the camera are good and managed to dig up the poorly documented HTTP API so it can be controlled and configured with automation. Right now I'm looking at picking up a few more and turning a raspberry pi into a device running Home Assistant, with which this integrates very well. The only problems are related to bad software that tries to make things easier to work with, but made some poor decisions.

If you're techy savvy (and I mean a programmer or sysadmin, not uses-excel-in-innovative-ways) you can take advantage of this camera's superior hardware with minor time spent setting it up correctly. If you're not, I'd steer clear and go for an IP camera that has patched the vulnerabilities that have been exposed. Likely not going to be as cheap as this one.

title: Case has several flaws
text:
TL;DR:

This is my third computer build. Did not enjoy building in this case.
Big flaws:
- PCIE slots have to be broken, not unscrewed.
- There is front glass panel which looks nice for the RGB, but the airflow was so much worse than expected.
- Front panel needs pretty much two people to remove, have to be careful with not ripping out the power/usb/rgb cords in the process.
Overall, I am going to rate my experience 2/5 with this case.

As I previously stated up above, this is my third computer case build. I have built a very cheap budget computer for around $450 U.S. As well as a $1500 U.S. build. So I have some experience when it comes to building within a computer case. This time, the build was extremely challenging. Some things were due to my own fault, and some things are faults of the computer case.

Let's get the things that I did wrong out of the way. First off, the case was a last minute change when I purchased everything I needed. I had a budget of $3,000 for this build, and when everything was all said and done I was at $3047. I dropped the computer case to this one, to make my budget.
I had previously went over the entire build inside my head with the other case, but not with this one. I made sure that the case would support the motherboard, but completely forgot about the AIO length I had selected. If you are wondering if this case will support a 360 rad.. it will. With some slight modding, and being willing to give up all your 3.5 hard drive space.
So that was my fault. Forgetting to check what rad this case would support. The other thing that was my fault is that I went out partying with some of our local Korean Nationals before building the computer. (I am in the military, and stationed in South Korea currently). They wanted to take out my section to celebrate American Thanksgiving a week early, and since they were paying, of course I went! But, that was a huge mistake when you are trying to build a computer super drunk.
Because of being drunk, I ended up breaking my top PCIE slot (the only x16 on the board).

Okay, now that I have rambled long enough, lets get into what I think the pro's and cons are for the case.

PROS:
- It looks very nice. Even though I am not getting the amount of airflow I want, I have to admit that it looks super sweet.
- The case comes pre wired for the rgb fans, with only needing to plug in the controller to the motherboard/sata, making it very intuitive, even for first time builders.
- The case is hands down the easiest I have worked with in terms of changing the rgb colors for the front fans. It is a simple button on top of the case, and it cycles through easily 15 different modes.

CONS
- The airflow for the front of the case is abysmal. Just on my rad mounted in the front I have 6 fans, 3 = pull, 3 = push, to get max ventilation, and even then, when I hold my hand up in front of the rad, I can barely feel the airflow. Now for me, I was forced to put the rad in the front because like I said, I had the wrong size. So you would probably get more airflow out of the top instead of the front. Although there is rad mounting options for the front, so in theory you should be able to have a rad there no problem.
- Removing the PCIE guards on the back of the case was a nightmare, and you'll definitely want to remove those before putting in the motherboard. I always put in the graphics card last, and by the time I was ready to install it and figured out that you need to BREAK any additional slots besides the top one, I already had everything wired up and the AIO with thermal paste applied. So I wasn't trying to remove all of that to make it easier to break those back guards. Simply put, I think it is a very terrible design to make someone break those off instead of being able to screw/unscrew depending on where you were going to put the gpu/sound card ect etc.
- Lastly, the case is not made to remove the front panel easily. I work out on a daily basis, and had to put some very significant force with me pulling in order to get it removed, and that was after spending about twenty minutes trying to loosen the pins that hold the case in. The pins are the ones that will pop in, and spread apart, as opposed to screws. Me personally, I think screws should have been the way to go, as when I finally got those pins loose enough to be able to pull, I almost ripped all the wiring right off the front panel. (I would like to note that I got the case and the radiator before the rest of my computer parts, and so was completely sober for this portion of the build, and not drunk like when I was installing the cpu/motherboard/gpu/ram/wiring.)

All in all, I think think this case would have been perfect for my very first build, as everything was already connected, which would have been nice. My GPU wouldn't have needed to have two PCIE back brackets removed and so the top one would be fine. But for anything past that, I think you'd be better off with something on the higher end. 2/5 for me, probably a 3.5 - 4/5 for a brand new builder with minimal parts.

title: This Boombox is a Bargain (and you get what you pay for)
text:
First, the good news: The sound on this little boombox isn't the worst. Don't expect top of the line and I think you'll be happily surprised. Also, I haven't purchased a boombox since I was a teenager in the 80s, so I was really excited to find one with Bluetooth functionality. And the light up panel is a fun little bonus (and don't worry, you can switch it on or off depending on your mood).

And now for the rest: You probably figured out there's no remote control with this. But there's more. You'll definitely feel the 80s returning as you navigate the clunky buttons and knobs. The CD lid clicks open and shut manually. The display is very minimalist. Do you want to know what track you're listening to? Well, too bad - the display won't tell you! And for the most disappointing feature: In terms of the Bluetooth feature, music sounds fine. But if you're trying to listen to podcasts or Audible, the quality is very choppy to the point of frustration.

This boombox is fine if you're looking for something on the cheap and you're willing to put up with a few quirks and rough corners. I've been enjoying it since I ordered it, so I can't come down too hard on it. But as a fan of podcasts and Audible recordings, I'm definitely let down. But for $40, I'm not gonna complain too much about it.

[[VIDEOID:ea9f498c3d3ebc422be410bfb535a7e]] I picked this monitor arm because it was the only one I was able to find that would work for my desk. My desk has a back so clamping was out of the question. Most other units when using the grommet installation leaves a the bolt that sticks down which would prevent me from closing my keyboard drawer. This was pretty much the perfect solution for me, other than having to drill a hole on my desk (which i really wanted to avoid).

After installing the base I tested out the 1st arm (which doesnt hold the monitor). It moved smoothly and easily. Once I mounted the 1st monitor (27in) thats when I started to have my doubts about this item. The arms no longer moved smoothly and when adjusting the monitor to a desired position the base would move. I decided to mount the 2nd monitor in hopes that it would settle the base down a bit, it didnt. Moving the monitors up and down worked great, but trying to move the monitor with out affecting the other monitor was impossible. My use case for these arms were to center the desired monitor based on my need. One monitor is a 4K display, the other a 1440 G-Sync display for PC gaming. I wanted to be able to center which ever monitor i wanted to primarily use at the time and either move the 2nd one to the side or on top easily. To adjust one monitor I have to hold the other arm down so it doesnt move.

text:
Been looking into getting a Yubikey some time ago and happened on these new U2F-style keys for cheaper so tried one out. This one registered fine on a Mac and tried it with Facebook with instant success. For setup on an iPhone it's a bit harder since not a ton of supported apps but tried it on a Gmail account I have and initially ran into issues where the Google Smart Lock App wasn't recognizing it via Bluetooth LE at all. After many tries and thinking I had a dud, I read some troubleshooting that included "reboot phone" as an option and low and behold, it worked. So now connecting to that Google account via Safari or initial setup in the Gmail App, it'll prompt to use Smart Lock to validate the U2F key with a keypress (works great), but downside is even unchecking "Remember this device" still saves the login, so seems I only need to do it once then just like the Gmail App, it won't ask for it again unless I go into Google Account Settings|Security and revoke all trusted devices. Speaking of Gmail App, it seems Google tends to want to "save" or "trust" devices probably for convenience, so trying to get it to prompt for U2F key every time doesn't seem to be a great option.

So while its usefulness will grow as more apps and websites support it or support it more fully, the U2F key itself worked exactly as it should for both plug-in USB and Bluetooth LE transmission to a phone. Oh, one thing that may be nice would be a still-compact version with both USB-C and USB-A capabilities (or attached adapter) since I have old MBPs and a 12" Retina newer USB-C-only machine.

Can't wait for more sites to support this standard!

title: The guts and the form factor just barely justify the poor material quality and low storage space
text:
(I own the 17" version of this product)

Hard Pros:
- The 1060 GTX handles a fair variety of new video game titles at 1080p and medium to high settings, some on ultra. Also note that the 1060 is currently considered the best card you can get for this purpose, and with a screen size of 15 inches, any more than that would be unrewarding/overkill beyond maintaining a consistent 60fps.
- The hardware covers the vast majority of your average user's multitasking needs, in addition to some resource-intensive software. The option to overclock the CPU would be useful for anyone trying to eke out a little more juice for anything that required it.
- It's slim, it's light, and I love to bring it to school. I can play what I normally play at home, on campus, and the weight is a big determining factor in being able to lug it around every day.

Cons/Thoughts:
- The SSD is hardly big enough for your average user, so you may want to choose the 500GB option
- Chiclet-style keyboard is low-profile and keeps the laptop thin, but leaves something to be desired in terms of ergonomics and finger-feel; may feel awkward at first for those used to mechanical keyboards.
- The trackpad is accurate and responsive but is very easy to brush over while typing, resulting in errant clicks.
- The frame is made of what I can only assume to be a cheap plastic, without any other information. This makes the screen extremely prone to color-warping or damage if it is impacted or pressured -- simply by carrying it in a backpack (which was designed to hold full-sized laptops, and had extra cushioning to prevent damage) with a few books resulted in fuzzy regions of the screen becoming green-tinted.
- Appears to kick fans into overdrive sometimes, which can be very loud. Testing temperatures while playing games, watching movies, etc. did not reveal anything out of the ordinary (50-60C at max). This occurs even when the laptop is placed on a flat surface with ample space to vent, and even when one is not even particularly challenging the laptop in terms of resource usage.
- Your laptop says, "Predator" on the front of it, which was really just a stupid move on Acer's part.

Bottom line:
For the price, you're paying for the form factor, really. It's a decent gaming machine, and would function well as a work or school laptop for many years to come, but similar, larger laptops in the same price bracket will outperform the Predator more often than not. The 1060 is powerful enough fits in this frame like a glove, delivering a solid 1080p gaming experience. The CPU is beefy enough for the vast majority of work you may need to do, and the overclock option is handy. Despite this, the material is low quality and it is prone to damage, even from light impacts or pressure. Other parts of the frame, where the hardware is housed, feel flexible enough to be damaged as well, so there is no telling if an errant elbow may be the laptop's demise. Buy the protection plan, honestly.

title: More functionality at 1/3 the cost
text:
Note: this review uses the VPB-XT2 as a benchmark for comparison. As such, it will not be a pure 1:1 comparison between the Meike and the VG-XT3.

Overall impressions:
The build quality and functionality between Meike and Fuji grips are very close. I personally cannot tell the difference between function in the two. Additionally, the Meike has the added remote-release baked in. If anything, it's disappointing that Fuji would not also build this into their grips that cost 3x more.

The Meike has slight differences in finish (e.g. the rubber is a bit softer, does not match the body like Fuji brand does), and shape/size/feel of its buttons. For the most part, which is "better" boils down to personal preference

A more in-depth field test will be required to further determine qualitative differences between the two grips.

-------------------------------------------

Differences:
-The only major differences between the two grips are the finish of the Meike and the buttons.
-The Meike has a softer, gripper, more matte rubber, while the Fuji's rubber matches their body 100%.
-The dials on the Meike feel slightly lower quality than the Fuji... perhaps a lighter plastic? They are also not as well dampened, HOWEVER, they do have a more definitive button press than the Fuji
-The joystick on the Meike is BIG. Much bigger than the Fuji (which is nice), but it also feels squishier. That being said, using it poses no problems thus far
-Boost switch is a switch instead of a dial! I find this to be an improvement over the Fuji, as the dial was easy to accidentally flip if it got caught on clothes or something
-Buttons protrude a bit more from the grip... this makes them easier to find/click

The Good:
- Price point!
- Remote trigger release included!
- Remote has multiple functions, including bulb and interval shooting
- Works great so far... really no complaints
- Boost mode switch instead of dial
- Clickier buttons
- Bigger joystick

The Bad:
- The remote has no off switch (weird)
- The remote is hard to figure out... multiple modes, but certainly not foolproof
- The instructions are not that great, translation-wise
- Grip does not feel as premium as Fuji brand... maybe just a tiny bit less solid in construction

title: Avoid. Insanely high temps. No fan controller.
text:
Move to 1 star vs 5 stars. I build 2-3 computers a week. This case started of great. It’s now my worst case purchase.

1. Pre-installed fans. They are not motherboard controlled so they just spin and don’t care what temps are needed. The front fans are mounted outside the case. This gives them little room to Intake air. So in return the inside case temps spiked with components exceeding 90c.

3. Hard drive slots. Just a pain. Best to install the hard drives before anything else.

Resolution. If you must buy this case, do this. Remove the front three fans. Install two on the front inside and one in the back. Take the back fan and install it on the top. Make sure to run that fan to the motherboard so at least one fan is temp controlled.

By doing this my temps went from 90c + to the mid 70s under heavy gaming.

It does hurt the front look of the computer a little. So prob just avoid buying all together.

I’m a huge thermaltake fan. Unfortunately they dropped the ball on this design.

title: Good enough for the price but it never ends there
text:
This turntable is quiet and does the job or spinning a vinyl record and reproducing what is picked up by the cartridge at phono level or line level to an amplifier. It looks decent and feet absorb most of the floor thuds.

Here are the things you need to pay attention to and spend money fixing:

Setting the tracking force requires a bit of work. The accompanying manual suggests use of the counterweight on the T mark - this results in way too much force. When you do it manually, you will find the counterweight ends up further back from the T mark. Ideally, you should check the tracking force with a track force meter (Price range $11-130)

The included conical stylus is very basic and you will need to change it for an elliptical stylus at a minimum. If not a better cartridge. (Price range $40 - several hundreds)

The factory setting on the cartridge is supposed to provide good alignment but if you notice inner track distortion - better cartridge alignment with a protractor will be necessary ($15-30)

There is a speed adjustment knob. because the speed of the platter may not be accurate. To make accurate speed adjustment, you will need a disc mat stroboscope or a strobe light (Price range 15-130)

The Music Hall MMF 1.5 is a good starter turntable to start spending on a hobby. And when you are hooked, it will make you turn your sights to the more expensive pieces out there, some in excess of 30K!

PS: The turntable speed is definitely off out of the box (34.5 RPM when I checked - crosschecked with multiple smartphone apps). For approximate speed correction, a smartphone app will do but for more accurate correction, use a stroboscope mat or disc with a lamp using an incandescent or halogen bulb.

This Sabbat earbud set connected easily to several of my devices (computer, pad, android), and they turn on immediately and re-pair with my device as soon as I take them out of their charging case. The case itself is smooth, compact and magnetically "clicks" shut in a satisfying way. The USB-C case, which is also a battery, will recharge the buds several times without having plug it in (I have not actually run out of charge yet, but I recharge the case every other day or so). You can see the charge level when the case is plugged in, as there are four lights on the back of the case- w four solid lights showing fully charged.

The sound quality on these earbuds is extremely good, with the the bass, treble and midrange all well-represented and well-balanced, and the sound cancellation is actually noticeable on these vs. many supposed "sound cancellation" buds. I am often not hearing people talking in the room when using these, and they have to motion at me. The earbuds fit in my ears well, and this came with many more gradations in sizes than the usual small, medium and large earpods covers They also are flush to my head, and don't stick out far like marbles. I use these the most out of my wireless audio devices now, and am very pleased with this set.

title: Control your smart phone remotely WITHOUT Bluetooth!
text:
These are for audio devices (typically, “head” or “ear-phones” using 1/8’’ (same as “3.5 mm”) jack/connectors.

BUT, they are “TRRS.” They have an EXTRA “ring” on the connector end for another conductor.

If you have a modern phone (say “smart”) you will need a TRRS cable if you want to use your audio device’s built-in controls for answering calls and doing things (like SKIP and REPEAT) from you device’s controls.

Handy if your device OR phone has NO BLUETOOTH or Bluetooth isn’t functioning (because batteries on headphones are dead, etc)

I got THREE foot by mistake. My bad.

Get the SIX foot.

IF you don’t need to control your phone (or other source) from your headphones, you do NOT need “TRRS.” Just get regular “TRS” connector equipped audio accessories.

Haven’t used much, yet. I’ll see how well these last and report back.

title: A Great Offshoot of the RX100 Line

Thank goodness this exists. Every camera before the ZV-1 were simply still photography cameras first and foremost but also capable of taking videos. The ZV-1 simply emphasized the other half of the equation because the RX100 line already took great videos. The wheel didn't need to be reinvented here, Sony just acknowledged that there are users of their cameras who use it for videos more than photos. The way this camera was designed, from the button placements and the flippy screen leaves no doubt who this camera is for.

This is also a friendly camera for people like me who are just beginning to take videos for travel and other things worth remembering through videos. The great thing is you can grow into this hobby with this camera because of the other features that this camera has that can be discovered while using it.

Is it a perfect camera? No camera is. But it's absolutely perfect for it's intended use. The price could be a bit lower but considering the features compared to the more expensive RX100 line, this seems to be a bargain.

This is good for you're "standard" listening, or shopping on a budget, or travelling.

Noise Cancellation: I use these at an office regularly, and I've found that I've not been able to hear the people sitting next to me when I wear this. Sometimes, vaguely, you can hear something, but not enough to be disturbed. There are probably better on the market, but for these at their current value, you're getting a good exchange. 4/5

For working out: 3/5 The cord is a bit to long, and I find it always being an issue for when I'm running or exchanging weights from the gym equipment. If you're intending to just do a walk on a treadmill for a half a mile or two, you'll be fine, but as far as running; you'll need to be careful. I think these are mediocre, at best, for actual gym equipment. You'll need to make sure you have the right sized in-ear bud to fit you're ear snug enough for it to not jar out of place and causing an problem.

Overall: The cord is a bit long, the noise cancellation the better feature, with good enough sound quality to satisfy most people. I'd say for the price you're getting these, with the included In-ear bud sizes and than some in case you lose any is a bargain. I've bought worse pairs for 5-10 dollars more, to be honest. I'd say these are a great pair for travel, work, and sometimes the gym depending on the exercise. Overall, 4/5 for the bargain and noise cancellation.

title: Love it, had to be curved though
text:
In one line: love it, returned it for being flat.

If you don't want a curved monitor, this is an incredible purchase. I had zero issues with the setup or resolution problems. One key part here is to make sure you're using DP, NOT HDMI and that your GPU can drive it. DP specifications are also tied to the card.

Colors are vibrant, the brightness is amazing and the picture quality is fantastic. By default on a Mac it goes to 2560 x 1080 which I find terrible as I got used to the iMac 27" 5k which does 2560 x 1440. As a result, I bumped the resolution up to 3360 x 1417 which is what the Mac offers and that was almost as good as the 5k Retina. Obviously not the same as there is about 25% more pixels on the 5k, but gosh, things looked great.

There are several profiles to choose from and I ended up going custom mainly for the brightness.

HDR was absolutely useless for me and actually quite disturbing. If you decide to buy this monitor make sure to play with that on and off until you can decide what to do. With HDR ON everything felt a bit "washed away", then I turn it off and it makes everything shine.

The monitor also comes with an automatic brightness adjustment based on the environment which I wish they would do gradually based on your preference. Say I set it 50% brightness then it goes 20% up or down from there. But that is not what it does. It just decides everything for you and it was just too bright for me. Perhaps it works great for someone with a very bright room abut at that point why bother? It will probably be at 100% anyway.

Lastly, the "coup de grâce" for me was the monitor being flat. After using a curved monitor for a few years I simply can't go back to a flat monitor if it is bigger than 27". I've tried to adjust to this monitor for about 10 days without success. The constant movement left and right to be able to read text completely defeats the purpose of having a wide monitor like that. I would probably be better served with a 3 x 27" 4k monitor setup (which would cost about the same) but that would allow me to angle every monitor to meet my eyes at about 28-30" distance from the panels.

Overall, extremely pleased with the image quality. When they make a curved version I'll buy it. For now, this flat version was returned.

title: Solid case, well built
text:
This case is very, very well designed. My old metal case was getting to be a pain to deal with, and I bought this to upgrade. I wanted lots of room and the ability to use any form factor motherboard. I currently have a micro ATX in there (it looks lonely), but I am planning to upgrade the MB to something like the ASUS ROG MAXIMUS XII, which is EATX, and I hate buying cases; I want one that will last a long time.

The case provides velcro straps for securing the wiring on the back of the mounting board, so most of the cabling is out of the way. There is a plastic panel that goes over the power supply to hide it; be sure to vent your power supply out the bottom (duh) or the cover will block it. That said, you can leave the cover out if you want. I included pictures of my installation both with and without the cover on the power supply. (I'm clearly not a fan of fancy lighting, as you can tell, but will also probably add some RGB at some point.)

There are caddies for drives that are accessible from the back (see the picture). Right now they are not populated, but I have lots of large spinning drives lying around (since I have replaced them with SSDs in every computer in the house) that will get mounted in here at some point for a file server.

I have two WD Blue SSDs that mount on rubberized holders in the case (you can see them in the picture). The power supply I had did not have long enough power cables to attach to both... so I got a new power supply.

The most surprising thing about this case is that it comes with a little plastic box that sorts your motherboard screws and connectors. Overall everything about this is very professional and the build is solid. Coming from an all-metal and glass case, it thought I might dislike the plastic, but the textured plastic actually looks good.

The only "gotcha" I saw online while researching this case was that you need to make sure to connect the power cables to the front panel. Apparently things will work if you don't, but not well (no light for power supply, front connectors fail, etc.). I've seen some complaints where the answer was to "connect the power cables." So you know... do that.

I don't water cool my PC, so I cannot weigh in on that. My PC runs cool with the stock CPU cooler and performs great in this case, and after four months of continuous running around a dog who constantly sheds, the interior is still clean. Highly recommended.

title: Its a really nice, budget case that does the job. I got a corsair rmx 850 watt power supply into it.
text:
Its a nice case and despite being fairly small there is a good amount of space in here. The case is fairly thin metal which makes it feel cheap but does it matter when its just sitting somewhere? In fact it may even be a good thing, less metal = less weight. And the plastic panel is light as a feather too. The parts inside will weight it down nicely. The case has a few usb ports at the top, and 3 fans included which is real nice. The fan at the back uses this tiny 3 pin cable that connects to the motherboard, the two front fans use this big molex pin connecter, my power supply had a cable for those thankfully. So the only one controlled by the motherboard is the back fan. They are pretty quiet fans tho, so running at full speed isn't really an issue imo. There is a hard drive area and it comes with a few plastic caddy guides you use to install them in the case, real nice for big storage.

Now lets talk about the issue ppl have with this case: The power supply area.
People are on here complaining about the power supply space and I'll admit it IS cramped but you can get a pretty big one in there with some patience. Really the problem is the cables being chunky, this corsair rmx 850 w has some of the chunkiest cables I've ever seen. They are massive, thick, woven cables and EVEN then with some problem solving I got them all in, no cutting the case or anything required. The trick is, connect up all the cables first to the power supply if you are using modular and get the power supply in first. The huge motherboard one you may wanna thread in first but other than that do it after, because getting the power supply in will be impossible otherwise, the cables get in the way and you kind of have to angle it in. Then once its in you can carefully thread all the rest of the cables in. I know you may be thinking I cheated, using modular because I only used the ones I needed. WRONG. I installed several extras for less hassle in the future, even two extra pcie power cables direct from the supply for an RTX 30-series upgrade soon. I used up almost all the cables included, trust me you can get it all in.

This is a good case, and I love the aesthetic. That ps2 ribbed look is a look I love and my laptop is a G5 with that look too. And in the case of this case there is a mesh behind the ribs so you get really good airflow. There is a magnetic filter at the top of the case and a slide one underneath the case for the power supply. Unfortunately not all the vents are covered by removable meshes. But this is a budget case so I'm okay with that. Overall I really recommend this one!

title: Avoid this monitor
text:
I can safely say that this is one of the singularly most annoying monitors I have ever owned.
Issues:
- Every time I need to change the input, I need to be ready for a 30-60 minute fight to get the OSD to come up and work if the previous display is not on. The soft buttons RARELY work unless there is an active incoming signal and you have to race it before it goes back into standby. So, turn it on... and button mash... cross your fingers. This may take anywhere from 10-1000 attempts before you simply reconnect the old input so you can get the OSD to come up.
- The monitor controls are some of the hardest to use, even when they work. They are awkward, unlabeled, impossible to get to if on a multi-panel arm without moving the displays and generally about as well thought out as the Chevy Corvair.
- And it's not all about control either... when it turns on, there's a 20% chance it will come up skewed. Where the left hand side of the monitor is several pixels lower than the side on the right. This creates an annoying and visible seam in the middle of the screen. Thankfully, it's one of the easier to fix since at least there's an 80% chance when you turn it off that it will be fixed when you turn it back on... BUT... welcome back to the OSD problem... because IF you have a second active input, when you turn it off... it may just decide to switch inputs and you're back to the OSD crap.
- Often can't change video modes. Mode switching is excessively slow. Slow enough that windows will often revert before you can see it to accept. (which would be dangerous anyway.) Sometimes, a game will switch it into a mode that never comes up (black screen) which leaves you just hard powering off your computer.
-The speakers are absolutely too low powered to really be useful and sound terrible. Think... someone wearing headphones beside you which are turned up way too loud. It sounds just like that.

What can I say that's positive?
- Well, the display looks good if you can turn it on and the game response time had no issues for me.
- I'm positive I won't be buying another ViewSonic anything. I got this on prime day, so it's almost brand new but it has me so infuriated that I want nothing to do with troubleshooting this. I'm keeping it as a reminder to not buy this brand again.

So what did I get for $300? The ability to post this warning to you as a verified purchase and a very good example of poor product design.

title: Great Set of Walkie Talkies with Added Features.
text:
Living high up in the mountains of New Mexico, in a remote town at least an hours drive to the closest small city, I try to have on hand at least some essentials in case of local emergencies or bad weather that cuts us off from the rest of the world. This happened last winter during a particular bad snow storm and the power was out for two days. No lights, no heat, and no way on hand to even contact anyone, i knew the next time I would be more prepared. Let me tell you, at 3 AM when everything is shut down, and the only noise you hear is the howling of the wind, and you can't see 6" out the window because there's no moonlight, you can start to feel pretty cut off from the world. After things went back to normal in a few days, I made a commitment to start on that emergency essentials list. Walkie talkies were on my list, and when I had a chance to order these, I did so without hesitation. I don't know much about walkie talkies, but I am familiar with the Cobra name, and that they make portable communication devices, among other electronics, so I knew I couldn't go to wrong. When they arrived, and I read the user manual, I was amazed at all the features that were packed into these little hand held units. The set comes with 2 walkie talkies (each with a removable belt clip), a charging stand, and charging cable (USB to Mini-USB), and of course the user manual. I actually had to spend a few nights learning all the features and how to use them, I wanted to be familiar with them and not wait until i actually needed them and had no idea how to use them. Once you familiarize yourself with them, they are actually easy to use, and have some useful added features. Besides the basics you'll find in most good walkie talkies, these included an LED flashlight, access to the NOAA All Hazards Radio Channel(s), a Weather Alert Mode, when set to your area, will automatically alert you to emergency weather conditions, and an Emergency Alert Mode, which, in short, will alert the other walkie talkie user (and others on your same channel/group, to an emergency you may be experiencing, and will alert them with an alarm, followed by your walkie talkie basically turning into an open mic, where the others can hear whatever is happening where you are without you having to do anything other than initially pressing the emergency mode button. When this mode is initiated, the other walkie talkies are automatically turned on to the loudest speaker volume, and users made aware of a current emergency. This could potentially be a life saving feature in some situations, and nice to have on these. Another nice feature is the ability to use these hands free, without having to depress the talk button at all. Set the "VOX" mode on and set the sensitivity for your voice, and your good to go hands free.

These are just a few of the handy features built into these walkie talkies. I tried them out at various locations around my area, and was impressed with the range of these. In the mountains, and surrounded by Pine trees, I could easily contact the other unit from 18 miles away. Most likely much further than I should ever need, but nice to know. These are dust and waterproof (not submerged under water), and have a bright LED panel where you can easily see the settings and active feature icons. Buttons are all rubberized, and depress easily. They are small enough to easily slip in a back pocket, or use the included belt clip. I haven't used walkie talkies in decades, and those were ones for kids to play with. There is a lot of great, potentially very useful features packed into these, and it's nice to know I will be able to contact others outside my home when an emergency arrives in our area. These are powered by Lithium Ion batteries, and a full charge is stated to last 18 hours before a recharge is needed. Recharge can be done by any device with a USB charge capability (most devices with a USB port are capable of this). Overall, and without going into all the features, you get a lot of bang for your buck with these. For just under $100 (as of this review), I can't imagine not feeling it's money well spent when an emergency arrives, and these help you through it. Something everyone living in a remote area, or who travels a lot in remote areas, should have on hand. Absolutely well worth the money.

title: Great Light, too bad about the app!
text: I have been looking at these small RGB lights for a while, then found the price of this light reduced significantly on Amazon.  So far it has been a great little light.  For a light that is slightly smaller than my iPhone XR it does more than you think it would  Using it for still photography it is nice being able to see the lighting and adjust before taking the photo.  After reading a lot of reviews on this light there were not any surprises, except I was a little disappointed with the app.  The app is very good for making fast adjustments to the light and it makes firmware upgrades very easy, but to make precise and repeatable adjustments to the light you have little choice but to use the tiny controls and screen on the light.  That works but it is a little slow.  After looking at the tutorials on the Aputure Sidus Link app, the Atomcube app looks very basic.  With the Aputure Sidus Link app, you can use the phone camera to analyze a color and their app will adjust the light to that color.  I can do that with this light, but I have to use another app to analyze the color and then get that information to the light using the controls on the light.  Works, but it would be so much easier and faster if I could use the Aputure Sidus Link app with this light (you can't, I tried).  Also, having a way to save a setting so you could quickly come back to it would be nice.  So, room for improvement on the app, but with the light being so nice I am sure improvements will come.

title: Battery life is awesome! Bbbuuutttt...
text:
I listen to audiobooks. A LOT of them. I listen to them every waking moment that I possibly can. You could definitely say I am fanatic about audiobooks. I'd been holding out for years and always using wired earbuds, as I was afraid I'd be stuck without headphones if the battery went dead. I tried wireless earbuds, but had no place to put them when I took them out of my ears. You can't carry around their charging case all over the place unless you have pockets, so they just didn't work for me. As for these, the audio quality is, well, eh. Not horrible, but nothing to write home about. People talking to me can definitely tell I'm on headphones. I struggled with the little charging flap, and decided it wasn't worth fighting with, and tore it off. But the battery! Honestly, these headphones have outlasted me. I have listened all day and into the wee hours of the morning, and have yet to run it down. I suffer from insomnia, so these have been with me at all hours and I have yet to run them down. My first set of headphones was a win.

Edit: After using these earphones for a few months, I am still in love with the long battery life. However... If you have long hair, I strongly advise against the folding earphones. Get the other style-I think it is called the sport style. Every night when I take them off, chunks of my hair go with them. When I move, hair gets stuck in them. I've been shopping for another set that doesn't fold so I can keep my hair.

title: Awful, horrible, ugly picture. BUY THE OLED instead!!!
text:
JANUARY 10th, 2021 UPDATE:

And we’ve got a dead pixel now. Fantastic. I had a mid tier Vizio 55” 1080p TV that never got a dead pixel. Ten years of ownership, two moves. Had this less than a year, one move (in original box) and a dead pixel appears, DEAD CENTER of the screen.

Avoid LG non-OLED at all costs.

****************************
After extensive research, I decided on this TV from LG. After having a fully calibrated 2K HDTV for the last decade, I decided it was time to jump into 4K UHD/HDR. Cannot emphasize how disappointed I am. I use this primarily with an Apple TV 4k and a Panasonic 4k BD player.

Seeing the attached pictures, even after full calibration, the backlight is completely uneven, blotchy, and looks so bad that my wife even cared to comment on how bad it looked, followed by the dreaded question asked in angst, “HOW much did you pay for this thing????” Not “we”, but “you”.

That is real bad news folks in case you’re not married. 😳

But she’s right. My decade old 1080P TV, also fully calibrated, has zero issues like this.

Example, in any dark scene, the screen appears significantly brighter in the same areas of the screen face, independently of the material being shown. This indicates an issue with the screen itself. So much for HDR, because in anything but a very bright room, this aspect (defect) dominates what you see on screen.

I’ll divulge that the TV that beat it so handily was a ten tear old VIZIO. And multiple $500-$700 models in Costco, from random brands, beat it as well.

With black levels being so off, that I actually couldn’t get a true calibration of the black levels. This is what you would expect from a $99 Westinghouse you bought from Walmart five years ago. Not from one of the two leading brands of TVs on planet earth.

I should have bought the OLED. And now I’m stuck with this hunk of garbage, wishing every time that I turn it on that lightning will somehow show up to give it a mercy k1ll just to put it out of its misery. So disappointing from an otherwise stellar brand.

Oh and no the TV wasn’t damaged in shipping. Box was in perfect shape and it was gently and professionally placed on its mount. All screws were tightened to the proper in-lb spec and we’re not over tightened.

So, I just blew $1200 and advise anybody reading this to skip this model. What a shame. I’d get a refund and buy the OLED if I could. $400 at Walmart gets you a better picture. I’m feeling sick just typing these words...

Note: the remote and OS are actually quite good and the sound from the speakers is actually VERY good for coming from such a slim device. Nipping at the heels of some cheaper soundbars for voice quality at low to moderate volumes. Impressive.

Songs streamed over Apt-X HD tug my heart back to my childhood spinning LPs and 45s.

The Woburn II is heavily at the mercy of room acoustics, highly susceptible to boomy room modes and suckouts resulting from poor placement. text:
I have been on the lookout for a home security system for a couple of years now. We don't want to pay ADT prices but we want something I feel safe turning on when I'm away for work but my family is here. My home has Google Nest cams all around and a 90LBS German Shepherd who really wouldn't hurt a fly but a home security system was the last bit to give me peace of mind. I've been on an email list for Simplisafe the last year or so but it's always expensive with no good deals and looked cheap with a basic keypad and I just wanted something more.

This is my first security alarm ever and it was a breeze to set up. and I know it works. Once after I set it for the night my wife later wanted to open up a window to hear the rain and the alarm went off. I darted over to the touchpad and disarmed it right away in less than 10 seconds I swear, but I got a text and phone call seconds later where the support center asked for the safe word and then they discontinued the alarm from their end.

It was nice to know that if something were to happen, heaven forbid, that the authorities would have my details and signal right away. Cove has my thumbs up.

title: Consider some reasoned counterpoints to the generally positive reviews
text:
After a few months of research I settled on the Garmin Instinct because of the coupling of GPS functionality with a simple, rugged wristwatch design.
However, after five days with it, I've decided to return it. Here's why:
1) Images of the watch give the impression of a proportionately large screen. However, in practice, I found that while running I couldn't check my data at a glance: the actual screen area was just too small. Meaning that I had to slow down and make an effort to hold my wrist steady to check my speed and distance. Customizing the screen to show only one or two bits of data somewhat mitigates this, but, not satisfactorily. And, then you have to switch between screens to see the different data.
2) Images of the watch, and many reviewer's comments, suggest a "Casio"/"G Shock"-like object. I'd say that analogy only somewhat applies to its appearance, while the light weight of the watch, its soft, stretchy strap, and plastic used in the case don't quite impart Casio/G Shock quality.
3) While I have a soft spot for old school dot matrix/monochrome LCD displays, I find in practice that the slightly too low resolution of the Instinct's screen, and the design language of watch faces and widgets, do not speak to me.
4) Images of the watch suggest a "near-black" graphite color. In reality, it is closer to grey.
The above considered, I feel that I will be frustrated with this as an activity GPS watch, and won't appreciate it as a wristwatch between activities.
While reviewers seem to concur that it is priced at a sweet spot in the sports watch/GPS/wearable market, I feel that evaluated on its own it's overpriced.
However, some positives:
1) The screen and control customizability is excellent
2) The UI has a nice logic to it and in 20 minutes I was sufficiently familiar with it
3) The Garmin Connect iOS app is excellent
4) It seems to establish GPS/GLONASS/Galileo connectivity very quickly

title: Not Quite a Five
text:
I have bought this keyboard/folio setup for some older Samsung tablets (Tab S2 and Tab E) and have been very satisfied. The Fintie keyboards work well. I have had no problems with them at all. The Fintie folios have been awesome, too.

I can't quite give this new one for my Tab A a "five" rating, though, because it doesn't have any provision for protecting the tablet screen when the folio is closed like the older ones did.

There was an upraised sleeve that went around the outside of the screen on the older style that probably couldn't be easily duplicated for the Tab A's different screen edges. The older style kept the keyboard from contacting the screen when the folio was closed. The new one provides no protection; the keyboard comes in contact with the screen when the folio is closed, which will eventually scratch the screen.

Some workarounds could be putting a screen protector on the Tab A's screen or keeping something between the screen and the keyboard. I bought a screen protector for it, but I still haven't put it on because I do not like screen protectors. I've been putting the keyboard in the thin paper sleeve from Samsung that the tablet was packaged in and hoping it will protect the screen.

What should happen, is that Fintie comes up with a solution for this issue. Hard plastic keys rubbing on a tablet's screen will eventually cause problems, I would certainly think.

I'm still giving this a thumbs up because the keyboard is great like the others were, but I am annoyed that I am having to come up with a solution for something that the designers and manufacturers of this keyboard/folio should have done.

I am including some photos to illustrate what I'm talking about. The older Tab E tablet with the older style Fintie keyboard/folio is on the left in the first photo that shows them both. The next two photos show more detail of the older style folio. The last two photos show the newer style folio for the Tab A. Compare the way the two tablets fit into the folios.

title: Duet 50 Slims..a great TWS earbud that easily competes with the best!
text:
As a previous owner of the original Back Bay Duet, I received an email from Back Bay describing the new Duet 50 Slim with a 20% discount offer. Given the fact that I was quite impressed with the original, and considering the very modest cost, I decided to give the Slim a try.
I found the same quality packing as the original but discovered that the new Slim seems to have been retuned as they are better balanced tonally than the original. Soundstage and imaging are superb with nicely detailed highs, accurate vocal presentation with non-boomy bass that does not color the mids.
The case has been improved with a metal covering that should easily fit in a jeans watch pocket. Charging is via USB 3 with easy to view charging indication. Pairing was nearly instantaneous and I have yet to experience a drop or connection artifact. Controls are intuitive with easy to activate buttons.
Although it carries the "Slim" label, the buds themselves seem to be similar in size to the original Duet 50 and fit comfortably and securely in my ears. None of the included 5 pairs of tips fit my ears but the large Spiral Dot tips fit the buds securely and also provide a perfect fit. I was also pleased to find that the large Spiral Dots fit perfectly in the charging case.
Given the quality build, excellent sound, 8 hour play time and modest cost, the Duet 50 Slim makes a superb daily driver!

title: Surprised what was Revealed
text:
First off, these speakers were purchased through the warehouse deals for less than $13. They are loud and sound good. If I come across another low priced warehouse deal, I would buy these again.

As you can see, from the pictures the top tweeter plate came lose and to my surprise noticed that one of the small tweeters isn't even wired. It's just for show. I point out the tiny tweeter and it's clear it's not wired at all.

Maybe this is why they are called Riot, because they were laughing all the way to the bank. The designer thought it was hilarious to dupe the consumers into the idea of 4 way speakers. In reality, this is a 3 way. Again they sound good for what they are but don't expect high end quality. These are entry level speakers, better than OEM wizzer cone paper junk.

I decided to disconnected the top plate and eliminate the 3rd tiny tweeters, that weren't even wired to work. Also removed the improper 3.3 capacitor from the large tweeter and added a 4.7, the same as the other speaker. It's currently a modified 2 way Riot, haha and sounds much better now.

If you are interested in 4 way speakers I suggest DS18 Select 6x9 has a 5 way, which can be purchased on amazon for a little more money than these boss riots and sound better too.

title: Not as strong or reliable as r7000 NightHawk, way more expensive
text:
I thought this router would be an update and upgrade from my trusty NetGear r7000 Nighthawk. No so.

The 2.4GHz radios have a hard time reaching by ip cams 175 ft from the house, the r7000 was almost 100% reliable. The 5Ghz ac signal is on average 5-10 db weaker than the normal 5Ghz radio and so is only good for about one room, certainly not 3500 square ft.

Turns out if you read the fine print about Beam Forming it's not all it's cracked up to be either. Mu-MIMO only works if the receiving device is capable. ETC.

In general, I have found this to be at best a so so router. I am thinking about returning it and going some different route. Maybe just add an extender to my good old Nighthawk r7000.

Edit: Feb 4, 2020.
After spending a good part of the day watching this router drop wireless connections, rebooting more times than I can remember, turning off then turning on features, fooling with the antennas and basically literally everything I know about routers I gave up and got approved for a return. I will now hook my old NetGear r7000 Nighthawk back up and enjoy almost perfect performance again, even with a wobbly antenna.

The essential problem of the r8000 router is the wireless performance is truly awful.

Edit Feb. 15:

After the last edit the router completely settled down and was running smoothly. I cancelled the return. Oops! Bad mistake. The very next day it became very erratic again. It turns out the various Smart features, beam forming, Mu Mimo and the like are either dumbed down features of the standard, don't do anything helpful, or simply makes things worse. One thing that DID help was move the router about 8 feet to the exact location I had the r7000. Everything fell into place at that moment and performance improved. I then set up the r7000 as a repeater, (not hard, but don't miss a step) and all is mostly good.

Except, the wireless performance is still erratic with power levels going up and down and to get my 10 cams running right I have to re-boot about once per day.

Last words: The Netgear r7000 router is a much better wireless performer and a lot cheaper.

title: Helps, but the PI4 could use more cooling.
text:
I don't have the Kodi Edition, but I did buy the Flirc Pi 4 case from the manufacturers website. They are the same thing, just different colors. Anyways the Flirc aluminum raspberry pi cases are definitely the best out there especially considering they are only $15 or less. I have three raspberry Pi 3B+ all of them each have a Flirc case. It absorbs heat very well and allows the processor to run smoother.

I do have one complaint about the design of this case. I believe that the aluminum design can be improved by adding small fins or grooves around the case to increase the surface area for passive cooling. I love the look of the case as is, but I think for it to be more functional they will need to sacrifice the smooth design. At the very least I wish Flirc would design an aluminum case more for functional than appearance. One with larger fins meant to be mounted vertically. Since heat naturally rises a heatsink with vertical fins allows for great passive cooling.

The Raspberry Pi 4 gets pretty warm. The 3B+ did too, but the 4 is noticeably warmer. Its a great hand warmer in the cold. It doesn't get hot enough to burn you. It is right on the edge of discomfort. My main concern with the heat though is I want to leave this on 24/7 near my TV for Kodi use and I don't get warm fuzzies knowing that this Pi 4 gets warmer than any other electronics I have and I don't like leaving it unattended.

text:

This looks just fine even when next to a 27" 1440p. Not as a sharp, but the same PPI as a 24" 1080p panel.

The HDR is awful but you shouldn't be buying anything but OLED if you want HDR.

Navigating the OSD is an exercise in frustration, but there's a (Windows) program you can use instead. SOL if you're a Linux user, though.

The hole in the stand to help manage/route cables works if you've only got two cables, but if you're using all the inputs then it's too small.

Would be 5 stars if it was ~$400, but if you're going to charge a premium and ask $700 for a DP 1.2 1440p monitor this late into 2020 then it should be flawless.

title: HOME / END hotkeys figured out
text:
I've had this for a while, but avoided using this for some reason. It's compact, comfortable, has good range, and I'm paired with 3 devices. Not having a numpad is fine, but not having dedicated PAGE UP / DOWN, HOME / END keys though, made me think I might switch back to my Logitech K360.

These HOME / END hotkeys in particular were not at all obvious from the other comments or even Logitech's website, so hopefully this info helps others out. FYI - I'm using Windows / ChromeOS / Android phone.

Web browser:
page up = FN+UP ARROW
page down = FN+DOWN ARROW
home (top of web page) = FN+LEFT ARROW
end (bottom of web page) = FN+RIGHT ARROW

Text / code editors:
page up = FN+UP ARROW
page down = FN+DOWN ARROW
home (beginning of line) = FN+LEFT ARROW
end (end of line) = FN+RIGHT ARROW
home (top of document) = CTRL+FN+LEFT ARROW
end (bottom of document) = CTRL+FN+RIGHT ARROW

Still getting used to these combo keys, but it's working for me. Haven't really used it for very long though, so I might change my rating.
