title: Great value wireless earbuds, with a few flaws.
text:
These wireless earbuds are a fantastic value compared to its Apple counterparts. For $50, you can get a pair of wireless earbuds that have a longer battery, better audio quality, and very good noise cancellation. However, my four main gripes with these earbuds are as follows (and they aren't deal breakers):

- The buttons are real, not touch capacitive.

The main issue with this is that when you press the button, the earbud goes further in, making it uncomfortable to use. Also, it prevents the waterproof rating to be higher than IP55.

- The earbuds become uncomfortable after an hour or so of being in the ear.

While many won't listen to the earbuds for this long, I feel that as I wear them longer, they become more uncomfortable, and I have to take them out for a few minutes.

- Only the right earbud connects to your phone.

While JLab remedied this with their higher end models of wireless earbuds, I still want the ability to only use my left earbud on this model, especially in situations where only one earbud is wanted, such as while running on a busy road. Currently, I have to take out both earbuds and leave the right one in my pocket or on the table in order to maintain a connection to my phone.

- The earbud commands are not customizable.

Currently, there is no way to be able to customize the commands of the earbuds. You are stuck with the configuration out of the box, and it is very disappointing, as I am right handed, and want to pause with my right hand, but I am forced to do so with my left (also, this requires me to take out my left earbud if I am listening to my right one only).

Despite these few flaws, however, the earbuds are certainly a great step into the wireless world, and with a few years of development, I am sure that we will receive better and better revisions of what we have now. If you don't own wireless earbuds already, I would recommend you buy these.

title: Not sure how to rate this
text:
No quality control problems at all.

You have to buy the most expensive model to get a useable number of ports. The cheaper model only has two USB-C ports, and one of them has to be used for the power supply, so it's like there's only one port, pretty pathetic. My cheap Windows laptop came with an HDMI port plus 3 USB ports, plus a separate input for the power cable. If you are going to dock a MacBook to a monitor, then I highly recommend a Plugable USB C Dock with Charging. Don't buy one of those super-cheap usb hubs, you won't be happy with how scarily hot they get.) Beware that if you want to drive a 4K monitor at 60 Hz, on a 13" Macbook you have to have one port totally dedicated to the monitor.

They say the keyboard is great, but it doesn't seem all that special to me, so the keyboard on the previous model must have been pretty bad.

Love the trackpad, MacBooks have the best trackpads.

I don't like the touchbar. It's a lot easer to adjust the volume or monitor brightness by holding down a FN key while pushing a button. The touchbar is really a pain in the you-know-what.

I'm not a fan of the glossy screens on MacBooks. Elsewhere, the standard for computers is matte anti-glare screens that are easier to look at without seeing reflections. Also, this "retina" screen has way more resolution than you need, the standard 1920 pixel width on PC laptops is more than enough pixels for a 13" screen. These Macs have worse battery life because they have to drive so many pixels. But colors are certainly great. There's no denying it's a great screen, but not necessarily the most practical screen.

It does a lot less weird stuff than my Windows laptop. But still not totally free of bugs.

But Mac's biggest fault incompatible it is with all the software you want to use. Not only does it not work with Windows software, that's obvious, but it also doesn't work with older Mac software such as Microsoft Office 2011. And as this is the last Intel MacBook (maybe), this means that there's going to be a whole bunch of future software that won't run on this.

Battery life is pretty good, it can last a whole day of work IF that work doesn't include Zoom meetings with video. Zoom meetings with video eat up the battery life.

Still my most favorite laptop computer ever, but annoyed about not being able to use Office 2011.

title: So far, so good.  Still early though...
text:
I literally just got it delivered an hour ago. I have to say, it's quite handsome. And hefty! My JBL Charge 2+ served me faithfully through countless camping trips, cookouts, basketball games in the driveway with kids, and even a trip to Cancun. The battery started giving me trouble about 8 months ago. Wouldn't charge all the way, and lots of amp clipping that got to be just too much. I didn't give up on it though. I bought a 3rd-party battery in hopes of reviving it. The sound was just so great. Didn't want to give up on it just yet. She still kept distorting and clipping, which was a bummer. Then, 2 weeks ago, the JBL stopped charging.

Once the mourning period was over, I dove head first into finding a replacement. I went straight back to JBL. I just had problems with some of the new designs and it seems JBL went to a mono speaker for my max pricepoint of $200. I'm no audiophile (probably way too many concerts and NASCAR races have crapped my hearing), but I sold home and car audio for 12 years at Crutchfield. So I kinda no good sound. My home audio system is the Polk RM7200, being powered by the Onkyo TX-SR604. Look it up. It's good stuff. So I don't want mono.

I'm rambling a bit. Sorry. I looked at every speaker under the sun. I was even willing to push my budget up to $300 to include some of the other options. Just always felt uneasy, and honestly, people either seemed to love or hate each option. Options from Bose, Kicker, Harman/Kardon, UE, etc. You name it and I spent time researching.

I bought my 10-yo daughter an Anker speaker a few years back. Nothing special. It was maybe $25. Just a blue rectangle. But it sounded fairly good. So the other night I went down a YouTube rabbit hole of nothing but BT speaker reviews. They kept using this Soundcore as a reference speaker for a lot of their sound tests. I'd never heard of it. Long story short, I bought two of these Motion+'s so I can get true L/R stereo while camping or whatever. I've played a few songs, nothing bass heavy, but I like it. Nice full range and separation. I just downloaded the EQ app and that's where I am.

I'll update after a good break-in period and messing around with the EQ app. Thanks for reading!

title: Great integration, Really poor tuner
text: The integration is great. However this is a really bad tuner. I think the problem is that it scans too fast and drops any channel that is less than perfect.  So if you have anything but a signal with a bit error rate other than zero, this tuner won’t pick up the channel. I used my signal meter on the channels that it can’t find and have a reasonable signal but the ota receiver won’t pick them up even though the TV on the other side of the splitter gets them fine. I tried pushing 5db of amplification into the device and it got worse. I added attenuation to the input and got one more channel but not the two I really needed. Just a note - I’m a dork and have engineered my antenna system to have the least amount of loss possible and no over amplification. The tuner seems overly picky. Thinking of returning it and getting another as it was used and possibly I might get another one that behaved differently.

title: Pretty decent, but needs some functionality improvements.
text:
One of my primary concerns after reading the reviews was picture quality of recordings. Given that it has to transcode the stream, and is limited to two concurrent streams at 720p, it seems like they would give you the option to only have ONE stream at 1080 to use the full processing power for that one stream. Some of the reviews have mentioned that the picture quality was not as clear as a direct antenna connection, so I was expecting somewhat poor picture quality. However I am quite happy to report that the picture quality of recordings is quite good, and is acceptable if you're okay with 720p HD. In my case I am very happy with it. Now, on to the issues I found.

Technical issue: Would not play recordings with the Recast hard-wired via ethernet, and the Fire Stick on WiFi. Only until I put the Recast on WiFi did it play the recordings. Makes sense if they're not on the same WiFi network, but seems like it should still work if it's on the same router network, but maybe not. I was just hoping to reduce any buffering issues by running it on ethernet.

Functionality Issue #1: If you cancel a recording, it does not appear to cancel it right away. And during that time it won't let you delete the recording either. I noticed this happen on two separate occasions so I know it wasn't just a fluke. I cancelled a recording and the red light stayed on like it was recording for a good 20 to 30 minutes before it finally cancelled the recording. Then, and only then would it allow me to delete it. Not a big deal. I can wait and just delete it later. The only time it would be an issue is if the other tuner was already in use, and I suddenly wanted to stop one that was recording to record a different show. I wouldn't be able to record the new show until it finally decides to cancel the other recording. That might be an issue at some point, but not very often.

Functionality Issue #2: As others have mentioned, the channels only show the station letter or the broadcast company (CBS, ABC, etc.) but does not show the channel numbers. A little confusing at first, but I figured it out. Not a big deal.

Functionality Issue #3: As others have mentioned, when recording a series, if the show airs on more than one channel, you cannot pick the channel. It's either the channel they have randomly chosen (which may or may not be the one you want to record the show on), or ALL channels in which case you will get duplicates. I thought I had a workaround by going into Scheduled Recordings and then pick the one I don't want to record (because it shows the channel icon there as well) and choose cancel recording, but that led to..... Functionality Issue #4 (see below).

Update 12/17/19:

Functionality Issue #4: If you schedule a series recording, and then later want to cancel ONE episode in the Scheduled Recordings, it cancels the ENTIRE SERIES. It doesn't give you the option to cancel the single episode, OR the series. It should. The only way I've found to cancel ONE episode is to schedule the recordings manually, one at a time. So football, for example: I can't just schedule the series NFL Football, I have to schedule all 4 games every Sunday ONE AT A TIME if I want to be able to cancel any of them individually. This is a design flaw that should be fixed, seriously.

OBSERVATION: Some reviews have complained there is no search function in the channel guide. This is not true. You can search the local channels by using the native Search functionality on the Fire TV Home page. Click the magnifying glass, and in the search results you'll have a separate rows for Movies and TV, and then Live TV (for Fire TV Recast channels) if there are any shows coming up in the next 2 weeks. So you CAN search the channel guide, but it's just not incorporated into the channel guide itself, and it really should be to be more intuitive.

OBSERVATION: The context menu button on the remote is your friend, especially when it comes to deleting recordings. When you select a recording, depending on where you're selecting it from, there is no Delete Recording button displayed on screen so it appears there is no way to delete it! The little context hamburger button on the remote will give you that option. The context button is also handy in the channel guide, as it allows you to filter the channels by Pluto TV, the Fire TV Recast, Philo, or ALL sources. This is pretty handy when channel surfing.

Summary: Overall I like it, I love the integration into the Fire TV menu, and I really like the new Live tab that shows the Live Sports, Breaking News, current Live channels from the Recast, and then a row for Pluto TV, and Philo. That's pretty cool. I really hope they add Sling TV live content into the Live channels at some point like they have currently with Philo TV and PS Vue. Still, with the issues I mentioned above, it doesn't have quite the same functionality as Tivo, but hopefully they'll come out with updates to correct some of those. It really needs some functionality enhancements for usability. Overall it does what I need it to, but the recording options are pretty basic at this point. I've had it now almost 6 months and I've seen no updates from Amazon to improve some of these things.

title: Buyer's remorse with this one. Operating system sinks this DAP.
text:
I've tried my hardest to really like the XDP-02u. I've really struggled with it. I think I have come to my final conclusion here. The sound of the DAP is good. There is no doubt about that. The real spoiler here is the operating system/software. The software is primitive though generally functional. When it comes to TIDAL though (which is why I bought the DAP) the software system is extremely frustrating. There are no thumbnails of album covers available to select albums among similar titles (like classical composers). You can never tell, for instance, which Bach or Mozart album you are selecting because they all listed as Bach or Mozart. You have no means of just selecting a specific album. Same with "Greatest Hits." Again, no means of selecting a specific album. And, again, the middle portion (the letters K and L) of "My collection" on TIDAL with this software just doesn't list.

So I write to Pioneer and ask them if a firmware update might be forthcoming to address these issues and they said no. It is a limitation of the operating system. One that Pioneer does not advertise.

Bottom line: For me, no matter how good the sound, if the software stinks, it blows the whole experience with the DAP. Lousy software trumps good sound. If you're looking at the XDP-02u for TIDAL nirvana, you won't find it here.

2-1-19 It's really a shame that the TIDAL software on this unit comes up short because, otherwise, this would be a fine unit. If you were to use this DAP with only an SD card, it is a great choice. For streaming with TIDAL using the installed software ( I haven't tried Deezer), it remains for me a no go.

title: Product and customer service dont work
text:
I bought this router because usually the more you spend, the better product you get and this one was basically advertised to be the best of the best. Well that is wrong. I had the router for less than a day and realized it wasn't broadcasting one of the 5Ghz channels. I did every bit of troubleshooting I knew how to do and nothing worked. So I called ASUS tech support and they walked me through all the troubleshooting steps that I had done and then told me the router was broken so I should get a replacement. So I sent it back and had a replacement ordered. The replacement took a week to show up. I got the replacement and it has the same freakin issue. However on my replacement router, I was able to set the 5Ghz channel that wasn't broadcasting to N-only mode and it seems to work under that mode. That isn't what you pay more than $350 for. It's advertised as an AC router and all 5Ghz bands should be on the AC standard. Why would I pay full price for a brand new car that's missing a wheel? So either their QA is non-existent or they have a firmware issue. I'm hoping a future firmware upgrade can fix this issue but this should have already been tested. You learn of the problems as soon as the thing is powered on and booted up.

If you don't already know, the N standard has a max speed of 450mbps and the AC standard has a max speed of 1300mbps. This is why I'm not happy with the state of my router. Sure the other 5Ghz band works on the AC standard but I expect that when I pay $350 the router works EXACTLY as it's advertised to out of the box with NO troubleshooting.

The customer service was acceptable even though I can barely understand them through their thick Indian accents. I spoke to at least 2 service reps and both were very difficult to understand due to ASUS outsourcing their tech support to India. Nothing against that other than they are hard to understand. They were helpful but I don't like being told on every call and then being called a few days later and being told to fill out a survey to say how I thought my service was. I think their service model is forcing the service reps to waste their time telling people to do surveys rather than focus more on their jobs. Just my opinion.

Update - After talking with customer service for about 2 weeks, they have gone silent so I am now left with a partially working router. Not buying ASUS routers ever again. And I hope I never have to talk with their useless customer service again.

title: Good, but much more annoying than the AfterShokz air
text:
This is the third pair of AfterShokz that I've owned. I am a fan, and will never move away from the bone-conducting technology. In fact I can't wait until this gets adopted by the motorcycle helmet industry.

The first pair was the regular AfterShokz which worked great for over a year before I left them in a rental car. No worries, it was a good time to upgrade to the AfterShokz air. A great upgrade for sure and lasted for over a year before the charging port broke.

The third set was the AfterShokz aerobic, which I was very excited about. The sound is amazing, Battery lasts longer but for a guy that listens to audiobooks and podcasts all day, it didn't really improve that much.

What I found disappointing was what seems like the software side of them. I'm not sure if they rushed to market too quickly but I did see plenty of reviews where the beep was way too loud. I can confirm that is an issue, even with the phone volume turned down, the beep seems to come over at 100% of the volume of the headset. If you have earplugs in to boost the sound, it's almost unbearable.

The second disappointment was the fact that I thought i could connect two devices but did not stop to read the instructions, so six months later I finally found the sequence you must do to pair multiple devices. but don't do it...

The largest problem I have with these is the fact that when a device is out of range, instead of beeping once to alert you that a device has been disconnected, it beeps every thirty seconds or so and gets so annoying. I don't see the point where you would want to hear constant beeps if a device lost its pairing or is out of the range of the headset. I haven't figured out a way to disable that without turning the headset off and back on again. Again that's probably my fault and I should refer to the manual but really.

Again, I am a huge fan of the bone conducting technology and aftershockz, my review is not to discourage you from testing any of the great AfterShokz devices, I would just recommend not starting with the aeropex as it might ruin the experience for you.

title: Great in most aspects, but starved for RAM
text:
This laptop has amazingly good build quality, and is very snappy to use. The achiles heel is that it only has 6 GB of RAM available to the OS, since it is capped at 8 GB non upgradeable, and 2 GB are dedicated to the integrated graphics. 8 GB would be OK if fully usable, but 6 GB is getting a bit tight these days due to the horrible new trend of desktop apps written in Javascript.

Apart from 8 GB instead of 16 GB RAM, this laptop is amazing, and I hope that Lenovo will continue to consider the AMD Ryzen processors instead of Intel processors for future laptops in this price range. The latest-gen Ryzen has excellent multicore performance. AMD's integrated graphics are also surprisingly good, especially considering that you get it for free from the processor. This computer should be able to run basically any AAA game released in 2013ish or before at high settings despite being an ultralight notebook with no dedicated graphics card. It can also run relatively less demanding modern games like Overwatch or Fortnite at high settings well.

The SSD could maybe be a bit bigger in this age of cheap 3DNAND SSD's, but it is very fast. The computer boots up instantly and has very little post-startup lag, making the fingerprint reader very nice to have as login time would be the time bottleneck in getting started otherwise.

The screen is great, both as an HD screen and as a touchscreen. It is larger than any ipad and gives an amazing touch experience. I expected it to be a bit bulky, but the laptop has an evenly distributed weight and balances well despite its size, so the tablet + pen experience is great. Used the pen to try writing and solving some physics equations with subscripts and superscripts, and it worked great, better than my old early-gen surface.

At this price level, this is the best offering out there imho for a 2 in 1 laptop. A microsoft surface tablet with similar performance would cost you twice as much.

EDIT: After learning that the RAM is in fact upgradeable, I increased my review to a 5. I ended up installing a 16 GB ram stick to increase the RAM to 20 GB (18 GB usable with 2 going to the GPU), and a 1 TB SSD stick from Sabrent:

https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B071KP8CGJ
https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B07LGF54XR/

This laptop is a pleasure to open up & work with. Replacing the RAM and SSD was a very straightforward operation. Might also add a new networking card as well. The current networking card works great on a strong wifi network, but frequently drops connectivity when the signal is weaker.

text:

(Away from where'd you would put the fan or radiator) And the PSU shroud needs a bigger cut out in front. No need for the shroud to cover the whole bottom. (Look at the NXZT 200s)

The picture on this things is deep, rich, vivid and brilliant. What also really pops on this is the black levels. It's as black as I've ever personally seen in a home theater projector, and the black level makes for a picture contrast that takes your viewing experience to an incredible level.

About the only gripe is that it's slow to boot up. Takes roughly 35 seconds to turn on the lamp, which is a bit slower boot time than my Panasonic. That said, the picture quality is simply phenomenal. Even with ambient light in the room, the picture is still crisp and detailed. The 4k content it renders is off the charts good.

If you can afford the crazy price tag, you will LOVE this projector. It's a strong 5/5 stars.

title: Very reasonable if you get it on sale. Be prepared for the usual Microsoft nonsense.
text:
When these are on sale, they are going very inexpensively indeed, often for well under $200. Monitor Amazon for discounts.

This review is intended for folks that are generally familiar with computing.

PROS:

1) Very light and very compact
2) Screen is reasonably bright and even
3) Audio is reasonably good and audible
4) Keyboard is eminently touch-typable (I have kids learning on them with Typing Club)
5) Design isn't embarrassing—very modern
6) Works and works reasonably well at very low price point

CONS:

1) Screen viewing angles could be better (though still far better than many Chromebooks)
2) The Windows 10 adventure (not really Asus' fault, but still)
3) Screen hinge is a bit floppier than I'd like—not due to hinge slop, just due to plastic

MEH:

1) Trackpad is modern and usable (i.e. of the post-Mac-Magic-Trackpad generation) but not super impressive
2) Placement of ports is not tremendously convenient (scattered all around outside edge)

PERFORMANCE:

1) Runs browsers and office apps (incl. video streaming) with no problems
2) Great performance with classic games (e.g. many from GOG or similar)
3) Not suited to run modern 3D engine games, don't bother
4) Runs about the same speed or even slightly faster than our Dell E6410s (ca. 2010 Core i5)
5) Can multitask within reason with few or no problems

HATE:

Windows 10. This is totally Microsoft's fault, not Asus' fault, and par for the course since you are buying a Windows laptop and presumably want one if you're not opting for a Chromebook at this point.

Comes with Windows 10 S, which is hobbled and won't run most PC software. This can be switched for free to Windows 10 Home, but you must:

- Launch Microsoft Store app to cause an update to Microsoft Store
- Hit Windows-X keys, then choose System Settings
- Find the link to upgrade to Windows 10 Pro
- Click that and instead of the paid Pro option, opt to switch to Home

Then, of course, you're in update hell, Microsoft style. There are a good 4-5 hours of updates that must be run. Do yourself a favor and do NOT try to do any app installs, system preferences, etc. until all updates have run, or you will break things and have to roll back.

Also note that the Microsoft updater downloads and runs updates in random order, and that updates step on each other, i.e. one update may force a reboot in the middle of another update, leading to chaos and a broken update database.

We got three of these and they sat side by side as we ran updates. The Windows 10 updater broke and got stuck on all of them in different ways—one lost the ability to launch anything but Edge, the other stopped downloading updates and the troubleshooter wouldn't fix it due to "corrupt updates database" and the other got to a state where it found no updates available, even though it was a pre-1803 version of Windows 10.

The solution in all cases was to start edge, visit the Microsoft page for the web-based Windows 10 Update Assistant (you'll have to Google it, as Amazon frowns on links in reviews) and run the latest update using that.

It will take a couple hours on this machine to download, pre-install, and then install across multiple reboots. After that, you can run the remaining updates that aren't in these rollups again using the regular update service.

*But YES,* once you're done, you have *Windows 10 Home* and you can install all the Windows software you want. I see a lot of one-star reviews here complaining about Windows 10 S and how you can't install Chrome, etc. but you absolutely *can* switch to Windows 10 Home for free, it just takes some legwork and finding the right clicks in the settings areas. Google is your friend.

As an aside, if you do this, I'd strongly recommend you get a 32GB or 64GB TF/MicroSD card to add to the machine, as the built-in storage isn't going to be enough to do everything you want. Don't worry, they're dirt-cheap these days.

OVERALL:

A better laptop all around than the Dell E6410s we're replacing. Dirt cheap, better screen and performance than these high-end-just-a-few-years-ago machines, while far thinner, lighter, and with better battery life and heat characteristics.

As long as you're not expecting a 2019 gamer ultra laptop at this price, you'll be presently surprised—better in every way than many mid-to-high end laptops of just 5-10 years ago, but priced (at least when on sale) such that you may be able to outfit each of your three kids with a very reasonable, non-Chromebook school laptop for under $500 total.

text:
PRO: I bought this system that came with 2 bullet cameras and 2 dome cameras. I also purchased 2 extra bullet cameras with the order. The system was fairly easy to set up, just time consuming and hot in the attic running the wires. The bullet cameras are well built and sturdy. The plastic housing dome cameras mount to a plastic mounting plate that slips into notches and turns about 1/2 inch. Did not feel very sturdy, should have had some type of screw to hold in place. I am electronically challenged but was still able to connect system to tv, laptop, and iphone. The clarity of the cameras are great.
CON: I get hundreds of motion detection alerts per day. I have customized the motion detection zones so no vehicles set it off. There is no bushes or branches getting moved by the wind. There are trees nearby that shadow part of my house and when the shadow moves, it triggers the alert. I have the sensitivity set as low as I can and it will still trigger me at about 20-25 feet from the cameras. There is no use having an alert set if it will not pick up a person. I know there is a setting to change the sensitivity settings for different times of the day, but I don't have a set pattern when I am home or gone.
I have read that this system uses numerical algorithms to judge whether there is motion or not, but surely the technology is out there to differentiate between shadows, bugs flying, and a person walking. I bought this system to alert me of any intruders on my property, but with getting hundreds of alert notifications per day it is not doing what I bought it for. I am planning on returning this system and buying one that will better meet my needs.

We really wanted to like this product. It's a great idea. For under $1,000 you get a decent PTZ camera, a solid speakerphone, and a DSP-equipped microphone with AEC (auto echo cancellation). No quick start guide or user manual included, but easy enough to get online.

Connecting the unit and making our first test video calls was super easy. The picture quality was excellent although the camera's autofocus struggles to find the sweet spot.

That's the good news.

The big issue is the mic in the desktop speakerphone. When the user at the Logitech Group end of the call first begins to speak, there is a very distinct and annoying crackling-popping sound. The unwanted added sound masks the talker's first 2 or 3 words. After that the audio is very good. However, if the talker is silent for a couple of seconds, as soon as speech is resumed the first few words are again masked by the crackling and popping.

This unit has pretty decent Amazon reviews, but after experiencing the audio issue, we read the reviews a little deeper. Other users have also had this issue and over a year ago at that. The big disappointment is that Logitech is still shipping these with the same defect.

I've always trusted Logitech. I'll be more cautious going forward.

title: Get what you Pay.  Disposable Chinese Quality.
text:
The center SMA pin on the Male-SMA-to-Male-BNC adapter broke off inside my factory stock Baofeng antenna. I should have bought a radio with BNC antenna connector to start with but look at me, can't afford to save my money for three months to be able to get that, so I spend $30 on a Chinese Baofeng not intended to be used by real hams who make their own antennas and like having quicker disconnect than the three and a half turns a tiny little SMA connector requires of my hamhock fingers trying to get to it around channel knobs and rubber-duck antenna bodies, so I get the adapters for $6 to make it work.

So it broke inside my antenna, making the duck antenna now useless. No pressure was applied to that junction, though. All forces I've applied have been to the BNC-BNC junction, where I had the antenna adapted to BNC so I could rapidly change from the antenna cable in my car to the rubber duck without having to sit there with an SMA screwing and unscrewing. SMAs are reputed not to be long-lasting to begin with across multiple connect-disconnect cycles, so I figured I'd adapt to a BNC to avoid the problem.

Lasted maybe a month.

Great, it's only what, like $6? I can afford $6 a month to keep replacing it, right?

And everything else I buy from China that breaks in a month, right? And also the item that the adapter left its bits in that I can no longer use now?

Look for better quality made somewhere with labor regulations. Of course, good luck with that. $30 Baofeng made to American standards of quality and workforce wages would probably cost $300 and be twice the size.

But it would work, it would last 50 years, and it would be designed to be upgraded to keep up with technology.

This projector's picture quality and watching experience exceeded my expectations by far. The picture attached is of a 133" display. Text is sharp, colors are excellent. Brightness i could say is almost blinding in medium/low lit rooms. You don't really need a ~$200 screen to enjoy this projector. This is great because you don't have distance restrictions and can use it in bedrooms or living rooms and don't necessarily need to place it on the ceiling. Use projectorcentral website for any projector that you might be interested to calculate the projector distance from the wall, it helped me a lot to understand projectors as a novice.
After having the experience with this projector. if i had the choice right now to either go buy a top tier $1000 Samsung 55" Q8F series Qled Tv or this projector and save $300 i would buy the projector without a single doubt.

title: A surprisingly feature packed battery charger!
text:
I've been using a Nitecore D4 charger for years. It's a great charger and has the capability to charge Li-ion, Ni-MH and Ni-Cd batteries as well as LiFEPO4. But there are times when I just need some additional capacity for just AA and AAA NiMh batteries so I thought I'd give this one a try. This product was provided to me as a Vine reviewer so I thought I'd give it a try.

This charger does not disappoint. It has the ability to charge, discharge, test, and cycle (to repair seemingly dead batteries). I did not try the cycle mode but all of the rest worked as advertised. I tested an AAA Eneloop and it showed the battery had a capacity of 777 mAH which is spot on with Panasonic's claim of up to 800.

The display is bright and informative. I did not read the manual when first using this device and it's just a matter of clicking and holding the mode button for a few seconds to change the different modes and cycling through them. If you click and hold the mode button while it's in charge mode you can also click the current button and change from .25 to .5 to .75 and ultimately 1A of charge.

This charger does not come with a wall wart; just the charger body, usb micro cable, and a manual. It takes a 5V 2A input so as long as you have a USB charging hub, or an old cell phone charger you should be fine. It would be nice if it had USB C in 2020. I can't speak to longevity but the build appears to be sturdy plastic. The buttons all have a very robust and positive click to them. I am highly impressed by this product and will keep dlyfull on my radar because they've done a very good job with this charger.

If all you need is the ability to charge your AA and AAA NiMh batteries, I think this charger is really a no brainer as it gives you some very convenient functionality that you just don't get with more simple chargers. Highly recommend.

title: Operates as it should.  Installation requirements clearly not thought through
text:
Functionally I would rate this 5 stars. For installation, I would rate it minus 31 stars. The issue is the power cord is not detachable. As a result, you must use a hole cutter of at least 2 inches to allow space for the plug to fit through from the outside of your garage/house to the inside. That means, that on the outside of your home, after the basic installation, you get to use a hole cutter and get through your garage, you then get to apply wood filer, smooth it, wait for it to dry, sand it, clean it, prime it, wait for it to dry and paint it. And then, if you care how it looks inside your garage, you get to do the very same thing.

The solution would be sooooo simple and would make this a 90 minute installation vs multi-day installation. And that solution would be to either make the cord detachable from the camera or make the plug detachable from the cord. THEN, you drill a 1/2 hole through the outside and inside, pass through the wire, caulk the two openings and you are done. If I were to do this again, I would simply cut off the plug, install it and rewire a new plug. If you know what you are doing, ZERO risk and a much faster AND CLEANER install.

That the company has allowed this massive inconvenience to exist boggles my mind.

title: Awesome drive. One big issue, one very small one.
text:
I got this drive and replaced my Samsung SATA 860EVO. For the most part, with this type of change you won't notice much of a difference. Windows doesn't load any faster but once I log in those application do load much faster. Most of Windows is still single-threaded. :(
I wanted to see how it did for writes so I created a RAM disk, copied a 3.9GB file to RAM from my HDD, and then wrote it to my MP600. 3.9GB took between 2 and 3 seconds to write!!! Now that's Fast!

The big issue I have is that the Corsair Tools, that's what they call it even though I think that the only tool is to clone the drive failed. It would get 3% into the cloning and fail. Nothing to help diagnose the problem. You have to than delete all partitions off of the MP600 in order to try the clone again. I found I had to use DiskPart from DOS command prompt as for unknown reasons disk manager wouldn't work with what was left on the drive.

The small issue is that when you insert this into your MOBO, they have created yet another size screw! And you won't have any of these on hand. Removing my ASROCK X570 cover I found out that I needed a screw for the MP600. I ended up stealing one from the MOBO second M2 slot. It runs at about 35-40C. I really haven't taxed it much.

Removing the heat sink was a breeze. Looking at the conducting material inside made me wonder if it was conducting material of packing material. I knew it wasn't packing material but you'll see what I mean.

I'm very happy with this unit.

Updated: 1 year later. The drive is still working great. It feels as if it has slowed down a bit. Not understanding why but I haven't done any tests on it to verify that it has.
Frustrating is that the drive does NOT show wear level in the SMART data. Weird.

title: Easy to set up and install, high quality imaging day or night
text:
I ordered this camera to mount at the edge of my two-story deck so that I can see both under the deck and into the fields behind my home at any time. These areas are not easy to see either from above or below, and the camera gives me a way to easily look to see what's happening when I hear something moving about, day or night. I think it should also act as a deterrent for any would-be thieves.

Installing the camera is fairly straightforward. I set up the unit to attach to the network BEFORE mounting it, making the process so much easier. The package includes a short Cat 6 network cable to simplify the process, although setup can be performed using WiFi only. The included documentation does an excellent job of describing all of the different types of installation methods.

Pros:
- The camera is a PTZ camera, meaning that it's capable of panning, tilting and zooming the view and can be remotely controlled from another device or application.

- The recommended app works perfectly on my iPhone, but the camera does meet standards to work with multiple software applications. The camera is designed to be integrated into many security systems and can support recordings, motion detection, etc.

- The images from the camera are bright, very sharp and clear, whether in day or night mode. This aspect of the camera exceeded my expectations.

- For what it's worth, the camera also has a built-in microphone and speaker, enabling you to listen as well as see what's happening at any given time, and to verbally interact with the scene. The audio at the camera also exceeded my expectations.

Cons:

- The camera is designed to use 4 screws to mount to a flat surface, making for an easy installation. However, the base of each of the Wi-Fi antennas is attached to this base, and they extend deeper than the base of the unit. In other words, you can't successfully and completely tighten the base of the camera to a flat surface because the WiFi antennas stick out.

- The wiring and controls from the camera are three white cables that extend from the bottom of the mount. This cables include a port for power, an RJ-45 connection for an ethernet cable, and a reset button to perform a manual reset of the camera. By extending these from the base of the wall mount, it practically guarantees that the cables will block the view from the camera if you rotate the head to look behind the camera. In most installations that may not be a problem, but in my particular case, the camera is mounted so that I can see in the full 355 degrees that it supports. It's difficult to keep the cables out of the way.

- The Ethernet and Power cables to not provide adequate protection from water. If the Ethernet cable is actively in use for a wired installation, then the provided parts should provide a water-tight installation. But, if you're using the camera via Wi-Fi, there's no "cap" provided to seal the Ethernet connection. I had to fashion a seal using vinyl tape and the supplied connectors to make the connection waterproof. Likewise, the power plug does not truly seal when installed. I wrapped this connection with waterproof tape to protect the connection. The "reset button" does have a waterproof cap included.

For most of the user base, this would be a perfect outdoor PTZ camera. For my particular requirements, it's not perfect but it does work well after a bit of engineering. However, its virtually impossible to find such a capable, advanced function exterior camera at this price point. I still recommend the camera and would likely order it again based upon my experiences.

title: Good Price Point for a Decent Laptop - Updated and Downgraded
text:
This is a nice laptop for the price, and it's very easy to upgrade the ram and add a second hard drive. Converting from Windows S mode to Home is also very easy. If you decide to order a second hard drive to upgrade it, be aware that you MUST order a drive that is 7mm thick. I originally ordered a 1 TB mechanical drive to install, based on an Amazon recommendation, and it was a 9.5mm drive. On the Acer website it clearly indicates that this laptop only supports 7mm secondary drives. I ended up installing a 7mm SSD and an additional 4GB of ram, and now it's blazing fast. I highly recommend this laptop.
Update:
Not as enthused as I was originally about this machine for these reasons:
1. Although it has a keypad on the keyboard, the system HOME, END, Page Up/down keys are tied to the keypad which means if you use the keypad on spreadsheets a lot, you can't jump around using Home and End keys - a real bummer if your job involves lots of spreadsheets like mine. IF I had known that I would have passed on this laptop.
2. I installed an extra 4 GB ram, but the system kept reporting only 5.9 GB Ram is usable. Defective Ram - I thought. Went ahead and slapped 16 GB Ram into it, but now using Speccy and Windows reopt only 13.9 GB is usable. Apparently, this is a known issue on Acer laptops with Ryzen and AMD graphics. The system seems to reserve 3 GB (give or take) for graphics and other stuff. To me, that's unacceptable and if I had known that I would have passed on it. IT is a nice machine. I like the build quality, the graphics are very good, etc. but this Ram issue is a bummer. If you are considering buying this machine, paste this into your Google machine:
Aspire A515-43 usable ram less than installed - and see for yourself. It's a known issue and there isn't a real fix for it. Now I have extra memory I don't need adding another $30 to the price of this machine.
Caveat Emptor leads to a 2 star deduction. See images for Windows system Ram report.

title: Easy setup, good features
text:
I have 16 cameras in my setup, all different makes so this is not a one off review.
First and foremost Amcrest should change the location or size of the wifi antenna. because my outdoor AP was "behind" the camera, the signal was terrible (even though my phone in the EXACT same spot was full signal.
Changing the mounting position by 90 degrees fixed the bad connection immediately (but not my first choice obviously).
PTZ functions are very good, I will that there was an easy way (or built-in logic) to slow down/step the Pan function so it was not so fast (I know, complaining about fast).
IR is decent, but that 328' is only achived when zooming in, looking from the standard zoom (all the way zoomed out) down my 300' driveway leaves a lot of area dark near the end, so literally a person could walk about 200' feet straight at the camera before it "sees" them.
Presets (through Blue Iris) are very nice and extremely responsive, and with BI, many things are achievable.
Two things I love about Amcrest cameras (7 cameras, 4 models, in my setup) is they force a password change on setup (so you cannot leave it with the default) and they are very easy to setup.
I am on the fence with the Amcrest app for Android, I use it until I have my camera running good in Blue Iris but then turn off the P2P function for security and bandwidth reasons.
I got this at a good price, catching it on a Daily Deal, would not have paid standard pricing since Sunba makes a competing camera for less money at standard pricing (I have two Sunba's).
I would recommend this but you should wait until it is $300 or less.

title: Major - as yet unsolved - boot failures.
text:
The RPI 4 is notorious for its boot failure problems. If you get one of these POS's here's the PI website solution:
Recovery
If your Raspberry Pi 4 will not boot, it is possible that the SPI EEPROM has become corrupted. To check, remove the SD card, disconnect the device from power, then reconnect it. If the green LED does not flash, this indicates that the EEPROM has become corrupted.
Raspberry Pi Imager provides an easy way to fix this problem, by automatically preparing an SD card that will reprogram your Raspberry Pi 4’s EEPROM:
Find an SD card that is empty, or does not contain any data you want to keep; it will be completely erased of all data during this process.
Download Raspberry Pi Imager for your operating system from the list near the top of this page.
Click “CHOOSE OS” and select “Misc utility images” then “Pi 4 EEPROM boot recovery”.
Insert an SD card, click “CHOOSE SD CARD”, select the card you have inserted, then click “WRITE”.
Once the SD card is ready, insert it into your Raspberry Pi 4 then connect the Raspberry Pi to power.
Once complete, the green LED will blink rapidly in a steady pattern. Disconnect the device from power. Now you can remove the recovery SD card, insert your usual SD card, and resume using your Raspberry Pi.

Alternatively, you can download the bootloader and create a recovery SD card manually:
Download the bootloader.
Extract it to an empty FAT-formatted SD card and insert it into your Raspberry Pi 4.
Connect the power and wait for the green LED to flash quickly.

This may or may not work. It didn't for me on either of the RPI4s that I've owned. If it doesn't work you're doomed to spend hours searching forums and YouTube videos looking for a solutions. Which also may or may not work.

The easiest solution is to do what I did: Keep sending the pieces of trash back until you get one that works. So far, I haven't been that lucky.

I attached the Nagoya NA-701 directly to a RigExpert AA-600 antenna analyzer and measured a number of parameters. See the VSWR plot. In the 2m band, the VSWR barely gets below 3:1, and in the 70cm band it never gets lower than about 4.5:1. Neither of these numbers indicate acceptable performance. I also tested the Nagoya NA-771. See the uploaded graph of VSWR. It is better than the 701, but not exactly stellar. The stock antennas that come with either the Baofeng BF-F8HP or the AnyTone AT-D878UV both outperform either of these Nagoya products. Save your money.
Bill McGrath

title: DON'T WASTE YOUR TIME BUY SOMETHING ELSE!!!!!!
text:
I built a new gaming computer and wanted a decent card and wanted to try the RTX series but BE WARNED!!!! During the first month of having this card my computer would randomly freeze and I would have to restart. I put this towards it being a new build and Windows 10 defects (which there are many issues). Within a month of all the freezing and checks using all sorts of tools (making sure it wasn't windows), I started getting blue screens of all kinds.
Getting annoyed I removed the card and tried to uninstall the drivers, well this just messed up everything and had to do a full Windows reinstall(2nd time). It removed other drivers that had nothing to do with graphics and wouldn't even allow manual installs of drivers. I am an IT Manager for a local company and am not completely ignorant to doing these types of things, for those of you who think I am being dumb about it. I even tried to put this in my other gaming PC and had the same blue screen and freezing issues.
So after my reboot and reinstall I contacted MSI about the issue. I filled out a RMA for them to repair/replace the item and after 3 weeks of NO updates or correspondence of any kind. I contacted them and they told me that the item has been through the repair process and should be shipped soon. I received an email the next day saying the item has been shipped, which raised some suspicion.
The card arrived 2 days later and I have had no issues with my computer for over a month(RMA+shipping+prep time and PC tests). SO, I KNOW there is no issues with my PC at this point and am excited to play some games with my RTX card. So I shut my PC down, unplugged everything to install my graphics card yet again. Boots up fine install the GeForce Experience stuff and get all the drivers downloaded everything is working fine. Go to start up a game and really test this puppy out and upon loading the game my computer freezes..... JUST LIKE BEFORE!!!! SUSPICIONS CONFIRMED!!!!!!!!! MSI NEVER EVEN LOOKED AT THE ITEM EVERYTHING IS THE SAME!!!!!!! I feel like they just had the item in a pile, assuming they didn't just misplace it, then I email to ask about my item and then they just said "Eh, probably user error just send it back." Games freeze I can't even play one of my games because the game crashes withing 5 minutes of playing IF it doesn't crash on loading into the main screen.
At this point I don't even want a replacement I WANT MY MONEY BACK! I am going to write MSI a response to the RMA on the card and just request a refund. (Not that this will ever happen and I'm probably out the 390 bucks that I bought this item for PLUS the $40 I had to spend on the shipping for the RMA).

What a waste of time and money BUY SOMETHING ELSE!
Hope this helps some people and if you have also had this issue I hope something good happened for you.

text:
Review of Artman 2-Pack BP-511/BP-511A 2200mah Batteries and Dual Micro USB Charger Set

I relied upon reviews of other Artman battery products as part of my decision process on whether or not to order this item. The reviews of other battery products were very good so I went with this. I have become extremely cautious about anything with Li-Ion batteries.

Per the seller/manufacturer the batteries need to be charged at 2A but only a USB-A to microUSB power cord is provided with a useful length of approximately 26 inches (66 cm). Typically, cell phone and other portable device charges are only 0.5 to 1 A and undercharging can more quickly damage batteries than overcharging so I waited until I received an appropriate power supply.

The initial charge took about 6 hours.

This did not come with any instructions so one must decode the LED although pretty simple – power available is steady green, charging is red and full charge is steady green again. Presumably flashing will indicate if there are any problems detected.

The batteries fit in my ancient Canon ZR-50MC and worked well.

title: Works with Dell Precision Tower 3620
text: I needed to install my new nVidia RTX 2060 Super video display card into my Dell Precision Tower 3620 computer. The original Dell power supply in the Dell Precision T3620 is only 260W and it has the 8-pin interface plugged into the motherboard (not the 24-pin). I had two issues: (1) More power for the nVidia RTX 2060 Super video display card. (2) 8-pin interface to plug the new bigger capacity power supply into the system board. The COMeap 24 Pin to 8 Pin ATX PSU Power Adapter Cable is the perfect "fix" for my needs. I got a new replacement power supply (460W). I attached the COMeap 24 Pin to 8 Pin ATX PSU Power Adapter Cable to the bigger capacity power supply and the Dell Precision T3620 system board (was easy to install). It works perfect. Then I removed the hard drives cage from the Dell computer case to make room for my full size nVidia RTX 2060 Super video display card (you need to remove more than just the pop rivets securing the hard drives cage to the computer case). Finally, the Dell Precision Tower 3620 computer is functional with bigger capacity power supply using the COMeap 24 Pin to 8 Pin ATX PSU Power Adapter Cable and the nVidia RTX 2060 Super video display card.

title: Don't expect them to honor your claim.
text:
Asurion won't cover "up to $399 of damage" -- they're coverage is limited to devices that cost under $399.

I purchased a Dell laptop through a third-party seller here on Amazon, and bought this protection plan to cover any failures. Amazon suggested the protection plan, presumably because it matched the price of the laptop.

Guess what? The hard drive failed. And Dell wouldn't cover replacing it, because the third-party seller (e@World) had upgraded the hard drive and RAM as add-ons to my purchase.

But those add-ons (apparently?) brought the total value of my laptop up above $399, which I guess voids the coverage of the plan.

Here's the transcript of our subsequent chat:

ME: So you won't cover the cost of a hard drive, even though that's under the $399 limit?
ASURION: For us to be able to file a claim, the purchase price of the item before taxes should be within the plan's price range.

So, even though a new hard drive would cost far less than $399, Asurion won't cover it.

They're refunding my purchase of the protection plan, at least, but as you can imagine, I have no faith in this company. "The refund for the plan will be processed within 3-5 business days and you will get the credit back in just 1-2 billing cycles."

title: Works well enough, but not easy to wall mount
text:
This product works well enough. I am about 40 miles north of Atlanta, and get 40+ digital channels with this. In fact, I was surprised at how many junk channels there are (QVC, HSN, etc.). Good for cord cutters.

Pros:
+ Inexpensive
+ When tuned, the picture quality of most digital channels in HD Broadcast is noticeably better than Comcast's highly-compressed crap
+ Fairly small, can be hidden behind a large TV
+ Comes with all the parts & cables you need
+++ Amplifier is powered by USB. This is really a differentiating feature -- I plugged it into the USB port on the TV, and it works fine. No need to mess around with extra power cords. This is actually pretty important if you're trying to put the thing up on the wall behind your big TV, and don't want to mess with adding outlets or power strips.

Cons:
- Somewhat sensitive, at my range -- takes a little playing around to get the stations to tune completely smoothly. Some occasional glitching, although I expect to get rid of that with a more accurate mounting setup.
- Not easy to wall mount: the coax enters the back of the unit at a 90-degree angle. Which means you have to have the thing stand off from the wall at least 2 inches, as the coax just won't bend that tightly against the wall (at least without kinking and signal impedance). I will probably fashion a bracket with adjustable angles, to carefully set the antenna's aimpoint. Not that big of a deal.
- The red light on it doesn't work. In some of the Monster product brochure photos, it's clearly illuminated. Mine doesn't, but the power light is lit on the separate amp. So I assume it's working correctly, but I'm not quite sure if the red indicator on the main antenna is supposed to mean something. Too bad the product materials suck...
- The product materials suck. It's only 2 pages, and basically tells you to plug it in. There is no configuration, no detail around what the low/high switch on the amp does, and no detail about the sensitivity lobes or width of the antenna for aiming purposes.

But hey, it was cheap and it seems to work. At this price point (two Hamiltons), I'm not complaining.

title: Learning after 1 year of use and NEW setup instructions (8/2020)
text:
I have been using these ZMODO Cameras for about a year and have learned a few things about them. I recently bought 4 new cameras and experienced some of what other reviewers complained about with difficulty setting them up - as I have this down to a science I will write the process that worked for me at the end of this review.

Functionality:
These cameras provide a decent but somewhat grainy image as far away as 150 feet when mounted high on a an outdoor pole. They are stable - in a full year never needing to be rebooted or repaired in any way. The picture quality is good - and the refresh speed is not bad at all. This camera is also a fairly low bandwidth device with good compression.

They motion detection is fairly sensitive but not discriminating - broad changes in lighting (IE the sun went behind a tree) will cause them to send you a real time alert. Sometimes minor changes are so hard to see I have to watch the clip replay several times to see what the motion detection was even triggered by. If you compare this to Amazons cloud cam "Person Detected" feature - it is really lacking.

The night vision is awful. It does illuminate out to maybe 30 or 40 feet but you really cannot distinguish anything unless it is right in front of the camera.

You DO have to pay for the Zmodo service to store data in the cloud. If you have one of their DVR solutions you can connect this camera to it but I have not tried removing the cloud based subscription.

To set these cameras up you they used to have an 802.11 share with the ZLINK process - none of that applies anymore. They no longer have QE codes and you DO NOT use the MESHARE application no matter what you read online.

To set these cameras up -
Start by plugging in the camera and making sure it is flashing green

1. Download the ZMODO app from the app store (NOT the MESHRE APP)
2. Launch the App and Click the + button in the upper right (not clearly a button but it is there)
3. Choose the right 802.11 network and supply your password
4. The app should generate a QR code on the screen of your phone (if the app instead opens your camera and is LOOKING for a QR code - try updating your zmodo application or rebooting your phone, once this took me 4 tries its a bug I believe)
5. When you phone is displaying the QR code hold the ZMODO security camera up so that the security camera can read the QR code on your phone - (put the phone down on something so it is still) and move the camera closer and father away adjusting the angle and tilt until the camera scans the app. If the app shows a QR code but it will not scan on the camera try making sure your screen brightness is maxed out on your phone - remove other ambient lighting hold the camera very still and very slowly pan it in and out. (this eventually worked for all 4 cameras)
6. At that point the cameras light will turn from green to blue and you should be good to go forward with the free trial.

Overall these are fairly decent cameras, the cameras are very reasonably priced but the Cloud service is fairly expensive and these cameras make no sense without it. I gave them 4 stars for value and stability.

Do your research before buying and make sure this solution is right for you.

title: Decent but needs to suit your needs to be worth it
text:
For $60 it's fine, given that it includes shipping and ReadyDesk is a small business.

The pros: it's sturdy, it's simple, it's functional, it's easy to assemble. I got it to fit into a very tiny desk space and it does accommodate that space perfectly. It also doesn't smell like weird chemicals, so I appreciate that. (It smells like wood when you open the package.)

The neutral: If you have a lot of wires (and a mouse) it's kind of a hassle to use, so I recommend only putting a small laptop (on battery, not plugged in) on it. That might be a limitation. But its key usage seems like its versatility (as a tablet stand/laptop stand), and therefore probably also its portability.

title: 10-core thermals are excellent - Good Job ID-Cooling
text:
I'll keep this simple and focused on the new builders. This is an excellent product for a first build. I put the 240X Snow on an ole' INTEL 7900x processor, fired from an ASUS X299 MB.
Results: my current ambient room temperature (71F, 22C) degrees. And, the MB temp around (30C); I'm seeing a nominal 32C in the Windows Core Temp software (which is reasonable). Once I fire up a multitask (i.e. rendering or video editing), the temperatures climb to around 58C (very good for a 240mm radiator and 0.30 amp fans)
Note: I'm not overclocking this particular processor - and, I recommend you begin temperature monitoring at baseline settings (not overclocked). Why: bc overclocking is an extreme profile - which presumes everything (cooling) is working properly. Also: overclocking is an extreme power draw - which the BIOS and Win software need to be properly matched (i.e. like setting the power in WIN and NVidia Control Panel to max performance)
Pros:
> Price to Performance is Excellent
> The LED lighting is fabulous and compliant to most MB RGB (3-pin, almost universal these days); I set my fans to RED to indicate warm exhaust and WHITE to indicate cool air coming in (personal choice)
> Noise levels are excellent - probably cuz the fans are low RPM (around 1200 max) - which is perfect for me - but not so good for hotter indoor temps; go Corsair ML 120mm for bigger RPMs (sacrifice noise)
> Universal fit and plenty of screws and brackets to match most configs; (LGA X299 has everything in the box) - which will normally fit the smaller INTEL setups (LGA 1151, 1200), no problem...
> Overall: beautiful design with good fit and price to punt - Well Done!
Cons:
> More like a personal gripe: but cable management is desperately needed (got wires slinging everywhere, no fun if you have a lot of spinning fans); I recommend velcro wraps or retractable zip-ties (velcro for sure)
Thanks, and I hope this helps the new builders and the Vets that forget about the simple things in life...

title: Good by better options for the money
text:
I bought these at the loca retailer on a Black Friday. They were not available at the store and had to wait a few weeks for delivery. In the mean time I bought the ASUS AX router.

When the Gryphon came I did a side by side testing for a week each. I bought 1 set of 2 routers.

Pros: 1. The user interface is only an app but it’s clean and easy to find the things you want. A web based app might be better for the power users but for most folks this should suffice. 2. Looks cool. 3. The extra router level security. 4. Speeds are solid. For my 250Mb plan on Comcast I got between 160-300 around my 3 story house.

Cons: 1. The speed was too variable. My 2 Gryphons had varied speed around the house whereas the single ASUS AX was within 10Mb regardless of the floor. 2. It would take time for the mesh router to get equipment linked to it. Most of the time my equipment wanted to go to the main router regardless of proximity. It would switch over but could take 1 hour before the phone laptop did so. I assume it’s an issue with the equipment and how using mesh. 3. I like the info presented in the ASUS admin page better. 4. The security features are a paid subscription after the first year, the ASUS is free.

All in it’s a nice router. But for 400 I expect more. The single ASUS router was about same speed, but more consistent speeds, better GUI, free security, and half the cost.

I wanted to be a US product that looked cool. The gap was too big though. If the single Gryphon was $200 but free lifetime security then that’s a fair deal. Still not as fast as the Asus but is more competitive and the Gryohon does look cool. The mesh router didn’t add anything to me. I also tried the Netgear Orbi and had issues keeping the second router connected to. Mesh seems good on paper but sometimes simple is best.

title: Awesome autofocus & very good image sharpness and quality
text:
[[VIDEOID:5326f7861adf4e67fa40a38763581dd9]] The auto focus is next level. If you are into portrait or animal photography this camera just locks on to the face and eye. Making it much faster to shoot moving subjects. Oh and auto focus points covering the entire screen, that's the best thing about mirrorless cameras.

The images come out sharper than my 5D Mark IV, when tested with the Sigma 50mm Art. The RF24-105L lens is also a very good improvement over the the EF version 1. Has better dynamic range, I can recover more highlights and shadows, but it won't do miracles. The low light performance is really nice, you can easily do ISO 6400 - 8000 with very pleasing results. I personally don't mind the grain up to 12800. (The cat picture is ISO 12800 with the RF24-105L).

Video 4K HQ looks amazing. I've not had any overheat problems, I shoot multiple 2 min or less clips, combined with photos, and a few 120fps clips.

The camera is light and fits my hand perfectly with all the buttons in the right spots. Very easy to transition from the 5Dm4. Has three main dials for shutter, aperture and ISO. The front ring is exposure compensation by default. The focus point joystick is super fast and responsive, I'm so happy they added this back in. The shutter is very quiet and one of my favorite things about shooting with it. The EVF is crystal clear like, especial in the faster FPS mode.

It works with all my EF and EF-S lenses, and all my 3rd party lenses with the addition of the R to EF adapter.

Here's what I don't like.

The one I got seems to have some built-in mic problem where it'll record random loud pops, usually a few at the start of the recording, or several seconds in. So this one may be sent back for exchange, I'm in the process of talking to Canon about the issue.

The swivel out flip screen has a little play in its joint when pressed and when closed has a little play in the recessed slot on the body, you can press on the LCD on the bottom and it moves a few mm up in the slot. It's nit picking, but my old 760D which also has a flip screen, is rock solid and doesn't have any play or wiggle in the LCD when open or closed, and I expected that from this camera.

The battery life could be better. I got about 350 photos with a few videos, with Blutooth/GPS on, and sleep set at 1min.

It's missing the focus area selector lever that is around the focus point joystick on the 5Dm4, and 7Dm2.

Doesn't seem to have an option to shoot only with the EVF, and use the LCD to review an image when play is pressed, otherwise keeping it off. Again this is probably nit picking, as it does auto switch between the two.

I think the auto focus, image quality and 4K HQ are justifiable for the high cost of this camera as an early adopter.

Update 9/6/22: There have been a bunch of firmware updates; one of them added the ability to turn off the LCD and shoot with just the EVF. Battery life was improved somewhat also. The MIC issue I had was resolved with a new camera, after return.

title: The usb/charging port fails too often
text:
I am old, I am angry, and I am rich. I have enough money to buy whatever I want whenever I feel like it. I decided that I would retire my old reliable glow light for a nook in 2018. I thought about the oasis, but that would be a waste of money. Now I doubt that I should have bought the paperwhite at all. While the glow light has performed and continued to display books, and charge reliably with a secure connection on the micro usb port, the nook has already become loose and is charging, at best, intermittently. I understand that Amazon wants to make a few bucks, and may feel that it is necessary to save a few dollars on what one would possibly see as a minor part. I can tell you on a user side I have bitched, moaned and complained for far less. I have no use for a product that wont function as expected for years and years on end. I have no use for a company that will not stand behind their products and remedy issues. I have no use for a company that would rather save a few cents on a part to hit a target price point.
The USB port on my paperwhite has failed. According to reddit, this is a known issue, and Amazon has refused to do anything about it. How can you sell a product that you know will fail?
The recommendation is to solder a new port to the board. While I can do that, why should I spend the hour or two to make the configuration, when I make more than what the damn device is worth in an hour?
So, I should buy a new device. Paperwhite? and go through this agony again? I think not.
Now, this infection is going to spread. When I go to work, and log into my AWS account, what am I going to think? I am going to turn to my coworker and ask, is AWS the only solution? NO. Google cloud, Azure, I'm sure there are others. Amazon, do you want me to ask this question? Do you want me, and everyone like me to ask these questions? Why don't you talk to HP, how are they doing? or IBM, do you think they payed attention to quality?
Its up to you. I am questioning weather or not I should ever buy an amazon product again, or shop at amazon ever again. Perhaps my business shouldn't shop there either, or my employers. Maybe my friends should start asking the same questions.
All because you decided it was ok to cheap out on a USB port. Is it worth it?

title: Need to knows for Filmmaker's Kit
text:
I bought the Filmmaker's kit directly from Nikon with their upgrade program due to a generous trade-in.

The Filmmaker's kit comes with an external recorder/monitor and gimbal for extra-steady shots. But it is not really possible to use it "out of the box." I'm not going to do an in-depth review of the Z6 or the other components - many people have done very thorough reviews of those. Instead, I want to help you get started quickly by highlighting a few things.

Additional things you need to have or buy:

SSD Drives for the Atomos Ninja V. Any 2.5" drive will work. You do not need to buy the extra-compact Atomos editions. Standard 2.5" drives are used with drive caddies (1 included in the box, you can buy packs of 5 for $30), and they project out the side a bit more than half an inch. Some might consider this beneficial, since it could provide some protection for the HDMI plugs from being knocked around. The special Atomos drives are far more expensive but fit flush to the unit with no projection. I bought 2 500GB Samsung 860 SSDs that are doing great as first recording units. They each hold more than 4 hours of 4K N-Log video. If I start using RAW (available in a future update) I likely will get some larger capacity units.

Batteries for the Atomos Ninja V. The unit ships with an AC adapter, but unless you plan on only shooting next to an AC outlet, that is pretty useless. It takes standard Sony-style NP-F batteries, and there are numerous options available. They recommend at least a 5200mAh battery for 2 hours of monitor/record time, and you can buy larger/heavier batteries as well. Beware that most sellers on Amazon do not offer a fast charger. This could mean very long charging times for the batteries, especially higher capacity batteries.

XQD Card for the Nikon Z6. At least 400Mb/s. I think most all cards sold do that now. I have used both Sony and Lexar with fine results in previous cameras. There is only one slot, so no backup capability. I've never had an XQD fail on me, but there's always a first time. So I will probably stick with 64GB cards and download them often to limit exposure to problems.

Options:

A hood for the Ninja V is awfully nice. Rather than pay the ridiculous price for a "genuine" plastic one, I made a foldable cardboard one.

A different HDMI cable - the coiled cable is nice and compact to connect the camera to the Ninja V, but is so tightly coiled that it interferes with the gimbal balance. The gimbal is strong enough to overcome this, but it's an annoyance. Also the connector on the coiled cable is too wide to use Nikon's cable clamp on the Z6, which if you're having the HDMI stick out a lot, might be good as protection. I have a habit of whacking and damaging cables and connectors.

Comments:

I love the Z6. It feels good. The battery life is shorter than my other cameras, but not really something to complain about. Auto-upload to SnapBridge on a smartphone uses a lot of battery, but is great for geo-tagging and viewing your pictures. I was disappointed to not find an artificial horizon in the menus, until I found it as one of the normal pages shown with the DISP button. And it's particularly good! I chose the D6 for it's better low-light sensitivity and all-pixel use of the sensor for 4K video. And it has delivered very well. It's a great all-around camera.

The Ninja V - If you want HDR type recording (and you do, if you want to high-end video), you need to use an external recorder. The camera will not record N-log (and presumably not raw in the future update) to an internal card. If you want standard recording, you can ditch the monitor and record in-camera. XQD cards are expensive compared to SSDs, and you can store a lot of video on an SSD. The Ninja V is a nice compact unit. Not lightweight including a battery. Several nice monitoring options. An additional stereo analog audio input supplements audio in the HDMI from the camera. The camera can send timecode to the Ninja V.

The Moza Air 2: makes superb steady video. Lots of stabilization modes with separate on/off and responsivity for each axis. If you want focus or zoom control, you need to get the separate iFocus module. Theoretically the gimbal has Nikon USB control through the USB-C on the Z6, but I haven't gotten that to work. Also, even if it does work, with current firmware very few functions are even theoretically available - basically just the record trigger. Perhaps a future update will bring exposure control, and even better, USB focus control. Focus pulls and zooms are unwieldy and will jiggle the camera when done manually. This is a heavy unit. The Ninja V is difficult to mount with the included arm in a fashion that will keep it from sagging. If mounted to the right side, it will unscrew itself. There are optional brackets that would solve that problem. With camera and Ninja V, this is a very heavy combination that will give you a solid workout.

title: Holy Smokes!
text:
So, I was reluctant to upgrade. My last router was an ASUS RT-AC668u, so it wasn't the cost or the brand that had me concerned. I just didn't think I'd get that much of a difference. Boy was I wrong.

As an appetizer, I have Comcast internet. 1000 Mbps download, 40 Mbps (LoL) upload. Some people have symmetrical internet... Comcast serves symmetric-lol. Anyhow, it's the fastest you can get in my area. I purchased my own modem opposed to paying them monthly for theirs (suggest doing this, for any who haven't, it pays for itself many times over as modems don't get tech upgrades as fast as other things like smartphones do).

Anyhow, onto the router. That signal strength though. I went from losing all bars completely near my fireplace which meant the yard was out of the question, to having to try really hard to see even one of my bars disappear. The CPU inside is much faster, too, making the UI page much faster than it ever was on the last one. And the speeds of Wifi itself? Yes. I went from around 250 Mbps on the last router (which was AC, mind you, and no slouch in it's day) to 650 Mbps on this one. That's very fast. 65 Megabytes per second. Buffering and watching a 4k video is seamless at that rate. It also seems to have less stuttering across all the devices in our house now which is ever important with the amount of devices a household has in 2020.

So long story short then, yes it's absolutely worth it. With a few exceptions. To really see improvements you'll need newer devices that take advantage of technology like MU-MIMO and Wifi-6. Your mileage may vary. It also helps to know what you're doing to take advantage of the tools in the router itself. If you just want the newest tech without a lot of customisation you might be better off with something cheaper. But the amount of control, from scheduling to URL filters to gaming prioritization, etc makes it worth it for me.

Lastly, I'll stand by Asus as long as I live. Their devices usually cost more than others, but it's always been worth it in my experience.
