title: Celestron - StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ Smartphone App-Enabled Telescope Review
text:
We purchased this telescope primarily for outreach purposes. As part of John Dobson’s Sidewalk Astronomy group, we setup a lot in the city where the people are, to expose those that never had the opportunity to experience astronomy. Often, we are setup under city and business lighting, finding deep sky objects can be very difficult. We needed a telescope with some smarts that was very portable, easy to setup and easy to use.

Assembly and setup of the StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ was very well documented and easy to follow, it doesn’t take an experienced technical astronomer to get this scope ready for observation. I use an iPhone so downloading the app from iTunes is free but requires the activation code included in the telescope kit to activate. I’m sure your 5-year-old could handle this part, LOL. Now assembled, in daylight, I did the typical aligning of the finder to the main eyepiece using terrestrial targets then I removed the cradle cover, I placed the phone into the cradle above the mirror. When I started the StarSense App, it opened and walked me through aligning the phone with the telescope view in the eyepiece. It is a simple procedure, so slow down and do it accurately, the pointing performance in use depends on this. In fact, I had to repeat this to correct my sloppiness.

Setting up on the patio of a Starbucks for one of our scheduled “Coffee and the Cosmos” events, the StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ was the only telescope I took. It was sink or swim to see if the scope would perform or not. Under the big Starbucks sign, in front of a large bank sign and numerous other businesses and street lights, could I show more than the Moon and Saturn?

With the phone aligned with the mirror and telescope view, you are ready to go. The app resolves the scope’s location and time and knows what is up and where the objects are in your sky. Calling up the list of available targets I saw 15 or so deep sky objects. Picking my first object in the list, the app had some difficulty plate solving (locating where it was pointing by comparing the stars it sees to its database) what it was looking at, I was disappointed. After a couple of attempts it dawned on me…. Duh so many lights, must be interference. I cupped my hands around the mirror, followed the arrows on the phone screen and EUREKA! object in the eyepiece. So then, I started at the top of the list and went after it. I would pick the next object in the list, cup the mirror follow the arrows, BAM! In the eyepiece. Rinse and repeat. I was able to complete all but two objects on the list. Those two were M81 & M82 directly above the bright Starbucks sign, I couldn’t overcome my observing environment, but the StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ was willing and able.

So far, my experience using this Celestron - StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ Smartphone App-Enabled Telescope has been “Over the Moon” (pun intended). I feel as though in the environment that I was using this telescope in was very indicative of what a new young telescope user would probably be in. I highly recommend this telescope.

title: Clarity and Quality are exactly what you would expect for the price
text:
let me start out by saying I was not paid or compensated for this review. I have installed 5 camera systems since 2013 and this is the best bang for the buck by far. I used to be an EZvision snob but have branched out to Hikvision and Annke. Out of the mentioned brands, EZvision has the cheapest systems, HIKvision has the most expensive, and Annke is the middle ground with all the options of the bigger brands.

I have a 5,000 sq. ft. house and used a POE switch along with 250ft of outdoor rated CAT6 cable to install. After learning how to install my own connectors I didn't use any of the included 50ft cables(although they are of great quality). All of my wiring resides in my attic. The POE runs to my basement where my router is located. This NVR doesn't come with a built in WIFI card but I always prefer hardwired Ethernet on surveillance systems. You can buy a cheap access point if you need to install away from your router($25 here on Amazon).

Setup was a little more complicated for my usage since I was not directly plugging each cam to the ports on the rear. After getting the IP addresses of each camera, setting up my ports, and registering the cameras with the NVR, I was up and running with about 20 minutes of software setup.

There are many functions built into the NVR but I chose just to use the surveillance without any motion detection. The night-vision was what impressed me the most. I can easily see 100ft in my side yard all the way to our communities access road.

We view the cameras on a cheap 1080p monitor but note this system is 4k resolution on its recording(much better to read license plates and distinguish faces). If you export the file to a supporting 4k device you'd be blown away at the clarity. Aside from the HDMI monitor, we access the cams utilizing our android phones with the Annkevision App. The app isn't as fluid as ones I've used in the past but has all the functions one would need to perform remote monitoring.

The only recommendation I could make is for Annke to include 100 CAT 5/6 cable clips to fasten to the exterior and interior of your attic/crawlspace. If not, they're less than $10.

title: This is a large supercapcitor array (not a battery) - treat it as such and you will be pleased
text:
My application is capacitor off-grid power storage with solar trickle charge. Due to environment considerations (temperature, reliability, etc.) I have chosen to use capacitors instead of batteries. This is a nice an relatively inexpensive way to get 6x 2.7v 3000F capacitors, balance boards, and a case. The balance boards start to take effect around 15.5v and start to bleed off charge at increasing rates as you push past that voltage (which is expected); however, be careful to not overwhelm the balance boards' ability to shunt current - you can overcharge these make sure to only supply voltage withing the specified limits.

My usage relies on efficient DC-DC step up/down circuits to produce the desired DC current for electronics that I power off-grid. This design won't for everyone but if you are looking large "high voltage" super capacitors this definitely is that.

Because I was curious I removed the screws from the top of the case and took a look inside - these are made of the older 2.7v 3000F Maxwell capacitors (newer version are 2.85 3400F or 3.0v 3000F) but they are still of good quality and use. Nice large wires are used to connect the capacitor array to the terminals - no concerns of overloading the current capacity or voltage drop due to wiring. Terminals are not standard for US car battery sizes (a little smaller overall and +/- are the same size); however, they do unscrew so ring terminals can be used (M6 size I think).

There is some relatively high self discharge (compared to some of my other Maxwell caps in various sizes, 350-3400F) but not so large as to matter in my application.

Over all I am pleased with the product. The minus one star is for use of older capacitors and the early current shunt behavior observed (I should be able to hold these caps at the rated 16V with minimal current to counter the inherent self discharge of the caps, this is not the case - technically based on the balance boards this should be the case all the way up to 16.2V).

I have waited two years for an Ultra Short Throw projector that I would be happy with investing in. I was going to cave in to a TV, but I am glad I didnt. This is one awesome piece of equipment.

The picture quality is superb. It is clear and crisp and everyone who has seen it is floored with how good it looks especially with a projector close to the wall. This machine has up to 3000 ANSI Lumens, which does fairly well at late morning or late afternoon. I have the projector in my living room next to a bay window (with a UV filter and non-blackout curtains) and when the sun hits the windows (afternoons), it basically washes the picture out. Mind you, I do not have a dedicated screen yet because I cant decide on an UST ALR projection screen. So right now, it is projecting on the wall. At night, it is magnificent. When it is cloudy, it still does really well.

My issue with the screen right now is the distortion. There is one portion on the upper line that is not entirely straight. I tried two different walls and there is a clear dip. I tried their on-board distortion fixing software. It is not shown when I am watching something, but it is noticeable because I keep staring at it. I am a bit of a perfectionist so I am not sure if it is a defect or natural for a UST projector.

The UI for this projector is not great. In fact, I do not depend on it. Instead, I use either a Chromecast or Roku to stream content via HDMI to watch and that has worked well.

As for the voice command, I have not been able to use it with Google because the software is missing to connect it through Google Home. Instead, I am forced to use Alexa Skills as that software/skill is available. I am not entirely sure why, but the Optoma platform/software is missing in connecting the projector to Google Home. Perhaps it was either taken away or it hasn't seamlessly connected yet. But, Alexa with the projector is doing well.

I have watched several action films (Avengers and John Wick) so far and I have been on the look out for a color wheel issue. I do not see an issue as of yet. Perhaps, I would need to keep looking for it. But, its a good thing that I have not encountered it.

It is a hefty piece of equipment and it is solidly built. There are plenty of uses for it with music streaming with Spotify and various connections for movies/gaming.

The package came in a big box housing the main box. I dont know why, but the big box is fine, but the main box had a punctured hole. title: Exceptional photo quality in a tiny camera
text:
My husband and I use the camera for still photography, not videography. I have, however, included details that will interest vloggers. I broke the evaluation down into the following categories:

Key Features
The camera has a 4.2x optical zoom lens with a range of 24-100 mm good for general use and for taking close-ups. It has an Optimal Image Stabilizer which adjusts the lens to compensate for movement. The lens is fixed and not interchangeable and has an integrated lens cover that is nearly flush with the body.

A 1-inch 20.2-megapixel sensor provides good clarity and sharpness for a very small camera. One convenience that the camera lacks is a viewfinder which helps when trying to take a picture in bright light. The LCD screen folds out and is adjustable, even folding up to allow viewing selfies.

With the variety of camera modes, the user can select the desired settings based on the subject and the conditions. The modes are: TV (shutter speed priority), P (shutter-speed and aperture values auto-adjusted to suit brightness), AUTO (camera-determined settings), Hybrid (a clip of scene recorded before each shot), Special Scene Mode, AV mode (aperture priority), M mode (manual shutter and aperture selection), C mode (saved shooting modes for reuse), Movie Mode (vlogger setting), Creative Filters Mode (variety of images when shooting added.)

Ease of Use
The camera is simple to operate. Its point and shoot design allows quick set-up for candid, spontaneous shots. For minimum effort, it gives great picture quality. (I’ve included a picture my husband took.) One problem we ran into was using WIFI to transfer photos to the laptop, not a cellphone. (My husband likes to see the photos on a bigger screen for editing.) This is a long cumbersome process with this camera taking up to an hour. There are two easier methods, purchasing a cable connection, or removing the SIM card and using a card reader. Note that a cable does not come with the camera and care must be taken to select the right micro-USB connection.

Durability
The camera is not waterproof or specially designed to be rugged. It is easily zipped in a pocket or backpack, however, to give it protection from the rain.

Battery Life
The lithium-ion battery in the camera does not provide for prolonged use. My husband needed to charge the camera after just several hours of picture taking. A battery charger is provided with the camera and the small battery is easily removed for charging. We have not used it for videos, so we haven’t experienced any issues with the camera overheating. The recommended video length is 10 minutes in 4K mode which some vloggers may not like.

Portability
For its small size (it fits in the palm of your hand and weighs only 304 g with the battery and memory card included) I give it the highest rating. This is the perfect camera to slip in your pocket or purse to get high-quality photos or videos anywhere at any time.

To sum up, this small size camera offers a lot of features to ensure high-quality pictures or videos. A beginning or intermediate camera user will love the easy to use options. Vloggers will love the picture quality and portability. They may not like the suggested 10-minute video limit. Because our use was primarily still photography, we didn’t run into any problems with the camera overheating, but we did have an issue sending the photos through WIFI to the laptop. For this, we ordered a special cable and a compatible SIM card reader. This little camera shoots quality pictures with minimal effort and set-up.

I'm glad that Ring has produced this new product at a good price, but they get 50 lashes with a wet noodle for not being more forthcoming about the delay in support for Mac and Windows machines, which I rely on heavily for security.

title: Very  impressed with optimus,,and follow up
text:
To follow-up after a few months of use. Nothing short of amazed. It reports vehicle speed,,even is vehicle is cornered too hard ,location down to 20ft accuracy, even opening a trunk sends a motion alert to my cell when car is parked. In even alerted everytime it loses a gps signal from driving in a tunnel(or someone loading your $100k car into a metal box trailer!!)
The units performs 100% same as day 1!! Would Definately buy again.

After carefully weighing pros and cons of several gps trackers(ex. Amazon reviews,buy cost,monthly fees,ease of setup and install, removable or hidden, features such as impact/ acceleration/ deceleration /ignition on/off/parked notification), lifetime warranty!!!)
I narrowed it down to Optimus and another similar well rated unit on amazon. After reading several pages reviews for both units..it seemed the optimus device ,tho had more features I was looking for,,had a few reviews about accuracy, and units that died very fast or discharged or ruined vehicle charging system??. I started to get the impression the reviews were false or intentionally negative from a competitor. Being a retired aerospace engineer and auto enthusiast, I know its not even remotely possible for a gps tracker that only draws 100milli amps.(CAR BATTERIES ARE 400-700AMPS,ALTERNATORS ARE 100-200AMPS APROX). So there is no way that these tiny devices could damage a vehicle system in any way. Even if a wire was to directly short out,simply it would just blow a fuse!! Also it didnt make sense since optimus claimed to have many commercial fleets using their product. Ups, fed ex,etc cant have malfunctioning gps systems for their fleet,it wouldn't happen for long,and optimus would be out of business by offering a lifetime guarantee if their products if they died quickly?? So I called to ask customer service at both of the companies i was considering. 1 did not take calls/ redirected me to send an email requesting support and wait for a call back. I dont have that sort of time or patience (very common now in a c19 world)..the other company(optimus), not only answered every call ,took calls up to 10pm est at night on 3 different occasions, were friendly /helpful/knowledgeable,,but even went to discuss implementing a custom software modification with their engineer,so my devices sensors could also detect light impacts/ tampering while parked. I was surprised they accommodated my request and took all of 10min to remotely update my devices software from another state, thru the air with a cell signal!!!
The photo i posted is my optimus gv75 built in device being updated and tested prior to install on my very cluttered work bench,,to verify the sensitivity of the tamper sensor modifications,, making sure they were in the ballpark.worked as requested 1st time out!!.
Soon as unit was powered up,after the simple 1 minute app download and 2minute registration process on the optimus website, it immediately pinged my cell with emails and texts from my gv75 device with alerts for being powered on and updating with its location..and this was inside my metal roof garage were no one can even talk on a cell phone without dropping a call!!
But being skeptical still after the negative reviews id read, I continued testing it for aprox 2 more hour's and shook it a dozen more times to verify the sensitvity functions alert me the way i wanted.
I noticed accuracy is good down to about 50ft,,which later optimus support explained was only that far off due to the metal roof preventing some satellites from communicating to giving the exact location.
I was extremely impressed and plan to purchase more of the obd2 plug in versions for family members that aren't able to hardwire theirs in.
I dont write reviews often but felt this product needed a clearer more detailed review.
With the slight modification to the opimus device, it now not only is a gps locator/tracker and speed sensor,but a security device with built in battery back up to alert me if ignition is turned on, vehicle power is disconnected, or vehicle is impacted or being tampered with while parked!!!
No other gps tracker has these features (non that I could find at least), came with lifetime replacement warranty, fantastic customer service day or night, and your own engineer to customize your device in the blink of an eye
( the last benefit im sure will have its limitations, lol)!!!
Im sold on their product and wouldn't be surprised to see this company expand in this field from the A++ support i experienced.
Im not affiliated with the company and was not compensated for my review in any way..
Hope the review helps.

text:
Wow, I have to admit, I'm impressed by how good this watch is. I've had an older model Approach for about 3 seasons now and got this one only because I saw a good deal on an open box. But I'm really glad that my old one is now my back up. The screen on this is very readable in all lighting, it is very light and comfortable to wear as I play. The accuracy is terrific, it locks onto the course very quickly and the battery life is very good. I'm sure I could get 2 rounds of golf from every full charge (tho I always seem to charge it before every round anyway - habit from the older model I suppose). It registers every shot you take - if you use this feature - extremely effectively. My guess is that it has automatically picked up at least 95% of my swings during every round (meaning that I've rarely had to add a swing/shot manually). The features of the watch are pretty intuitive after you've used it a couple times. The Garmin golf app is also really good and appears to have been upgraded and improved recently, but I haven't checked it out thoroughly yet.

If I had any criticism at all - more suggestion really - it would be to reorder the menu options on the watch. For example, the Last Shot option - i think - should be one of the first listed while you're playing instead of being 5th or 6th. While I'm playing each hole I should be able to get to Last Shot right away, certainly before the Scorecard since I won't use that until the hole is completed. As I said, a suggestion more than a criticism.

Great watch for golfers and works great add a watch and fitness tracker. Highly recommended!

title: Traveling Audiophile perspective
text:
I am writing this review at 35,000 feet, which is why I use headphones. I am in airplanes about 400 hours per year, and good and accurate music is a huge benefit in reducing the tedium.

I have both the most recent Sony 1000 xm3 and the Bose QC 35II for a comparison. Also important for context, I am 62 years old and a bit of an audiophile. When I am home, I prefer excellent speakers to headphones, and while I have spent some time with the excellent Sennheiser HD800s open back phones ($1,500 or so) I much prefer the B&W or Dali speakers. And since you need a quiet space for open-back phones to really deliver, there is no practical benefit to the cans over speakers in a listening room.

However, I realized that I was enjoying music through phones much less while traveling than I used to, and I think that is due to my aging ears that have been subjected to too much loud music - both recorded and live, as well as jet engines and other sounds. The Sony and Bose phones really were not giving me what I expected, especially with delicate jazz and classical. The great recordings seemed muddy and flat, and I just assumed that my old ears were past getting a great experience from travel phones.

When I heard about the Nuraphones, which had mostly positive but somewhat mixed reviews, I figured that the claim that they would tailor the sound to my ears (which I had tried to do with eq settings with the Sony and Bose - with only minor success) might be worth a try.

Happily, I can say that I was very pleased with the result. After going through the calibration process several times in a VERY quiet room, I got a profile that sounds more like great speakers than any other headphones I have heard. And my old ears are enjoying frequencies that have been hidden for some time. While the active noise cancellation is less effective than either the Sony or Bose phones, the physical isolation from over-ear and in-ear components combined with the ANC has a combined effect that is at least as good as the other two phones. And they don’t have the subtle hiss that those other phones’ ANC introduces. For the very first time I can fully enjoy Chopin, Rachmaninov, Claude Bolling or Oscar Peterson on an airplane to almost the same level as in my listening room. And music with less delicacy sounds equally great - the bass is very adequate and the highs are clean. Steely Dan’s AJA sounds just right.

While certainly not as comfortable as the Bose, I find them adequately comfortable - the inner earbud component can become a bit painful for me after 3 hours, but a 5-minute break is adequate to restore happiness, and I am good for the rest of the flight.

So, if you find the current crop of NC phones inadequate, or if you suspect that your ears are cheating you out of part of the frequency spectrum, these phones may be worth a try. They go everywhere with me now

We actually recycled our clock after giving it a long term test. We purchased the clock as soon as it was available. The real reason was to use the clock to keep track of timers usually set for cooking. It IS an easily readable clock. That's about it.
The clock was difficult to pair up with the Echo, it took several tries.
The clock eats batteries at a prodigious rate.
The clock is cheaply built and it bot feels and looks like the cheap clock it is, even from a relative distance.

The real disappointment is that the clock CAN pair up with ONE Echo unit. The real purpose of having an "Alexa household" is the mesh of Echo units spread throughout the house. What that means, to us, is that things like timers should be shared throughout the house rather than be tied to one specific unit.

In out case, that would mean pairing the clock with the "bedroom Echo" and interrupting the cooking process to walk close enough to the bedroom to set the timer on the "bedroom Echo" instead of the "family room Echo", defeating the purpose of the whole thing.

If the clock is ever redesigned to be able to consider the entire Echo ecosystem in a residence or business, AND the battery life was decent, it would be a great product.

title: Really nice sounding set of headphones. Easily beats the HE4xx. However the wire is the worst ever.
text:
I bought these because I did not feel I was getting all the planar sound I should from the HE4xx even after owning them for almost a year.
I did not want or need the bluetooth module (I have other ones) so I was happy when a significantly lower priced version was released without the bluetooth.
So here is my story and review.
But first and I will probable get some hate and down votes as I open with a disclaimer that I am that guy.
You know the 1 person who hates the Sennheiser HD6xx. The most boring and overrated headphones ever.
First of all I have several other open back headphones to compare these to:
- Grado rs2e
- Sigva P II
- SHP9500
- Fidelio x2hr
- Fostex rp50
- Fostex rp90
- Dakoni Blue
- K7xx
- AUD ATHAD1000X
- Sennheiser 6xx
So I have some experience with the sound signature of an open back set of cans.
I find in the Deva what I was looking for in a headphone.
A slightly warm sound with good imaging and, depending on how the track was mastered, lots of soundstage.
The have several times caused me to take them off because I thought a sound was coming from the 'outside world' and when it was in the music.
This is even more surprising when you consider my main genres are classical, jazz and 70s/early 80s rock.
I mean I was able to hear the pedals and the resulting mechanics in piano only music (but it should be noted that is a sign of bad mic placement), finger slides on guitars, drum stick impacts before the actual drum sound and brass players (in jazz music) taking a breath in solos.
These are for anyone who appreciates well mastered music and wants to hear everything sounding wide and where the mics were placed.
They are not, however, for bass heads.
The bass is there, but it's clean, true to life and not boosted.
They are also probably not the best choice for those who value imaging above all else.

Now for the elephant in the room. The cord.
It is the worst cord I have ever seen on a headphone. After almost a week and trying every trick I know I cannot get the loops out of it.
Hanging over doors (with and without other headphones connected for weight), a hair dryer and counter twisting it is still a 6 foot pigtail from end to end. and I will be buying a replacement if i can find one.
I was able to find a 3.5mm balanced to 4.4mm balanced pentaconn cord on eBay and can't wait for it to arrive.
All of this make the cord an effective <2 feet long.

So the obvious question and how I ultimately judge a headphone is would I buy them again?
And the answer is yes. In a heartbeat.
The quality of the sound and the soundstage, which is why I was even looking for another planar while owning so many, is an unqualified yes.
Buy these, connected them to a good amp and sit back for a listening experience you will not expect to be so good from a $200 headphone.

title: Great entry level monitor, but also consider the G7.
text:
The Odyssey G5 rounds off the curved gaming monitor series from Samsung at the low end. It’s still a great monitor, even if there are no quantum dots here.

The new 1000R stands for a more aggressive radius of curvature of 1000 mm (1 meter, -3.3ft), unlike the previously common 1800 mm. That essentially means all portions of the screen are at the same distance if your sitting about 1 meter away, which is relatively typical.

The curvature is given as a more immersive experience as it also covers slightly more files of view, but for me the main benefit is that all sections are essentially perpendicular to the viewer and varying viewing angle is a nonissue. Hence, the color rendition and black level should be more consistent.

Generally, the 2500:1 dynamic range is more than double the typical 1000:1 and that’s partially due to the supported HDR10. It also shows fairly decent black levels, which I didn’t expect in this price range.

The color space is not listed and measuring via screen calibration tool (Spyder) reveals a fairly good match of the sRGB color. That specifically shows a bit more weakness in reds than expected. In other words, this may not be the monitor for professional graphics and photography work.

Another feature that arguably stands out for this monitor is the curved screen. It does help with immersion in games or movies. It does, however, also distort the image a bit and certainly makes prints a bit more difficult.

There is one USB input, but that’s for uploading firmware updates. There is no USB hub in this monitor, and frankly, after a year or two Samsung hardly ever publishes updates anyway.

The two inputs are one display port 1.2 and one HDMI 2.0. You can have the monitor sense the inputs automatically, but that function is turned off initially. The on screen display (OSD) has a bit of a gaming character, but the issue is with navigating the menu with the unusual combination of power button and joystick. It’s oriented down and requires some getting used to.

The stand is likely the weakest part of this monitor. It generally works, but only allows for tilt and the height is both fixed and a bit on the low side. As this is a curved screen, the pivot between landscape and portrait orientation is not available either.

The screen is decent and a positive surprise is the effective anti glare coating. I suspect if this was glossy in any way, you’d quickly be tired of seeing yourself in all parts of the screen.

The screen has an impressive response time of 1ms and the WQHD resolution (1440p) still suits the 32” size without feeling too grainy. I’ve been relying on 27” screens so far and the curved 32” are noticeably bigger but not dramatically so. The brightness tops out at 250 nits, which is about the lower end of average. It sounds like a huge drawback, compared to the 340 nits of my other monitor, but the office is typically darker and the difference only matters in direct comparison. (In my case they're next to each other and brightness needs to be considered in the calibration.)

As the colors tend to be a bit muted, I keep my secondary display (99% aRGB) for photography proofing. Other than that, the Odyssey is a great monitor for gaming and videos. If you can afford it, consider the G7 as that gets you quantum dots for more brilliant colors (125% sRGB) and significantly brighter (320 nits).

Btw., the HDR10 capability resulted in an odd failure during calibration with the Spyder 3 Pro. A proclaimed “SanityCheckLUT” error kept the tool from calibration and it turns out that the Spyder 4 software doesn’t know how to deal with HDR. Turn that off temporarily for the calibration and it will be fine.

title: nearly perfect - sturdy, great price, but had to figure out install
text:
i've had these cord clips up and running for a couple months now and they have been great once installed:

i have them installed to clip an ethernet cable that's basically running through my entire house. they are sturdy enough that if someone accidentally hits them, they do not budge. however, if you need to take them out, it's as simple as just pulling/twisting them off the surface with your fingers - won't hurt your wrist and hasn't done any damage to the paint or wooden floors that i've pried them out of (your mileage may vary though depending on what surface you're using).

they can be clip cables both from the left and from the right, so they're pretty versatile as well. i have them running all sorts of shapes across the edges of my floor.

OK! so why the minus one star? installation...specifically installing with tape instead of screws. i figured out a good way to do this so don't worry, but it took some trial and error. let me explain:

the package gives you a bunch of double-sided tape if you want to install this via tape as opposed to screws. the tape itself is clear colored but the covers on both sides are read. it's really really hard to peel off one side of the tape cover. like i destroyed several of these double-sided tapes in an effort to peel the cover off the second side of the tape. what i eventually started doing is as follows:

1) peel the tape cover off the side of the tape that's easy to peel, and stick that peeled side onto the cord clip.
2) take a knife and cut that tape (the one already taped to the cord clip) in half. now, the tape is already stuck to the cord clip so the tape isn't going anywhere. the plastic of the cord clip is sturdy so it should be easy to cut just the tape and not the the cord clip.
3) use the knife (or your fingers) to find the newly formed edge(s) that you just made on the tape cover by cutting it, and peel the second side of the tape cover from there.

it wasn't so bad after i discovered this... but it would have been nice if i didn't have to cut the tape cover for every clip installed.

on a final note, i'd definitely recommend these for home use. i'm comparing this to the Command Round Cord Clips, which i actually replaced these with. the Command Rounds cost a ton more and didn't last a whole day, whereas these are still going strong.

title: Great sound, awkward controls
text:
I use earbuds for hours upon hours every day, for many years. I have settled on BT neckband style because I am repeatedly using only one side (while driving, etc) and taking them out completely for certain tasks. I like to be able to simply pop them out and they dangle until I'm ready to use them again. I usually have two sets, one charging while the other is in use, then swap. They typically last me a year or so.

The Linklike design needs work. Typically with neckband style the controls are on the neckband itself, but on this model the controls are on the wire, so using the controls pulls the earbud out of the ear, or jostles it to dislodge it. The button needs to be very FIRMLY pressed, making it more likely to come out of the ear during operation. Poor design.

The other problem with this is the control "bar" built into the wire causes it to be heavier than the other side, so when working out/running it is more likely to pull the earbud out of that ear (right side in this case). This is the reason I don't like the BT earbuds that are simply a wire connecting the two buds. If you remove one, the weight pulls the other out of your ear, and the controls in-line with the earbud wire is extra weight that causes imbalance. If you always keep both earbuds firmly in place, this may not be a problem for you. Since I am using them while doing things, interacting with others, driving, etc., I very often have only one bud in place.

On the positive side, the sound and noise-canceling is EXCELLENT with these things! Much better than other, more expensive neckband earbuds I have used. Very, very nice listening experience for a range of music styles, podcasts, audiobooks, etc. Battery life is superior as well.

I am going to have to return these and find a style that hopefully has good sound like the Linklike, good battery life, but has the controls on the neckband. Seems like a dumb, fussy thing to be a deal-breaker, but it interferes with the functionality for me and how I use earbuds. The price was certainly right, though!

text:
I am building a computer for a friend who has a limited budget, but still needed some decent specs to play games. This machine looked liked a good choice.

As part of setting up a new machine, I always run MEMTEST to be sure there are not issues I need to address before delivery. In this case, the stock RAM is showing entire blocks as failed (no-name brand I've not heard of previously; as shown in pic #1). This is consistent over 5 seperate tests; always fails. Using other (name brand) RAM and performing the same test battery, and the RAM passes fine, so is not machine/CPU/mem controller issue (pic #2, which is consistent over multiple tests).

The choice at this point seems to be buy and install other RAM or ship the computer back. Either way, there is a delivery delay to my friend.

Good machine, but seems to me like even a little quality testing would have prevented bad RAM being shipped to a buyer, and resulting in a 2-star review, which could have otherwise been prevented.

I cannot recommend this machine to someone not skilled with computer hardware. The buyer needs the ability do some testing of their own before putting the system into service.

title: The solid and quality product one would expect from Japan
text:
When it comes to quality products I still remember the old "Made in Japan" logo. Try to find anything NOT made in China these days. Well, I found one - the Fostex HP-A3 DAC. My main reason for considering a DAC was to replace my computer's built-in sound card. At very high volumes I could detect 60 cycle hum, with a bit of static that would come and go -- like a bad connection. Using the output plugs at either end of the sound card offered no improvement. My only option was to bypass the built-in sound card entirely.

Researching several DACs within my $350 price point, I kept coming back to the Fostex HP-A3. The HP-A3 implements the rare high-grade Japanese AKM AK4390 32-bit DAC chip, offering automatic up sampling of any USB audio signal to 96kHz, this is mirrored on the S/PDIF optical output.

It is compatible with Windows XP (SP2 or later) / Vista / 7 / 8 / 8.1 / 10 and Mac OSX (10.6 or later). No software is needed. No drivers required. It is strictly a plug and play device right out of the box. Another advantage - its power is derived from the USB. No external power supply necessary. The 5 volts from the USB is more than ample to run the DAC and power its headphone jack. It was only required to change my default setting from sound card to Fostex, and select the bit/sample rates. Done! My computer Hi-Fi is now completely quiet at full volume. No background noise issues.

The Fostex HP-A3 DAC is old school design, very 80s, with its angular casing and multiple buttons. In other words, it doesn’t fit in with modern aesthetics, which was probably a conscious choice from Fostex. But I like a few lights, buttons and a knob or two on my components. A lot of the latest DACs look positively barren and home built for lack of a gew-gaw or two.

The Fostex HP-A3 features an optional S/PDIF digital output, which allows the unit to act as a digital to digital converter from USB to optical. The input and output routing is selectable by front panel buttons. In my situation it was only necessary to plug the included shielded USB cable into the DAC and the computer's USB.

When ordering the unit I had little interest in its optional headphone jack. But now I find it gives me the option of not operating my pre-amp and amplifier just to get sound. My amplifiers are tube type and generate a lot of heat, pulling 100 watts of extra power as well. The DAC and headphone jack has great low bass. A portion of the sound spectrum I never heard or felt from the sound card.

How does the Fostex HP-A3 sound? The greatest improvement was with my considerable archive of .mp4 files. They now sound as good as my CDs did. And my CDs are also much improved but with little to quantify them. A friend sent me a few test high-res master files, but the downloaded player brought malware along with it which set me back a couple days. That killed that experiment! But my CDs sound just as good as his few high-res master samples.

Using my Sony MDR-6 Studio Monitor headphones, the sound stage is very wide. I have heard a few instruments sitting on my shoulder, or a tad behind it, if that is possible -- a sound stage effect not easy with "closed" headphones. My tube amps are now fed a clean, high quality input which only improves their performance as well.

Overall, the Fostex HP-A3 is a very strong performer, backed with the Fostex brand and "Made in Japan" logo. You can't lose on that one! The sound is very clean with zero grain. The sound stage is wide and deep. Tonality very natural. The mids nice and full bodied. The tonal balance is quite similar to the DACport HD, except that the Fostex has a wider and deeper sound stage. The Fostex tonality nips at the heels of the Bryston BDA-1 DAC, a $2,000 gadget for sound quality. The sound of this DAC is very impressive. It is smooth and not sharp, harsh or digital sounding. For gaming with headphones my sound system is absolutely at another level now.

Addendum:
It is being used with a Hewlett Packard tower gaming PC with Windows 7, a SUCA AUDIO two-tube pre-amp, a Nobsound 6p1 7-tube amplifier; a pair of Fluance SX6, high efficiency bookshelf speakers and Sony MDR-6 Studio Monitor headphones.

It has been five months since its purchase. The Fostex HP-A3 has been a rock solid performer, and I am delighted with my choice.

Addendum:
I am shocked. My Fostex DAC is already a year old. Not a whimper of a problem. It is used probably 12 hours a day and is still as perfect as the day it was plugged in.

Absolutely love my Fostex DAC. Don't be misled. This is a top notch quality - MADE IN JAPAN - audio product. It is a Rolls Royce DAC.

title: Phenomenal but DEFINITELY check for Quality Control
text:
Ultrawide, 1440p, FreeSync, 10-bit color, 400 nits, DisplayHDR400, 144hz, 1ms Response Time. At this price it doesn't get better than that.

I don't know if it's just because I went from two 23" 1080p IPS monitors to this beast, but it's an amazing upgrade. "But how is VA better than IPS?" You may ask that and believe me, I was concerned about it too when upgrading. But my previous monitors were only at 250 nits of brightness. A 400 nit VA display is worth it over the 250 nit IPS. The color is still amazing and the contrast ratio is tenfold better. Ghosting is slightly noticeable in darker color schemes, but it's still better than my previous monitors so I guess it depends on what you previously had.

My only issue with this monitor is quality control. After inspecting, I found over 10 disoriented and a few dead pixels along the borders of the monitor. You can only see them up close or if you're really looking for them. They're honestly not that bad and I could still thoroughly enjoy using it. What really bummed me out then? Finding a clump of dead pixels that smacked you in the face when you first turned the monitor on. I didn't have to inspect it to see the black dot that took this exciting day and turned it into what'll become a long process to get a replacement. I really hope the replacement turns out better than this and I will update you all when it shows up.

As of right now I honestly say this is a great purchase, all except for the abysmal quality control on this particular unit.

- - - UPDATE 10/14/2020 - - -

I got the new monitor and quality control is much better. There is unfortunately a dead pixel on the new one, but it's off to the left side and it's not noticeable when gaming or browsing the internet. I've had a week now to explore and make use of the previous unit that I'm returning but here's my input:

I highly recommend this over any 1080p or 60 hertz monitor. You will like the higher quality and the higher frame rate. Personally, my favorite upgrade is the brightness as this is a 400 cd/m2 display (I haven't used anything higher... yet). I'm not an expert at color identification or determining what looks best by any means, but I made the following adjustments to the monitor on its menu:

Brightness = 100
Contrast = 50
Black Boost = 1

In NVIDIA's Control Panel, under Display "Change resolution", I changed the output color depth to 10 bpc which can be run at 144 hertz (some monitors require a drop in hertz first in order to choose a higher bpc; this one does not). After making these adjustments to the monitor's menu and NVIDIA's Control Panel, the screen looks incredible. Try to get this monitor when it goes on sale, but honestly for $500.00 you can't go wrong. It's a great upgrade in all aspects if you don't require the use of dual monitors.

title: Good performance & build quality
text:
It simply works well.
Although manufacturer was kind enough to include a driver CD, I didn't even need to use it.
Before installing the card; I downloaded latest Intel Wi-Fi6 drivers from Intel's web site (you'll download two files; one for wifi and one for bluetooth).
Then I installed the card. On next bootup; I installed above drivers. It worked just fine.
Beware; if you have another bluetooth adapter on your computer; make sure to remove all paired devices (from Windows bluetooth settings) before unplugging that bluetooth adapter. Otherwise; your new card simply won't "takeover" those previous bluetooth pairings. Worst; it'll still populate your bluetooth devices list - but you won't be able to connect them with your new card.
If you forget doing that as I did, you can still cleanup AFTER removing your old bluetooth adapter and installing your new card. Just follow these steps to completely clean out both driver for your old bluetooth adapter AND paired devices to that adapter:
a. Press Windows key + X.
b. Click on Device Manager.
c. Click on View.
d. Click on Hidden Devices (these will have light blue color).
e. Look for your old Bluetooth adapter and paired devices (they'll all have light blue color).
f. Right click on each entry and click uninstall one by one (again, only the light blue color ones). Items for your new card will have darker blue color - do not delete those.
Then pair your devices to your new bluetooth card as normal.
I actually bought this card only to add Bluetooth 5.0 capability to my home-made PC. I had a plug-in USB bluetooth 4.2 adapter. I was (keyword is: was) hoping to achieve wider coverage area with bluetooth 5 (as marketing makes you believe). But I have about same coverage distance. That's OK. At least I can use later codecs with my bluetooth 5.0 headphone. I even tried an external antenna; trying to see if I can extend bluetooth coverage. A 12" external antenna with a 15' extension cable. My aim was to "pull away" bluetooth signal from electrically noisy signal neighborhood of my PC case. I tried many different placement and directional positions with that external antenna : no improvement at all. On that regards; take a look at my photo: that marked 2.4GHz antenna also works for bluetooth.
As I have wired gigabit network connection to my PC; I'll not be using the wi-fi portion of the card for foreseeable future. So I disabled it thru Windows network adapter settings. I tested wi-fi connection before disabling it though; it connected with high signal strength. Good to know that I have wi-fi6 capability when I need it.
Note: Bluetooth works even if you disable wi-fi driver.

title: Decent camera, but field of view is way too narrow (58-degrees)
text:
Outside of using the built-in webcam on my Surface Pro laptop, it wasn't sufficient for the number of meetings I needed to participate in lately with Covid. So I bought 2 different brands from Amazon (Papalook PA452 [This review] and Amcrest AWC201-B) to try them out on my Dell Desktop, which has more computing power and 2 larger screens. After hooking up both webcams at the same time and trying them out side-by-side, I learned alot... unfortunately neither of these webcams fit my needs, so they'll both be returned and I'll continue my search.

Pros of the Papalook PA452: Nicely packaged in a small box, with clear instructions inside. Overall the build quality seems good, it pivots well side-to-side, and it mounted to the top of my thin, widescreen monitor fine. It was extremely easy to install/setup, and Windows 10 plug and play recognized it immediately, allowing me to use it right away in Zoom and Google Hangouts. Plus it shipped/arrived very quickly.

Cons: Although the microphone was sensitive and properly picked up all the spoken words, I found it to sound a little muffled/distant (although it was better than then other model). Maybe there's a 3rd party app/driver that could have helped with this, but out of the box, it was just ok. As for image quality, I admit I don't have the best lighting in the room, other than an overhead light built into the fan, so a big concern of mine was if the camera could compensate/color correct. Although this camera was better than the other model, in that it was clearer and adjusted for the yellow tint of the light bulb and brightened the image a little, it still wasn’t what I was hoping for in terms of auto correction. However the biggest issue and deal breaker for me, was the narrow field of view. I couldn’t find this anywhere on the website or box, but in the manual it lists it’s only 58-degrees, and I believe it. Although I don’t need it to see the entire room, this camera zooms in very close, almost like head and shoulder only. And when you turn of the “HD” option it gets even closer. Too close for my taste (the other was 70-degrees which makes a big difference). And as others had said, the On/Off button on the back doesn’t do anything. The only way to turn off the camera is to unplug the USB. And although I knew it didn’t come with a privacy cover, with the design of this camera, the lens sticks out of the body. So there’s no easy way to attach a 3rd party “stick on” cover (like a hinged toilet seat) or a piece of paper.

Overall I’d say it’s decent for the money. But given the amount I’ll need to use it, and the type of calls I’ll been involved with for work, looks like I need to buy one of the more expensive models.

text:
I love everything about my SL3 other than the fact it refuses to pick up sound from an external mic (hooked up via XLR to 3.5mm jack on the side of the camera).

The photo and video quality (regarding picture) are excellent and I love the 4K resolution feature for the SL3 since I most often use tripods. Handheld 4K video? I don't think the hands of a surgeon could execute a stable video but perhaps that's just me.
Features are extremely easy to maneuver through and you can choose a guided mode or Canon's typical digital display (the one you use once you know what you're doing). There's a "Q" button you have to hit before changing any settings on-screen so you don't acidentally do it by bumping a button.

title: Best 13" laptop out there right now
text:
I've been using this laptop for a while now and it's a fantastic laptop. The keyboard feels good to type on. The touchpad is fantastic. The gaming performance is impressive for a laptop this size. The fans remain relatively quiet even at max speed. The screen is nice and bright and you can get away with it at less than half brightness most of the time without having it look too dim. The keyboard backlighting is nice, though I usually leave it turned off unless I need it, and even then I keep it fairly dim to conserve battery. Battery life on this thing is actually quite good. If you keep the screen at a reasonable brightness and turn off the keyboard backlight you can easily get 6 to 7 hours out of this if not more. I haven't noticed any of the problems mentioned with the previous model of this laptop. The speakers don't crackle, the usb-c ports are solid. The only thing I've noticed is that there's some coil whine if you charge it using a charger that's lower than 100watts. So if you use a 60 watt charger for instance it will charge fine (as long as you aren't gaming or something), but you'll hear some coil whine, which really isn't that big a deal. I don't hear any when charging it with the included 100watt charger.

Tips to improve battery life:
1. Remove the Xbox game bar / overlay as it's a big battery drain. You need to remove it by running commands in the powershell window as they don't let you remove it via add/remove programs. There are guides online for how to do this.
2. Set the keyboard backlighting to either solid red, blue, or green as it will only use 1 of the 3 sets of lights under each key and will save battery. Keep it as dim as possible as well (or turn it off when not needed).
3. Uninstall any apps that run in the background but you don't intend to use, such as OneDrive.
4. Disable the nvidia game overlay if you don't plan to use it.
5. Make sure you have the power profile / mode set to "Battery saver".
6. Set the screen brightness as low as possible while still being comfortable.
7. Turn off bluetooth! (huge battery drain).

The versatility of this laptop, being able to stretch a full work day worth of battery out of it while also being able to run triple-A games on it is just incredible. Also the portability. I highly recommend getting yourself some dbrand skins for this as it's an absolute fingerprint magnet and the skins resolve that.

Bottom line: great laptop with excellent performance, very snappy. If you're on the fence about getting one of these after hearing all of the build quality problems with last year's model, this year Razer has definitely stepped up and ironed out the problems. This thing is stellar.

title: Not suitable for continuous high current applications, will heat up and melt.
text:
The fuse that is shipped with this socket is not suitable for continuous high current applications, because the internal resistance is too high.
200 Amps across the 250 Amp fuse I measured a Voltage drop of 120 mV, that makes a stunning 0.125 * 200=24 Watts of loss to heat. If that current was drawn for hours and as in my case the fuse was mounted inside of the engine compartment of my van, the plastic housing would start to melt.

Recommendation: Do not use this fuse and socket for Inverter type, or battery charging kind of applications. If continuous current close to the rating of the fuse is drawn over a longer time, it will heat up and possible pose a fire risk.

text:
This could have been a great device. Unfortunately Caavo chose to mislead their customers about adding Dolby Vision support and subsequently if you have a source that sends a Dolby Vision signal you are likely to have stability issues (I do) AND you simply cannot use Dolby Vision. This is unfortunate as most new devices (and a lot of older ones are getting) support for Dolby Vision.

I own two Caavos and I've had to shelf one of them since it locks up multiple times daily forcing me to get up, unplug the device, plug it back in and wait for it to power cycle to bring everything back online again. A real pain.

Another issue is if you are using Plex on an Nvidia Shield (or likely many other devices) the play/pause buttons do not work and the Caavo team acts like this is normal. My Harmony remote works just fine. I can hit play/pause and the button works just as expected.

Lastly the D-Pad on this thing is horrible. It's way to shallow and it's almost completely level with the large OK button inside the ring (that acts as the directional pad) so you will CONSTANTLY press the OK button accidently and end up launching the incorrect item, or other random things.

I'm pretty disappointed in the device at the moment but should Caavo make good on their initial promise of Dolby Vision support I will revise my review. I'm hoping to see a proper redesign of the remote to address the Dpad button issue such as how the fantastic Nvidia Shield remote (the new one) is setup.

title: Great little computer, especially for machine learning
text:
The Jetson Nano is one of the most underrated SBC's on the market. First, just as a general purpose Ubuntu 18.04 LTS desktop, it's great. Yes, the image is based on the previous LTS, not the more recently released 20.04, but it's a very polished image that Nvidia provides. Even with just 4GB of RAM, it runs very well, thanks to a proper set of Nvidia drivers that allow for fully accelerated composited window management, WebGL acceleration in Chromium. The Nano has a generally snappy feel while running a REAL full desktop Linux distro that even the 8GB RaspberryPi 4 can't match.

And then there's the main show: the GPU, GPU programming and machine learning toolset: it's all preinstalled, and configured. What isn't there can be added quickly via container images. The Maxwell based 128 cuda cores are not latest gen (or even close) but they get the job done as a teaching tool. The key here is that it's a self contained setup, that takes just ten minutes to get up and running.

For the money, you can't beat it, especially as a self-directed learning tool.

title: Bad, bad, bad
text:
Follow up to my initial review:
Wrote the initial review too fast. We immediately noticed that the sound was out of sync with the video. Not much, but def. annoying.

Bigger problem--the sound would completely drop as we were streaming (BTW--when the sound drops so does the closed captioning, so couldn't use that as a work around)

I am NOT a techie. Hit the owner's manual--waste of time. Support? Also. Youtube yielded some options and in trying I found that indeed I DO have HDMI-ARC (on side of TV). Changed out the cords and...no difference. I had hoped the optical cord was the issue. It wasn't.

I tried various setting adjustments. Nothing. Unplugging the unit for 10 seconds did correct the sound drops for a day or two--and then repeat. Annoying but do-able. But the out-of-sync persists.

This thing has wasted too many of my hours. Disappointed with Roku on about 7 levels. Am boxing it up and shipping it back.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Sounds great. Voice-activated feature is cool. But seriously, why do I have to spend a half-hour trolling YouTube videos to figure out how to install the product?

Specifically--my TV does not have HDMI-ARC, just regular HDMI. So I needed to use the optical cable that comes with it. Except--they don't say that there are not-easy to remove plastic tips covering the ends of the optical cable. I don't do this every day. This was my first optical cable installation and likely will be my last. You can't tell that there is a cap. Tried seventy-five ways to install and then looked at 5 videos until thankfully one guy says, oh, yeah, make sure you take off the cap, it's hard to tell it's there!

So-- Roku geniuses--how about including each step in the installation process?

(I recognize how silly this is. I'm complaining about a minor installation issue with the sound bar to my flat screen TV. Ridiculous, and I feel like a jerk for whining about it. But.... I was 5 seconds away from putting the whole thing back in the box and shipping it back. So maybe this will help someone.

title: Beautiful monitor if you accept its flaws
text:
Pros: awesome colors, incredibly clear, massive real-estate, stand an housing incredibly solid and ergonomical

Cons: IPS glow, HDR low, 60hz, right at that point where it's almost to big to not be curved

Once we have hardware that can readily push 4k above 60hz is probably when you should really get something like this if you intend to do gaming, particularly competitive gaming. For normal gaming and other tasks this is more than adequate and you really benefit from all those extra pixels. I use this primarily in a work capacity so it's browser tabs, consoles, and IDEs. This monitor is almost perfect if that is all you're going to do. Almost because even in that context, it still suffers if you like to do those things in low light, but it's not to noticeable. Even watching movie with black bars is good enough that I really don't notice the glow, at least not to the extent that it's turning the screen yellow or anything like that. It's also a little weird doing things/using windows that cause my eyes to approach the corners. Maybe it's just because I'm also used to using a 34in curved monitor during the day, but it takes a bit to get used to the view angle going back and forth. I knew what I was getting into with this monitor, but accepted those concessions as there don't seem to be any others of this size and clarity with USB-c available outside of a few LGs that come with their own compromises. Speaking of which, LG makes the panel in these. They really need to get it together quality wise. I know they can when you look at the displays they produced in partnership with apple, but I'm also not going to pay 1300 for a display right now. But even at this significantly lower price point I don't think the quality should be this poor. I also opted for the Dell because of their warranty commitment. Overall I'm content with this model but with ready acknowledgement that things could be a lot better.

title: Photographer and Mac User - Decent Drive for Backup
text:
I bought two of these drives a little more than 1.5 yrs ago. They both work GREAT. I carry them in my computer bag everywhere I go. As with anything "electronic", you have to practice care. Mine have a few dents from slightly rough handling, but overall they have worked wonderfully. I have one 5TB that functions as my primary storage/backup of my photography (set my Lightroom to keep catalog and all images on this drive). The second I have partitioned into 2x 2.5 TB drives, one for my TimeMachine Backup and the other for additional Document and Website backups.
My only complaint is that since these are "spindle" HDD, when trying to tether from Camera to Lightroom, the drive performance via the USB 3.0 is slow. Also at times, Caching seems to get bogged down when doing major edits (this could also be because of RAM limitations on MacBook).
Overall I'm happy and I think other Mac users/ Photographers would be happy with these drives as a portable system.
(NOTE:: always perform you backups of your stored data - I use Backblaze as an additional layer of backup. These are portable HDDs... that means they get jostled, dropped, bumped, etc. - you have to use a little common sense and realize that there is the possibility that one minor bump may be the bump that renders your HDD non-readable)

title: Great gaming monitor that works with G-Sync as well.
text: Beautiful screen. Great performance. Didn't like the wait (over a week) to receive the product but once I plugged it up and seen the screen all was forgiven. I made this review to help others fix an issue this monitor have with enabling G-Sync (unoffically works) using a Nvidia graphic card with this monitor. If you enable G-Sync with this monitor everything will work fine. But once you run a game your screen will flicker. I have came up with a fix that fixes this issue. I fixed G-Sync flicker for the ViewSonic VX2458-C-mhd freesync monitor by following these steps using the CRU program. I changed my V-H rate values by selecting the edit button to the right of the pull-down menu, labeled VSC36AF-VX2458 Series (active*) in cru. The changes are 120-144 for V rate and 120-160 for H rate. Then under Detail resolution (3 slots left) click on 1920x1080 then hit edit. Change the refresh rate from 143.996Hz to 144.000Hz. I looked all over the web and this should be the only post that gives detailed info on how to make this work. I hope this helps buyers of this great monitor! Happy gaming!

title: Great buy for $20
text:
Great value for the $20 price tag!
There are a lot of similar styles of laptop tables out there on Amazon, but I chose this one specifically due to the lock that keeps the table flat when unfolded. That feature is a game changer and that’s what set this product apart from all the other foldable laptop tables I saw.

Some things I liked about this product:
- Easy set up/unfolding and folding back up again. The table includes locks for when you want to keep the surface flat, and also for when you want to keep it folded up.
- Good height for me as a short person who is 5’2. High enough to allow room for me to easily sit with my legs crossed, but not so high that it becomes uncomfortable to write or type.
- Lightweight and can be easily moved around, especially when folded to take up less space and be more portable. Even includes a handle to carry it around with when folded.
- The legs can lock in place when the table is unfolded, so no worries about the legs collapsing while in use.
- As a bonus, the table also came with an extra plastic tool that can be used as a laptop stand. Haven’t used it but it was a nice addition that may come in handy.

If I were to nitpick and complain about some things/ areas to improve:
- Top surface creaks and bends slightly in some spots if I lean my elbow on it.
- Doesn’t align perfectly when folded up so there is a small gap between the sides. The product in theory could probably be used similarly like a suitcase to store books inside, but since the edges don’t line up too well when folded up I probably won’t be using it in that way if carrying it anywhere outside of the house.
- The finish on the legs gets scratched easily and this leaves small black marks.
- Not the hugest fan of the off-white, fake marble pattern. I don’t mind it because it’s neutral enough, but I do wish there was a better selection of colors and patterns available for this design.

These are all just off the top of my head. I think this table still wins for the value I got for paying just $20. I prioritize utility over aesthetic and this table gets the job done. Overall, I am happy with the product and hope to be able to use it for years to come.

Why? They say 'it's intended to reduce battery usage.' But that should be on customer's decision. Foscam don't have to make decision instead of customers. Even if I have to charge camera once a day because I'm using 24-hour live view, but that's my choice.
I think the actual reason is, to make customers forced to use their cloud stroage plan.
If these cameras are attached to other BETTER programs such as surveillance station on synology, maybe many people (including me) wouldn't pay for foscam's storage plan.

title: Great Product - Buyer Beware Not Wireless
text:
As reported by many this product is NOT wireless. Some reviews seem to indicate it was but had a proprietary dongle. My version is decidedly not wireless at all as there is a built-in cable that must be plugged in.

Lack of wireless is not a deal-breaker, but I feel it is completely misleading to advertise as such. That is why this product is 1-star. Otherwise it is a good product.

Working at a computer all day I was looking for a product that avoided the stress of repeatedly moving my hands from keyboard to mouse. This hits the spot. The rollerbar feels very natural to move the mouse, I was expecting a huge learning curve. Meanwhile clicking did take some getting used to avoid pressing and moving my mouse pointer simultaneously. Although there are dedicated buttons for single click these are a bit too far from the home row and so I tend to use them much less.

Configuring the mouse speed was easy to figure, but configuring the click force and the sound was not. The product came with no manual and I had to look this up online. Looking it up online was not easy because there are several subtlety different versions of this product and I had to try several PDFs before I found the one with the right instructions.

The many different versions that all are named very similar are probably why there are bad reviews here. My suspicion is that the seller can't easily tell the difference.

Overall it is a great product to reduce strain, though a bit expensive. Buyer beware that you may not get a wireless version.

title: Great upgrade from combo modem/router but took hours to set up
text:
So a full 6 hours of setting this up is insane and google needs better support when they launch a product. No instructions, and 2 hours on the phone with their tech support. Issue was the 2 routers vs the standard extra point (which would have been a simple setup).

My first router plugged into my Motorola MG7550 modem with no issues, I disabled the wifi on it so that wouldn't be an issue. For some reason my speeds were not any better than the modems wifi though. I was really disappointed since I spent $300 on this setup. After resetting it a few times and trying to install the other point I started seeing the speed pickup (using third party app on phone). All of a sudden I was getting 230mbps wifi which is the same as my hard wired speed! I was getting 80mbps max on the motorola wifi. My home server movie files were too big to ever stream with around 50mbps in my bedroom but now its no issue as I am also getting over 200 there.

The problem was the second point, which I needed badly in my office across the house, never got a good wifi signal but I have a hard line into there, so it was just annoying for phone use. Figured it would be simple, hook up the hard line (from a switch) to the second router, then since it has the extra port plug that into my computer to keep the hardline going. Yeah no such luck, kept saying "problem connecting to cloud" on the final step of setup, so the wifi networks wouldn't sync (even though my phone was picking up the second one, it was under a different name) and it wouldn't connect my computer to the rest of the network.

Took an hour of explaining to google support until they finally understood there is a 2 pack of routers that only amazon sells (they kept trying to tell me I had 1 router and a point). Then they said it wouldn't work with 2 routers unless I wanted 2 wireless networks (which defeats the purpose of this). It turns out the problem was my motorola modem/router still wanting to act as a router, I unplugged everything from it except for the 1 cable going into the nest wifi, then had the witch going out from the nest wifi and even though I turned off wifi on the actual modem I also went in and changed the setting to be a bridge (not sure if that did anything, but goolge help person mentioned it). Then it picked up second router as new mesh point and connected but it was acting like a regular point and not a hard wired router, so the connection sucked. The whole point of me buying this 2 pack instead of the $269 one directly from google was having the 2 hardwired routers for better coverage. Well something finally clicked along the way not exactly sure what it was as we did so many things over the 2 hours on the phone, but its all working now. I have 2 routers hooked up, both hardwired and both sending 100% full strength signal as wifi even though they are completely across the house (where a regular non hard wired point wouldn't be able to communicate with a router). I am paying for 200mbps from cable company but getting 230-240 on all my tests, hard wired and wifi, which is amazing and anywhere from 3-5 times what I was getting. This is a better/cheaper solution than buying the 3 pack with 2 points unless you really want the google speaker functions (which I didn't care about).

This would easily be 5 star with better support on hooking up multiple routers in mesh mode, and was so painful I almost gave it 3 stars, but the product simply works really well once setup and is easily managed along with all my other google devices and hue lights thru a single app.

title: Great laptop, good value
text:
Background: I bought this six months ago, weeks before the pandemic. I have been using it 10-12h every day, mainly for work (PhD in biochemistry). I installed Kubuntu on the first day and seldom boot on Windows. Main software I use is Firefox, PyCharmm, Zoom, and office stuff. I do not play games.

Overall, it is a great computer. The CPU is quite fast, the NVME SSD is excellent, and 16 Gb is more than enough RAM for my needs. The i5-1035G1 has 4 core/8 threads, and my experience with it is great. I don't recall a single slow down, and some times I even run small 5-10 min jobs. I cannot comment on the GPU, as I don't play games.

The usable screen to overall size rate is good, as there is only a small strip of plastic around it, so the laptop it is not that large, as some 15.6" models. It feels light and thin. But the screen is a bit dim, and not HD. The keyboard is responsive and there is a numpad, which some may seem as useless, but is a pro by me. The touch pad is ok, but I sometimes wish it to be larger.

What I dislike most about the laptop is the thermal design. The cooler is noisy and it runs too often. It's annoying. For some reason, the hot air is blown towards the screen, and I think it makes the noise even more obvious. For some reason, I think the fan was even louder on Windows, so be aware! There are some other annoyances (see below).

All in all, it's an excellent laptop for the price tag, if you are not playing games or do not need a good GPU for any reason.

Pros:
- CPU/RAM/SSD combo, ie, great speed
- Touchscreen
- Good keyboard
- Battery lasts for 3h-4h
- Light and thin
Cons
- Noisy fan
- Screen is a bit dim, and it is not HD (res is 1366x768)
- Keyboard is not backlit

title: Inconsistent speed and random drops off of network, until I gave it an antenna upgrade (UPDATE)
text:
Some will need antennae upgrades.
I purchased this for a 12yr old 2008 Mac Pro 3,1 that I've upgraded to be compatible with the latest Mac OS (Catalina). Out of the box it outperformed the built-in 802.11n chip, though, suffered random drops off the network - often - as well as inconsistent speed. The drops were a deal breaker and I was on the cusp of repackaging it and sending it back, until I borrowed the external (4x) antenna array from my ASUS PCE-AC88 card that I use in my Windows machine. This time, it joined the network utilizing the speedier 802.11AC protocol with speeds consistently triple of what I'd get using the N protocol. Most importantly, I'm happy to say that there have been NO DROPS in 6hrs of heavy use!!!

I wish I could give it 3.5 stars, though I'll round-up to 4 stars because it works out of the box with MacOS, it's cheaper than alternatives and delivers on its promise *AFTER* I provided my own antenna upgrade.

Unfortunately, the antenna array has to go back to the Windows machine. I'm shopping around for an alternative array and believe I have settled on the following and will update this review after some testing.

Eightwood 2.4GHz 5GHz Dual Band WiFi Antenna with 3 RP-SMA Male Connector Magnetic Base for WiFi Wireless Router Mobile Hotspot PCI PCIe WiFi Card PC Desktop Motherboard External WiFi USB Adapter

UPDATE: 08/13/2020
I purchased the above mentioned antenna by "Eightwood" and have been receiving very good, consistent speeds with no drops/disconnects. I'm not quite getting the same maximum throughput as I was with the antenna from the Asus PCE-AC88 kit, though, the latter high performance kit cost me nearly two hundred dollars a couple of years back and was meant for gamers. I am very pleased with the Eightwood antenna.

UPDATE: 08/29/2020
A little over two weeks after purchase and the card/antenna combo has still had NO problems in 24/7 usage. To give you a little background, my computer is in the basement and the Comcast WiFi router is on the 1st floor. There are 2 Comcast xFi pods (wifi mesh extenders) on the first floor and one in the basement, to help the Wifi cover the whole house. However, the basement pod frequently falls victim to significant interference (a result of being within feet of plumbing, HVAC, water heater, etc. - all items Comcast says NOT to put a pod near) so it - mostly - connects to a pod on the first floor. While this does lead to a small decrease in bandwidth (100mbps+ down to around 70mbps+. Doesn't affect latency, however!), it's a testament to how much reach this antenna has given my 12yr old Apple Mac-Pro 3,1.

title: Solid product.
text:
Build quality seems good. Really like that it has a separate power adapter, rather than hard wired.

Right out of the box I started experimenting. Plugged up my monitor using HDMI and plugged in my wireless dongle for my keyboard and mouse. I have been using Chromebooks for a while now. The main page said NOTHING about Chromebook compatibility. Plugged up to my Acer R13 and within seconds docking station began working including the attached screen. While you can click on preferences to make changes, I shut the Chromebook's lid and started working away at my new workstation. I can't say it will work with all Chromebooks but it worked with the two I own just fine.

Windows 10 laptops installed the drivers after plugging the USB cord. In order to get the thing to work once you close the lid of your laptop there is a switch under power setting that must be changed. I set our to never turn the screen off while plugged in when closing the lid. Works fine. Occasionally the audio flakes out and you have to reselect it as your audio output device. (this is a windows issue)

On to my negative part of this review. Mac OS. I know the Displaylink website claims the driver works for newer versions with some system tweaks, but in our tests we had NO LUCK getting this to work with any OS past High Sierra. Once you upgrade the video just stops working. We reached out to Displaylink support, read through every forum we could, and still ended up rolling the Macbook back to High Sierra. This next little bit is more on Mac OS in general. ALWAYS DO A SYSTEM BACKUP TO A SEPARATE STORAGE DRIVE BEFORE UPGRADING. This will save you a lot of headaches because once you go from the Itunes store to whatever they are calling it now, getting to where you can download older versions of the OS will really try your patience. "And that's all I have to say about that." Your mileage might vary.

I can neither confirm nor comment on how well this dock work with any other devices, like the MS Surface, as I don't currently own one.

I may come back later after trying it out with some ODD stuff, like a linux laptop or some SBC's running various OS's and add to this review. Sorry this has gotten so long.
