title: For the price, this is the best. Better than devices which cost 2x as much.
text:
First, this is for the actual Hi10X tablet. Which is a windows tablet, which by itself is both a big plus when it comes to functionality/openness/backwards compatibility and a big negative when it comes to resource utilization.

Mostly I purchased this device to replace a 7" dell Venue 8 pro 5855 (4G ram/128G storage/1080p) I use mostly for media consumption, and once in a while some light application use (ssh, email, etc). In that regard is a definite upgrade. Its got a nice screen, plenty of ram, and the storage is more than adequate. I wanted a smaller lighter x86/windows tablet, and this is probably the best device in that class, now that it is impossible to buy a 7" x86 tablet that isn't using ~5 year old processor design. I find the surfaces and most of the competitive machines too bulky to hold up in bed or while on an airplane. Which is why you always see them on the tray tables instead of peoples laps like you see with phones, kindles, etc.

That said, this device isn't going to win any speed awards. Once you turn off windows idiotic virus scanning and telemetry/spying, install a firewall to block it from downloading updates without permission/etc its completely usable for most non-gaming tasks. Given, its probably more compute power than most people had in their win7 machines 10 years ago, one can only blame MS for the lag that is sometimes seen. OTOH, its just a couple watts full bore, so about a 20-30x reduction in power utilization from that 10 year old machine.

The battery life situation is frustrating. This tablet is super low power, but that doesn't mean it should come with a phone battery (which is basically what it has). As it stands, the battery life ranges from 12 hours to about an hour depending on what your doing. Reading a book, 12+ hours, watching netflix 10 hours, light web surfing 6-7 hours, watching a video in firefox that doesn't have hardware decoding, 4 hours. Compiling code, about an hour (not many laptops survive for long when compiling code two hours is a lot). If this were running android it would be a 12+ hour device, but windows is all to happy to let random background tasks eat battery, or run software that doesn't let the core sleep between user interactions/etc. Doubling the battery capacity would have made this tablet a no-compromises device. As it is, it battery life is similar to most < $900 laptops. Although on the battery charging, I wish it were possible to charge from a random 5V USB port. The brick it comes with says 12V output, which AFAIK isn't one of the standard USB PD voltages, which explains why none of my other chargers works with the device.

Yes, its got enough ports for most uses without having to have a pile of dongles. I did pick up the keyboard for it after owning it for a few days. That is a fine purchase as well, although given how large/heavy it is, they should have put a massive battery in the keyboard. It adds a couple full size USB-A ports which are very useful.

In the end 5+ stars, the only shortcoming is really the battery life, and that is fine as long as one doesn't try to run heavy applications. The weight form factor, and price more than make up for the battery life gripe. Most of the rest of the gripes are windows related (minimum back light setting, etc). That is the price of avoiding the apple walled garden that makes it painful to just copy a movie file to the device, or the garbage ware of android that won't get updates in a few months and a long list of functional shortcomings.

BTW: Extra star for not dumbing down the BIOS options, its crazy complete.

title: Quick and Easy Review.
text:
Quick and Easy Review.
Clock Radio with amazing amounts of features, setup can be a challenge.

Extended review below.
I will write this review from the point of answering questions I had and got conflicting information.

1. This unit IS an Atomic clock in the sense it uses the signal from the NIST Radio Station WWVB, which is located near Fort Collins, Colorado, to set the time.

2. This clock also can be set using a local FM radio station that transmits a special time sink signal.

3. this radio has TWO external antennas, one for the FM which is a little wire and one plastic cigar shaped unit for the Auto setting feature.

4. The auto clock radio features have a signal indicator on the upper left of the display and you MUST position the antenna to get the best signal so the Radio will set itself.

5. if you use either one of the Automatic time settings available, the clock will set itself for Daylight savings time.

6. you can set up the Clock manually without any automatic setup if you want, but then you might as well buy a regular old clock radio.

7. you MUST turn on any Automatic settings in the clocks menu.

8. This Clock Radio does NOT have a battery backup, but it DOES have a capacitor backup which will keep the setting for sometime in a power failure.

9. you can turn the backlight completely off on the clock, you have to use the dial on the BOTTOM of the unit to do this.

10. the Backlight button (bottom right on the front) will cycle between your setting and full.
if you have the display off as I do, simply push the button and the display will turn on the light and then go back off.
11. when the Alarm goes off, the back light will come on FULL, which is nice because it's trying to wake you up!

12. this has TWO alarms, when you set any alarm it gives you many choices, One time, Daily, Weekly, Weekend.

13. The clock has a month, day, year feature.

14. The AM/FM radio works well, use the loudness feature for full effect.

15. If you want to use the huge amount of features available on this clock radio, you have to use the Manual, without the manual you will be frustrated very quickly.

This is an AWESOME Clock Radio that will do everything for once you set it up.

Hopes this helps.

title: Outrageously exaggerated claims, 100 Watts x 2 RMS TOPS!
text: I knew that for $150, 800 watts RMS was not going to happen. But I figured even if it only puts out half of that, it's not a bad deal for $150. Well this amp doesn't push even close to half of what it claims. I bought it to push two single voice coil 12 inch subs at 4 ohms. It was pretty much a joke. I compared it to my home theater set up by listening to it next to my one 12" Klipsch sub which is rated at 800 watts Max. The Klipsch sub was blowing away the two 12in hooked up to the supposedly 3000 watt Max amp,  it was barely enough to push them. Just to be sure I didn't screw something up or there wasn't something wrong with my subs I rewired it twice tried it in bridged mode, stereo, and wired in series and parallel. No real noticeable difference in the subs. Before packing it up to ship back I decided to hook it up to my Klipsch bookshelf speakers: 6 1/2" drivers + compression horn tweeters rated to max out at 75 Watts RMS. Cranked It up about 90% of the way before backing off and the tiny speakers took every bit of it. so either my little bookshelf speakers can handle 3000 Watts or someone needs to retest the power output of their amplifier, I'll let you be the judge! On the plus side the seller (Audiosavings) was cool about it. I told them I was unhappy and they accepted the return but I did have to pay for shipping. I knew I was taking a chance so that seems fair.

text:

are something I have never seen on a TV before. OLED's have 4 layers of that make up the screen and LCD LED's have 8.
I would describe seeing a OLED for the first time like having cataracts (LCD LED) and then having them removed (OLED). Plus on LCD LED TV's you have to sit directly in front of it. Anything slightly off center, it starts to get washed out. Again because of the 8 layers. And I'm really getting sick of people talking about "burn in". I have no issues with "burn in" and don't expect any. But then again I don't watch TV 20 hours a day. But maybe if you watch TV 20 hours a day, "burn in" might not be your only problem. I believe people who have "burn in" are the same people that buy a new car and 6 months later it's a junker because they did not take care of it. If you spend 1000's of dollars on something maybe you should care for it a little better. Try turning it off after a few hours and go out side and get some fresh air. Go to the store and compare for yourself and see the difference. You will be amazed. And don't worry about "burn in", as long as you have a "life" you'll be fine. I have a 6 year old top line LCD LED and the difference is amazing. I will NEVER go back to LCD LED. OLED for life!!!

title: AMAZING FOR THE PRICE; REALLY QUITE GOOD, ACTUALLY
text:
Upfront: I am giving these five stars because they are an exceptional bargain, and deliver really good sound at a low price - not because they are "five-star" quality like Bose or Beats or whatever. The ratio of quality to price is a winner.

LIke others here, I am a chronic earphone/ headphone/buds purchaser. I love gadgets, plus I use these for phone, gym, hiking, etc. Swapping them out. I have the Bose QC15, I have over-the-ear Alpatronix, in-ear buds, etc.

My first assessment: I was quite amazed at how good they sound. It took me by surprise. Two things: there seemed to be more noise-cancelling effect than I expected. And the sound quality was way better than I expected. Yes, perhaps the bass can have a bit more boom. And the treble can be more bell-like. But considering I paid $35 on a promotion, I was shocked. Delighted and shocked. I've worn them four times. They appear well made. Indeed, they hug the ear, and my ears are larger rather than smaller - so I can imagine that I would find them confining or warm after several hours. But I have only worn them a half hour at a time, and it's been fine. I can't imagine an over-the-ear headphone not being warm. At the gym, they were way loud enough, and it muffled the loud ambient music that is played at the gym, so I was happy about that. And unlike my Bose, I love that they are cordless. So far, I quite recommend these. They are quite good, especially at the price. But they are simply quite good, I think.

title: Useful and at a good price, but with a few minor Cons
text:
I usually purchase 3ml Polypropylene 12 3/4" x 13", 2 mils thick, outer jacket sleeves via a different brand (BCW Record Album Sleeves) but I thought I'd search for a better price and discovered these. I was influenced by the fact they are Polyethylene which is preferred by audiophiles and the price.

The PROs: I found these and the price was @ .22/ea for 100 pieces. That's better than I was paying before. I liked the 3mils protective thickness, I liked the strength and durability of these. I liked the "archival quality", "polyethylene" material. The single and double/gatefold sized LPs fit well and were easy to insert and accommodated these sizes well.

The CONS: These were labeled as "high-clarity" and they actually a bit cloudy. They are not crystal-clear like the bags I usually use. So, my collection will be a mixture of this cloudy brand and the crystal clear kind which is probably about 95 percent of my collection. Oh, well. Also, these bags are sized a bit odd. Not square. They are wider and shorter. So when inserted the top of the album is mostly covered but barely and if you have a double album, there will be a 1/8" peek out at the top. The sides are a bit baggier and that's okay. It's just not as tailored. They are more like the plastic sleeves used in record stores. It's flexible and elastic. Not crisp, clear and sharp; showing off the album cover art.

But in the end, they are perfectly functional. I am protecting my vinyl collection, I can live with the plusses and minuses and enjoy my music regardless. It's a perfectly fine choice. But be aware of these differences when making your choice if these things matter to you. I hope this was helpful. Jc

title: Great So Far
text:
I have only begun to explore the capabilities of this Reolink RLN8-410-E so I will likely need supplement this review as I learn more. But, so far, the NVR has done everything I expected and done it well.
I ordered the version with NO hard drive because I already had several unused Seagate 2T green drives on hand. I understand that the “-410-E” model (vs the -410 model) is designed for higher resolution (5M, and 8M) cameras. I believe the several informative Amazon reviews for the “with hard drive” version are equally applicable to this diskless version; so check out those reviews too. By the way, Reolink online technical support has been excellent; they tend to reply at night (US time) so I always got answers by the next morning and often sooner.
There are basically four local ways to control the NVR: (1) direct (monitor and mouse connected to NVR), (2) web browser, (3) PC/Mac client, and (4) smart phone app. The PC and phone software are free. Personally, I find the PC client the most intuitive but some functions must be done by direct connection to the NVR. The smart phone app is fine for viewing but that’s all I use it for. In addition, the NVR can send alerts and video clips by email, FTP, P2P, and DDNS but I have not used any of these yet.
My NVR arrived with “old” firmware. Even so, setup with Reolink cameras is very easy. Just plug in the cables (power, network, monitor, mouse, and PoE cameras-if any) and the NVR will find and connect all Reolink cameras. It doesn’t matter if cameras are plugged into PoE ports or just connected to the same LAN subnet, including by WiFi. If you previously gave passwords to any camera you need to input the passwords in the NVR using the mouse and monitor. Hint: click the “ab/AB” icon at the right end of the data entry box to toggle capital/lower-case letters (thank you tech support). I had Reolink RLC-410, RLC-410W, RLC-411WS, and D400 cameras running on my NVR “out of the box.” I also had two ONVIF cameras on my Lan; the NVR “saw” those cameras on the LAN but would not display video until I updated the NVR firmware.
PoE cameras can be connected to the NVR PoE ports or just connected to the wired LAN using a PoE switch or PoE inserter. If a camera is on the LAN you can also access it directly with a web browser or the Reolink client. But if a camera is connected to the PoE port that camera can only be accessed through the NVR.
I needed to update the NVR firmware but initial attempts using the PC client and using a web browser interface failed. My first attempt with a direct update with new file plugged into the NVR (on a USB drive) also failed. But another attempt using a different USB thumb drive worked perfectly. Go figure? With the updated firmware, the NVR recognized and displayed video from my ONVIF cameras and all Reolink cameras as soon as I entered the passwords.
My NVR did not come with a fan (apparently not really needed) although older models had one. I installed a Noctura NF-A4x10 FLX using the existing chassis holes and 2-pin header on the circuit board. The fan ran at full speed all the time; not bad but louder than my idling PCs. So I inserted the low-noise adaptor (included in Nocturnal kit) to reduce the speed from 4500 to 3700 rpm. The noise is hardly noticeable now but the box feels cooler.
I use a Keyboard/Video/Mouse (KVM) switch for several other computers and that KVM had one unused set of VGA/USB cables. I just plugged these into the NVR and it works fine; less clutter in my work area (no second monitor or mouse). Eventually I want to hide the NVR where potential thieves won’t find it. I may usea Cat5 KVM extension when that time comes.
There is at least one IP camera web site that is very critical (to put it mildly) of Reolink products. I am not an experienced professional in this area but the Reolink cameras seem to do everything I need.
I have only tried the basic functions at this time but to summarize: (1) NVR does everything as advertised, 2. Setup with Reolink cameras very easy but the firmware update was needed to get ONVIF cameras working, and 3. Reolink online tech support has been excellent

text:
I bought the Move Shoot Move (MSM) rotator from their website directly for taking Milky Way and other night sky pictures. The rotator is well built and compact. I have used it to get up to 10 minute exposures with a wide angle lens with a good polar alignment. Attached is an example, straight from the camera, no post-editing.

Unless you want/need the small size however, I would recommend a StarAdventurer package. By the time you add the polar scope and a wedge to the MSM, the cost is within spitting distance of the Star Adventurer. That product supports a heavier payload (11lbs vs 6.6), has replaceable batteries and a auto-guider port should you choose to go that route.

title: Replaced it in less than a year
text:
The last couple months in my house: Family complains about internet, I reboot my Netgear CM1150V. It works for an hour, or a day. I call Comcast, they send a "refresh" signal, it works for an hour, maybe a couple days. I ping google's DNS: 10-15ms for a while, then a few timeouts, then back to 10-15ms, then timeouts for a few minutes. I've scheduled two appts with comcast, and for both they called back saying they "found something upstream - does it now work?" It does, for a while. Then it doesn't. The voice phone service cuts out as well.

I read about the Intel Puma chipset problem in many of these reviews - it sounds awfully familiar. On the way home I picked up a broadcom-based motorola mt7711 and just hooked it up. A solid 10-12ms ping replies for the last hour. I hope it works.

title: Great affordable cpu cooler
text:
Just received this cooler today and just finished install. Wow I'm impressed. I previous had ryzen 5 3600 with stock wraith stealth cooler, which did a good job at cooling. Idle temps were 53 c to 63c and gaming 75 c to 85 c (kind of high) but I live in a warm place. The issue I had with the stock cooler was the fan, it has a coiling sound and when the fan ramps up it quite loud. So I decided to try and find a decent cooler, I seen most of the name brands but they were $50 to $100 price range. Seen this one on sale for 22.50 and checked few youtube reviews and saw good results. Another reason I chose this cooler was the design, with the fan it doesn't cover ram slots like other beefier coolers. I have rgb rams and didn't want it to be blocked out.
Installation was pretty straight forward, it uses the AM4 backplate and a few brackets and screws. There is a youtube video of how to install, it's a good watch before you do it. I used the thermal paste it came with, which seem adequate but will get artic 4 paste later. Currently my idle temps are 40 c to 49 c and gaming highest yet is 73 c, I'm amazed for this value cooler. The fan it comes with is pretty quiet and I don't have anymore humming noise. The only con I say is the fan cable plug is pretty long for a cpu fan, it's a standard fan cable length so you will have to do some cable management. I just wrapped it around the fan itself, hoping later on I don't hear any rattling noise. It also comes with extra clips if you decide to add a extra fan on the other side for push/pull.
For the price, this is a steal and easy install. Huge improvement of the stock cooler.

title: Beaten by Sonos
text: I went through so much research time, ordered and returned so many speakers, including these and Klipsch R-51PM and a Kanto SYD speaker, I can't even tell you.  After comparing all of those I settled on the R-41's  (paid $399 on Amazon initially then saw them marked down to $319 and I'm still working through that return and refund complication).  But I was at Costco today with my girlfriend and we saw "Sonos Two Pack Play-1" for $259 so we brought those home and played them side by side with the R-41's.  No contest!  Sonos is birghter, clearer, better separation, just as much tight base as the R-41's.  Set-up is a pain in the neck and involves apple passwords you've forgotten you ever had but when that's done the R-41's are toast and getting packed up and returned.  In addition to better sound, Sonos does wi-fi. Klipsch is bluetooth that, at least in my house, stutters occasionally, and if you're playing from your phone, means no music when a call comes in.  Also, each Sonos speaker is plug-in powered--no connection between the two, so they're easy to move around independently (but they sync seamlessly if you want them in the same room).  On the other hand, one R-41 is plug-in powered and there's an old -school cable connecting it to the other one--clunky and inconvenient.  I might go back to Costco for another pair of Sonos just because.

title: Goodish but Buggy - You get what you pay for.
text:
The Good:
It's got lots of screen real estate, which is helpful for capturing gestural sketching or having a bunch of tool pallets open simultaneously. It's got a reasonable amount of resolution, though, compared to the Retina screen it's currently sitting next to at my workstation, it looks a bit dated. The pressure sensitivity is great, much better the ancient Intuos3 it replaced. The tilt-adjustable stand feels solid and is easy to adjust. *Lot's of hotkeys. **Customer service is helpful.

The Bad:
The OSX install instructions are in Engrish. You may get through them in one piece; I did not. The supplied USB-C cable on my copy doesn't inspire confidence. They stick out further than they should in my iMac. It needed to have the plugs rotated, flipped, etc. in order to get the tablet running. **Reaching out to XP-Pen for help will be a bit of an exercise in patience and persistence. I've needed to uninstall/reinstall the tablet driver, and dump my prefs file for Adobe Illustrator 2020 alarming often since installing this equipment for the first time. *The hotkey and scroll-wheels haptics feel cheap.

The Neutral:
Before buying ANY screen tablet, think about your lighting situation. If there are lights directly above your desk, the reflected glare is going to give you a migraine. This is just a personal anecdote, but the lighting in the cube-farm in which I work significantly reduces the number of positions the tablet (and my head) can be in without catching reflected glare from one or more lights. Because my job allows me some freedom/authority over my workstation, as a solution, I've removed the lights above my desk. This may not be feasible for some.

Conclusion:
If you NEED the extra screen real estate and don't have the budget for a Cintiq, and you're willing to deal with some headaches and downtime, this is a good fit.

title: Does NOT work well on GFCI outlets! Do NOT plug into surge protectors. (Here's some speed tests)
text:
If you're looking for basic internet browsing needs and Wifi doesn't work due to walls and floors and stuff, just buy this and be done! It works well enough. If you're looking for HIGH SPEED data throughput, however, and have to use any outlet connected to a GFCI-protected line, get wifi instead--this won't cut it. Here's some real numbers:

I'm paying for 100 Mbps download / 20 Mbps upload. On my $400 Orbi mesh router wifi system, 8 ft from the router, over wifi, my laptop gets 90 Mbps download / 20 Mbps upload. With this device, I get 6~12 Mbps download and 6~12 Mbps upload, across the same air distance, but probably over 25 ft of wiring. Why? Because this device works poorly on GFCI outlets. The problem is, however, my router has to be in the kitchen because that's where the internet comes in, and the kitchen is all GFCI-protected so you don't get electrocuted around running water. So, this device doesn't work well for me. I need to use a wifi repeater instead.

If neither end you are connecting to is GFCI-protected, however, DO buy this, as it appears it will work very well!
Note also: it may not work *at all* in a surge protector, as they interfere too. Plug directly into a wall outlet.

Powerlinks 2 ft apart, both on GFCI outlet:
30~35 Mbps download, 20 Mbps upload
Wifi 3 ft from router: 90 Mbs download, 20 Mbs upload

Powerlink Kitchen GFCI outlet to Living Room NON-GFCI-outlet (~15 ft open air, through 2 walls, probably 50 ft of wiring):
6~12 Mbps download / 6~12 Mbps upload / 0 Mbps (no connection) if plugged into surge protector
Wifi (high-end Orbi router, to laptop at same location--through 2 walls 15 ft away): 70~90 Mbs download, 20 Mbps upload.
- as you can see, the GFCI outlet here is killing my signal with the powerlink so I'm buying a wifi repeater instead. I've returned this product and gone with the repeater. I'm now getting a consistent 30~70 Mbps download (usu ~50 Mbps) / 20 Mbps upload at that location when wired to the repeater, which picks up the wifi from the router. This is much better than the powerlink (again, due to the GFCI outlet in the kitchen that is making the powerlink not work well).

Powerlink laundry room to living room (probably 100+ ft of wiring):
18 Mbps download and 18 Mbps upload
- this is impressive, because my mesh router had to bring it up to the laundry room in the first place, so this is actually quite good for it.

title: Sennheiser PXC550 simply do not compare to their Sony and Bose competition
text:
The Sennheiser PXC550 headphones are 1/3 of the trifecta of ANC wireless headphones (along with the Sony WH1000XM3 and the Bose QC35-II headphones). Unfortunately, the Sennheisers are a distant 3rd place to both the Sony and Bose offerings.

The Sennheiser's touch controls are nicely implemented, but I do not like that the on/off "switch" is activated by unfolding the headphones. That just seems like something that will break or at least cause the headphones to accidentally turn on and drain the battery. Again, I really like the touch controls and think that gives the Sennheisers an edge over the Bose (which uses physical buttons for everything), but they really should've stuck with a physical power button. Honestly, I'm not sure how you would use the Sennheisers wired without it still using the battery (???) since there's no way to have the folded out and on your head without them being powered up.

The materials used and the craftsmanship on the Sennheisers is excellent. They're very nice looking and seem like they would be very durable. Unfortunately, the craftsmanship and design does not include the ear cups. They really tried to do something new and special with the odd oval shape (presumably to mimic the shape of a human ear), but unfortunately it was a fail for anyone who doesn't have tiny ears. Humans have two different types of earlobes -- free earlobes and attached earlobes. Free earlobes hang below the lower attachment point of the ear, whereas attached earlobes don't go below the lower attachment point. The most common of the two are free earlobes. However, if you have free earlobes, and anything other than tiny ears, you are likely going to find the Sennheiser headphones very uncomfortable, if not even downright painful due to they will pinch the top of your ears as well as your earlobes...A LOT. I don't have this problem at all with the Bose or Sony headphones.

The connection to my phone, Chromebook, and laptop PC was quick and easy. The sound was rather good, but definitely not great, the rather anemic bass makes it seem like you're using a really cheap pair of headphones.
I actually get better bass out of $10 earbuds on these same devices. The noise cancellation is also rather good, but no where near as good as the Bose or Sony offerings. The companion app seem minimalistic compared to Bose and Sony's app, but in the case of Bose, at least Sennheiser (and Sony) actually have an Android version of the app.

The included accessories/cords are pretty much the same across all three, except the Sennheiser case is rather flimsy and cheap looking, it only offers micro-USB charging, and the wire/cord for using the headphones wired has a more proprietary (and difficult to replace) 2.5mm to 3.5mm connection.

I have/had several different full-sized Sennheiser headphones, and I really liked them, which is why I expected a little more with these. I really don't know why some professional reviewers actually rate the Sennheisers as superior to the Bose and Sony offerings when they're really no where close. The only headphones the Sennheisers beat are the cheap, lesser brands (usually without ANC), but even then I suspect that quite a few of the cheaper brands are painful to wear like the Sennheisers are.

I ended up returning the Sennheisers and went with the Sony WH1000XM3 headphones, which offered very similar touch controls (but with a physical power button), are VASTLY more comfortable to wear, offer much better sound quality (especially the bass, and this model of Sony isn't exactly known for its bass), USB-C charging, a 3.5mm to 3.5mm cord, and a much better case. My wife ended up with the Bose QC35-II headphones, but a lot of that was due to Bose offering them in pink (yep). This allowed me to try the Bose and compare them directly to the Sony and Sennheiser headphones. My ranking of these three is following:

1. Sony WH1000XM3
2. Bose QC35-II (very close second with the only real negative being the lack of USB-C charging and lesser battery life)
3. Sennheiser PXC550 (very distant 3rd primarily due to the significantly lacking comfort, but also rather poor sound quality)

title: If you think about it carefully you probably want a standalone device-- this isn't it.
text:
I have the SE+ and decided to get this one. It has been nothing but trouble. First, full disclosure, the mini software is not up to date. So some of the issues below may be due to that problem. The software update requires a windows or MAC computer and I have only chromebook. For most people this isn't an issue. But be aware of you don't have easy access to a mac or PC. To update the software you'll have to borrow someone else's computer and install the garmin software on it to upgrade your device.

But my complaint isn't just about the difficulty updating the software. I really love the Garmin Inreach SE+ and hate this device so if you are considering purchasing one or the other, read on.

One more word of caution. Don't make the same mistake I did of not returning this when you still have a chance. I called in during the return window after using it on two trips. But I made the mistake of letting Amazon transfer me to Garmin and allowing Garmin to convince me to stick with it. Then after a couple more trips when I decided--no this really isn't for me-- it was too late to return. OK. Now on to the meat of it.

What do I hate about it?

1) The user interface is awful. But you want small and you are willing to make that tradeoff right? Consider carefully. How to do any one thing on the device isn't so hard to figure out but nothing was intuitive to me. Some features are in the standard menu system, others are only in a special menu system you find when you hit OK on the home screen. Some features that clearly are "settings" aren't in the setting menu but buried somewhere else. Also, don't think you can just use your phone instead of messing with the device itself. Much of the functionality (for example changing the device settings, or doing the most common activity for me --sending a preset message) is not available through the phone interface so you'll have to use the actual interface of the physical device--which as I said is awful.

2) To compose a message you'll want to use the phone. Typing character by character is incredibly slow and difficult. I found myself keeping messages I composed through the MINI as brief as possible because they are so difficult to send that way. But then I found out that they were misunderstood (compounded by the fact that the messages didn't go out in order and were much delayed (see below)). If I ever found myself in an emergency situation I would so much rather I had the SE+ than this thing.

3) When you put the problems of 1 and 2 together what you end up with is a device that is pretty usable so long as you are the only user. That may not sound so bad but think about it. If one of the main reasons you are getting this is to deal with an emergency situation--do you really want a device that only you can use? For me that is the deal killer. To use the device well you need it paired with your phone (see item 2) but others in your party may not be able to use your phone in an emergency. The user interface isn't terribly hard once you spend a couple of hours playing with it but will the other people in your party have spent that time? Compare by way of contrast to my experience with the SE+. For example, when I went camping with me 11 year old, I showed my daughter how to use it, had her compose a test message with it and send it to Mom. I talked with her about how the SOS message works and had her send a message with that. She felt confident as did I that if there were an emergency she could use it to get help if I weren't available to help. Try that with the Mini. It won't work. It isn't isn't just that she is 11. I believe a lot of adults would have a hard time picking this thing up on its own and getting the proper info out through the SOS. Also I have two devices because when I am hiking sometimes I want to split up and we still want to communicate. It is so nice to be able to hand the other device to my wife or friend or child. But do I ever give them this one? No way. It's just too hard.
4) my particular device is very fussy when it comes to charging. Garmin said it was probably because I was using a non Garmin charger. What? This is just USB. The same charger that works with other items doesn't work with this. The also suggested that a software update may solve that.
5) my particular device doesn't reliably send satellite messages. Again Garmin believes that a software update would resolve this. But anyway here is what happens and I can help but compare this to my experience with the SE+ that always works fine (also with no software update). The difference between the SE+ and this was most obvious when hiking in canyons. Both my SE+ and the Mini had a hard time sending out a message because of the high canyon walls--you pretty much have to wait for a satellite to pass over head which in my experience could take 20-30 min. But with the SE+ there was a screen that showed me what was going on--i.e. when the message check happened. There was no way to tell what was going on with the mini. Also, one thing I saw is that the mini would send some but not all the messages I had written between satellite fly overs. Why? who knows. After the hike I drove an hour home and then after I had been home for more than 30 min my wife (who had been home in cell phone range the entire time) got two additional message from the mini spaced apart by some time on her cell.

As noted above, problems 4 & 5 may very well be because I don't have the ability to upgrade the software on the mini. But even if I trusted the device I wouldn't want the Mini because it just doesn't work as a standalone device.

title: A Sonic Disappointment within a Beautiful Headphone.
text:
Great build quality, accessories second to none, but disappointed with the overall sound. The bass has too much bleed into the upper voices, it is slightly bass bloated, and the headphone produces a bass pillow that smothers the other sounds somewhat. As a result, a flat sound is produced that can be boring at times. With that said, this presents high resolution and you hear all the sounds with clarity, which is at times beautiful. Much too inconsistent though, and the sound requires significant break~in and external tweaking.

The wire is similar to an earbud wire and although it favorably goes into both sides, the connection to the headphones is hard to put in and pull out. These headphones are aesthetically beautiful, but are smaller and fall on the ear not over~ear.

This headphone is definitely overpriced. I kept the headphone because the sound can be tweaked with an equalizer or external DAC/AMP, and it sounds better assisted. Still, it should sound very good on its own for the price.

Better alternative headphones~ Klipsch On~Ear, Grado On~Ear, PSB M4U1/2, even Edifier Audiophile. I also enjoy the sound of Superlux headphones more. In this case, 1MORE fails to rise to the level of the competition at a better price, and is in fact undercut in price by better sounding alternatives. Again, I still own it for quality other than its sound, the high resolution, and my ability to enhance the sound through external tech.

COMPARISON SHOPPING IS A MUST.

01/2021 Update: After many hours of listening with this headphone, the bass has settled into the mix & there is much better balance to the sound. It is a relaxed, highly detailed sound. Not the largest soundstage, but just enough instrument separation. It is a coherent, coordinated overall sound. Although the headband fit could be tighter, earcups do provide a good seal. It took a long time for the sound to settle into a balanced presentation~ too long.

title: It Works!
text:
I was hesitant to buy because there were no reviews so here goes.

1) It's cheaper than most of these bridging cables.

2) This one comes WITH needed software; other cables (see those reviews) you have to apparently purchase the software separately, making those cables even more, more expensive than this one.

NB: No need to download software and open accounts you do not want. Simply plug in one cable in the USB slot of your computer, and a folder pops up showing you the software for both windows and mac. The cable comes preloaded with the needed software (Prolific PCLinq5). Click on that, and it will install in about a minute.

NB2: Install that PCLinq5 software on BOTH computers between which you want to transfer files.

3) It's USB 3.0 but backwards compatible with USB 2.0.

I have a Windows 7 laptop, support for which has stopped so it no longer goes online. I have software on that laptop I still use, which creates files that are 14-15 GB large. In order to transfer those large files to my new Windows 10 laptop (so they're included in the latter computer's cloud backup), this cable is great. Note, my windows 7 laptop has only 2.0 USB slots; my Windows 10 has only USB 3.0 slots.

I tried transferring these large files to a flash drive and than uploading to the other computer, but that is a two-step process and took about 40 - 60 minutes. This cable cuts that down to 10-15 minutes in one direct transfer.

Great cable. I hope it holds. If not, I'll be back to update this review.

Update 2/14/20: Transferring a few large files as described above went without problem. Later, I transferred thousands of small files and noticed the transfer process getting cut off because of a perceived problem with a single file. It wouldn't skip that file and continue with the rest. No, it would stop transferring altogheter. This happened a few times. I solved it by transferring smaller batches of still hundreds of files, and then transferring the folders that contained the problematic files by using a flash drive. The flash drive had no trouble transferring those files. I'm not sure what is going on here, but I don't think that's an issue with this cable. If anything, that's an issue with the PCLinq5 software, which is not unique for this cable.

title: Saved my tablet from total destruction no exaggeration!
text:
Heads up, this review is long, but I think it's worth reading (and hopefully a bit entertaining).

Ok, so I have had this cover and keyboard for a little over two years now. It has served me well enough, but I don't normally leave a lot of reviews. Probably because I don't like reviewing things I haven't had for a while, and then when I have, I tend to forget to go back and do it. So what made me leave a review for this cover after so much time? Let me tell you a story of my stupidity and this products stupendousness (I know, not a word, it is now).

After two years of being carried almost daily to work, church, and just in general the case is starting to show some wear and I've been thinking about seeing of I could get just a replacement case without the keyboard (as the keyboard is still fully functional), so it has just been on my mind in general. As I said, the keyboard still works great. Honestly, I may not use the key board a ton (actually, I'm not using it as I type this... Maybe I should switch) but I have literally only charged it like... twice? maybe three times in the two years I've owned it! To be fair, I'm good about turning it off, but it is also good about turning itself off and waking back up quickly, so it holds a charge for a long time. The bottom corner by the s-pen broke off some time ago because I dropped it, and it still held the tablet fine, so I was in no rush to replace it. Also, I have lost one of the little inserts on the edge that, I guess, are supposed to support the flap when closed and maybe help keep it closed. Again, I think that's from a fall it took.

Then about a month ago I was on a business trip... This is where it gets really good (or bad, depending on how you view it). I was unloading my cat to go into my hotel after a long drive and apparently set my tablet on top of the passenger side of my car and forgot it. Later I left to go get something to eat. As I was pulling onto the interstate (about a quarter mile away from the hotel, btw) I heard a big thud on my trunk and stopped almost immediately thinking I hit something (fortunately it was late and not a lot of traffic on this highway). I saw something on my back window, and when I got out I saw it was my keyboard. Needless to say I was extremely upset, realizing my tablet had just gotten thrown off my car into the highway. I frantically searched for it and found it (minus the case) in the road. I then continued to search by my phone's flashlight and eventually found the case. I just assumed the tablet was destroyed and the case was useless...

I WAS WRONG! Other than some cosmetic damage from it sliding across the road after popping out of the case at 30+ mph the tablet works fine! The camera got scratched up, but strangely you can't tell when you start the camera app. The case took a beating, but it is still fully functional! In fact, the tablet is in it as I type.

Do I need a new case? Yes! Would I get a different one? Not a chance! Are there others that might have protected it more? I suppose some big rubberized case might have (then again, maybe this one would have a year ago). But most of those also don't have a keyboard, let alone one that works this well (I will say, my one complaint is that there is no delete button on the keyboard... which at this point means very little!).

All I can say in summary is, if it weren't for this case, at best my screen would have been shattered, at worst the $200+ tablet would have been in pieces. Will I ever do something that stupid again? Probably! But I trust my cover will keep my tablet safe! Buy it, it's a great case, super protection and a bargain price!

title: Screen was tilted - had to return
text:
Was very excited to get this laptop, despite some of the negative reviews. I love the form factor and the power they packed into it. Unfortunately, when I received the laptop, the screen inside of the laptop was crooked. That is, the left side of the screen was ~1mm higher than the right, so it slanted downward noticeably from left-to-right. That's ultimately why I returned it to Amazon (I tried to call Razer's support, but they had apparently closed a few days early before the Holidays...).

I also ran AS SSD on the laptop when I got it, and confirmed what others had noticed: the SSD was performing @ ~1GB/s sequential, which is < 1/2 of the performance you would expect with a Samsung PM981 (which is what's installed). The i7-8750H only has 16 PCI-E lanes off the chip, and since the GTX MAX-Q 1070 requires 16 lanes, the SSD must be running off of the chipset. The i7-8750H has 8GT/s to the chipset, which is 1GB/s without the overhead, so the 1GB speed cap makes sense and is all you can really expect out of this hardware. AFAIK, all of Intel's 8th gen mobile CPU's are limited to 16 lanes off the chip, so this is really par-for-the-course and isn't the fault of Razer.

(That being said then, the PM981 might actually be overkill for a laptop like this, unless you really need the random IOPS or slightly faster access times.)

title: Very Dissatisfied
text: I ordered this hub because I have a number of portable external hard drives that I use to back up music and videos. I needed to connect no less than 3 portable hard drives to the hub,and the port had a total of 7 high speed transfer ports which meant that I could theoretically connect additional devices. I have two desktops, one was an older Dell and the other a brand new Acer that I bought last week. I tested the hub on the older computer first. I used the AC adapter and powered the hub, next I plugged in the USB cable from the hub directly into my PC. Next I connected my first portable hard drive to the hub. The computer recognized it. Then I tried portable hard drive #2, but the PC rejected it, so I switched it to a different port in the hub and then it recognized it. But when I connected portable drive #3 to the hub, one of the first two drives was disabled (no longer recognized). I tried it a few times and every time I connected the #3 drive one of the previous drives would be disabled. Then I tried connecting a flash (thumb) drive to the hub and the same thing happened. In other words, the hub would accept no more than two devices at a time. I contacted the seller who suggested that the problem may involve the PC, so I connected the hub to my brand new PC - an Acer, and the same thing happened. I connected the hub to the USB port in the front, which only recognized ONE of the portable drives. The second was rejected. Then I moved the hub to the back of the PC and tried one of the ports in the back. The PC would not accept ANY of the my portable drives through the hub. Then I connected my portable drives individually to each of the ports (bypassing the hub) and all were accepted, so there was nothing wrong with my individual drives. In conclusion, something is wrong with this hub. It may have a total of 11 ports, but the hub will only accept no more than one of two devices at a time. So my only option was to return it for a refund.

text: This is a great little docking station from Dell. I've not used a docking station that does not have some positives and some negatives. This dock is mostly positive from my experience. I've had it working for a while now on Windows, macOS, and Linux. As one reviewer noted it's a good idea to check the firmware and update it if possible to avoid any issues. Another reviewer noted it's best to remove the dock before booting from a shutdown or it may not recognize all your devices. There are very few docking stations with the versatility of this model to work on multiple platforms though not officially supported by Dell. For me the feature that is most important to me is the three video outputs. Two DisplayPort and one HDMI. Most of my other peripherals are wireless so the additional USB ports go unused. The network adapter is useful and a feature found on most docks. The headphone jack is a nice feature for the audiophiles with quality plug in headphones for music or gaming. text:
The Orion Astroview mount/tripod/RA drive is a good value for an EQ-3 category setup. The mount itself is identical to Celestron's CG-4 mount, but with an aluminum tripod instead of the steel legs of the CG-4 (making it somewhat lighter in weight). Some frown at the aluminum legs of the Astroview setup, but really it performs just fine for most amateur visual work. I wouldn't use this mount for long-exposure AP, but it does perform reasonably well for rudimentary beginner short exposure AP interests. It's solid enough for an amateur's first serious mount and a lot of enjoyment can be had with it.

The supplied simple RA clock drive is excellent for this price range. At clock speed and at 2 X clock speed, the drive is entirely silent, and nearly silent at 8 X clock speed. Some criticize the conventional D-size battery pack, but the upshot of this approach is that one can use run-of-the-mill rechargeable Ds and when they fatigue, just purchase another set from the local hardware store (fully user-serviceable).

The Astroview mount has a decent weight rating, but a little thought should be applied here as there are considerations other than simply the weight of the telescope, eyepieces, finders or trackers, and so on to contend with. To ensure that your scope is not under-mounted, I would suggest mounting telescopes no larger than those listed below:

1) A long focal length 90mm refractor (say, in the f/10 range)

2) A 120mm short focal length rich-field refractor (say, in the f/5 range)

3) Or maybe a 6" rich-field Newtonian, or a 6" Mak or Cat.

If larger, more unwieldy scopes are to be used, I would suggest moving to the EQ-4 category, like the Orion Skyview Pro (at about the same price as the Astroview kit, but without polar alignment scope or clock drive). The Skyview Pro is a superb mount for the price, with a heavy stainless steel tripod. The dual-axis drive for the Skyview Pro comes in at about $170. So, if you're thinking of, say, a 6" long-focal length Newtonian; an 8" short focal length rich-field Newtonian; or a 102mm or 120mm long focal length refractor; or an 8" Mak or Cat, then the Skyview Pro is the much better choice.

Otherwise, the Astroview mount and clock drive is the point at which beginners start to get excited about their equipment. As long as they don't over-scope this mount, most beginners will be overjoyed with it.

Clear skies.

title: Decent but there are others with more features for the same price...
text:
I’m using this dock with a universal usb-c power supply. https://www.amazon.com/Charger-Adapter-Latitude-MacBook-Charging/dp/B0813TDBPT

I have been using the dock for 4 weeks now and haven’t had any problems. I leave it powered up and my Lenovo T480s on 24/7. It runs a little on the warm side but nothing overly concerning. I have not experienced any device shutdown due to over heating. Using the above power supply I get a noticeable amount of static noise using some inexpensive speakers connected through the docks 3.5mm audio jack. The noise is about half as much when using the OEM Lenovo power supply plugged into the dock. In reality I think this may be a function of the value of the dock, value of the charger, and inexpensive speakers. It may also have something to do with the audio jack being located directly between the usb-c power input and the usb-c power/data port to the laptop.

However, after looking at other universal docks on amazon I did notice there are others with 12 or 13-in-1 features that contain an additional usb-c port and or a third monitor output (usually 2-HDMI and 1-VGA). Some also have more usb 3.0 ports as well.

It’s pretty clear most of these little docks are virtually identical or a variant of the same dock with slightly different features as noted above. They may all be produced by the same manufacturer and rebranded.

title: Plenty fast and easy installation.
text:
This is my first experience with NVMe storage in my personal computer. I'm honestly completely blown away with how fast this drive is. Over the years I've gone from 5400RPM mechanical drives to 3D NAND SATA SSDs to this NVMe PCIe storage. I was initially very put off from this style of drive because of the price, but I decided to give it a try with my latest "revamp" of my desktop gaming PC. I was going to be replacing the motherboard and CPU so I figured it would be a decent time to try NVMe M.2 storage. I got the 1TB version with the heatsink; it was on a pretty great sale so I didn't want to pass it up. I've bought a lot of WD drives over the years and have NEVER had a single issue so I find the brand to be incredibly reputable.

Installation was very straightforward. My motherboard came with a thermal pad to place underneath the drive to keep the heat away from the underlying PCB. It installed and screwed down without incident. I cloned my old Samsung SATA SSD to the WD drive and expanded the main partition to fill the additional space. The computer booted from the new drive as I hoped and everything is just SO MUCH SNAPPIER. Granted, I made a significant CPU upgrade at the same time, but I can tell that read and write speeds are helping dramatically with opening applications, particularly large and resource-heavy applications like Adobe Lightroom and Photoshop. Aesthetics are nice. I find that a lot of PC components anymore are gaudy and "gamery". I don't own a windowed case so I don't really care what the gear inside looks like or what color it is, but the black and silver scheme should match pretty much anything. The heatsink is made by EK Water Blocks who have a very solid reputation the PC water cooling scene.

I'm not the kind of guy that benchmarks drives. I'm also not going to go out of my way to buy the absolute "best" drive on the market because it writes a few more bytes per second than the other one. You can go down a rabbit hole really quick of finding the "best" and "fastest" of every computer component. Having said that, it's plenty fast for my needs and I have respect for the WD brand. I can get applications, games, and large photo collections/catalogs open without hesitation. Overall, I'm glad I bought it. It does seem to be expensive, but I do have to remind myself that there's an ENTIRE TERABYTE on a little tiny aluminum stick that just sits right on the motherboard and doesn't require additional power or cables. I will absolutely be sticking with M.2 NVMe drives going forward (at least until something new comes along).

title: Stealth 700 turtlebeach
text: Easy swap. You'll need a pair of tweasers and a small screwdriver. Remove the earmuffs from the headset to expose 4 screws underneath . Be careful when removing the plastic piece since the speaker is in it and you don't want to pull the wire out. Once pulled apart use the tweasers to lift up the tape and it should give you some more speaker wire. So you can lay it to the side . Now there are 2 more screws in between the aux jack and chat volume . Remove those . Now push the aux jack in just a bit till it pops out of the plastic housing. Now you should be able to lift and pry the board out from the opposite side. Just be careful not to flex the board or pry to hard. Once up , flip the board and remove the old battery and unplug connector.  I removed some of the double sided tape and stuck it to the back of the new battery.  Because of the size when your putting it back together just lay the battery into the housing then put your board in place. the tape should stick  wherever it touches. Now just reassemble the way you took it apart.

title: Does the Job - Mostly - Dish Network Installed
text:
This Televes DiNova Boss Mix UHF/VHF HDTV Antenna w/LTE Filter is the same model provided and installed by Dish Network. I purchased this from them in January 2020, with installation for $150 for 1 television, with additional televisions being $50 each. After about 1 month of use, here is my experience...

REASON TO GET ANTENNA
We watch more streaming than regular television. Paying over $100 per month for a lot of channels that we don't watch was getting too expensive for what we use. With OTA (Over-the-Air) televison having HD quality channels, we decided to get an antenna for local stations and drop cable. We were already watching streaming television on-line. We still use cable for internet, for that.

ANTENNA
The antenna is a dual UHF/VHF antenna system with a 2 television amplifier that is plugged into power where your cables go from the antenna to the television(s) in the house. We live within around 50 miles from most of the local television stations. After installation, we were able to get 56 stations, including sub-stations. However, 1 VHF station and its sub-stations did not come in at all, and it is less than 50 miles from our home, even with the antenna pointing in the direction of that station. The station is a FOX affiliate, and we watch it mostly for the news. I am disappointed that it will not come in. We tried several scans and repositioning, as well as scanning channels without power from the amp, but it did not come in. I am not sure if this is the antenna or the station. I think it is the station, because I found others on-line complaining about the same station.

INSTALLATION
This commentary is only for those choosing to have their antenna installed by Dish Network. I went this route because I did not want to chance climbing on the roof and not installing it correctly or in the right place. I also chose Dish Network, due to recommendations by some reputable on-line cord-cutter web sites, as being the lowest cost antenna installation package. They were right, because the others that I did find were over $500 to install. Here are the pros and cons of the installation process:
PROS
1. The customer service reps were very courteous.
2. The antenna was installed within several hours (the promised amount of time), and is working for the most part.
3. The installer was very courteous and covered his shoes when he went into the house to check the TVs and cabling.
CONS
1. The 1st installer actually called me to try to talk me out of having it installed, as I would not get many channels (I ended up getting 56). After saying that I wanted to try it, he never showed and noted that I wanted to schedule a dish install (not true). I had to call Dish Network to have my appointment rescheduled. They could not explain the installer's behavior. This wasted an afternoon, that I stayed home to have this done.
2. The 2nd installer showed up on time, but had to travel from out of state, as our state was low on installers. This would be his 2nd antenna installation, as he usually only installs dishes. So he was mostly winging it.
3. After you sign the work completion order, there is no warranty from Dish. They will not come out to correct anything without a further charge. I found this out when I discovered on-line the next day that the installer had not pulled out the VHF antenna on the sides. After calling Dish, who wanted to charge $150 to come out again, I called the installer's cell phone. He claimed that there was no VHF antenna to pull out of the sides and he did not remember how to get to my home, even though he had just been there and was still in the area. I later had someone else climb up and pull the VHF antenna out of the sides (see attached photo of the installed antenna). So FORGET WARRANTY SERVICE.

Overall, I recommend the antenna, but even after the VHF antennas were pulled out and TVs rescanned several times, I still cannot get that FOX affiliate or its sub-channels. All the other channels come almost perfect (sometimes they garble, but not much).
=======
UPDATE (June 2020):
The local FOX affiliate station and sub-stations started coming in, although not perfectly stable, after rescanning all of my TVs’ antenna channels. Not sure if the weather or station corrected the issue. So this is an improvement.

title: Frontier subscriber be aware
text:

Frontier has a policy in place that doesn't allow you to use your own equipment, hence the monthly rental charge for their equipment will stay on your bill, no matter if you use their's or your own equipment.
I call it "rip off, gouging or whatever you want to call it (to use Mr. Trump's words)".

** The D-Link modem works as expected, though. ** Makes it harder to return!

Frontier provides a modem with built in WiFi (Netgear) and charges you a hefty rental fee.
When I asked if I can use my own modem to save the rental fee, I was told that I could use any modem that has an RJ11 (telephone receptacle). What they conveniently forgot to tell was that they still will charge the rental fee.
This I learned when I inquired about the return of their equipment.
In other words, it is useless to purchase a DSL modem replacement, the charge stays on your bill.
I am writing this so that other Frontier subscriber are aware of this dubious business of Frontier Communications!

title: Measure twice, modify once
text:
The modularity of this design made it easy for me to modify it safely to add an extra shelf. I might have wanted to make a special purchase of only the one extra shelf, four shorter cylinders, and 8 plastic end caps, but at this price I didn't mind purchasing a second TV Stand. When I'm ready to replace the older stand in the bedroom, the cylinders and shelves I have left over will make it easy to craft an even taller unit for that location, after buying one more TV Stand.

My TV room has a perfect space for an entertainment center, a grotto and another inset space, just beneath the stairs. This constrained the size of the TV and Stand, so measurement before any purchase was crucial; I can't understand why so many reviewers didn't measure properly before they ordered. I wanted the TV to sit on the top shelf, far forward, which means the new center speaker would need room to fit in the space beneath the top shelf; this unit fit the bill perfectly. That would leave me only one more shelf on the bottom for the AV Receiver, Disc Players, Game Consoles, Logitech Harmony Hub, and Amazon Dot. I didn't want to use the space on the top shelf, just beneath the TV, for Disc Players, because that's a more convenient spot for remotes and media packaging to live. The size of the cylindrical spacers for the Stand's base adds enough height for the SACD and UHD Players to fit side by side, with the addition of one more shelf between the Center Speaker and the AV Center. I did not have room to place the shelf at the height of the taller cylindrical spacers, so this modification added only 8 centimeters to height of the unit.

In hindsight, I might have looked for four replacement rods that were 80 millimeters longer, but four bolts and nuts were easy enough to order online, after learning what the measurements meant at the local hardware store which didn't stock anything that short. Here are the specs for the extender, threaded the same way as the provided rods: Thread Size: M8 x 80mm/0.3" x 3" (D*L), Thread Pitch: 1.25mm

I decided to put the extender just below the top shelf. I seriously doubt that the extender, or the weight of the additional shelf (heavier than the Disc Players it holds) make the unit any less sturdy. The chrome cylinders are the only thing keeping the shelves apart; my only concern is that I would like to have a slightly heftier chunk of metal than the shiny tin cans provided. The inspiration for this was seeing another reviewer who bought two units and simply stacked them, without anything other than weight connecting them, to my mind a highly precarious situation. My approach is far more stable and sturdy; I wouldn't be comfortable adding more than one shelf. I was very happy about how safely everything was packaged, each unit double boxed. I would have preferred honeycombed cardboard spacers to the styrofoam. Also, while I was shopping for new speakers, the 1980's called and asked to have its black and chrome back.

title: You Won't Find Better At This Price
text:
[[VIDEOID:f21df9a407a03ed24d90f806e21e1f78]] This is for the AKASO V1 Dash-Cam

First off, let me say that the dash-cam arrived in good condition, packaged well. It was easy to set up, although the included instructions are a bit hard to understand at times. (Obviously written by someone who's first language is not English, lol} If you have any problems, most answers can be found in the questions section on the Items Amazon page.

Let me start off by listing what this item IS NOT, as it seems a few people in the questions section seem confused about this.

1. This is a dash-cam, for recording videos of driving incidents/conditions/etc. It is NOT a GPS unit. It cannot show you how to get from point A to point B. If that's what you need, then look for a dedicated GPS unit. This dash-cam has built in GPS to show info on the recorded video only. It cannot show real time GPS info.

2. While this dash-cam does have a built in WiFi hot spot, it CANNOT stream live video over the internet to social networks such as Facebook, etc. The WiFi is for transferring video files to your phone, and accessing some settings of the dash-cam, as well as monitoring live video from the dash-cam. It does not stream live video. It cannot access the internet.
Just remember, that while the WiFi setting is enabled, it disables the GPS data function for the videos. You must disable it when you're finished, if you want GPS data recorded with the videos.

3. If you want to view the GPS data along with the video, you have to download and install the Android or iphone version of the AKASO app and install it on your phone. There is also a PC version of the app.
I've seen some people say they've had problems with the PC app, running it on Windows 10. I only ran into 1 problem myself.
First off, I suggest running the program as Administrator. Secondly, I've found that the PC app (for some reason) does not recognize .mp4 files, which is what the file extension of the downloaded videos were on my PC. To fix this, I simply changed the file extension to .avi, which the PC program recognizes. It also recognizes the .MOV file extension.
All videos can also be opened on whatever video player you choose, such as VLC, Windows Media player, and most other video apps. Just remember, that when using these apps, the GPS data will not be available. Video and sound only.

Now that those few points are covered, about the quality. The overall quality of the Cam are very good. Solidly built and looks good. Screen is small, but it is mostly to adjust settings and getting the camera positioned properly. If you want to view the video files, I'd suggest you use your phone or transfer the files to a tablet or PC.

The included 16 GB microSD card works fine, but I wanted more space for saved videos, so I upgraded to a 64GB card. I used a formatting utility on my PC to format it to FAT32 as described in the instructions, and also formatted it once it was installed in the Cam. It worked flawlessly, and I've had no problems with it.

Videos can be saved to 1, 3 or 5 minute increments. Once the card is full, the older videos will be overwritten. This can be disabled in settings, but if the card runs out of space, it will not record new footage. I have mine set to 5 min. increments.

To transfer videos to my PC, I just download them to my phone. All you have to do is enable WiFi, connect to the WiFi with your phone using the password listed on the Cams screen, and open the AKASO app on your phone. It's relatively simple, and easy to figure out if you just play around with the app for a while. You can also just view the videos on the phone app.
If you don't want to mess with it, you can just take the microSD card out, and plug it into a compatible card reader on your PC. You might need a microSD card adapter for this, as there is not one included with the 16 GB card.

There are 3 video quality settings to choose from. 1296p, 1080p, and 720p. I prefer 1080p myself, as the aspect ratio is what I prefer, but once again, play with it and find your preference. Overall video quality is great, imo. The night time quality is also very good.
I've seen a few people complain that you can't see license plates well with this cam, but after watching tons of dash-cam videos on YouTube, I can say it does as well as most others. You pretty much need to be right behind the vehicle to get a good shot of the plate with almost all of the ones I've seen. Maybe some of the super expensive ones might do a bit better, but this unit is affordable. If you are involved in an accident, this will definitely catch the important details. Video quality is great...color details, etc. You can't ask for more in this price range.

I uploaded a screen capture of the phone app in use, to show the GPS function at work. I have seen a few people complaining that the GPS doesn't function correctly, but I've had no problems at all with it, myself. I think it's possible that some may be forgetting to turn off the WiFi setting, which disables the GPS.
I wanted to upload additional videos, such as night time quality, but Amazon would only allow me to upload 1 video. If I can upload additional in the comments, I'll do so. Just remember, the quality you see in the video on Amazon is not the actual video quality of the cam. They compress it or something, degrading the quality. Believe me, it's much better than shown.

I know I have missed several points, but I'm pressed for time. I'd like to say, in short, I'm VERY pleased with this dash-cam. I would not hesitate to recommend it to family and/or friends. It was very easy to install, and if you just read the question and answer section, and play around with it a bit, it's pretty easy to set up and use. I've had it for 3 weeks now, and have had zero issues or problems with it.
If anyone has any question, feel free to ask & I'll answer anything I can. Thanks for your time!!!

title: Great for landscape view, less for portrait
text:
FIrst, the good stuff: the fit is perfect and secure for the tablet (Fire HD10, 7th gen). The flipout card holder is not very useful to me now, but may become very important in traveling. The cover is stiff and slick (great for keeping clean) and the inside lining is very gentle on the screen. The elastic bands (one to hold the cover closed, one for hand while open in portrait view) seem strong and do the job well.
Now the not-as-good: the swivel allowing portrait or landscape viewing is just very friction-free so in use, the tablet seems to readily flop. In setting the case up on a table for hands-free use, in landscape view the grooves hold the tablet in correct orientation pretty well, but in portrait mode, only one of the positions is usable at all because the relative height of the tablet causes it to overbalance and fall on its back. The position that is usable is not terribly secure--any slight jostle and again the base of the tablet jumps out of the groove and the tablet falls on its back. It's hard to fault this because the size and weight of the tablet militates against very many design options. This case is probably doing the best it can.
Finally, the tablet in the case is probably twice the thickness of the (unprotected) tablet alone. That's not bad or good, it just is.
Overall, I think this is good value--I think the branded Amazon case is slightly sturdier for viewing, but not nearly as comfortable for holding (I have one on a Fire HD8). And the branded Amazon case is listed at about 50% more money than this one. The color is perfect, the fit is very secure, standing in landscape with the speakers pointed downward the sound is much improved from the tablet. If hands-free portrait mode isn't terribly important to you, this might be your best bet. If hands-free portrait mode is your main use and critical, you probably want to do something else.

title: Very, very good. Only one or two flaws.
text:
What do I like about this laptop?

-Value for money: you won't find a laptop that looks and feels this good for the price with the specs.

Build quality: immaculate. It's not metal, but it's damn tight nonetheless. No screen or keyboard flex, and it feels as solid as a brick-- not overly heavy, just solidly built.

Screen quality: amazing. The 240hz display really shines, and the colors are very accurate and vivid. Some other laptops in this price range only cover about 60% of the srgb color gamut, but this one is very close to, if not 100%. For a gamer or someone not doing precise art or visual editing, this is fantastic. Response time is great at 3ms.

The included asus software is intuitive for the most part, but I do still have to mess around with it a little bit to master some of the more advanced settings.

Thermals: the thermals are typically in a very good range, even under load. I don't own a desk, so I have it resting on my bed when gaming-- that's typically bad for cooling. However, I've kept an eye on the temps, and it hasn't yet gone into a range where I felt it was in danger of throttling. The computer itself stays cool to the touch too, with the exception of the heat vents.

Fan noise: even at full speed, they're not annoying. They don't have the higher pitch that some other laptops have (ex: acer helios 300). And when you put them on silent mode? They're inaudible.

The keyboard will take some getting used to, I think? But it's still good. The arrow keys are shrunk a little, and I often hit the caps lock key instead of the a key. Also-- can't find the number lock key to turn the trackpad into a touch numberpad? Not a big issue, but very confusing.

The lights: very flashy! They aren't as reactive as I'd like when put into music mode, but I'm sure I'll live lol.

All in all, there's a few minor things that I'm not crazy about, but I still love that laptop. 9.5/10 from me!

title: Really nice amp for your sub, easy to install
text:
This is my second Pioneer Class D amp and so far I'm really pleased with them. I paid full retail for this, no promo deal for me unfortunately.

This is a great amp if you only need to run a sub. It's very efficient and can easily run a 12" subwoofer past the point of comfort. RMS (continuous) power is what you want to look at when comparing amps and 300 watts RMS at 4 ohms is plenty for the aging parent who harkens back to their younger days of bass laddened songs. The amp is stable down to 1 ohm so you have a lot of flexibility in how many speakers and in what layout you wire them up.

I really liked the line level input feature on this amp. This feature means you can tap an existing speaker input (which in my case was the stock 8" "sub woofer") to provide both the input signal as well as the activation signal for the amp. In my particular car it already had a factory amp buried under the dash with no easily accessible sub output. Being able to get the signal from the existing 8" speaker (which wasn't doing much to be honest) was great. The amp will auto turn on when it detects current from your car's stereo which is really nice so you don't have to run another wire up to the car stereo (it will also turn off when the signal stops).

The bass boost remote is really handy as well. It always seems that some songs have too much and some have too little so being able to easily dial up or down the bass to suit the song in question is pretty awesome. You can mount it anywhere but I have mine mounted on the left side of the steering column out of sign but within easy reach so when I (or my kids) want some more bass I can easily dial it up. When you see the police car up ahead you can dial it down and look & sound unassuming :).

Overall it's a nice amp in a small package.

I’m using this on my 2020 MacBook Air. Works great. I use one Thunderbolt 3 port for my external ssd, and the other for this Satechi adapter.

I use the USB C port for the MacBook’s plug adapter (as it’s only used for pass-through power and not data transfer). Other’s have noted that the USB A ports are a pretty tight fit, but I think the more you use them, the less that will be an issue. But for the time being, it’s a little difficult getting my Samsung Ultra Fit out.

The HDMI port I use to hook up to my TV so I can watch Apple TV+ without having to pay $150-$200 for the Apple TV device. I don’t use 4K so 1080p at 60hz is fine by me.

If you line out to a TV or external monitor, it’s best to set it up as a second monitor. Don’t mirror the image. Drag whatever program you want out to the second screen and there you go. title: Best suited for laptops/chromebooks....too power hungry for smaller devices
text:
I originally avoided this adapter mainly based on its price, but decided to grab it since it was discounted 50%.

Background... I was looking for a way to provide an ethernet connection to my new Chromecast w/ Google TV (CCWGTV) and knew that I needed a USB-C to Ethernet adapter with power pass through. My benchmark for price is the Google official ethernet/usb-c/power adapter which unfortunately is stuck in the 20th century with it's 100Mbit speed. I wanted something with a gigabit connection. Enter the Belkin adapter.

Testing... The adapter arrived and I quickly tried it on my CCWGTV. I plugged it into the dongle, plugged in the cord from the dongle's power adapter, and plugged in an ethernet cable. As the dongle booted up, it stopped at a screen indicating there was not enough power. Darn. For reference, there are other adapters out there that work with the Google power supply so this is a black mark against the Belkin dongle. The Google power supply is 5V/1.5A (7.5W), and that wasn't cutting it. Not to worry. I had a fast charger on hand that was rated at a very beefy 5V/3A (15W) so I figured this should be plenty adequate at twice the power. Nope. Seriously? Now I wondered if it was the adapter not working properly. I grabbed a Chromebook and hooked everything up. Success! The Chromebook power supply is 45W (!!), for reference. So I moved on to my Note 9 with it's 5V/2A (10W) charger. It worked, but my phone was basically getting a trickle of charge (8 hours from 90% to full????) which means the Belkin adapter was probably consuming somewhere in the neighborhood of 8-9W, or at least was unable to pass through enough power (efficiency?). The bottom line for the CCWGTV is that this adapter needs >15W, which would require using a laptop/chromebook charger, or investing in a very high power charger for a small device (20W? or more). In either case, I cannot recommend this adapter for the CCWGTV, especially when other adapters out there work directly with the 7.5W power supply. It's probably fine for laptops/chromebooks but it'll really hinder your ability to charge/power things like tablets or cell phones when used with the OEM chargers. Definitely not worth the high price tag this device normally carries.
